THE
TROPICAL AGRICULTURIST

VOL. LX.

PERADENIYA, JANUARY, 1923.

No. 1.

THE POSSIBILITIES OF WATTLE BARK
IN CEYLON.

In the present number of the TROPICAL AGRICULTURIST are reproduced articles relating to the wattle bark industries of South and East Africa. These articles have been extracted from the SOUTH AFRICAN JOURNAL OF INDUSTRIES and indicate the importance of these industries. They are of particular interest to Ceylon at the present time because it has been pointed out by the Director of the Imperial Institute that the prices for bark have improved, and that the demand is steadily extending owing to its growing popularity with tanners.

The black wattle has been grown in Ceylon for many years, and an attempt was made to export the bark for commercial purposes. The margin of profit was not, however, at that time, sufficient to warrant large scale operations. The rates of freight from Ceylon were heavier than those from South Africa, and further efforts to undertake commercial shipments were not made.

The wattle, or—as it is known in Ceylon—the Acacia—is grown over large areas of up-country as a fuel supply, as wind-breaks, and as a green manure plant in tea.

It thrives well, and has been increasingly planted in recent years. There would be no difficulty in regard to its growth for the production of bark if the margin of profit were sufficient. It has however been suggested that all acacias cut for fuel for tea factories might be barked, and the bark dried and exported. It is possible that this would prove remunerative, and that the demands on labour would not be excessive.

2[JANUARY, 1923.

With a view to testing the values of acacia barks from Ceylon, samples have been prepared from Hakgala Gardens for analysis locally, and for investigation at the Imperial Institute.

These barks were prepared from a tree of Acacia dealbata aged 6\frac{1}{2} years which yielded 30 lb. of dried bark; a tree of A. decurrens aged 5\frac{1}{2} years which yielded 54 lb. of dried bark; an old tree of A. decurrens (exact age unknown) which yielded 84 lb. of dried bark; a tree of A. mollissima aged 10 years which yielded 18 lb. of dried bark, and another tree of A. mollissima aged 7\frac{1}{2} years which yielded 18 lb. of dried bark.

The ruling prices of chopped wattle bark in London during recent years are reported to have been as follows :

Year. Price per ton.
1916 ... £10—16
1917 ... £12—10 to £23
1918 ... £16—10 to £17
1919 ... £13—£19
1920 ... £13—22-5
1921 ... £ 8-10— £11
1922 (Early part). £ 9-10— £11-10

If the analyses of Ceylon barks are satisfactory there would appear to be prospects that wattle bark could be produced commercially in Ceylon.

It is however necessary to sound a note of warning to the growers of tea. The leaf disease caused by Cercospora Theæ appears to become more prevalent upon acacias up-country, and from acacias it spreads to tea. The attention of the tea industry has been drawn to this by the Mycologist of the Department, and it is possible that some revision of the policy of planting acacias amongst tea may have to be considered by the tea industry.

This does not however preclude the growing of defined areas of acacias for fuel supplies away from the tea, and the production of bark from such areas is well worthy of serious consideration.

JANUARY, 1923.]3

RUBBER.

GENERAL PRINCIPLES OF ECONOMIC PLANTING.*

The subject chosen by our Society for me to lecture on this evening is a very wide one and in the short time at our disposal we shall only be able to touch upon the mere fringe of many of the aspects of the matters affecting economic planting. Further we shall have to restrict our thoughts mainly to matters affecting the planting of Hevea from an industrial standpoint, though I think that many of the general remarks I shall put before you, will equally apply to the economic planting of crops other than rubber.

The basis of all economic planting must be the using of land to the best advantage for the crop chosen so that the capital and labour invested will give the largest return. We have thus two things to consider, the one dependent to a large extent upon the other, viz., capital invested and crop harvested. These two matters are further affected by two other factors, one, the nature factor, i.e., the lie of land, soil conditions and climatic conditions, and two, the state of the market for the crop produced. Round these factors the whole business of a planter—and I use the term “planter” to include those who cause to have planted as well as those who actually plant,—hangs. To unite these factors we find that economic planting aims at getting the biggest profit per unit of capital invested. The biggest profit can be measured in two ways, viz., the biggest immediate profit or a immediate satisfactory profit combined with a good assurance of a continuation of such satisfactory profits. Which one is sought by the planter must necessarily depend upon his view of the industrial value of the crop raised by him. If he considers that the crop he is growing has only a transient market value then he seeks the largest immediate returns possible, while, if he is confident of the permanency of the market value of his crop, then he is willing to forego some of these immediate returns if necessary, in order to stabilise his efforts, which establishment will ensure both immediate as well as future satisfactory returns.

Let us consider for a short time the factors around which the business of an economic planter hangs. Since the last two factors I mentioned, viz., the nature factor, i.e., lie of the land, soil conditions and climatic conditions and the state of the market for the crop produced, are less within the control of the planter than the former two, we will consider these first. It will be obvious that the thoughtful planter will, in selecting the site for his plantation, choose such areas where the lie of land, natural drainage soil conditions and climatic conditions are most favourable to the crop he wishes to plant. Not only are these points of the greatest importance to

* A lecture delivered under the auspices of the I. S. P. at the Klang Club on 14th September, 1922, by MR. H. C. PINCHING, Senior Scientific Officer of the Rubber Growers Association.

4[JANUARY, 1923.

him but he has also to consider the position of his selected area with reference to the geography of the country, i.e. with reference to railways, navigable rivers, main roads or seaports, in order not only to facilitate the disposal of his crops when harvested but to render the obtaining of stores for his plantation as easy as possible.

SELECTION OF LAND.

When the planter, who, in searching for land for his plantation, finds a site where all these factors are existing in his favour, that is, where lie of land, soil and climatic conditions and position are ideal, he is extremely fortunate. In the early days of economic tropical planting the position of the estate was of more importance than it is to-day when we have easy motor transport, and in some cases it would seem that the pioneer planters placed more importance upon this point than they did upon the actual condition of the land. In my opinion, and I think you will all agree with me, the selection of the land is one of the principal factors in the success of economic planting. In these days, when much of the land of easy approach has been taken up, the selection of suitable sites for further planting generally needs considerable thought. It is not that the best agricultural land in the Peninsula has been already taken up—for there are thousands of acres of first class agricultural land as good as, if not better than, much of that already planted up in the more easily accessible parts, still obtainable in such states as Pahang.

Unfortunately, in the rush to open up land under Hevea during the boom period, sufficient consideration was not given to the state of land planted. Thousands of acres were planted up which cost heavy sums to maintain and many, if not all of these, have since been abandoned. Such unsuitable lands cost more to open up, to maintain, to supply, to weed and to drain than suitable lands, and after that was all done one obtained smaller returns (if any) from such lands. As I have said, most of unsuitable lands have since been abandoned after absorbing a lot of money, and I often have remarked that had I the money, so spent by rubber companies, I should be a millionaire to-day. It is not only the preliminary opening up costs in connection with these unsuitable areas which have to be considered but also the heavy cost of maintenance. I feel that the blame for opening up such unsuitable areas under rubber is not to be laid wholly, and in some cases not at all, at the door of the early rubber planters. Instructions were received from Home that the work was to be carried out in spite of the recommendations from men on the spot that such a procedure was extremely ill advised. In those days the thing which mattered was the number of acres planted up rather than the quality of those acres.

The planter has therefore carefully to weigh up the pros and cons of the land he proposes to select for his purpose. In the cases where the soil conditions or lie of land are not all that he could desire, but there are other points which favour him, then he must consider whether it would be possible, and then would it be worth his while, to attempt to improve the soil conditions. In the first place it is a proper appreciation of these matters which makes a successful economic planter.

Since the economic planter grows his crop for the market it is highly necessary that he should watch the state of the market and order his work

JANUARY, 1923.]5

in the light of the possible future of the market. When he sees the possibility of a shortage in the market he must be prepared to take every advantage of it and at the same time guard against flooding and so spoiling the market. This matter is of special importance in the case of minor agricultural products. With the rubber growing industry these matters are generally left, or rather, have been generally left, to the people at Home and the actual rubber planter took very little interest in them. Indeed, due to the previous state of the rubber market, no one had to worry much about such matters. The depression in the rubber market has made a very great difference, however, and I must state as my opinion that I feel that the present day rubber planter has a better school of real economic planting to pass through than his predecessor, the pioneer rubber planter. To-day is the day of decimals of a cent while years ago ten cents was of no very great importance. Cost of production to suit a depressed market is the aim of every planter at the present time, and I can assure you, in my visits to estates, such replies as "such and such work will cost say, 2 cents a lb. on my rubber" are getting very common. Such surely shows a keen appreciation by the planter of the economic aspect of his work.

MAXIMUM RETURN FOR CAPITAL.

After this somewhat preliminary ramble on the more general side of affairs let us turn to the more particular and consider the position of the planter who has already selected his land and wishes to plant up his crop. The first and main question which confronts such a planter is "How much capital does it pay me to invest in an acre of the land I have selected, in order to obtain the maximum return per centum of capital thus invested?" All his programme of work must be planned out with this question in view. If, say, he sinks $500 worth of work or material into an acre of land in planting, cultivating, etc., and his crop yields him an annual profit of say 20% on that capital, would it have been better financially for him to have sunk, say $400 instead and had a smaller total profit (but may be an equal or larger % return upon the money invested)? Or would it have paid him better to have carried out his work on a more elaborate scale and say invested $800 an acre and perhaps thereby gained larger returns per acre? When I say returns I am also including the stabilising of his efforts as well as actual cash profits.

Every cent spent on, or rather invested in, an estate must therefore be expected to give some return, otherwise it is not economic planting to spend that cent. Such returns are sometimes very difficult to assess in cash equivalents. It is easy enough to calculate actual cash profits or tangible assets such as the value of a factory or bungalow securing to a company during a year's working but some of the items of expenditure can find no compensating item on the other side of the balance sheet. Some of such expenditures are made in the form of insurances, others on general improvements to the property, the actual cash values of which improvements are very difficult to define. Let us take two works on estates illustrating these two latter forms of expenditure. Under the heading of insurance might be placed the money spent on the daily disinfection of the tapping surfaces of the trees in areas affected with, say, "Mouldy Rot," while under expenditure on the general improvement of the property could be placed that spent on the liming of the

6[JANUARY, 1923.

soil, which has been carried out in the past by some estates. In either of these cases it is difficult to state in £ s. d. what return has been obtained for the expenditure made. To give a concrete illustration of what I mean. I once visited an estate which was full of jungle timber and stumps in all stages of decay. The rubber trees were seriously affected with root diseases—principally Fomes lignosus and White Ants were rampant. Groups of twenty trees and more had been completely wiped out by disease and pest and without wishing to alarm the owners unduly I recorded my opinion of the state of the property, and strongly advocated the clearing up and burning or removal of the jungle timber and stumps. Further, another area was then being opened up and I suggested that that should be cleared of timber either before, or directly after, it was planted up. The reply to my letter from the agents stated that before the owners of the property would consider my proposals it was necessary for me to state in £. s. d. the profits which would accrue to the estate by carrying out such work as I recommended, and, whether they would ever see the money again were they to spend it on such work. Needless to say, it was impossible for me to give the required figures. Unfortunately no tables have yet been drawn up showing the chance of a tree, living in a disease-infected area, catching that disease.

PRELIMINARY AND SECONDARY WORK.

Let us consider for a few moments certain operations carried out in connection with the planting and cultivation of Hevea, the economies of which are still a matter of difference of opinion. There are certain preliminary works which we will all agree are necessary in establishing a rubber plantation and the costs of which we will all accept as being unavoidable. Thus we have surveying, felling, clearing and burning the jungle timber or changkolling, or in some way eradicating the lalang. I might add here that it has been suggested by some in the past that it was not necessary to fell all the jungle, but merely to fell parallel rentices along which the trees could be planted. This view has been put forward on the basis that since HEVEA in its natural habitat is a forest tree it should grow better when under jungle conditions. The few attempts to put this into practice have not been successful as far as I know and very little is ever heard nowadays of this theory.

It is over the expenses incurred by what one might call secondary work, however, that the differences of opinions in planting circles arise. Under such a heading I might place such works as planting systems and planting distances, methods of raising plants, weeding, growth of cover crops, leaf pruning, pruning, thinning out and the method of selecting trees for this purpose, manuring, clean clearing of timber, disease work, cultivation etc. It may be of interest to us to consider these debatable matters for a few moments in the light of the economics of planting. As I have already stated it should be the object of every economic planter to see that every cent of capital invested in an acre of land is yielding the maximum return possible. In order to procure this desideratum it will be obvious that the planter must use the land at his disposal to the best advantage, that is to see that every acre is bearing the optimum number of trees which will give the maximum yield from that acre of land. This means that every square inch of land must be assisting to this end, which in other words means that the trees must

JANUARY, 1923.]7

be properly placed. The correct placing of trees must be obviously a variable term, the variation depending upon the lie of the land and the class of soil being dealt with. This, I am afraid, is a matter which has not been fully appreciated by rubber planters and directors of rubber companies.

OPTIMUM NUMBER OF TREES,

There is nothing magical about certain numbers in economic planting. I have heard planters make general statements as to their opinion of the number of trees it is advisable to plant per acre of land. Some have said that they believed in planting up say 108 to the acre (20 in. \times 20 in.) and then thin out down to 80 to the acre eventually, while others have stated that they preferred 150 trees to the acre (say 17 in. \times 17 in.) and thin out drastically during the first few years the trees are in bearing, or some have even advocated the planting of such a large number of trees per acre on the grounds that losses by disease would not matter and diseased trees need not then be treated. Undoubtedly there are reasons behind these expressions of opinions, but in my opinion such have been expressed so dogmatically that it would seem to me that the speakers failed to realise that what might be a correct number of trees to plant per acre on one class of soil or lie of land, would be incorrect for a different kind of soil. Thus a really good soil can accommodate fewer trees than a poorer soil in order to obtain the best returns which the soils can give. I do feel sufficient attention has not been given to this point in rubber planting. It is quite possible that a comparatively poor soil bearing a large number of properly accommodated trees will give as big a yield of latex, as a good soil on which the trees are also properly accommodated, though of course, the harvesting of that crop will be dearer than in the case of the few trees. Directors at Home are in my experience, very prone to consider all rubber estates as being alike and to forget the great variations which exist in soil conditions. Thus some years ago a certain rather poorly grown estate in the Malacca district was the cause of some controversy between the agents, the visiting agent and myself. It was at the crest of the thinning out wave, when the universal panacea for all diseases, etc., on estates was thinning out. The directors of the estates in question wrote out from Home that all their 10 years old rubber and over, was to be thinned out immediately from the existing 110 trees to 85 trees to the acre. The Visiting Agent visited the property and opposed the suggestion. The Directors then called out from Home that the thinning out was to be proceeded with. The agents and Visiting Agent then had a consultation with the result that I was asked to visit the property and give my opinion. This I did, and you can believe me, in spite of the fact that the trees over 10 years old were standing at an average of 110 to the acre, yet the shadow of one tree hardly fell upon its neighbours. The soil conditions were so poor, the fields having raised untold crops of tapioca prior to being planted with rubber. In a case like this with such poor grown Hevea it was absurd to thin out as suggested by the Directors. They had failed to appreciate that the number of trees which an acre can properly accommodate must depend upon the quality of the soil and the consequent rate of growth of the trees.

8[JANUARY, 1923.

It is now usually accepted that about 100 trees per acre is sufficient for the initial planting. The possibility of diseases and pests too must be considered and in lands where efforts have not been made to reduce this possibility to a minimum, i.e. by clearing away the jungle timber and jungle stumps, then it may be advisable to plant more trees to the acre. This is certainly preferable to planting few trees and then having to replace those lost through disease by supplies. I hasten to remark, however, that in my opinion it is better to clear the timber at the outset and so not to make the planting of a large number of trees necessary. Anyway we have all appreciated the general fate of "supplies," how that they are the first to be removed in thinning out, generally before they have yielded any return.

Another view has more recently been put forward in planting circles in connection with the number of trees it is desirable to plant per acre. It has been suggested that it is advisable to plant very closely say 14 in. \times 14 in. giving 222 to the acre, or 10 \times 20, giving 201 trees per acre, with a view of making an early selection of the 70-100 best yielding trees and then to remove the remainder during the first few years of the history of the field, that is, about 80 trees per acre, all good yielders, will remain by the time the trees are five to six years old. An article by MR. BANNERMAN of Java on this subject appeared in the Rubber Growers' Association Bulletin for August 1921, in which he suggests planting 10 in. \times 10 in., giving 410 trees per acre. This number he suggests should be reduced to 70 eventually, the selection to be based on the individual yields of the trees. The thinning out is to take place over five years. He suggests that it is possible to select by crop 2\frac{1}{2}-3 years' old rubber by mild experimental tapping. Personally, I do not care to criticise such a scheme until I have seen it in working and obtained some results from it. It would seem rather a big scheme to plant up 410 trees per acre and then remove five-sixths of them and it would seem to me that the results of tapping such young rubber as he suggests would be difficult to compare—the majority of the crop being taken up as "tree scrap."

It will be obvious that the thinning out would have to be promptly carried out for the 410 trees per acre would quickly overcrowd and interfere with the development of the best yielders. I should consider with such a scheme a smaller number of trees would answer better, the saving in planting, in thinning out etc., compensating for the slight advantage obtained in the extra scope in selection given by planting 410 trees to the acre. Not content with the above scheme, MR. BANNERMAN suggests the introduction of grafting and buddings with the planting of the 410 trees per acre. Personally, I consider this is a case of "precaution run amok" for if "budding" holds good for our purpose, i.e. if the bud which we place in the small rubber plant does give rise to a tree which yields a similar amount of latex to the tree from which it was taken, then as all the buds will necessarily be taken from high yielding trees, what is the practical use of the enormous scope of selection obtained by planting such a huge number of budded trees per acre.

I am afraid I have spent more time on the subject of the number of trees to plant per acre than we can afford this evening. Still it is a very important point and what I desire to emphasise is that there is no fixed "correct" number of trees to plant per acre. The number of trees to plant up and to maintain per acre must depend upon the quality of the soil and the rate of growth and development of the trees.

JANUARY, 1923.]9

SQUARE, AVENUE AND QUINCUNX PLANTING.

Before leaving the subject of planting up, I would like to mention briefly that of the allocation of the trees on the acre of land. The three methods of planting—square, avenue and quincunx—have often been discussed and I have very little to add to what has been already stated beyond to criticise avenue planting in the light of recent developments on the thinning out question. Selection of trees for thinning out is now largely based—and rightly so—on the yields of the individual trees and the spacing of the trees must therefore receive less consideration. Take for example a field planted up in avenues 12 \times 24. If the trees obliged us by becoming high yielders every alternate tree then after thinning out we should be left with an evenly planted area of 75 trees to the acre, in which the spacing both aerial and subterranean was being evenly divided among the standing trees. Chance, however, does not favour us in this way and what is usually found is that in a row six good yielders exist together and then two poor yielders, and so on. In thinning out, the two poor yielding trees are removed—but how does that benefit to any extent of spacing of trees which remain. All that one then gets are open spaces where weeds grow more heavily and with the exception of the trees surrounding the few spaces caused by the thinning out, very little advantage is obtained. I saw the extreme of the avenue planting method a few months ago in a young area, under a year old, in which the planting was 7\frac{1}{2} ft. \times 30 ft. The idea behind such a scheme must be eventually to thin out 30 ft. \times 30 ft., but will the trees favour the management by producing good yielders every fourth tree along the row? On the yield of individual trees basis for the selection of trees for thinning out I can foresee trees—probably three or four of them—having to be left 7\frac{1}{2} feet apart.

Personally, I favour square or quincunx planting. It would seem to me that thinning out can be carried on with greater advantage to the remaining trees with these systems than in the case of avenue planting. In avenue planting, it would seem that the trees make no particular effort to accommodate themselves to the distances under which they are placed, i.e. they do not appear to put out all their largest branches towards the avenues and then smaller ones in the direction of the rows.

WEEDING.

The next point I would like to consider for a few moments is weeding. On hilly land, and in fact, on all slopes where Hevea is planted clean weeding from the time of planting is a faulty policy. HERBERT WRIGHT as far back as 1912 stated "Planters, even in Ceylon, are convinced that it is impossible to exaggerate the soil loss that must take place when young clearings are year by year exposed to tropical heat and rain and scraped by weeding contractors. Nobody seems to entirely like or approve of the system. The proprietor knows it is costly, the planter regards it as his most troublesome task and all who have studied the pros and cons pronounce it as injurious to the soil." Further he stated "Clean weeding in the tropics though appalling in its effects on the soil and costly to the enthusiasts accustomed only to agriculture in temperate zones, seems nevertheless to be the most desirable system from the commercial point of view. Once an estate is perfectly clean it should be maintained in that condition for all time." Well, gentlemen, several years have elapsed since this was written

10[JANUARY, 1923]

and I think that the evidences which have accumulated during these years show that while clean weeding may or may not be the least expensive policy in the long run from the actual expenditure point of view, yet it has a most marked detrimental effect upon soil and consequently upon the rate of growth of the trees. I know of hillsides which have been clean weeded for 12 years and where now the weeds will not grow—and I might add neither does the rubber. A most pointed illustration of this came to my notice a few months ago. Part of a hillside was planted up with rubber some 12 years ago and kept clean weeded until about 2 years ago. Of course, in the latter part of the clean weeding period the cost of weeding was practically nil. About three years ago the other part of the hill was opened up and clean weeded for a few months only. An attempt was made at terracing this newly opened part and it was allowed to go to grass. Lalang was carefully eradicated. To-day this more recently portion of the hill is covered with a fine growth of grass, but the early opened part will only produce a few spasmodic blades of grass. The solution to the question is easy to find for the low land adjacent to the originally planted part of the hill is covered with all the silt and humus which the tropical rains have scoured from the clean weeded land. Only unfertile subsoil is now left, upon which the grass will not grow—and if the grass will not grow how can one expect the rubber trees to grow!

It is quite probable that it takes a less monetary outlay to keep a place clean weeded from the outset than to establish cover crops or to put into practice the other artifices for holding up the surface soil and so preventing wash. The great question for the planter to decide is whether this possible smaller expenditure is real economy in the long run. Is it not possible that the original possible heavier expenditure due to such works as establishing a cover crop will be more than compensated by the increased development and growth of the trees and hence the bigger yields. In the case of a clean weeded hillside, the tropical rains soon cause the valuable surface soil from which to obtain its necessary food to be washed off and permanently lost and the surface then exposed under the sun's influence is rendered more or less sterile. Further the physical character of the soil is changed by the severe baking influence of the sun. This may occur to such an extent that the soil is almost irretrievably ruined. Rain which falls on such surfaces does not penetrate deeply and the soil loses its power to conserve moisture. The result of these influences may not be immediately apparent, but after a few years, when the trees are in tapping, the trees do not continue to thrive as they should in spite of the fact that they may have made fair progress at the start: bark renewal becomes slow and in extreme cases it is so backward that a long resting period is necessary.

Consider for a moment the benefits which would have accrued to the land had it been planted with some cover crop from the outset:—

  1. (1) Wash would have been prevented and at least the major portion of the top soil retained.
  2. (2) The sterilising action of the sun on the surface would have been prevented.
  3. (3) The humus content of the soil would be increased and the physical properties of the soil (e.g. its power to conserve moisture) would not only have been retained but improved.
JANUARY, 1923.]11

(4) By using the cover crop as a green manure and periodically mulching it, or by pruning and leaving the prunings to decay on the surface, the actual chemical composition of the soil is improved.

Personally I am still sceptical that clean weeding is the cheapest line of action. I know of young estates covered with centrosema where the upkeep costs in 3-4 years old rubber are very little, much less than what weeding would have cost in such areas.

The next point I would like to mention is pruning. Pruning has largely fallen into disuse nowadays and the word is rarely found in the rubber planters' vocabulary. In the early days of rubber planting pruning took much the same place as thinning out does to-day. It was used to prevent overcrowding of the aerial portions of the trees. Since these days, however, we have appreciated that the growth and development of the trees depend to a large extent upon the amount of branching and leaf surface they possess and that the encouragement of branching is desirable rather than the restriction. Occasionally it is now advisable to carry out slight pruning work on an estate with the object of preventing the breaking off of heavy lopping branches. In any case of pruning it must be remembered that a badly pruned tree is a danger to both itself and those in the immediate neighbourhood. All branches to be removed should be cut off flush with the stem or parent branch. "Hat pegs" should on no account be left or disease is bound to follow as a matter of course. By leaving such "hat pegs" the length of life of the tree is reduced.

THINNING OUT POLICY.

I have been particularly requested to introduce some remarks into my lecture this evening on the questions of thinning out, its economic value, and the selection of good yielding trees. I think we will all agree that the planting up of a larger number of trees per acre than the acre can sustain properly when the trees have reached say ten years of age is a financially sound policy. The first and foremost argument at the present time in favour of planting more trees than we subsequently require and then thinning out, must be that we cannot guarantee the latex yielding powers of any young rubber seedling or stump we may plant out in a field. Thus by planting more trees than we really require—or rather than the soil can support when the trees are say, ten years old, we have the opportunity of selecting the really required number of trees—all the best yielders present—and of removing the unrequired poor yielders. Most of us have had some chance of appreciating for ourselves the variation which exists in the latex yielding powers of the trees existing on an ordinarily planted acre of land. We always find that a certain percentage of the trees consists of poor yielders, some of which hardly pay for being tapped, especially at the present price of rubber. Thus unless we plant a greater number of trees per acre than we really require we shall be unable to remove these poor yielders, for, if we do, then our land is not being fully occupied.

Even if we could have an assurance that every tree with which we planted up a new area would become a high class yielder, would it then be advisable to plant up more trees than we really required and so have to thin out? I think the answer is still in the affirmative. Not only have we to consider the possibility of loss or the spoiling of the tree by disease and the risk of breakage or damage by storm or wind, but we have to bear in mind that we must always make the most out of the soil at our disposal. Thus supposing we require an ultimate stand of say 60 trees per acre—should we just plant up those sixty trees only at the outset? Such proposal, in my opinion, would be a very wasteful, and also a very expensive one.

12[JANUARY, 1923.

The object of the rubber planter must be to accommodate his trees as they grow. As the trees demand more subterranean and more aerial space for expansion then he must see that this demand is fulfilled. One does not place the food requirements of a hearty man before a child of two on the ground that the child when he grows up will require such an amount of food, neither does one equip a boy of five with men's clothes and boots, because the boy, if he lives, will eventually require such.

ELASTICITY.

Planting up a larger number of trees than will be eventually required is, in my opinion, economically sound, both with ordinary planted areas as well as with those areas planted up with trees for which one may have some guarantee that they will develop into high latex yielders. The yields from those trees eventually removed in thinning out will compensate for the cost of their planting and ultimate removal, while the matter of the earlier shading of the ground by the greater number of trees per acre and the saving on the weeding expenses where weeding is carried out, will be advantages acknowledged by all.

Taking fields of ordinary planted Hevea as they exist to-day in the East, the basis for the selection of trees for thinning out must depend upon the revenue value of each tree, i.e., its latex yielding power. Only on such a basis can the greatest return be obtained from an acre of land. Since the rubber content of the latices from different trees varies to a considerable extent, in some cases the rubber content of the latex from one tree being less than half of that of the latex from another tree, it will be obvious that, strictly speaking, the volumetric latex yield of a tree is not a correct indication of the tree's revenue value as compared with another tree, and that it is necessary, in order to make a correct comparison, to find the actual dry rubber yield of each tree. Though the finding of the actual dry rubber yield of each tree is not a very difficult task and is quite within the scope of the planter, yet on account of the extra time and attention necessary in carrying this work out, as compared with merely recording the volumetric yields, I have often been asked whether this latter method is not sufficient for ordinary estate purposes. In my opinion the answer to such a question is both yes and no, depending upon the condition of the estate under consideration. In the case of an ordinary planted estate where no thinning out (or no thinning out on the yield basis for selection) has already been carried out, then it is sufficient, in my opinion, to select trees for removal on the volumetric yield basis only. The slight errors which will enter through the usage of these volumetric records will be so slight as to be negligible from a practical standpoint. Let us consider such an estate for a moment. I have already stated that there is a considerable variation in the yields of individual trees on such an estate and thus there will be a certain percentage of the trees yielding say less than a quarter of a cup of latex. Thinning out when carried out at the proper time rarely necessitates the removal of more than 15-20 trees per acre. It will be no trouble in most unthinned fields to find 20 trees per acre which yield a very little latex—say enough to cover the bottom of the cup. If, for example, one of these trees which was yielding so poorly gave latex of a very high rubber content, say more than twice that of the latex from a neighbouring tree which gave \frac{1}{4} cup, the loss admitted by removing the low volume but high rubber content yielding tree in thinning out, and the reserving of the higher volume but low rubber content yielding tree would be very slight. In my opinion it is in the latter stages of thinning out, when all the four and five drops of latex yielding trees have been removed, and the remaining trees all yield large volumes of latex that the question of the rubber content of the latex will become of importance. I do not want you to think for a

JANUARY, 1923.]13

moment that I am against the recording of the actual rubber yields of individual trees, but having preached yield recording for some years with but comparatively little response from the managements, some of whom look upon it as a high flown impracticable idea of a scientist, I should be only too pleased to see estates tackle the easier, though slightly less accurate, method, rather than confront them with the more tedious but correct one. I fully appreciate that European staffs on estates are now working very short handed and with the present depressed state of the rubber market every thought has to be expended on the curtailing of expenditure. Of course in old rubber the yield recording is of less importance except as a means for indicating suitable mother trees for "budding" work. This brings us to the question of late thinning out in old rubber. Experiments have shewn us that thinning out in old rubber, no matter whether the basis used for the selection of trees to be removed is the individual yields or the spacing of the trees, is not financially sound. Consider for a moment thinning out in old rubber with the selection of trees for the removal based on the spacing of the trees. Such a thinning out may remove some of the best yielders and then, further, will the remaining trees respond to the improved environmental conditions? The yields of the remaining trees will not materially increase, for generally speaking, the majority of the trees will have reached (and perhaps passed) their normal maximum yielding period. Anyway, any slight increases per tree which may be experienced will be more than negatived by the loss of the yields from the removed trees.

OLD RUBBER.

Let us turn to thinning out in old rubber on the yield basis. It is possible in a field of unthinned old rubber that certain trees yield so poorly that they do not pay to be tapped. Thus if such were removed a tapper could tap a larger area, bring in a larger amount of latex and thus a reduction in the tapping cost per lb. of rubber would be obtained. Still if these very poor yielding trees were merely taken out of the tapping round and the tapping tasks readjusted accordingly, the result would be the same. Of course, there is the possibility of the remaining trees responding slightly to the somewhat improved environmental conditions brought about by removing such poor yielders, but would the response, measured in extra crop, increased girth or growth or increased rate of bark renewal compensate for the outlay necessitated in the thinning out? Further, as I have already stated, only a comparatively few trees would be placed under improved environmental conditions by the thinning out and personally I do not think the game would be worth the candle. With reference to the suggestion of merely selective tapping and not thinning out in old unthinned rubber I have personally been able to reduce my tapping costs from 10 cents to 8 cents per lb. with a reduction of yield per acre of under 50 lb. per annum in old unthinned fields. The trees stood about 100 to the acre and about 20 poor yielders per acre were taken out of tapping and the tasks re-arranged. In the event of the price of rubber justifying the work, the trees now out of action could be tapped again.

There are many more matters affecting the economic planting of rubber, which, had time permitted, I should have liked to discuss with you, but I think in what I have already said there may be several points upon which some of you gentlemen present may like to express your views and opinions or to ask questions, I will, therefore, thank you now for the very patient hearing you have given me. I am afraid that I haven't been able to bring forward much that is novel, but I trust that what I have said may provoke some questions or expressions of opinions from you.—

MALAYAN TIN AND RUBBER JOURNAL, Vol. XI. No. 18. 14[JANUARY, 1923.

COFFEE.

COFFEE CULTURE.*

J. HAGEN.

(Translated from the Dutch by H. L. LUDOWYK, Librarian, Department of Agriculture.)

CHAPTER IV.—Continued from November issue.

g. SHADE.

Whether shade is beneficial to coffee or not is yet an unsettled question in Java. Everywhere, especially in estates of higher elevation shade is used for coffee. In Sumatra, however, where no well marked dry and wet seasons exist, no shade is used. I believe that the Coffee Leaf Disease facilitated the settling of the question in favour of shade.

The existence of shade regulates the productivity of trees; and it was observed that the more productive the trees were, the easier prey were they to the leaf disease, and the damage they sustained too was great. But, setting aside the question of disease, the fact remains that the more dense the shade is, the less is the harvest.

The characteristics of a good shade tree should be these :

  1. (1) The tree should grow fast, so fast that at the end of a year they should already have begun to give some shelter ;
  2. (2) The shade should not be too dense ;
  3. (3) It should be possible to prune the trees easily ; and they should be able to bear pruning well ;
  4. (4) They should bear up well against the wind ;
  5. (5) Far from impoverishing the soil, they should possess properties for manuring it ;
  6. (6) The root systems of the shade trees should not interfere with the roots of the coffee plants.

It is admittedly difficult to find one tree that fulfills all these necessary conditions.

The Dadap (Erythrina lithosperma) was for a short time the tree most widely used for shading coffee. There are two varieties of it, namely the Dadap serep and the Dadap solo. The first brings forth seeds that germinate whilst second does not.

The plants of the serep raised from seed have generally a profusion of thorns : so the method of propagation by cuttings is commonly resorted to. The cuttings should be about two feet long and of the thickness of an average pole or stake. They should not be too much matured ; the pithy canal should be white. These should be planted obliquely, and the earth should be well pressed down under foot in order to fix them well in. Buds will soon begin to sprout out ; and the tree will be observed to be a very fast grower.

* ONZE KLNIALE LANDBOUW VII, DIE KOFFICULTUUR, DOOR J. HAGEN, and Planter TWEED DRUK-HAARLEM, 1917, H. D. THEIME EN ZOON PRIJS £ 2'25.

JANUARY, 1923.]15

The Dadap has the following qualities. As it belongs to the Papilionaceæ, it fulfills condition No. 5 : it grows fast, gives not too dense a shade, and is easy to prune. In addition, a regular defoliation leaves on the land a layer of leaf mould which the roots of the coffee thrive on. But unfortunately, the dadap is not very long-lived everywhere, and has been, in the past few years, the victim of many diseases and pests.

The Albizzia, another leguminous plant, has been largely used. Two varieties of this too have been grown on estates—the Albizzia moluccana and A. stipulata, both of which grow to be large trees. The growth of the first of these species is even more vigorous than that of the Dadap ; but its wood is very brittle, and the falling of branches from the tree, which occurs pretty often, injures the coffee plants. The second is much stronger, but its growth is slower, and it drops its leaves during the East Monsoon.

The Albizzias too have many enemies, and it is fortunate that we lately found a tree that to a great extent satisfies the conditions required of a shade tree. The Lamtoro, Leucaena glauca, belonging to the Mimoseæ, is also one of those plants that fix nitrogen in the soil. It gives rise to a mass of seed that can also be collected, ground fine and given back to the soil as manure. The point will be dealt with in the Chapter on manuring.

The distance at which shade trees are to be planted depends on a number of such conditions as the altitude of the estate in question, and the kind of coffee one intends to plant. Generally, one is careful to see to it that the shade is neither too dense nor too scant. The ideal shade would be obtained if the tree be so planted that the space between them when viewed from North to South is such as leaves a rather wider opening for admitting light, than the open space seen when viewed from East to West.

As has been said before, coffee is easily affected by winds. On this account it is often necessary to provide unprotected spots with shelter belts. For this purpose Kosoemba (Bixa orellana), or, yet better, the Lamtora can be used. These should be planted as hedges.

The Lamtora should be propagated from seed sown either in beds or directly in the open. With systematic pruning the trees should be made to assume a decent form. The tree does not become exceptionally tall ; and unhappily, the leaf-fall is not great enough.

h. CARE.

Once the coffee plants have been planted in their permanent positions on the estate, they begin to claim all the care and tending due them. One cannot be too careful with them ; and nothing of the most minute importance to the welfare of these plants ought to be neglected.

All kinds of weeds begin to appear. They should be instantly and thoroughly eradicated. If at the beginning weeds are regularly kept down, then, as the shade trees and coffee plants grow, the trouble required will be noticed to decrease. As a rule, two months after the plants have been put, the ground should be well tilled with a mammoty, and this should be repeated once or twice again during the first year. If the ground be sloping, then the small terraces should be improved and enlarged. Then again holes should be dug on the land in order to catch up the surface soil that would otherwise be washed away by heavy rains.

16[JANUARY, 1923.

If the estate be so managed and looked after, the coffee plants will grow and thrive and soon it will become a settled and perfect plantation in bearing, and the growth of weeds in it will be greatly hindered. One should always try to have on the ground a heavy leaf mulch. This prevents the denudation of the surface soil, and the root hairs of the coffee plants find for themselves a favourable bed in such a layer, and flourish on the mould.

Once this stage has been arrived at, there is, in our opinion, no more need of digging the land with a mammoty. But whether on old plantations the mammoty might be used with advantage, has for many years remained a debated question. Whilst one person convinced by experience holds that the land can never be cultivated enough, another is wholly in favour of giving up cultivation of the soil by digging once the plantation has grown up. We shall not discuss this matter, but leave each superintendent to take into consideration all circumstances and decide for himself whether estates whose trees are in bearing need to be tilled or not. One should not forget that cultivation does away with the layer of leaves under which the roots, in combination with the nitrogenous moulds nourish the tree.

i. PRUNING.

The aim of pruning should be to prolong the life of the tree, and to make it bring forth a regular crop. To attain this aim the tree should have a well developed root system, a stout and healthy trunk, together with strong branches bearing a lively profusion of leaves. When this healthy condition exists, the planter should yet take care to have recourse to a rational process of pruning which, while it prevents over-production, will not diminish the crop more than is necessary.

It is obvious that each species or variety of coffee will have to be handled in a manner different from others. Besides, as climate too exerts great influence, the mode of pruning in dry areas will have to be different from that used in the wet zones. The principal matter is the topping; and since, as a result of topping, there is a quick and copious output of secondary and tertiary branches, the topping might have to be followed up by a thinning out of these branches. Topping is done in order to make the gathering of the berries easy, especially in the case of certain species which have an abnormal tendency to grow very high if left to themselves; in addition to this, it is done in order to obtain the sooner a great girth of trunk, and make the tree come fast into bearing. This process involves the lopping off of the top of the main stem at the required height below the primary bud and just above a node. At the same time one of the side branches left at the top is taken off, for, if this were not done the weight of the branches on either side tends to split the stem. Arabian coffee is topped at 5 ft. from the ground, and Robusta and Liberian coffees at 8 ft. and so on.

Primary branches once cut off or withered can never be regrown. But they give rise to a number of buds; and of these a branch should be trained so as, nearly as possible, to take the place of the one which was lost, and thus regularly maintain the condition of the tree. The best among the shoots should be encouraged and the rest removed; for if they all be allowed to remain the symmetry of the tree would be irretrievably lost.

JANUARY, 1923.]17

The discarding of the shoots whilst they are yet young should be done by rubbing or pulling them off by hand. The process is often known as "handling." This prevents the great wounds the tree would have to sustain by the removal of developed branches.

In Liberian trees, and also in Arabian trees, more often in the former, there appear branches, sometimes termed wild branches, which possess to some extent the habit of the main stem. These grow obliquely upwards, have in their turn, branches, etc., and bear a very large quantity of fruit. But these branches should be removed for they develop at the expense of the tree, draining the resources of, and even killing, the other heavy bearing branches.

There is yet another secondary branch that has to be removed ; those growing very near the main stem. If they be not removed, especially in the case of trees that have been topped, there results what is known as a "crows' nest," a tangled mass of branches that totally screens off the light, prevents free ventilation and hold up in its meshes the leaves that fall from the shade trees.

Especially in a wet climate, it might be found useful to let trees that have been topped shoot out again. Just as it happens that, usually, young trees and the upper branches of trees bear more fruit than old trees and the lower branches, so it might lead to getting a more abundant crop. It is as an application of this principle that what is known as the "bayonet" system came to be used. According to this system one out of every two shoots at the top is spared ; but this one has to be replaced by another after the crop has been gathered, as it may be considered to have fulfilled its course after bearing once.

Finally I should call attention to the great importance of regularly breaking off the tree all dead wood.

j. MANURING.

Every crop deprives the soil of a certain amount of plant food ; so any rational mode of culture, in order to prevent having to be suddenly faced with an appalling deficit, aims at restoring, as much as possible to the soil the elements used up. In the case of coffee, however, the matter is rather different. Coffee impoverishes the soil but little—so little that even a very poor soil can for an adequate number of years provide the coffee on it with the necessary salts.

One, however, sometimes notices the crop of rather old plantations deteriorating while new plants just come into bearing on old land is just as bad. If this is due to the deterioration of the physical conditions of the soil alone, then cultivation can in many cases prove effectual. It is obvious that cultivation alone will not pay in the long run ; and the remedy will be found worse than the thing we try to overcome.

Prompted by personal experience, I give precedence to farmyard manure. All rubbish and waste such as coffee pulp should be put in with the farm manure ; and this not only turns the waste to some account but also gives to the manure some of the advantages of green and artificial manures.

18[JANUARY, 1923.

GREEN MANURES.

By preference we use for green manures plants of the Papilionaceæ. These plants, as is widely known, possess the property of fixing in the soil nitrogen from the air. The green manures should be planted between the rows of coffee. They should be cut from time to time, dug up and buried. This method has been found to be very successful especially where the shade is not too dense, for the Papilionaceæ require a fair amount of sunlight.

If we replace the Arabian plants on our estate with Liberian or Robusta coffee, then, it would be very useful to sow, simultaneously with the planting of the new species, a green manure crop of some papilionaceous plant that would enrich the soil. The land that had been used for nurseries too should be thus treated. Among the crops that would be suitable for green manuring I would name the Kratok (Phaseolus lunatus), the indigo varieties, and the Lamtor, Leucaena glauca,

As regards artificial manures, I have myself in the course of many years subjected the prescription of DR. KRAMERS to a series of comparative experiments. Plots with a certain known number of coffee trees were treated with different artificial manures. The crops of the different plots were separately gathered, prepared and weighed. These experiments have given no definite results; but the results clearly showed that sulphate of ammonia was the most successful. Sulphate of ammonia, however, was found to be too expensive, as the accounts, when made up, showed. The quickly operating nitrogenous manures can with great advantage be applied to help a tree to rally after it has borne a heavy crop, or after it has got over an attack of leaf disease. And in such cases, sulphate of ammonia should be chosen.

The question of coffee manuring, far from being settled, is barely out of its infancy, and so I may easily proceed further in this matter. A number of experiments will have to be performed, keeping in mind the financial side of the question too.

In the Chapter on shade trees, I have already said something regarding the nitrogen which the seeds of the Lamtora can provide. This tree which serves as a green manure in the ordinary course can be turned further to good account if the seeds be harvested, ground and given back to the soil. Here, indeed, would be such an abundant source of nitrogen as would be of immense importance to our coffee culture. (Vide the Publications of the NETHERLAND INDIES AGRIC. SYNDICAT, 5th Year, pt. VII).

JANUARY, 1923.]19

DYES AND TANS.

BLACK WATTLE BARK INDUSTRY IN SOUTH AFRICA.

The following report by MR. C. WILLIAMS, B.Sc., A. R. C. S., Chemist, School of Agriculture, Cedara (Natal), has been reproduced from Volume 1 of the SOUTH AFRICAN JOURNAL OF INDUSTRIES :—

South Africa has, in the Black Wattle Bark, a raw tanning material that has proved to be of very great value in the leather industry, and is rapidly increasing in favour amongst tanners in various parts of the world. Apart from this commodity, no other tanning materials have been exploited in South Africa to any great extent, although it is well known that several native trees and plants are important sources of tannins, and others might easily and profitably be introduced and cultivated here.

With regard to dyeing materials, very little attempt has hitherto been made, as far as the writer's knowledge goes, to establish an industry of this nature in the country, although several species of the wild indigo flourish here, and several other plants are known to yield dyes that probably would be of commercial value. It is not proposed to deal at any great length with the technicalities of the various processes involved in the production and marketing of the particular materials embraced in this report, but rather an endeavour will be made to give an outline of the commercial position of these industries at the present time, together with their possibilities in the future.

BLACK WATTLE BARK.

The Black Wattle Tree.—This tree is known botanically as Acacia decurrens var. mollis Benth., or Acacia mollissima Wild, and is a native of Australasia. There are about half a dozen varieties included in the "Acacia decurrens" species, and, according to BENTHAM, although these forms appear at first sight to be well defined and very distinct; they pass into each other by many gradations. The consequence is that Australians are not agreed as to the common names applied to these different varieties, the terms "Black Wattle," "Green Wattle," "Sydney Wattle" and occasionally "Silver Wattle," being used more or less indiscriminately for all of them. The variety under consideration is, according to MAIDEN, the form which yields the best and the most tan bark, but since it passes imperceptibly into other forms, he advises landowners not only to have a botanical examination made of their wattles, but also to have a chemical examination made of the bark (1). The Department of Agriculture of the British East Africa Protectorate realized the importance of this precaution to such an extent as to have an ordinance enacted, which prohibits the planting and sowing of the Silver Wattle (A. decurrens, var. dealbata), a variety which yields bark of much lower tanning value than the Black Wattle, which for the purposes of the ordinance is taken to include A. decurrens varieties mollis and normalis (2).

20[JANUARY, 1923.

EARLY HISTORY OF THE INDUSTRY.

The introduction of the wattle into South Africa does not date back much more than half a century; it is supposed to have been brought from Australia to Natal by JOHN VANDERPLANK and his brother, the first seeds being planted at Camperdown (3). The wattles were at first planted for ornamental purposes and as shelter-belts for stock, the wood being used for fencing and for fuel. BARON VON MUELLER in his writings, however, drew attention to the value of the bark as a tanning material. The credit of being the pioneer of the wattle bark industry in Natal is generally given to the late SIR GEORGE SUTTON. In December, 1884, he first sold to a local tanner a few tons of mixed bark from the Silver Wattle (A. dealbata) and the Black Wattle (A. molissima), and during the following years several more lots of the mixed bark were sold to the same customer, who soon realized, however, that the latter variety was of considerably more value as a tanning agent than the former, which he ceased to buy.

In May, 1886, samples of the bark were sent to the Colonial and Indian Exhibition in London, and in the same year 39 packages were shipped to the London market, for which the total sum of £11 was realized (4). From that date onwards, the trade has rapidly increased, until of late years it has become one of the most important industries in Natal, while in the neighbouring Provinces—the Transvaal and the Cape—the industry is making satisfactory progress. Mention might also be made of the marked expansion of this industry during the last few years in East Africa.

Consumption and Use in South Africa, and Amount Exported Overseas.

According to the particulars given in the industrial census it is estimated that about 3,700 tons of wattle bark, valued at £22,600, are used annually for tanning purposes within the Union itself, and the amount is rapidly increasing.
