It has been usually contended that Germany imported the wattle bark chiefly for conversion into extract, as bark, being a raw material was admitted duty free, while there was a duty of 14 marks on every 100 kilograms of liquid extract and 28 marks on a similar weight of solid extract. Although it is true that a great deal of the bark was thus consumed, there is no doubt, however, that a considerable proportion of it was sold as bark to tanneries in Germany, Austria, Russia, and other countries of Central Europe.

It is often stated that the hitherto limited market with Britain is largely due to the conservative tendencies of the tanners generally and their want of knowledge concerning the tanning value of wattle bark. It has frequently happened, after the British tanner has been induced to give the bark an extended trial, that he has become convinced of its good qualities, and that large orders have in consequence been placed, thus proving that this tanning material only needs a fair trial in order to convince tanners of its merits.

22[JANUARY, 1923.

SUITABLE LOCALITIES FOR PRODUCTION.

It is generally recognized that the best type of soil for the growth of the Black Wattle is the deep red or chocolate soil resulting from the disintegration of the dolerite (locally known as whinstone) which covers such a large proportion of the surface of Natal and contiguous Provinces. The wattle, however, flourishes on any medium, well-drained loam, with a rainfall of about 30 to 40 inches or less if the soil is well supplied with moisture from a neighbouring river or from underground sources. It is also partial to a misty climate and a humid atmosphere, so that the "mist belt" of the Natal Midlands is the home par excellence, of this tree. The young trees cannot very well stand severe frosts on the one hand, nor extreme heat on the other, hence they do not thrive in the low-lying portions of the vlei at the moderate altitudes of the midlands of Natal, while in the northern districts the climate is altogether too rigorous for this variety, although the Green Wattle (Acacia normalis) flourishes in those parts. The Black Wattle does not do very well, as a rule, on the Natal coast, although here it seems to come to maturity sooner than elsewhere, at any rate, in so far as the tannin content of the bark is concerned.

There are many districts in the Transvaal and Cape Provinces where this variety of Acacia does well, and several samples of bark from these two Provinces have been analysed in the laboratory at Cedara, showing that the amount of tanning material compares very favourably with the Natal product. Black Wattles grow well in the Eastern Transvaal, and in the neighbourhood of Johannesburg and Pretoria. In the Eastern Province of the Cape, especially in the neighbourhood of Kingwilliamstown and Stutterheim, in the Transkei and Griqualand East, there are several wattle plantations. The district around George also supplies a fair quantity of Black Wattle bark to tanneries in the Western Province.

In order to make the growing of wattles a profitable undertaking, it is necessary, besides a suitable climate and soil, that the land should not be very far from the railway and the port of export, and that there should be a good supply of cheap labour available in the district. Having regard to these considerations, Natal is also more favourably situated for this industry than her sister Provinces, and will undoubtedly continue to be the premier wattle bark producing portion of the Union. On the other hand, the proximity of certain wattle-growing districts of the Transvaal to the Rand, which requires the timber for mine props and laggings, should assist considerably in making the planting of wattles there a sound financial proposition.

AREA UNDER CULTURE AND AMOUNT OF PRODUCTION.

It is estimated by SM that the area under wattle in Natal at the present time is roughly 160,000 acres (5). The Forest Department estimates the acreage in the Transvaal at 20,000, and the aggregate for the remainder of the Union (chiefly the Cape Province) at not more than 10,000 acres. The total for the whole Union is therefore approximately 190,000 acres.

With regard to Rhodesia, it is estimated by the Secretary of the Rhodesia Munitions and Resources Committee that the land under wattles is not more than 500 acres.

The average yield of bark is from 3 to 3\frac{1}{2} tons per acre, when the trees reach their maturity, at the end of about seven years usually, but it must be remembered that a small quantity of bark is also obtained as the result of

JANUARY, 1923.]23

thinning out the plantations at the end of about three or four years; this usually amounts to about \frac{3}{4} ton per acre. ANGUS estimates the yield as being about \frac{1}{2} ton of dry bark and about 3 tons of dry wood per annum per acre of the total area under trees.

METHOD OF CULTURE AND THE DRYING OF THE BARK.

This hardly comes within the scope of this report, but a short resume of the most up-to-date methods applied is given for the information of readers who are interested in the industry, but who have not had the opportunity of visiting wattle plantations in South Africa.

The seeds, previous to sowing, are softened by being placed in boiling water, and allowed to stand for about 24 hours. They are usually sown in lines, the ground having been previously prepared, and after sowing the ground is lightly harrowed to cover the seed. The espacement between the lines is usually about 9 to 12 feet, the seeds being planted in patches at a distance of about 3 to 6 feet apart in the rows. At the end of a year or so, the seedlings in each patch, except one, are removed by hand, leaving always the healthiest-looking tree. When the plantation is about three or four years old it is further thinned by removing any injured or badly-growing trees, so as to produce a crop of straight, clean-stemmed trees of even growth. SIM, however, advocates still wider espacements in the first stage of thinning, and allowing the trees to stand for a longer time before felling (5).

The trees are usually stripped when they are seven to eight years old, the stem being first denuded of any twigs or small branches within reach, then ringed at a height of about 7 feet above the ground, and the bark of this bottom portion pulled in strips downwards towards the roots, so as to remove as much bark from the upper portion of the roots as possible, for at this point the tannin strength of the bark is at maximum. The tree is next felled, and the remaining bark stripped, after removing the upper branches. The bark is then weighed and removed as soon as possible to the drying sheds or to a convenient spot where it can be spread or hung out to dry in the sun, carefully avoiding exposing the inner side of the bark to the light, otherwise the colour would be darkened very materially. This drying process takes from a week to a fortnight if the weather is not too unfavourable.

A wattle area, after the trees have been cut down, is regenerated by burning the wattle branches in lines, thus causing the seeds to germinate in those narrow strips of ground. In this way no second sowing is necessary, and experience shows that the yields from the second and successive harvests are, if anything, greater than from the first crop.

PREPARATION OF THE BARK FOR SHIPMENT.

When the bark is thoroughly air-dry it will have lost nearly half its original weight. This "stick bark," as it is called, is sometimes bundled and sold in this form to agents and buyers, who usually prepare it further for the market, for very little bark is shipped in bundles at the present time.

The sticks are mostly chopped by means of a chaff-cutter (worked by steam or water power) into pieces about an inch long. Most of the bark is exported chopped, the chopped bark being packed tightly into strong

24[JANUARY 1923.

hessian bags holding about 200 lb. each, this being done either by manual labour or by means of special mechanical packers.

One ton of chopped bark occupies 90 cubic feet of space in the ship's hold, and many attempts have been made to reduce this by compressing the bark by some means or another. Under normal conditions, there is not much difficulty in finding freight space for the bark in home-going ships, but at the present time freight charges are very high and space difficult to obtain. One method of overcoming the difficulty is to press the chopped bark by means of a hydraulic plant into bales, approximately 2 feet long 1 foot 8 inches wide and 1 foot 3 inches high, the cubic measurement being about 4 cubic feet. These bales hold approximately 200 lb. each, and are tied and held neatly by broad iron bands or by wire. Another method is to pulverize the bark by means of special disintegrators, and compress the product in a hydraulic press, as is done with chopped bark. A serious disadvantage of this method is the loss of the finer and richer material that takes place when the bark is ground, for a great proportion of it gets blown away unless means are adopted to conserve it.

A ton of compressed chopped bark occupies about 49 cubic feet, and one ton of compressed ground bark 45 cubic feet, the latter being only half the space occupied by ordinary bagged bark. Besides saving space in the ship, the space saved in storage at the docks is also a matter for consideration, and the compressed bales, besides, form a very handy package to deal with when loading and unloading.

A few of the largest growers in Natal have plant of their own for grinding and compressing bark, and the Agricultural Co-operative Union has established a factory at South Coast Junction with machinery for chopping and for grinding wattle bark, and bailing either variety under compression, as explained above.

It may be pointed out that in compressing bark into bales of this description, it is very essential that it must not be damp when put in the press, otherwise it would be liable to ferment and become mildewed.

COST OF PRODUCTION.

It is difficult to give any reliable figures under this heading for so much depends upon the size of the plantation or estate: the larger the acreage the more economical it is to work it. Also, the methods adopted, and the cost of labour, etc., vary largely throughout the country.

Ploughing, planting, weeding, thinning etc., till the plantation is established, will cost anything from 15s. per acre upwards. The matter of firebreaks, re-weeding, etc., necessary for the upkeep of the plantation till it is ready for stripping, will depend on the local conditions and the manner in which it is dealt with in the first instance, and may cost quite a considerable amount more.

Stripping, transport, drying, chopping, bagging, and handling will probably amount to 20s. per ton of bark at least for labour alone, to which a further sum of 10s. or 12s. has to be added for cost of bags, and 7s. per ton for cost of railage for the average distance to the Point. To this total we must also add the cost of machinery, maintenance, oils, renewals, etc., which is a very variable item and of which it is almost impossible to give an estimate.

JANUARY, 1923.]25

When it comes to re-establishing a plantation, the cost is likely to be much greater than the initial one of establishing, the expense of burning litter, weeding, thinning, and keeping clean being usually more in the case of subsequent crops than the first.

The above figures are those for the actual working of the plantations, and do not include interest on capital, depreciation of plant, machinery, buildings, etc., loss of live stock necessary for the working of the plantations, road repairs, accidental breakages, fencing repairs, damage by fire, insects, drought, hail, frost, unsuitable weather for drying, besides administrative expenses, and the numerous incidentals in addition which contribute to the total cost of running an estate. Some of these are very high in comparison, and vary too much to allow of anything like even an approximate estimate being made.

SHIPPING CONDITIONS AND FINANCE.

The usual practice previous to the outbreak of war was for the bark to be shipped to approved consignees—generally agents—who entered into contracts, as a rule for six months, in equal monthly quantities. The contracts were generally made during June and December for the half-yearly periods July to December and January to June respectively. The usual commission was 1\frac{1}{2} per cent. to a 2 per cent. del credere.

Shippers, as a rule, drew through their bankers on consignees at arranged currencies—generally 30 days' sight—with shipping documents attached. It lay with the consignees to arrange the necessary credit, to take up the documents and get possession of the shipment. Although contracts were, as a rule, made c.i.f., the consignee generally paid the freight to save bank exchange.

The freight from Durban to London or Hamburg immediately previous to the outbreak of war was about 25s. per ton, plus 2s. 3d. shipping charges. At the present time the freight to London is about £4'15 per ton measurement (40 cubic feet), or about £9 per ton weight when shipped as chopped or ground bark in bags, estimated at 90 cubic feet per ton weight. It will be noted that a very considerable saving in cost of freight is effected by compressing the bark.

GRADING OF WATTLE BARK.

The bark has not been generally sold on its tanning content, but a certain price is fixed for bark of fair average quality (f.a.q.), and if the quality appears to be appreciably of lower grade than this the price is usually fixed by friendly arbitration. Under what was known as the Hamburg Contract, the arbitration clause gave the Hamburg Chamber of Commerce the official adjudication on points of dispute, and debarred sellers from having any voice in the selection of arbitrators unless outside friendly arbitration were agreed to by both parties.

This method is unsatisfactory from many points of view; first, it is very difficult, and practically impossible, to establish a consistent standard of quality of bark, by ocular judgment alone, especially when there are so many different people called upon to act as judges and referees, many of whom are unqualified to give a judgment. Again, the seller does not get any benefit from a consignment of bark that is appreciably above the average

26[JANUARY, 1923.

quality, although he would be immediately penalized when selling bark that is apparently below the standard, the reduction in price being often out of all proportion to the real deficiency below the standard quality.

This question of grading of wattle bark received the attention of the wattle growers and exporters in Natal for several years, and became a subject of serious consideration in the year 1907, when several letters of complaint were received from brokers and buyers in Britain and Germany concerning the deterioration in the quality of the bark exported, involving numerous cases of arbitration and reduction in prices.

The Natal Wattle Bark Union was instituted in August, 1907, and one of the first questions it devoted its attention to was the feasibility of establishing a standard in the quality of exported bark and arranging for the inspection and classification of all bark shipped by its members. The Union first took steps to ascertain the views of representative commercial men in Europe, besides those of the chief growers and experts in Natal, on this question of grading, but the conclusion it came to was, that while it would be a very desirable object to attain, the difficulties in the way were insurmountable at the time.

In December, 1907, the Minister of Agriculture for Natal called a meeting of the growers and those interested in the industry to consider this questions of grading bark and to discuss the Government's suggestions in connection with it. They proposed to appoint a grader, who would open a certain proportion of the bags in every consignment and decide whether the bark was up to the standard or below grade, the latter to be refused the Government certificate and to be penalized with regard to railway rates. This scheme did not find favour with the meeting, and the matter dropped for the time being.

Although the importance of maintaining a uniform grade of bark, and thus establishing a recognized standard for this produce in the European market, ought to have been obvious to the growers and sellers in this country, strong complaints continued to come in from buyers and tanners in Europe about the variable character and the deterioration in the standard quality of the bark shipped. The United Tanners' Federation of Great Britain and Ireland considered the question of grading wattle bark at a general meeting in 1912, and expressed the opinion that steps should be taken to settle this matter without delay. It was desired that growers should be informed that much of the bark that was being shipped was immature and unsatisfactory from the tanners' point of view, and that by sending over immature and badly graded bark this excellent tanning material was being brought into disrepute, having the effect of depressing prices. The Federation suggested that the bark might be classified into :—No. 1 quality, a good, bright coloured, heavy bark from mature trees ; No. 2 quality, lighter, thin bark ; and No. 3 quality, including bark spoilt in harvesting, by rain, or by having been allowed to become mildewed, or for any other reason.

In 1913, the Union Department of Agriculture called meetings in Durban and Maritzburg of those interested in the wattle bark industry, and propounded its scheme of grading bark, which had previously been considered by the Wattle Committee of the Agricultural Co-operative Union. This scheme came into force by Government Notice No. 2032, of 23rd December,

JANUARY, 1923.]27

1913, and a Government Grader was appointed. The classification originally adopted was, however, amended by Government Notice No. 655 of 11th April, 1914, to the following :—

  • H. 1.—Heavy (choice)
  • H. 2.—Heavy (fair average quality)
  • M. 1.—Medium (choice)
  • M. 2.—Medium (fair average quality)
  • T. 1.—Thin (choice)
  • T. 2.—Thin (fair average quality)
  • B. G —Below grade.

This should have worked satisfactorily, but it was discontinued in September, 1914, owing to the dislocation of the market caused by the war, but chiefly owing to the fact that very little advantage was taken of the scheme.

That the above scheme of grading is not quite so arbitrary and unscientific as one might at first think it to be, was proved by the writer during an investigation carried out in 1913 and 1914 on the composition of Natal Wattle Bark. The results of a large number of analyses carried out on trees of different ages, from the neighbourhood of Cedara, showed that there was a close connection between the thickness of the bark and its tannin-content. The figures as given in the two articles published (6) seem to prove that a bark of a thickness of 0·15 inch and upwards may be relied upon to have a tannin content of over 35 per cent., and bark of thickness between 0·10 and 0·15 inch has over 30 per cent. of tannin, while bark below 0·10 inch almost invariably has less than 30 per cent. tannin. The figures agree very closely in cases of trees varying widely in maturity—from three years up to nine years. They also show that the thin bark from the top portion of a mature tree should not be mixed with the thicker bottom bark, if a uniform consignment is desirable.

It may be pointed out, however, that subsequent investigations carried out by the writer, on the composition of bark from the North Coast of Natal, showed that bark of a similar thickness to that grown around Cedara was richer in tannin in practically every case. The actual figures have not hitherto been published, so no definite comparison can be drawn.

In view of the fact that a large proportion of the bark is now exported in the compressed form, chopped or ground, the question of grading has to be reconsidered. It is possible that a satisfactory method will be found by sampling a certain proportion of the bales in a consignment at the port by means of an auger, and submitting a composite sample to chemical analysis, which need not take more than a day or two. The analyst's certificate might be attached to the shipping documents or posted by the next mail, if not ready when the consignment leaves the port. By this scheme the bark might be sold on the guaranteed analysis, or be graded according to the results of the analysis. If the practice of shredding or grinding the bark, and then compressing it into bales becomes general, the sampling and analysis of the bark would be facilitated, and, the results would be more trustworthy.

DR. PARKER states, in the article previously quoted(3), that South African growers have been misled to a certain extent concerning the importance of the colour of the bark. He mentions the well-known fact that the lighter coloured the bark, the younger it is, and, consequently, the lower percentage of tannin, as a rule. He also points out that, of course, the bark may be damaged, both as regards colour and the richness in tannin, by bad harvesting, rain, etc., but if proper care is taken in the harvesting, it still follows that the richer bark is darker in colour. It may, however, be mentioned that the markets, both in Britain and Germany, have always laid undue stress on this question of colour, and a deep colour in the bark has generally

28[JANUARY, 1923.

caused it to be penalized as regards price. As a rule, a bark must be of a light colour if it is to fetch the tip-top price in the market, no matter how rich it is in tanning matter. DR. PARKER seems to insinuate that this question of colour does not weigh very much with the tanner, provided the bark has a high percentage of tannin, but I am afraid that in a good many cases it is taken too much into consideration, and it is to be hoped that the opinion expressed on this point by DR. PARKER and other experts will convince them of the falsity of their standard of judging bark.

DISEASES AND PESTS OF THE WATTLE.

Up to a few years ago, the Black Wattle tree in South Africa did not suffer to any great extent from diseases and pests, but lately great depredations have been caused in most wattle neighbourhoods by the "Bag-worm" (Acanthopsysche Junodi, Heyl.), an insect which originally frequented the indigenous mimosas of the thornweld. This moth when it pupates weaves a very tough chrysalis or "bag" which is suspended from the branches, and the pupa or caterpillar which ultimately emerges from the case feeds on the leaves and sometimes on the bark of the trees, thus seriously interfering with their healthy growth. As a result of investigations carried out by POLE EVANS, FULLER, HARDENBERG, and others, several schemes have been advocated for the control of this pest, but hitherto without much success. The Division of Entomology is at present experimenting with a method of dust-spraying the trees, which was instituted a year or two ago by HARDENBERG, and it is hoped, with the loyal co-operation of the planters, to give the scheme a thorough test at the first favourable opportunity.

Probably owing to the exceptionally wet weather that has prevailed this year, the bag-worm is practically non-existent in most wattle districts at the present time, for this insect thrives best in a dry climate. In fact, its activities are largely confined to the drier neighbourhoods, and in the heart of the mist belt of the Natal Midlands it is not such a very serious enemy to the wattle grower.

Another pest is the "Cockchafer Beetle," which in the adult stage also devours the leaves. Granted favourable conditions, it is likely to become a serious menace in future years. It is believed that the dust-spraying mentioned as a control for the bag-worm will at the same time keep this insect pest within limits.

A third pest is what is known as the "Frog Hopper," which gives some trouble in certain neighbourhoods. This insect lives mainly by sucking the juices of the bark, and will probably also require serious attention before long, if it is allowed to multiply unchecked for any length of time.

Certain kinds of "Tree Borers" are known to do great damage to wattle trees, especially near the coast, where white ants are also troublesome.

A serious disease is that commonly known as Mottling in Wattles which has been studied in this country by VAN DER BYL(7). He attributes it to physiological derangements caused by unfavourable conditions of growth, which produce dark coloured areas in the bark, and afterwards gummosis sets in in these diseased portions. It is suggested that methods of controlling this disease should be directed towards improvement of the conditions which produce this disturbance; for instance, the trees might require a greater amount of light and moisture, and this might be satisfied by increasing the espacement.

SUITABILITY OF THE WATTLE BARK AS A TANNING AGENT.

The composition of the bark from Black Wattle trees of various ages from Natal was lately investigated by the author, and a resume of the results was published in the two articles previously mentioned(6). The richness of

JANUARY, 1923.]29

the bark in tannin seems to increase continuously with age, provided the bark does not become corky, for old, corky bark is found to be very poor indeed in tanning matter. As stated in a previous section, it was also demonstrated that the tannin content of the bark decreased with the height above ground, so that the bark from the uppermost portion of a mature tree may be poorer in tannin than the bark from the bole of a much younger tree.

The properties of wattle bark as a tanning material have been very thoroughly investigated by a number of scientists and experts in various countries where the tanning industry is conducted on scientific lines. Amongst others, PROF. PAESSLER, the celebrated leather chemist, of Freiburg, has published the results of an elaborate and interesting research carried out by him on this raw tanning material(8).

PAESSLER in this article strongly advocates a still more extended use of wattle bark in German tanneries. He points out that it is a very rich tanning material, the average result of the analysis of over 260 samples made at his laboratory during recent years being 31.6 per cent. of tanning matter; but it may be pointed out that the results of a large number of analyses in the laboratory at Cedara, Natal, give a higher average still (not far short of 35 per cent.) for mature bark.

PAESSLER also shows that apart from its richness in tannin, wattle bark has the advantage of containing only about one part of the soluble non-tanning matter to every three parts of tanning matter, and that the proportion of sugars in this non-tanning extractive matter corresponds to about three parts for every 100 parts of tanning matter, whereas in oak bark, for example, the sugars amount to 26 parts, and in hemlock bark to about 32 for every 100 parts of tanning matter. Liquors made from wattle bark are consequently far less liable to fermentation than those from most other tanning materials.

This investigator also carefully calculated the actual relative cost per unit of tanning in case of the principal tanning materials, and his results are given in the sub-joined table:—

Oak bark .. 10.5 9.0 1.17
Valonia ... 25.0 27.0 0.93
Quebracho wood ... 12.0 19.0 0.63

It is evident from the above table that wattle bark is a very cheap tanning agent as compared with other raw tanning materials.

Another advantage that PAESSLER claims for wattle bark is that the tanning matter is very easily extracted from it, and at a comparatively low temperature. In fact, at 30°C. more than 90 per cent of the total available tanning in the bark is extracted.

If, however, the extraction of the wattle bark is carried out to the extreme limit, and at too high a temperature, there is the danger of extracting an undue amount of red colouring matter, which is objectionable from the tanner's point of view. Owing to the fibrous character of the bark, it may with advantage be used for mixing with other raw tanning materials that require extraction, for its admixture with these finer materials facilitates their extraction by preventing clogging and the formation of channels in the leaching vats.

30[JANUARY, 1923.

Further, PAESSLER proves that wattle bark liquors lose very little in strength, or deposit but a small proportion of insoluble matters or "blooms," on keeping, and compare most favourably in this respect with "liquor" prepared from most other raw tanning materials. This fact is borne out by the results tabulated below, the figures given representing the percentage loss of tannin in liquors of 2° Baume after keeping for 60 days :—

Source of Liquor. Percentage Loss of Tannin.
Gambier 0.0
Mangrove bark 0.0
Wattle bark 2.0
Quebracho wood 3.4
Oak bark 7.5
Galls 16.0
Myrabolans 24.0
Valonia 29.0
Divi-divi 29.0

Finally, PAESSLER praises the value of the tanning matter obtained from wattle bark for the weight-giving properties it has in the tanning of heavy leather. He places the chief raw tanning materials in the following descending order of merit as regards this property :—

Quebracho Wood, Wattle Bark, Oak Bark, Mangrove Bark, Divi-divi, Myrabolans, and Valonia.

In addition to its suitability for tanning heavy leather, PAESSLER considers that wattle bark might also be used with advantage for the production of certain kinds of light leathers.

The vegetable tannins are divided into two main classes, the pyrogallol and the catechol classes, the tannin from wattle bark belonging to the latter, whereas oak bark contains tannings of both classes. EDWARDS (9) points out that although materials of the catechol class are not usually reckoned to be very suitable, when used alone, for the manufacture of heavy leathers, wattle bark, when used in conjunction with materials of the pyrogallol class (like Myrabolans and Valonia) may perform a very useful service in this direction.

In the same article he points out that owing to wattle bark being so rich in tannin, and to the case with which it yields up its tannin on extraction with water, it is possible to obtain strong liquors very readily from it, which is a great advantage in the modern methods of tanning. For this reason also it is especially suitable for placing, when ground up, between each hide or butt in the "dusters" or forward "handlers."

EDWARDS also draws attention to the fact that wattle bark is an astringent tanning material, which arises chiefly from the low proportion of soluble non-tanning matters in the bark as compared with the tanning matter. These soluble non-tanning matters usually consist largely of glucosides and other sugary matters, which not only help to modify the astringency (i.e., to mellow the liquor), but also yield acids by fermentation, which always takes place in tan liquors, and these acids also assist in modifying the astringency of the tannins and thus help to swell the hide fibres. As pointed out by PAESSLER, not only is the proportion of non-tannins low, but of these non-tannins actually present there is only a very small proportion of sugary matters or acid-forming substances. The non-production of acidity can be corrected by the direct addition of acid, or by the use, along with the wattle bark, of some material rich in sugary matters and which will produce acids by fermentation. The material which perhaps best fulfils this condition is Myrabolans, which not only gives a mellow tannage, but is rich in glucosides and produces abundant acidity under suitable conditions; Valonia is another tanning material that is also used with wattle bark for the same purpose.

JANUARY, 1923.]31

It is further mentioned by EDWARDS in this article that, on account of the astringency of wattle bark, it is advisable not to use it in the early stages of tanning, when the grain is liable to become drawn, but rather later when the grain has become set and when the pelt is partially struck through. The most astringent tannins are removed from a liquor first, and this fact, in itself, is an added reason for not using such tannins in the earlier stages of tanning.

Wattle bark when used alone as a tanning agent, owing to its astringency, produces a leather whose characteristics would be harshness and shortness of fibre. It also imparts a slight pinkish colour to the finished leather, which darkens if the newly tanned leather is exposed to light. As previously pointed out, this astringent effect can be obviated by the use of Myrabolans or Valonia in conjunction with it, and, in addition, the slightly reddish colour of the wattle tannage is hidden by the strong yellow of these other materials; in fact, the very presence of the slight pinkiness of the wattle helps to brighten the colour produced by these materials.

BY-PRODUCTS.—THEIR USES AND MARKET VALUE.

The chief by-product of the wattle bark industry is the wood, and under the present conditions it might be stated that timber is the product and the bark only a by-product; this is especially the case with plantations in the Transvaal or those at a great distance from any port.

Assuming the total area under wattles in the Union to be 190,000 acres, and that each acre during an average rotation of eight years will yield 20 tons of timber, we find that there are nearly half a million tons of timber produced from the wattle plantations of this country annually. A large proportion of this is grown in plantations that are too far from the railway for the wood to be utilized, but it may be safely reckoned that at least half of it is available for commercial purposes.

From the more mature trees, the timber is sold as pit props, chiefly for the Rand mines and the coal mines of Natal and the Transvaal. The poles from the smaller trees are also utilized by the mines as "laggings," or are sawn up and used for fuel purposes, for which there is a good demand in South Africa, as the wattle makes a most excellent firewood.

The timber is being made use of to a large extent for box-making but unfortunately it takes nails rather badly, and it has been found desirable to use a softer wood for the ends of the boxes.

For the last fifteen years or more, inquiries have been made by some of the larger and more progressive growers with regard to the possibility of erecting plants for the distillation of the waste wattle wood and of finding markets for the numerous products of such a factory. For instance, estimates were obtained by SIR T. K. MURRAY as far back as October, 1905, from experts in London as to the cost of establishing such a factory. Based on prices and cost of labour, etc., ruling in England at that time, it was estimated that the daily working costs of a plant utilizing 10 tons of wood would be £10 4s., while the value of the products would be £12 3s. 6d. The cost of such machinery for treating 10 to 15 tons of wood per diem was estimated at £3,000.

The following figures give the results of a trial carried out in London in distilling Natal wattle wood:—

Weight of wood sent for trial amounted to 15 tons to 16 cwt.

On distillation, the products were as follows:—

Charcoal, 4 tons 7 cwt.
Acetate of lime, 11 cwt. 2 qrs.
Pyroligneous acid, 1,280 gallons
Wood tar, 55 gallons
Naptha, 20 gallons

32[JANUARY, 1923.

The acetate of lime could easily be converted into acetone, for the additional apparatus required for the manufacture of this latter material would not be a serious item, and practically no additional labour would be required.

The expert opinion expressed in connection with this test was favourable, the proposition being evidently a sound one, judging from the yield, and since the capital outlay is comparatively small the inducements are correspondingly great.

About the same time SIR GEORGE LEUCHARS and his brother (MR. J. W. LEUCHARS) made some investigations on the question of wattle wood distillation. They arranged for two separate and independent laboratory tests to be made in England on samples of wattle wood. One was conducted by DR. N. WIRTZ, London, and the other by MESSRS. DAVIS BROS., of the Manchester Technical Laboratory.

DR. WIRTZ reported: "I find that the wattle wood compares very favourably with other woods generally used in destructive distillation. As a matter of fact, it comes quite up to birch and oak, which are the best, as gives even a little more acetic acid than the latter."

The results obtained by MESSRS. DAVIS BROS., were practically the same as those of DR. WIRTZ, and they found that the quality of the charcoal compares very well with the best English charcoal.

Estimates were also obtained of the cost of machinery and production. It was reckoned that the cost of a plant for dealing with 10,000 tons of wood per annum would be £20,000, from which the receipts were roughly estimated at £8,600 and the expenditure £5,200, leaving a profit of £3,400.

It is a pity that such an industry had not been instituted in the country some years ago, for, owing to the war there is a tremendous demand for acetone at the present time in the manufacture of explosives and the price is correspondingly high. It may be mentioned here that the British War Department was approached some ten or twelve years ago by certain parties in Natal interested in the wattle industry, to see if the Home Government would be prepared to purchase the acetone provided a distillation plant was erected here. No such guarantee was forthcoming, however, although I believe the War Department at that time was largely dependent upon Australia and other European countries for its supplies of acetone.

With regard to the charcoal, the wood tar, and wood naphtha, it is considered that satisfactory markets for these would be found in the Union,

In 1907 inquiries were instituted by SIM, who was then the Chief Conservator of Forests for Natal, with regard to the possibility of utilizing the timber from the wattle tree for paper-making. The results went to show that the wattle wood taken alone is not very suitable for the manufacture of a good grade of paper pulp, the fibre of the wattle being rather short, and consequently the paper is deficient in strength. It is considered, however, that if it were mixed with an equal weight of pulped sugar-cane or other grass fibre, the paper produced might be satisfactory.

Wattle Gum.—MAIDEN states that the gum exuded from several species of Acacia, including A. decurrens, is in commercial demand, especially the clear light-coloured samples.

Wattle Blossom.—Bees are very partial to wattle blossoms and do well on them, the honey produced being of good colour and excellent flavour. The blossoms from the Black Wattle and Golden Wattle also yield a very delightful perfume, which is coming more and more into favour.

JANUARY, 1923.]33

PRESENT CONDITION AND FUTURE PROSPECTS OF THE WATTLE INDUSTRY.

On many occasions the wattle growers in this country have not shown sufficient foresight and energy to place the industry on a firm and permanent commercial basis, and during the past decade many warnings have been sounded by people conversant with the trade against this laissez faire policy.

When the Wattle Growers' Union was established in 1907, the endeavour was made to bind all the growers and others interested in the industry, so as to be able to protect their interests in every possible way. The immediate aims were to represent the needs and wishes of the wattle growers to the Government, the shipping companies, agents, dealers, etc., with regard to railway rates, freight, conditions of shipment, etc., and especially in an endeavour to institute or arrange for the inspection and grading of all bark shipped from the country. The Union also immediately instituted investigations into the possibility of manufacturing wattle extract in the country.

In spite of the strong committee formed under the rules of this Union to carry out its programme, its efforts met with but feeble response from the growers generally, and the result was that the industry for some years subsequently did not make the progress that it should have done had the difficulties been faced firmly and the desired unanimity of action been established amongst the growers.

Subsequently the Wattle Growers' Union was merged into the Wattle Committee of the Agricultural Co-operative Union, Ltd., and great credit is due to this committee for what it has done in fostering the industry and for its endeavours to find new markets for the bark.

It was chiefly due to its representations that the Government took steps to establish the machinery for the grading of wattle bark, referred to in a previous section of this report. As far back as 1912 this committee made special efforts to open up markets for the bark in the United States and Canada, and the comparative failure in this case was due to the fact that the American tanners had then other sources of raw tanning materials to draw upon at a cheap price. The committee's representative, however, was assured over and over again by people who had a thorough knowledge of the tanning trade over there that there would have been a good sale for the tanning material if it could be placed on the market in the form of an extract at a reasonable price.

Subsequent to the outbreak of war, the committee's efforts to find new markets have been redoubled, and have met with some success in Russia, Japan, India, etc., and at the same time the price has been fairly well maintained. As mentioned in a previous paragraph, they have sought to overcome the freight difficulty by establishing a factory at South Coast Junction for grinding and compressing the bark.

Owing to the want of efficient co-operation among wattle growers the export trade in wattle bark seems to have been allowed to fall too much into the hands of speculating buyers, apart from the genuine broker and commission agent. The actual producer finds it practically impossible at the present time to obtain any preference in the matter of freight space, unless he is an old shipper of bark and has been a regular customer of the shipping companies in the past. The consequence is that the small grower, who in the past only shipped through his broker or commission agent, has now no alternative but to sell his bark to these speculators, who are recognized by the shipping companies as old clients and are thus granted so much freight space. The speculator has no interest in keeping up the price and quality of the bark, for it does not matter to him whether he can buy at £3 or at £6, provided he can make the same amount of profit in each

34[JANUARY, 1923.

case. To the presence of the speculator in the wattle bark market is chiefly attributed the amount of really bad bark that is exported from this country, for he is ready to give a price, albeit a small one, for almost any quality of bark, so long as he can make his profit on it. The question of keeping up the good quality of the bark on the market does not affect him any more than does the fact that the low price he pays for it will ultimately affect production. The seriousness of the position is realized if it is correct that the best price for bark at the Point at the present time is £4 15s., although the price in England is about £16, the freight insurance, etc., per ton being about £10.

It might be pointed out that the grower who produces and sells to the speculator the low-grade bark is the one really to blame. That may be, but it must be borne in mind that all growers are not far-sighted enough to see the damage they are thus inflicting on the industry and on themselves in the future. It is only efficient co-operation amongst the growers, and a compulsory scheme of grading bark, that will do away with this evil.

About six months ago two representatives of the United Tanners' Federation came out to South Africa to institute inquiries as to the condition of the wattle trade here and to encourage the production of wattle bark for the British market, so as to keep the trade as much as possible within the confines of the Empire. Judging from the results of the interviews these two gentlemen had with the Wattle Committee, the principal growers, and other representative men in the industry, hopes were raised that the Tanners' Federation were going to give real support to the industry and assist in placing it on a sound commercial footing. It was stated by these representatives that if the effort were made out here to keep up the quality of the bark and to have an efficient system of grading it (preferably on the results of an official analysis at the port), the Federation would be willing to give a fair price for the bark, according to its quality, and would be able to take practically all the bark that was produced in the country. The disappointment amongst the producers was most keen when they heard, shortly after the return of these representatives to England, that they had made a contract for 7000 tons of bark at £5. 7s. 6d. per ton, f.o.b., a figure that in the opinion of those best conversant with the industry is too low to make it profitable (especially at the present time) for growers who are anxious to maintain a reputation for good quality of bark.

By making contracts at such low prices the Tanners' Federation has missed a good opportunity of ensuring a permanent supply of an excellent tanning material for the British tanners' use, and of obviating the need on the part of the Natal growers to seek markets outside the Empire.

The consequence of the lack of co-operation amongst growers, and the dislocation of the trade since the outbreak of war, is that a large acreage in Natal, previously under wattles, has either already been diverted to other better paying crops or is lying idle, and there is very little or any breaking up of new ground for wattle planting. I understand this policy is not only adopted by the inefficient growers, but also in the case of the more up-to-date plantations, where they find that only the best and most favourably situated areas can be worked at a satisfactory profit.

THE WATTLE BARK INDUSTRY IN
EAST AFRICA.

The following extract is taken from a report by MR. C. WILLIAMS, B. Sc., A. R. C. S., Chemist, School of Agriculture, Cedera (Natal) from Vol. 1, No. 10 of the SOUTH AFRICAN JOURNAL OF INDUSTRIES.

In 1908 the possibilities of a large wattle industry was realized in the British East Africa Protectorate, as a result of a favourable report on wattle

JANUARY, 1923.]35

bark produced there. The following year samples from several localities were sent to the Imperial Institute for investigation, and the results were very encouraging. It was found that bark between three and four years old had 40 per cent. of tanning matter in it, although samples from older trees were not so rich, but in no case was the amount less than 36 per cent. The quality of the leather produced in each case was very satisfactory, being of good colour and texture, and free from harshness.

As a result of these favourable reports and the good prices realized from trial consignments, a number of the settlers have been induced to put down large areas under wattles. In 1914 there were about 11,000 acres of wattle trees in the Protectorate, and the expected annual output for the next few years was to have been not less than 7500 tons of bark had the outbreak of war not interfered with the trade.

A scheme was on foot in 1914 to erect a factory at a cost of £15,000 for dealing with 7000 to 10,000 tons of bark annually, but the same deterrent mentioned above caused the erection of this factory to be delayed.

The bark by all reports seems to compare very favourably with the Natal product, and this Protectorate is likely to prove a keen competitor in the wattle market in the future.

The Government has issued stringent regulations governing the wattle bark industry (2). As previously stated, they prohibit the planting of the Silver Wattle and the officers of the Agricultural Department are given power to destroy any of it planted or grown from seed. The Governor is also empowered to make rules (1) prohibiting the export of wattle bark that has not been officially inspected, (2) providing for the official grading and branding of bark prior to export (3), for the licensing and inspection of Black Wattle plantations in which seed is harvested for sale, (4) prohibiting the sale of seed of the Black Wattle harvested in the Protectorate on any place other than a duly licensed plantation, (5) prohibiting or restricting the importation of Black Wattle seed for use in the Protectorate, and (6) prescribing the fees to be paid for licences, inspection, and services rendered under the ordinance.

It may also be mentioned that wattle bark of a similar quality to that grown in Natal and British East Africa is grown in German East Africa. Samples of the Black Wattle bark gathered from trees from two to six years old have given an average of 44 per cent. tanning, and, similarly, barks from the Green Wattle have averaged 38 per cent.

SOILS AND MANURES.

RETAINING THE SURFACE SOIL.

One of the biggest problems in agriculture as carried out on hilly or even moderately undulating land is the maintenance of surface soil. So many influences are at work depleting the soil surface that measures have to be adopted to prevent or counteract this loss. In some places a periodic renewal of the soil has to be effected to grow any crops at all.

For example, certain hillsides are exposed to heavy rains and winds and the fertile surface soil would be lost if precautions, such as terracing and carrying soil from lower parts, were not taken.

Owing to the fine particles of soil that are being continually swept down and deposited, the valleys and lowlands are more fertile than the hillsides and higher lands. The fertile lowlands of Bengal have been formed in the course of the centuries by matter carried down from the Himalayas and Central Asia in the drainage water.

Consider the method in vogue in the valley of a river like the Humber in England. The river carries in suspension solid matter from the Yorkshire hills and moors, but the tides have the effect of pushing back this matter in suspension and by arrangements of sluices, channels and drains the water is spread over the surface of the land, the sediment settles and the water is then drained off; the silt thus deposited improves the fertility of the soil.

A somewhat similar natural process although on an immensely large scale takes place in certain areas in India, Egypt, and Mesopotamia where the land is periodically covered by muddy flood water from the rivers.

In Lincolnshire the marine silt has been retained for ages by means of walls and banks built to keep out the tide, but the most notable case of this nature is in Holland, where land has actually been reclaimed from the ocean, and very fertile land it is.

The farmer who relies upon maintenance of fertility by replacing with manures and fertilisers what is taken from the soil by the crop should look to the question of the maintenance of depth of soil, as well as its fertility, for some is being lost every year.

Earthworms bring fine soil to the surface and by their action do good in many ways. Whilst on some land worms may bring up fine mould to the extent of 10 tons per acre in the castings they leave on the surface, yet this may not be a permanent addition. The very fact that they bring up soil and leave it on the surface may help in reducing the soil surface for the castings may be blown away as dust.

There are other ways in which soil is carried away, lowering the soil surface in one place and raising to it in another. In volcanic regions dust is formed and may travel round the earth before it settles.

JANUARY, 1923.]37

Dust may often be observed on the leaves of tea bushes after monsoon rains; this has obviously been carried there from a considerable distance by the wind. In various parts of the world there are wind storms which, where the soil consists of fine clayey or sandy, particles, become dust storms. Thus whilst in some regions the surface is denuded to a depth of several inches, a similar or even greater amount may be accumulated in other places.

The loess lands of Manchuria and Western China are made up of wind-borne dust. This was accumulated to a depth of many feet and has a dark rock-like appearance but is really composed of very fine particles of dust carried by the wind hundreds of miles from the great desert wastes of Central Asia.

The action of rain and rivers tends continually to reduce all land to one level. Rain wash along brings particles down, and even on apparently level lands torrential rain makes channels and grooves in the surface and carries forward soil particles. The tendency is naturally for soil to follow the slope. Those who have not previously studied the subject are amazed to learn of the immense quantities of matter that are actually carried from high to lower levels by natural forces constantly at work such as winds, rivers and floods. Were it not for the fact that there are, happily, opposite forces, including earthquakes and earth movements, also at work, the surface of the world would long since have become level and, in fact, would be entirely covered by water.

Regular cropping has a conserving effect as it preserves the soil from denudation and prevents too ready drainage of fertilisers during the wet season.

The application of manures and fertilisers adds to the soil content but if not properly selected and judiciously used they may reduce fertility instead of increasing it. Green manures, and similar methods of adding to the organic contents of the soil, have a beneficial effect and a soil may become richer every season if a suitable blend of fertilizers is applied and if the surface soil is not allowed to wash away.

Normally there is a continual drainage of the nitrogenous and other substances from the soil, continuous oxidation of substances ploughed in; and with these regular means of escape or utilisation or exhaustion, the balance due to ordinary agricultural operations generally finds the soil less able to bear the strain than the previous season. The maintenance of the soil surface has indeed been hardly considered during the year's agricultural work.

It would seem desirable to have something in hand, to have a reserve upon which to draw, and to ensure that the soil shall be able to grow crops for several seasons without annually making it up. From the crop producers' point of view it would be an advantage but is difficult of attainment. This desirable end was obtained in England in the past by marling. To quote from an old writer: "That marl is most esteemed which contains the most lime. The farmers say that it strengthens the soil, enables the growing crops to maintain their vegetation during a dry season, and that it fills the kernels of corn. It does most good on light land, but even stiff lands derive benefit from it.

A field was said to be well marled when 128 cubic yards were spread over a statute acre.

38[JANUARY, 1923.

Its effects last for from six to eight crops. Unfortunately marl is not everywhere available but the application of tank scourings and lime would be equally effective.

Top dressing with surface soil from neighbouring jungle or with the accumulated peaty soils found in neighbouring bheels and hollows had been and is still practised in India as in other countries. The system is effective—indeed it is the only feasible method that can be adopted in those cases where surface soil has been more or less completely washed away.

The method is however very costly and can only be done to a limited extent. Prevention is better than cure in this as in so many other cases and can be effected best by keeping the land under continuous crop as far as possible, arranging a suitable drainage system to encourage water to pass down through the soil instead of rushing over the surface and by making terraces or bunds across the slopes to prevent the rushing flow of water.—

INDIAN SCIENTIFIC AGRICULTURIST, VOL. 3, No. 8.

THE MANURING OF BANANAS.

R. G. BARFLETT,

Assistant Fruit Expert.

Although the manuring of bananas is now receiving more attention than formerly it is not even yet carried out by the great majority of growers on the right lines.

Bananas are a crop that, both in regard to the fruit itself and to the large quantity of vegetable matter produced, make heavy demand upon the soil. They may be said to be voracious feeders, and to ensure maximum returns year after year, therefore, it is most essential that the fertility of the soil be maintained by every possible means. In a measure the truth of this is coming home to growers, who, however, have not yet given a great deal of consideration to the means by which it may be most profitably and efficiently done.

Fertilisers are being used by a number of growers, but too often incomplete mixtures are being applied where complete ones are needed, and in other cases where the mixtures are more complete they are not being supplied in the best proportions, while upon almost all hands insufficient attention is being given to the maintenance of the supply of humus in the soil. This all-important substance not only provides plant-food in itself, but it has a very valuable general influence upon the soil, opening it up, aerating it, receiving and retaining the maximum amount of moisture, and thus providing conditions favourable for the soil bacteria to act upon the mineral matter in the soil and to turn the plant-food therein into a condition in which the crop can make use of it.

THE IMPORTANCE OF HUMUS.

A number of cases have occurred on the North Coast where soils lacking in humus have made practically no response to artificial fertilisers, and the only hope the grower has in such cases is to adopt a practice that will repair the greatest deficiency (that of humus), and thus provide the conditions that will make expenditure on fertilisers worth while.

JANUARY, 1923.]39

It is, suitable, therefore, that in dealing with the matter of manuring banana lands, reference should be made first to the means by which humus may be added to soils.

Humus is decayed and decaying vegetable and animal matter. There is a certain amount of it in most soils—least of all in sandy soils, and most in heavy loamy ones. It is continually undergoing change, however, and the supply is always diminishing, whether the soil is being cultivated or not. Indeed cultivation has the effect of hastening the oxidising or burning up of this decaying vegetable matter, and hence it is that soils that are in cultivation require to be supplied with material that will become humus.

Any vegetable matter that will decay fairly rapidly is suitable for the purpose, be it weeds, leaves, or crops grown for the purpose. In the banana districts of this State there is usually an abundant growth of soft weeds in the wet season, and banana growers might well take advantage of this as one means of supplying the soil with vegetable matter. Quite rightly growers like to see their land free from weeds, but an inexpensive cover-crop could be obtained by allowing the weeds to run up in the rainy season, then chipping them off and allowing them to lie on the surface to decay and humify there.

WHAT COVER CROPS DO.

Cover crops may be grown for the purpose of supplying humus to the soil; and, indeed, on account of the abundance of material they provide and the contribution they make to soil fertility, they should be part of the practice of every grower. Their advantages as a general feature of farm work may be stated thus :—

  1. 1. They supply humus, thus adding to the amount of plant-food in the soil, improving the texture, and increasing the capacity for receiving and retaining moisture.
  2. 2. They provide a useful mulch while decaying, preventing evaporation during the dry period.
  3. 3. They prevent the washing away of the rich surface soil during heavy falls of rain, being of especial value in this respect on steep faces.
  4. 4. They protect the surface roots of the bananas from scorching and drying out during hot weather.
  5. 5. They reduce work by saving two or three chippings in the season of greatest weed growth—January, February, and March.

The only advantage attaching to cover crops is that the runners of certain kinds of crops have to be pulled away from the banana stools occasionally, but the amount of work so entailed is so small that any one of the advantages named greatly outweighs it.

Failures with cover crops may be said to be traceable to two things :— (1) Neglect to cultivate the soil and to keep it free from weeds until the young crop is fairly well established; (2) planting among old plantations where there is not sufficient light and air to allow the cover crop to grow properly.

WHEN AND WHAT TO PLANT.

The best time to plant cover crops is November and December, following a good fall of rain. They will quickly establish themselves to the exclusion of weeds.

40[JANUARY, 1923.

Various plants are suitable for the purpose, but none are so good as the legumes, which fix atmospheric nitrogen and store it in roots, stems, and leaves, thus adding substantially to the nitrogen content of the soil when the growth is cut down and allowed to decay.

Of legumes suitable for the purpose mention may be made of Rice bean, Velvet bean, Giant Red cowpea, Mauritius bean, and pigeon pea. Rice bean has several recommendations, its haulm being less woody than those of some other legumes, and therefore decaying more rapidly after being cut down.

The ploughing under of cover crops in the autumn cannot be practised among bananas as among other fruiting plants and trees—the disturbance of the surface roots would be too great—but chipping off is sufficient and the crop roots on the ground.

When cover crops are grown among bananas less nitrogenous manure can be used in the fertiliser mixture.

FERTILISERS THAT ARE USEFUL.

Great as is the value of cover crops, commercial fertilisers are also essential to the banana grower, and, as already stated, various mixtures have been used with more or less success.

Analyses of Cavendish banana plants and fruits have shown there to be more than twice as much potash present in their ash as of nitrogen and phosphoric acid combined. This seems to indicate the necessity for including potash in some form in banana manures, but in the past often only nitrogen and phosphoric acid have been supplied—largely the result of lack of knowledge on the part of growers. Actual experiments have shown that a complete manure containing nitrogen, potash and phosphoric acid gives the best results, and, further, that when the potash is omitted the fertiliser barely pays for itself. Departmental tests have demonstrated that among the best mixtures for average soils are the two following, either of which the grower may try :—

No. 1-2 lb. dried blood } per stool every
six months.
1¼ lb. superphosphate
1 lb. sulphate or muriate of potash
No. 2-1¼ lb. sulphate of ammonia } per stool every
six months.
1¼ lb. superphosphate
1 lb. sulphate or muriate of potash

One of these mixtures may be applied in March and September of each year.

Inquiries have been received from time to time from banana growers with reference to guano, it being apparently thought that that material has some value, but it must be pointed out that guano is of variable chemical composition. In any case, sulphate or muriate of potash should always be added when guano is used, as it is deficient in that respect. One part of potassic manure to four parts of guano may be found suitable.

Lime may be necessary on some banana soils. It should be applied at the rate of 2 to 4 tons agricultural lime per acre, at least six weeks before the application of artificial fertilisers. The autumn is the most suitable time, and dressings may be made every four years.—AGRIC. GAZ. OF N.S.W., Vol. XXXIII, Part II.

JANUARY, 1923.]41

PESTS AND DISEASES.

DESTRUCTION OF RATS.

H. W. JACK, B.Sc., B.A.,

Economic Botanist.

Department of Agriculture, F.M.S. & S.S.

This subject has been brought up so frequently that it is worth while recording my own experience in Krian and Kuala Kangsar, as well as the experiences of writers in England and Java.

Rats play an important role in the dissemination of disease germs, plague (carried to man by fleas which infest rats), trichinosis, and other parasites, and fevers, by mechanical damage to drains, etc., but in this country, their chief crime is their great destruction of food and food crops.

They are the enemies of the henroost, the coconut, the paddy field and all sorts of stores. The gradual waste and consequent financial loss caused by the depredations of these vermin is not easily detected but is continuous and soon amounts to a considerable sum.

In the Krian district of Perak, it has been estimated roughly that rats destroy at least six per cent. of the crop or approximately one million gantang of paddy, which would be sufficient to feed 10,000 Malays for one year. This computation does not include the damage done to paddy stores in every cultivator's house, which must be considerable.

Thousands of rats can be found in every large rice store and even small stores harbour hosts of them. Recently, in a store belonging to the Department of Agriculture, containing only 55 bags of paddy, six coolies in one hour caught and killed 78 large rats, and about forty escaped.

The damage done to young coconuts by rats in the Bagan Datoh district can be estimated in thousands of dollars. Two thousand acres in one locality have been known to be completely destroyed and, on all plantations, precautionary measures, which are fairly costly, have to be taken to combat this pest.

Although the problem of rat extermination is a difficult one, owing chiefly to the migratory habits of these rodents, it is necessary both from an economical as well as from a sanitary and medical point of view, that stringent measures be taken to combat the nuisance. In Europe, rats have increased at an alarming rate during the last five years, owing to the war, lack of labour, accumulation of stores and neglect of ordinary precautionary measures.

At the London docks, rats do incalculable damage and in 1919 the port rat-catchers killed over a million. In rural districts farmers suffer severely from the depredations of these rodents as they consume and destroy root-crops, fruit, eggs, vegetables, etc., and it has been estimated that in 1908 they caused damage to food-stuffs to the value of £15,000,000 in England alone, which is but a mere fraction of Europe, and the value of food has

42JANUARY, 1923.

increased very considerably since then. There are two species of rats in Europe—the black and the brown, but the latter predominates in the proportion of 10 to 1 and is thus the chief source of destruction of food and spread of plague. The brown rat migrated westward from China, appearing in hordes in Europe in 1730 and is almost identical with the destructive rat common to Malaya, though several other species are said to abound also. Rats breed very prolifically and commence at an early age. They may have several litters a year, averaging six to nine young but the writer has seen litters of 17 in Krian and litters of 22 have been known. It is said that one pair of rats will give rise to a progeny of 880 in nine months and the average gestation period is only 21 days. Abundance of food leads to larger and more frequent litters and a lower mortality of young rats, for, when food is scarce, the parent rats eat their young and are not able to support large litters. They are fierce, voracious, cannibalistic, agile, cunning, good climbers and swimmers and can adapt themselves to almost any surroundings. The migratory habits of rats are well known. In large paddy areas, for instance, when the fields are flooded and cleared for planting and food is scanty, they will tour in hordes and destroy every rice nursery in a block of land of some 100-200 acres in one night. The writer has seen hordes in Krian, which he estimated at anything between 150 and 400. These hordes are more common at a sowing time following a bad harvest than after a good harvest and the rats eat up every grain of paddy in every nursery they encounter.

Similarly in Europe many instances of hordes migrating in search of food or frightened by disease are well known. The rat menace to food, property, and health became so acute in the British Isles that in 1919 legal powers were given to the Ministry of Agriculture to enforce rat destruction in areas which proved to be particularly badly infested, and similar powers in force in this country might be more rigorously pursued, especially in rice growing districts. In a campaign against rats it is essential that energy and zeal should be displayed by all concerned in carrying out the necessary methods of destruction; half measures are practically useless.

PREVENTIVE MEASURES.

Preventive measures consist in the protection of all food supplies from rats, the careful removal and destruction of waste, the rat proofing of buildings, the protection of ventilators, drains, sewers, etc., by gratings, fumigation of ships and store-rooms from time to time, the filling up of rat burrows with sand or glass and tar or similar material.

Methods of destruction :
  1. (1) Protection of natural enemies ;
  2. (2) Poison ;
  3. (3) Trapping and hunting.

(1) Large numbers of rats are killed daily by their enemies (herons, owls, snakes, ferrets, hawks, cats, dogs, mongoose, etc.), which should be protected. Snakes and mongoose are probably the most important of our local fauna in this respect. In Krian rice fields, where they both abound, the writer has found three medium sized rats in one average sized (five feet) cobra and it was found that the season following one in which snakes were killed almost daily on the Rice Experiment Station area was characterized by unusually large numbers of rats, and consequent excessive damage to the paddy crop.

JANUARY, 1923.]43

Fatal snake bites are so uncommon in this country that it is questionable whether snakes should be killed at sight as so frequently happens, for even when they bite, their poison, though causing intensive pain and temporary paralysis, is I believe, rarely known to cause death. To give another instance, as many as twenty freshly killed rats have been found in a single owl's nest, though these birds are persecuted because their presence is regarded as an ill-omen.

(2) The number of rat poisons in use now-a-days is legion, some are effective and some are not. The active poisoning agent is usually one of the following. Barium carbonate, phosphorus, arsenic, strychnine, squills and plaster of Paris. In using poison great caution must be observed so that only rats can have access to it. Domestic animals must be safeguarded and unused baits should be collected and destroyed, if placed where there is any chance of their being eaten by useful animals. Dead-rats should be burnt or buried. Frequent change of bait is essential, as rats are very cunning and if any of their number die from eating any particular kind of food, they quickly learn to avoid that food, unless it is artfully disguised. Also poison and bait must be handled as little as possible as the rats will easily smell anything which has been handled and become suspicious. A little aniseed or musk oil will prevent this contingency and simple dyes will serve to disguise baits.

(a) Barium carbonate.—This poison is tasteless and odourless, efficient and fairly safe. It can be used as a powder sprinkled on fish, bread and butter, etc., or mixed with rice in the proportion of 1 part of poison to 8 parts of rice, or made into dough with oat meal or rice flour, rolled out and cut into half inch cubes. In the dough form the proportion should be 4 parts of meal to 1 part of poison.

(b) White Arsenic.—This is commonly used by Malays in rice fields and kampongs and known as "warangan." A grasshopper or other insect is caught and killed and into a split in its back a pinch of powdered white arsenic is inserted and the bait is then placed in a conspicuous position, often amongst paddy husks. "Warangan" is also used mixed up with rice in the proportion of 1 part powdered poison to 12 parts of rice, or made into dough with flour in the same proportions, with a little sugar added and the mixture cut into half inch cubes.

(c) Arsenite of soda.—This is also effective and is best mixed with oat or maize meal in the proportion of 12 parts of meal to 1 part of poison and made into a thick dough by the addition of the white of egg or coconut oil and the mixture cut into small cubes. A good mixture is one kati of meal, one kati of brown sugar, and two teaspoons of arsenic well mixed up together and put in small heaps near the rat runs.

(d) Strychnine.—This is a very effective poison but too dangerous for general use, owing to its highly poisonous nature. Crystals may be inserted into grasshoppers, raw meat, or fish, or made up with powdered biscuit and sugar. A good preparation is half an ounce of strychnine dissolved in one pint of boiling water, to which is added one pint of molasses; the bait, paddy or maize, being afterwards soaked in the diluted syrup.

(e) Phosphorus (Yellow).—Many of the patent rat poisons contain this chemical, which is a good poison, but its use is too dangerous, owing to its inflammable nature.

44[JANUARY, 1923.

(f) Carbon bisulphide.—This liquid is deadly in its effects and is especially useful where rat holes are apparent, when a little cotton wool or kapok moistened with the liquid is placed in the burrow and all the rat holes are blocked up with thick mud. It should not be used near dwellings, on account of its highly poisonous fumes, and great care must be exercised to avoid bringing any flame near the liquid, which is highly inflammable.

(g) Sulphur dioxide, chlorine, carbon monoxide, and hydracyanic acid are useful gases for fumigating rats in confined spaces, sheds, houses, rat-holes, etc., but they are dangerous to use and are only efficient if all air inlets are thoroughly blocked. Ordinary white ant pumps are useful for injecting gases into rat runs.

(h) Local poisonous plants.—The chief poison plant used by Malays for destroying rats is a specie of Dianella which they call "sisiak." The root-stock of this plant is pulverized and boiled up with ten times its volume of rice and the bait is then placed about the rice fields in little heaps. There are also a few other plants but little is known yet as to their poisonous properties.

When poison has to be laid near poultry houses, the bait can be put into the node of a bamboo, wide enough to admit rats but not fowls or domestic animals and beyond the range of their beaks or paws respectively. Another method is to use two boxes, one considerably larger than the other and each having two or more holes in the sides just large enough to admit rats. The poisoned bait should be placed on the bottom and near the middle of the small box and the larger box should then be inverted over it.

(3) TRAPS.

(a) Guillotine traps.—Numerous patent traps are available, but many of them are ineffective, owing to the sagacity of the rats. The best kind is the "guillotine" type, but it must be used intelligently, frequently moved and differently baited. There are several forms of this type of trap but the simpler the form the better, and an all-metal one is preferable, as it is less likely to absorb and retain odours. Good baits in this country are pieces of dried fish, sections of maize cobs, raw meat, cheese rind, buttered toast, fresh vegetables, rice, oat meal, etc. The "schyler" trap was found very effective in Krian and Bagan Datoh.

(b) Cage traps.—Cage traps are useful, but expensive and troublesome, where rats are numerous. They should be baited and left open for several nights until the rats are accustomed to enter them for food. They should then be closed and freshly baited, when a large catch may be expected. It sometimes pays to conceal a cage trap by covering it with thrash or putting it into a wooden box having a hole at one end, against which the opening of the trap is fitted.

(c) Dead fall traps.—The simplest trap and that which has proved far the most effective in the rice fields is a "deadfall"—a heavy plank or sod of grass resting on a light bamboo frame, supported by a figure—4 trigger, which is well known to the Malays, and temptingly baited.

(d) Barrel trap.—This consists of an ordinary barrel with a sheet of stiff brown paper tied across the top. Rats are fed with baits placed on the brown paper top for several nights and then a cross is cut in the top so that the rats fall into the barrel. It is advisable to prop a few bits of wood

JANUARY, 1923.]45

against the barrel so that rats can easily reach the top. The barrel should contain about eight inches of water with a surface film of kerosene. There are numerous other traps, but the above are easily the best.

(e) A scheme which seems worthy of experiment, is to trap rats alive in cages and to kill only the females and liberate the males. This scheme should, if carried on with sufficient intensity, result in a large excess of males, which would so harass the females and each other that little effective pairing would take place and the mortality of the litters would greatly increase. This might be tried experimentally in the first place with caged rats.

HUNTING.

Organized rat clubs, which have done much good in England, America and Java, might be instituted in badly infested areas where there is a fair population. In America these hunts take the form of contests between two sides or villages, the beaten party having to entertain the winners. In England rat and sparrow clubs are numerous, prizes being given for catches during definite periods, in order to sustain interest and effect. Thus one club in Kent destroyed 28,000 sparrows and 16,000 rats, by the trivial expenditure of £18 in prizes. Such clubs would do much good in large paddy areas in this country, if energetically organized, for it is estimated roughly that local sparrows (burong pipit) take five per cent. of every rice crop, in addition to the amount destroyed by rats.

The following are approximate local prices for some of the various poisons mentioned in the text and for rat-proof wire netting and expanded metal.

Barium Carbonate ... 10 cts. per lb.
Arsenite of soda ... 10 " " "
Carbon bisulphide ... 30 " " "
(best purchased in drums of 4 fallons)
White arsenic ... .. 20 cts. per lb.
Sulphur ... .. 10 " " "

" " lathing 1'00 " " "
