CONCLUSION.

In these trying times, when food is scarce and expensive the rat problem is one of serious importance and ought to gain the attention of every agriculturist and every business man in the country : if any organized destruction is to be carried out, it must be done thoroughly over as wide an area as possible, must be repeated periodically, and the methods varied or combined to get the best results.

SUMMARY OF RECOMMENDATIONS.

  1. (1) Protection of the natural enemies of rats.
  2. (2) Increased cleanliness about markets, stores, houses, etc.
  3. (3) Construction of rat-proof stores, houses, drains, granaries, etc.
  4. (4) Removal of garbage, of straw, husks, etc., from paddy fields.
  5. (5) Systematic destruction of rats by poisoning and trapping.
  6. (6) Organization of rat clubs for continuous and systematic warfare against rats,—AGRIC. BULL., F.M.S., Vol. IX, No. 4.
46[JANUARY, 1923.

POULTRY.

BABY CHICKS: HOW TO GROW THEM
THE NATURAL WAY.

T. F. MCGREW,

(In the Western Poultry Journal)

Comparatively few people realise the tremendous waste that annually takes place in hatching and growing chicks. As ordinarily conducted there is not more than one chicken for every four eggs incubated. This has been stated in the following form : from each dozen of eggs set there will be hatched on an average not more than six chicks and from each of such lots of chicks not more than three will be reared. Such waste is due to a number of causes, among which are bad management of the sitting hen, improper nesting places, allowing filth to accumulate and vermin to multiply and above all the use of infertile or weakly fertilised eggs. Such waste is unnecessary.

The chief cause of poor hatches is found in the infertility of the eggs incubated. During the natural breeding season, when all living creatures mate and strive to perpetuate their species, the eggs of hens will be at their highest fertility. When frosts come and cold days are the rule, the fertility of eggs begins to decline. This declination reaches its lowest point in the middle of the winter ; then, as the days begin to lengthen and the hours of sunshine to increase the fertility begins to increase and when spring arrives, the grass begins to grow and the trees to bud and leaf out, the highest point is again reached for spring is the natural breeding season.

During the cold weather the physical organisation has to look after itself, to preserve its life, and has less vitality left for the increase of the race. Of course something can be done to combat these unfavourable conditions, the fowls can be to some extent protected from the excessive cold by proper housing, exercise can be compelled by feeding the grain in deep litter, and the decline in fertility can be partially arrested. But nothing can make the winter the natural breeding season.

The remedies for other causes of waste will sufficiently appear in the following pages.

The natural way to hatch eggs and rear chicks is to permit it to be done by the broody hen. All hens do not become broody. While there are no breeds or varieties of fowls which are absolutely without the incubating instinct, there are many specimens among the Hamburgs, Leghorns, Spanish and the like which do not become broody. But among breeds like those in the Asiatic, American and other classes the greater part of the hens will at some time or other evince a desire to sit. This desire is evidenced by the hen remaining on the nest, by bristling up her feathers when approached and by uttering a clucking note when at all disturbed. The signs are so plain that a beginner need not err therein.

JANUARY, 1923.]47

Every hen which wishes to sit should not be permitted to do so. Not every hen is fitted to hatch and hover a brood. To get the right kind of a hen for this purpose is to make the right start in the work. The first requisite in a sitter is that she should be calm, peaceful, of gentle disposition. The quiet, gentle hen is less likely to break the eggs which she attempts to incubate and less likely to injure the chicks when they are breaking their way out of the imprisoning shell. If she is two years old or older, she will be more likely to have this characteristic than if she is a pullet. She should be neither too small nor too large.

Very small hens are not desirable because they can cover too few eggs; very large hens, unless the eggs have especially strong shells are more likely to break the eggs. A hen of medium size is to be preferred, because she can cover a fair-sized clutch of eggs and because her weight is not a constant menace to the eggs. A hen with an abundant, rather long, and very soft plumage will cover her eggs to the best advantage, preventing them from becoming chilled and thus avoiding a common danger to successful incubation.

Hens with extra long legs, like the modern Exhibition Game, are less desirable than those with medium to short legs, because the long-legged birds are more liable to become cramped during the time of sitting, and therefore, more apt to become restless. And, finally, the sitter should be persistently broody—have the broody fever thoroughly developed. Some hens will show an inclination to sit, but will not stick faithfully to the nest, and will break up easily. Such are not desirable.

The Plymouth Rock, Wyandotte, Rhode Island Red and Orpington hens of all varieties, especially those of medium size for the breed, make excellent sitters. The incubating instinct, where special pains have not been taken to breed it out, is well developed, and they are naturally of a mild and peaceful disposition, two prominent characteristics of a good broody hen. A cross of the Silky and the Wyandotte is said to make an ideal sitter, and if one rears a few for his own use, he can easily keep up the strain by using a Silky male, one year upon the cross breeds and a Wyandotte male the next year, so alternating from year to year. The cross gives a desirable size, with a soft, fluffy abundant plumage, together with a gentle disposition and a persistent broodiness. The Cochin bantam, except for size, is an admirable fowl for this purpose, and crosses of the large Cochin on small fowls are also excellent.

When one has found one or more broody hens he should not be in too great haste to remove them to the eggs, but should allow them to remain on the nests for forty-eight to seventy-two hours to make sure that they have fully determined to rear a brood.

Having made sure that one has a really broody hen, the next consideration is the preparation of the nest in which to place the eggs for hatching and first it should be settled where the nest is to be placed. Where it is possible the nest for the sitter should be placed where the laying hens cannot disturb her. It is possible, of course, to hatch a clutch of eggs in the pen where the hens are laying even in the nest where the hens lay, by heavily marking the eggs undergoing incubation so that they can be quickly and easily distinguished from all others, but this is never desirable and should be avoided if possible.

48[JANUARY, 1923.

There are many ways in which the desired seclusion can be had, by having a pen reserved for sitters, by having nests placed in separate coops, by having covered and closed nest boxes and removing the sitter from them daily and the like. But, however it is done, the seclusion should be secured if best results are expected.

The nest should be ample in size, in length, depth and width. Depth is especially important in the early spring, when nights are chilly and sometimes very cold. A deep nest once warmed through will hold some of the heat imparted to it, and prevent the eggs from becoming chilled from underneath.

One reason why hens, which sit upon the ground, usually bring off full broods, is that the earth, warmed by the hen's body, holds the heat and prevents great and sudden changes in the temperature about the eggs. If sods or earth are placed in the bottom of the nest box some of the advantages of sitting upon the ground are secured. This is a case, not of "just as good," but of as good as circumstances will permit.

The essentials of a good nest for a sitter are that it shall be roomy with sufficient depth of material to secure the eggs from becoming chilled, secluded from the approach of other hens or creatures that would annoy the sitter, and properly made and shaped. For hens of an average size a nest box that is fourteen inches square and ten inches deep will answer admirably. The crates in which oranges are usually shipped will make nests for two hens or if one prefers, the middle partition may be knocked out and the crate used for a single sitter.

If late enough in the spring and the frost out of the ground and the earth dry, one can provide hatching places quite cheaply by laying down barrels on thin sides, first scooping out enough earth to keep them from rolling and filling the thin bottom of the barrel—the side next to the ground with earth. Holes should be bored through the side of the barrel next to the ground, so as to provide drainage in case water should get into barrel.

Upon the earth placed inside the barrel the nest may be built. A burlap to hang on the open end secures darkness and tends to keep out disturbers. Where several barrels are placed near together, the separate hens may be tethered each morning to a peg driven in the ground and released and placed back in the barrel after they have eaten and relieved themselves.

The nest is best made by placing in the bottom earth or an inverted sod over which is placed soft hay or other materials. Chaff is excellent, fine straw well softened is good. The earth at the bottom of the nest should be slightly hollowed out—just enough to properly hold the eggs in place, but not enough to cause them to roll together at the centre. This shape should be retained as the nest is carefully built up with other materials.

If one can procure them, tobacco stems are excellent to be placed in the nest next to the earth. Sulphur in its powdered state, may be sifted through the top materials of the nest. Insect powder should be placed in the nest. These are all precautions against vermin, than which nothing will make a sitting hen more restless and uneasy. Take time to do the work properly. Make the nesting material as firm as the nature of the material will permit. Time and care spent in preparing a good nest will be fully repaid in the results obtained.

JANUARY, 1923.]49

When the nest has been prepared, as a final and necessary finishing touch, place in it one or more china eggs. If one has enough nest eggs the best plan is to place a sufficient number of them in the nest to properly fill it out to the size desired for the clutch of eggs to be incubated.

When the nest has been finished, the next step is to remove the broody hen to the awaiting eggs—china at first, to be replaced with the real article as soon as it is certain that the hen will remain on the job. Before removal the hen should be thoroughly dusted with some good insect powder to free her from any vermin. The removal should take place after dark.

Don't carry the hen by the legs with her head hanging down and her wings wildly fluttering, but gently place her under your arm with the legs firmly grasped by the hand, so that no fluttering will follow. The quieter the removal, the stronger the prospect that the operation will be a success.

When the hen settles down quietly upon the china eggs with a contented note, and remains so settled for a day, the time has arrived to remove the nest eggs and substitute the hatching eggs.—SOUTH AFRICAN POULTRY MAG. AND SMALL-HOLDER, VOL. XIV, No. 128.

CORRESPONDENCE.

SOME NOTES ON RUBBER ESTATES OF
THE FUTURE.

THE EDITOR,

"TROPICAL AGRICULTURIST."

DEAR SIR,

MR. VICTOR RIS'S "Some notes on Rubber Estates of the Future" is quite interesting as far as it goes, but he has not given us his views on the very important question as to what he considers to be a suitable number of mature trees that an acre should support if it is planted up with a specially selected plants raised as indicated by him. From observation extending over many years, I have found that virgin forest grows 70 to 80 well-developed trees to the acre. Considering that these trees have a continual struggle for existence by reason of the fact that a fairly large percentage of the available plant food in the soil is absorbed by the undergrowth, it would seem that in the case of an ordered and well-regulated plantation where every tree is afforded exclusive facilities for absorbing food and thus developing to its fullest possible extent, sufficient room for this purpose should be considered of paramount importance. If the original planting is done on the triangular system, providing 25 feet from point to point, this would work out to about 75 trees to the acre. Allowing for loss of trees from various causes, after the time for supplies has passed, such a plantation might reasonably be expected to average about 70 trees to the acre at maturity, and a harvest of 1,000 lb. of rubber from 70 trees, or about 14 lb. per tree per annum, does by no means seem to be an over-optimistic output from specially selected trees, making allowances for all other factors.

When I suggest 70 trees to the acre, I would add that I certainly do not consider this to be ideal planting. Taking the "crown spread" of the rubber tree into consideration, a far wider spacing would seem to be indicated, but one has, of course, to take commercial necessity into account.

YOURS FAITHFULLY

"3103."

50[JANUARY, 1923.

APICULTURE.

THE CAUSE OF SWARMING.

GEO. S. DEMUTH.

Ever since bee-keepers quit looking upon swarming as desirable in adding to the number of colonies for the brimstone pit in the fall, they have been struggling with the problem of swarm control, which in some localities is still one of the most difficult problems in honey production. Instead of the old-time thrill of pleasure at the announcement that the bees are swarming, the progressive bee-keeper of today hears such an announcement with disgust. It is interesting to note that some of the terms he uses in connection with swarming indicate that he looks upon swarming as an abnormal thing. He speaks of the "swarming fever" and talks about treatment for swarming colonies as though swarming were a disease.

In the fight against swarming, naturally one of the first questions is that of its cause. The back volumes of bee journals are replete with suggested causes of swarming. Thousands of pages have been filled with plans for the prevention of swarming, each plan based largely upon some theory as to the cause of swarming.

SWARMING INSTINCT SOMETIMES DORMANT THROUGH SEASON.

Since swarming is the natural method of reproduction of colonies, upon which the existence of the species depend in nature, bee-keepers are willing to accept this deeply seated reproductive instinct as the fundamental cause of swarming, but they want to know just what it is that calls forth this instinct at certain times and why it is apparently dormant at other times. They know that some colonies go through the season piling up a large surplus of honey, apparently without a thought of swarming; while other colonies in the same apiary waste their energy in swarming; that some season practically all colonies go through the season without attempting to swarm, while in other seasons a majority of the colonies try to swarm; and that in some localities, as in some parts of the tropics, well-managed colonies seldom swarm, while in other localities, especially in the far north, swarming is troublesome nearly every year. No wonder that bee-keepers have been searching for the thing that throws the switch which leads some colonies headlong into swarming while others continue on the main track of gathering and storing.

MANY THINGS HAVE BEEN PUT FORTH AS CAUSE.

In the search for the thing that throws the switch, some have looked upon swarming as a taint in the blood that might be bred out, and at one time American bee-keepers made serious efforts to eliminate swarming by breeding. Some even claimed to have actually accomplished this, but to-day no one really hopes that a swarm-proof strain of bees will ever be

JANUARY, 1923.]51

developed. Swarming has, of course, been reduced by the elimination of stock that shows a great tendency to swarm when there is but little if any excuse for it.

Lack of sufficient room is generally recognized as contributing to the tendency to swarm. As a rule, colonies in large hives swarm less than colonies in small hives. Formerly much was said about colonies of bees established in attics never swarming, because such colonies had the whole attic for a hive. But swarms do issue from colonies housed in attics and other large cavities, and have been known to issue from colonies established under the eaves of buildings, having the whole out-of-doors for a hive. Swarms sometimes issue from the largest of hives, even when tiered up five or six stories high. I have seen swarms issue from two-story hives having 20 combs in which only four or five frames contained brood, the rest of the combs being practically empty and not occupied by the little colony. While large hives and an abundance of room in the form of good empty comb greatly reduce swarming, they do not prevent it in all localities every season.

It has been said that bees swarm because of the honey flow, which makes them feel sufficiently prosperous to divide the colony and build a new home. In the North swarming does usually come during the early honey flow; but in some localities, especially in the South, swarming occurs before the main honey flow, swarms sometimes issuing when the colonies are gathering scarcely enough for a living. In some places swarming ceases entirely on the arrival of the honey flow. While the honey flow often influences swarming, it cannot be considered the cause of swarming.

Some thought that the presence of drones causes swarming. Working on this theory ASPINWALL, many years ago, constructed wooden combs by drilling holes into the ends of blocks of wood to form the cells in order to have all cells of worker size to prevent the rearing of drones. After years of research along this line he abandoned this theory of the cause of swarming and took up another theory to be mentioned later, which finally resulted in the invention of a non-swarming hive. In this hive instead of eliminating the drones he provided wide spaces between the combs, inserting in these spaces slatted dividers to prevent comb-building in the wide spaces.

Old queens have been put forth as the cause of swarming. Some said that the old queen becomes broody in her second year. Others said that a queen, after laying so many eggs in the spurt of spring brood-rearing, becomes tired and seeks a rest by swarming.

At one time it was believed by many that a queen does not swarm during the first season of her life, and several bee-keepers in the North tried to prevent swarming by requeening their colonies in the spring with young queens from the South—only to find that many colonies so treated swarmed, though, of course, they no doubt had less swarming because of the young queens.

Much of the trouble from swarming in colonies having old queens, is no doubt from supersedure during the swarming season when colonies often

52[JANUARY, 1923.

apparently depart from the original plan of supersedure and swarm because queen-cells are present. In many respects such swarming is quite different from normal swarming.

INFLUENCE OF AGE OF QUEEN UPON SWARMING.

GRAVENHORST laid down the rule that a colony having a laying queen reared this season will not swarm this season, provided the queen was reared in this colony. If she was reared elsewhere, the colony may swarm this season. But we know that if the old queen is removed at swarming time and all queen-cells (if any) are destroyed, then all queen-cells again destroyed ten days later, a young laying queen from another colony may be given a few days later with the same safety from further swarming as if the young queen had been reared in this colony. The important thing to note here is that when a young queen is reared in this colony this year, there is (except in some cases of supersedure) an interval of at least 16 days during which no eggs are laid. When a similar break in brood-rearing is brought about by removing the queen, it does not make any difference whether the young queen is reared in this colony or elsewhere, so far as swarming is concerned. Even when the old queen is given back to the colony after 16 days, there is usually no further swarming. Apparently the condition of the colony brought about by the period of queenlessness has more to do with the prevention of swarming than the age of the queen.

HOW YOUNG BEES CONTRIBUTE TO SWARMING.

GERSTUNG, a German investigator, put forth the theory that swarming is brought on by a preponderance of young bees. This fits in well with the well-known fact that the swarming tendency is strongest early in the season when young bees are emerging in greatest numbers. This theory would also explain why colonies are willing to give up swarming when their brood is taken away as in artificial swarming, as well as why the swarming impulse disappears completely about 20 days after removing the queen when the dequeening plan is used to prevent swarming. Using this theory as a basis, comb-honey producers about 20 years ago worked out plans by which the brood and youngest bees were taken from the colony at swarming time, kept in a separate hive until old enough to do field work and then returned to the main colony. Producers of extracted honey, instead of putting the brood and young bees into a separate hive, placed the chamber containing the brood above the queen-excluder, the queen being confined below, thus separating the young and emerging bees from the Colony below. In 1908 COVEYON advised placing the chamber of emerging bees above the supers to separate them still further from the colony (See Gleanings, 1908, pages 640-641). This was further emphasized by A. C. ALLEN in 1910 (A. B. J., 1910, page 94) and by CHALON FOWLS in 1915 (Gleanings, 1915, page 574).

The Aspinwall non-swarming hive was based upon the young-bee theory as the cause of swarming. It provided extra room for these young bees between the combs.

GERSTUNG, however, carried his theory so far as to attempt to explain swarming as caused by an excess of nurse bees in proportion to the number of larvæ to be fed, the unused larval food causing a physiological condition in the nurse bees bringing on the swarming impulse. He evidently quite forgot that when an artificial swarm is made by shaking there are no larvas to feed during the first three days; yet the bees are willing to give up swarming if properly handled, even though these same nurse bees are shaken with the older bees and there should be a much greater excess of larval food than before shaking.—GLEANINGS IN BEE CULTURE, VOL. L., No. 6.

(To be continued.)

JANUARY, 1923.]53

GENERAL.

DRIED BANANAS.

C. HAROLD WRIGHT, M.A., F.I.C.,

Government Chemist.

In a former article* on dried bananas in the Agricultural Circular, Vol. 2, No. 3, the yield of banana flour was given on as varying from 5.05 to 7.58 lb. per bunch, but I now find that I under-estimated the yield. The above figures were arrived at by supposing that the number of bananas in a bunch varies from 100 to 150, and that the average weight of a single banana is 132.4 grams=4.67 oz. av. The latter figure was obtained by using China bananas; but I have since found that the weight of a single green Gros Michel banana varied on one bunch from 5.7 to 8.3 oz., and that the average weight of 19 of these bananas was 7.05 ozs. The weight of banana chips obtained from 54 of these bananas (mostly from the upper hands) was 4.2 lb.

A far better way to find out the yield of banana flour per bunch is to calculate it from the weight of a bunch of bananas, which varies from 20 to 100 lb., with an average of 50 lb. I found that the banana chips are 17.3 per cent. by weight of the whole green banana. The whole bunch consists of bananas and stalk, but since this is only a rough calculation the weight of the latter can be neglected. Hence the yield of banana flour per bunch will vary from 20 \times .173 = 3.46 lb. to 100 \times .173 = 17.3 lb. with an average of 50 \times .173 = 8.65 lb.

COMPOSITION.

Banana flour prepared as described in the previous article by grinding banana chips in a coffee grinder was analysed in the laboratory, and the analyses are given in the following table, which includes other analyses of banana flour for comparison:—

Banana Flour.

No' 1 2 3 4 5
Water ... 14.21 14.48 10.88 13.0 11.10
Protein ... 2.69 3.00 0.71 4.0 3.55
Fat ... 0.29 — 0.22 0.5 0.83
Carbohydrate ... 79.04 — 84.83 80.0 81.70
Fibre ... 0.85 — 0.72 — 1.50
Ash .. 2.92 — 2.64 2.5 2.23
100.00 — 100.00 100.00 —
Nitrogen ... 0.43 0.48 0.114 — —

In the above table Nos. 1 and 2 are the analyses of banana flour prepared at the Chemical Laboratory during the months of July and October

* Vide T. A. VOL LIX., No. 3, Sept. 1922.

54[JANUARY, 1923.

respectively. No. 3 is an analysis of banana flour by H. M. COUSINS Director of Agriculture, Jamaica (W. FAWCETT. The Banana, p. 110); and Nos. 4 and 5 are analyses of banana flour quoted by FAWCETT, pp. 110 and 116, on the authorities of DR. R. HUTCHINSON and DR. W. TIBBLES, respectively. It will be seen that my analysis (No. 1) agrees very closely with MR. COUSINS' (No. 3) with the exception of the protein. MR. COUSINS found 0.114 per cent. of nitrogen, corresponding to 0.71 per cent of protein. In the sample of banana flour prepared in July, I found 0.43 per cent. of nitrogen (as a mean of 3 determinations, the actual values being 0.43, 0.42, and 0.44), corresponding to 2.69 per cent. of protein; and in the sample of banana flour prepared in October 0.48 per cent. of nitrogen, corresponding to 3.00 per cent. of protein. The percentages of protein I have found in these two samples are very similar to the quantities in the analyses given by DRS. HUTCHINSON and TIBBLES

Analyses No. 1 in the above table gives the composition of the banana chips prepared by drying the pulp of the green banana. I found that the latter contains 68.8 per cent. of water, hence its composition can be calculated from the above analysis. No. 6 below is the composition of the pulp of the unripe green banana found in this way and No. 7 is an analysis by LEUSCHER given for comparison:—

Pulp of Green Banana.

It will be seen that I have found far less protein than LEUSCHER and of course more carbohydrate, since the latter is found by difference. LEUSCHER found 5.0 per cent. of protein in the ripe banana, but the writer of the article on Banana in Thorpe's Dictionary of applied Chemistry from which the above analysis by LEUSCHER is quoted states that "American analyses show much less protein in ripe bananas than is given in LEUSCHER's figures, the average being 1.3 per cent." Thus LEUSCHER found 5.0 instead of 1.3 per cent. in the ripe banana; and if we suppose that the same error was made in the analysis of the unripe banana, then the correct percentage of protein in the latter is 1.3 \times 3.9 = 1.0, which agrees with my figures.

BANANA BREAD.

Banana flour contains far less protein than wheat flour which contains on the average from 10 to 15 per cent. of this constituent. It also differs from wheat flour in not containing any gluten. It is owing to this constituent (really several proteins) that wheat can be used in making bread. Owing to the absence of gluten banana flour cannot be used alone in making bread; and if it is mixed with wheat flour it behaves like a weak flour.

JANUARY, 1923.]55

Through the kindness of MR. N. B. CREASY, the Superintendent, Suva Gaol, who took great interest in the subject, banana bread was made at the Gaol from mixtures of wheat flour and banana flour. When mixed in equal quantities the loaves were small and flat, like those made from a weak flour. They had a crisp brown crust, but the interior was dark coloured, damp, and close textured. This bread had a distinct banana taste, and though its appearance was not attractive, it was appreciated by everyone to whom it was given. Bread was also made from a mixture of one-quarter banana flour and three-quarters wheat flour. These loaves were of far better shape; the interior was light and spongy, and was very similar to brown bread in appearance. Loaves of this kind of bread were sent to a meeting of the Council of Planters of Fiji on 2nd November. Portions of this bread were given to great many people, and I think that all who tasted it liked it.

PREPARATION OF BANANA FIGS.

Banana figs are prepared by peeling ripe bananas, cutting the pulp lengthwise and drying them in the sun or in a dryer. It is well known that an ordinary steel knife discolours many fruits, hence in my experiments a rustless steel knife was used both in peeling the fruit and cutting the pulp; and for the same reason all contact with metal was avoided during the drying. The pulp of each banana was cut into three or four slices to shorten the time of drying, but in Jamaica the bananas are generally cut into two slices. If the bananas are fully ripe and the slices are dried quickly in the sun they are yellow-brown in colour, if the bananas are not quite ripe they are whiter; and if the bananas are over ripe or the bananas are not dried quickly they are darker in colour, and in some cases become almost black. Hence to make banana figs of an attractive appearance only fully ripe bananas should be used, and they should be dried as quickly as possible.

The drying presents some little difficulty, as the slices on drying soon become very sticky. Attempts were made to dry the slices on brown paper, but the results were not at all satisfactory: enamelled iron plates and a sheet of glass were then tried, but under these conditions the slices dried on one surface only, and although they were frequently turned took a long time to dry. The most satisfactory method so far tried is to dry the slices on butter muslin. In my experiments the butter muslin was fastened with tacks to a framework made from a benzine or kerosene case, which can be seen at Chemical Laboratory by anyone interested in the subject. This arrangement has been found most satisfactory. When exposed to the sun and wind the bananas dry above and below at the same time and hence require very little attention; the framework can be very easily made and the muslin can be easily removed and washed. I can strongly recommend this method to anyone who wishes to prepare figs on a small scale for home consumption. Of course on a large scale a drier would be absolutely necessary, so as to be independent of the weather. Another advantage of a drier is that during the drying the slices would not be contaminated by flies and other insects settling on them. Owing to their sticky nature figs cannot be wrapped in ordinary paper; butter paper or biscuit paper can be used, but on a larger scale they should be packed in wooden boxes like Turkish figs.

YIELD OF FIGS.

The proportion of skin in a ripe banana, and the yield of figs were determined by weighing a whole ripe banana on an enamelled iron plate which had been previously weighed. The banana was then peeled and the peeled banana weighed on the same plate. The pulp was then cut into slices and dried in the sun on the same plate until the weight of the plate and figs no longer lost weight. As an average of six experiments, which agree very closely amongst themselves, I found that the skin of the ripe banana amounts to 29.4 per cent. by weight of the whole fruit, or in other

56[JANUARY, 1923,

words that the pulp is 70.6 per cent. by weight of the whole fruit. The figs are 31.0 per cent. by weight of the peeled banana and 21.8 per cent. by weight of the whole banana. From the above data the yield of figs per bunch can be calculated. A bunch of bananas weighs from 20 to 100 lb. with an average of 50 lb. Neglecting the weight of the stalk, which is very small compared with the weight of the bunch, the yield of figs per bunch would vary from 20 \times .218 = 4.36 lb. to 100 \times .218 = 21.8 lb. with an average of 50 \times .218 = 10.9 lb.

PROSPECTS IN FIJI.

I think everyone will agree that there is a great wastage of banana in Fiji. The number of bunches which ripen between shipments or are too ripe for a particular shipment must be considerable. Then too, large quantities of bananas on the upper Waidina and Wainimala are wasted because in certain states of the river they cannot be brought to Suva for shipment. And lastly there are the small bunches too small for shipment and the small fruit too small for packing in cases. With a little enterprise all this fruit which has so far been entirely wasted could be dried for export. According to W. FAWCETT., The Banana, p. 254, the number of factories for the manufacture of banana figs in operation in Jamaica in November, 1922, was 11, and the output of these varied from \frac{1}{2} ton per week to 3\frac{1}{2} tons per week.

In order to show what use could be made of rejects which so far have been considered as fit only for pig-food, I brought a case of bananas which were rejected from the "Tofua's" shipment of the beginning of November, and from them prepared figs. The bananas were of very poor quality, and there was no wonder that they were rejected; but the figs prepared from them are very similar in appearance and flavour to figs prepared from some very fine Gros Michel bananas. Both kinds of figs were handed round at a meeting of the Council of Planters held at Nausori, on 17th November, and many members preferred the former to the latter. This shows what use could be made of all the bananas too small for export, which so far have been absolutely wasted.—AGRIC. CIR., FIJI, Vol. 2, No. 5.

HUBAM CLOVER.

(MELILOTUS ALBA, VAR. ANNUA.)

H. A. MELLE, B.A. (Agr.), N.D.A.,

Officer in Charge, Botanical Experiment Stations, Pretoria.

The necessity of winter feed for live stock is now recognized by most South African farmers, yet it is surprising to find how few attempt improving their native pasturage by judicious grazing and laying down permanent pastures. In other countries it is considered a fundamental part of good farming to make provision for an adequate supply of food for stock during winter months. South Africa is essentially a pastoral country, the greatest portion of it being devoted to animal husbandry, and, as a general rule, all live stock are dependent for their sustenance on the natural veld herbage. The veld during winter, in most parts of the Union, cannot keep stock in a thriving condition, and every breeder knows that stock should be kept in that condition to obtain the best results.

The Botanical Division has been investigating these problems of suitable pasture grasses for the last twelve years, and has now pure cultures under cultivation of most of the best native grasses and also exotics from different parts of the globe. Great difficulty has been experienced in finding a legume which would not only be able to adapt itself to our adverse conditions, but

JANUARY, 1923.]57

would also grow with grass and not become choked. Some clovers, especially English Wild White, have been found to grow very well in conjunction with Kikuyu grass. But, owing to the exorbitant price of the seed and the moisture requirements of this clover, it can only be grown under favourable conditions and under irrigation. At last it seems that we have a plant that will answer our requirements, and that plant is Hubam clover.

DESCRIPTION.

Hubam clover (Melilotus alba, var. annua) is a variety of sweet clover (stink klawer). It makes about the same growth in one season that the ordinary sweet clovers do in two. Most of the common clovers are biennial, or two-year clovers; if seed is sown in spring the clover makes a small growth the first season, remains dormant during the winter, completes its growth, matures seed, and dies the next summer. In contrast to this, Hubam clover continues its growth until it reaches a height of from 3-8 feet within 3-7 months from the time the seed is planted, matures its seed, and dies, all within the one season.

The following description of Hubam clover is taken from an article by MR. W. S. HALL on the subject, which appeared in this JOURNAL November, 1921 (page 463):—

“It is an herbaceous plant, with trifoliate leaves; the flowers are disposed in long-stalked, loose racemes growing from the bases of the leaves, and are white in colour; the seed-pods are marked with irregularly netted veins, and each contains one seed. In the early stages growth is slow, but subsequently firm stems are formed and a height of from 4-8 ft. attained. It flowers irregularly over a period of at least two months.....; in the later stages the lower stems are somewhat woody. The plant has a pleasant odour, resembling Tonquin beans. It has a well-developed root-system, which penetrates deeply into the soil, loosening it, and providing favourable conditions for succeeding crops. After seeding, the plant dies.

“It resembles the biennial form of melilotus in appearance; the annual has a smaller, more woody root, and crown or resting buds are not formed. The stems, branches, flowers, pods, and seed are indistinguishable from the biennial form, but during the season of seeding the annual grows more rapidly, blossoms, fruits, and dies.

“In the case of the biennial, the slender stem of the first season’s growth dies and is represented by a stub of dead tissue.

“Around the stub, and coming from the crown two or more strong branches form in the second year (the growth from the resting buds); such branches never occur in the annual form. The seed of the annual cannot be distinguished from that of the biennial form.”

ORIGIN.

A few plants were found by PROFESSOR HUGHES in greenhouses at the Iowa Experiment Station in the winter of 1915-16 among biennial white clover plants being tested from various parts of the United States. Its probable point of origin was determined to be a limestone ridge in Alabama. There PROFESSOR HUGHES found it growing wild, crowding out weeds, and over a considerable acreage being cultivated and cut for hay.

USES.

Although Hubam clover can be used for several purposes, its best use is that of a pasture renovator and soil builder owing to its vigorous growth it is an ideal plant for green manuring. It is reported that a seedling of Hubam made in New York put on a growth of 9 ft. in 3 months and 16 days. At the Groenkloof Botanical Station within 3½ months it grew to 7 ft.—7 ft. 6 in. Here, too, it has proved to grow very well with established Kikuyu grass. It not only renovates the Kikuyu, but supports the slender stems of the Kikuyu. In some places the Kikuyu attained a height of over 3 ft. when growing with Hubam.

58[JANUARY, 1923.

It commences growth much earlier than Kikuyu. At the time of writing—first week in August—Hubam from self-sown seed is showing about 3 inches above the Kikuyu. It is apparently an excellent pasture-renovator. Kikuyu, after the third year it is established, becomes sod-bound, but when grown with Hubam it does not “go off” as when grown by itself. Hubam, through the agency of its deep-growing root-system, prevents the Kikuyu becoming sod-bound, and, being a legume, keeps the grass well supplied with nitrogen. The Rural New Yorker states: “Inside of 100 days annual white sweet clover will bring to the soil and distribute as much nitrogen as a farmer can hope to get from fifteen loads of manure to the acre. . . . We have never seen any legume grow as fast as this does.”

It cannot be recommended as a hay-plant; it has coarse woody stems and the leaves drop off before the rest of the plant is fit to be stocked.

As a pasture it can be strongly recommended, as it commences to grow early in the season and remains green, and, if sown late, throughout the winter. When once stock acquire the taste for it they eat it readily. The chief objection to it as a pasture plant is that it becomes very coarse unless grazed down, but, if grown under irrigation, it affords a good bite for stock from about August and is eaten greedily.

In America, Hubam is regarded as one of the best bee plants ever grown.* Progressive bee-keepers consider Hubam clover the greatest of all honey-producing plants. This is because of its richness in nectar and its long blooming period that, in most regions, comes when the main honey flow is past. A beekeeper who has his apiary located on Hubam clover fields reports that “my stronger colonies are each producing one super of finest honey per week.”

DROUGHT AND FROST RESISTANCE.

As yet we have not tested the drought-resistant qualities of Hubam. In America it is considered remarkably drought resistant.† “In one instance without irrigation and with less than one inch of rainfall after the clover was seeded, it grew to a height of 7 feet, and showed no ill effect of the drought when other vegetation perished in the worst drought experienced since 1882.”

At Groenkloof, this season, Hubam has shown itself to be more frost-resistant than barley. A plot was sown in April last. In June it attained a height of 3 ft. 6 in. and commenced flowering. It was still green in August, and only a few stems have become affected by frost. It has continued to flower since June.

A plot was seeded in May and another in June. In both these plots the seeds germinated and grew about an inch, and then stopped growing. In August they again showed signs of growth.

PREPARATION OF THE SEED-BED AND SEEDING.

The seed-bed should be prepared in a manner similar to the seed-bed for any other standard farm crop. It should be planted on a firm seed-bed with a surface mulch of loose soil.

* Hubam Clover: The A. I. Root Comp.

† Hubam Clover: The A. I. Root Comp.

JANUARY, 1923.59

The seed-bed should not be planted deep—just covered with soil is best; in fact very similar to sowing lucerne. If required for seed the best time to sow is in the spring with the first summer rains. But if intended for winter grazing, sow late in February or early March.

SOIL REQUIREMENTS.

Hubam clover is said to thrive wherever other clovers grow, and may be made to grow well on soils not naturally adapted to it by the application of lime and proper inoculation. Being a legume, it is naturally a lime-loving plant, and will not grow on a sour soil, but grows best on a soil having a good supply of limestone. The bacteria found on the roots of a leguminous plant will not develop and thrive in a sour soil. To get the best results the soil should either be previously inoculated, i.e., on soils where "stink klawer" (melilotus officinalis) grows naturally, or the soil can be artificially inoculated. A satisfactory way of introducing the necessary bacteria is to use the soil obtained from around the roots of sweet clover plants (stink klawer) that are known to be inoculated. To ascertain whether a crop of sweet clover is inoculated, dig up the plants and carefully wash off the ground adhering to the roots. If the plant is inoculated, wart-like excrescences will be found attached to the roots of the plant. This soil should be pulverized, thoroughly dried carefully by exposure to the air, and sifted. It may then be sprinkled over the sweet clover seed which has first been slightly moistened with glue-water (1 tea-spoonful of pulverized glue to a pint of water); 1 pint of this mixture will treat from 1-2 bushels of sweet clover seed. If not seeded at once, spread it in a thin layer to dry. The bacteria are said to live only about a week on the seed after inoculation, and, if in the sunshine, only a few hours, hence the necessity of sowing soon after treating the seed.

QUANTITY OF SEED PER ACRE.

In America, Hubam clover is grown either in cultivated rows or broadcast with or without a nurse crop, or with any of the small grains as is the custom of seedling the common clovers. In cultivated rows, 3 feet apart, 3-4 lb. per acre are generally sown to ensure a good stand and, at the same time, allow loose cultivating. If sown broadcast, 10-15 lb. of seed per acre are sufficient; for green manuring a thicker sowing is advisable, about 20 lb. per acre.

TIME TO CUT.

If it is desired to be cut for hay, and only one crop is to be harvested, it may be left until it reaches its maximum growth. When two or more crops are to be harvested, the first crop should be cut when the plants have made an average growth of 30 inches. The crop should be cut for hay before the plants bloom and the leaves begin to shatter.

The crop is more difficult to cure than lucerne, and the leaves are likely to shatter before the stems are cured. For this reason it is very unlikely that Hubam clover will be exclusively used as a hay crop.

60JANUARY, 1923.

If it is desired to raise seed, Hubam should be harvested when the seed-pods are turning brown. Anything from 5-10 bushels of seed can be expected from an acre.

SUMMARY.

Hubam clover can be regarded as a rival to cowpeas, as it very largely fulfils the same function as the latter crop.

1. Owing to its upright growth it would be very much easier to cultivate and reap than cowpeas.

2. It puts on far more foliage in a season's growth than cowpeas and for this reason may be more valuable as a green manure.

3. In places like Natal, where cowpeas are badly attacked by rust, Hubam clover may wholly replace it as it is only drought-resistant, but thrives in plenty of moisture.

4. According to reports it is one of the most drought-resisting plants under cultivation, and at this station it has proved itself to be more frost-resistant than lucerne and the common clovers.

5. As a bee-plant it is unequalled. By sowing at different times of the year at the Botanical Station, Pretoria, we have had Hubam flowering throughout the year.—JOURN. OF DEPT. OF AGRIC., UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA, Vol. V, No. 4.

EXPERIMENTS WITH HUBAM CLOVER
IN CEYLON.

The Secretary, Ceylon Bee-keepers' Association, secured some seed of Hubam clover, a few months ago, and distributed them to members for trials in different parts of the Island. MR. R. NEVILE ROLFE, who tried the seed in the Kelani Valley, has sent us the following report:—

"In September, 1922, a sample packet of this seed was sent me. It was put out broadcast in a portion of an old vegetable garden set aside this year as an orchard, and in close proximity to the hives.

It was unfortunate that we had some very heavy "plumps" of rain prior to its having got well established, and seed was no doubt buried, and plants suffered in the hollows by being silted up.

The elevation here is 866 feet, and the climate that of the wet portion of the Kelani Valley.

The clover started flowering 1\frac{1}{2} months after being put in and when at a height of 18 inches, and has been flowering up to the present time, when the best plant is just six feet in height.

It appears to me that the older it gets the stronger gets the scent. Bees certainly go to it, but I could not see that at present it had any greater attraction for them than other flowers."

JANUARY, 1923.]61

The rainfall summary of December is extremely simple. There was a general deficit throughout the island which was most marked in the areas where the December averages are highest, namely the Eastern Province and the whole North East face of the main hill country which may be interpreted generously from Nalanda to Numunukula. In both these areas deficits of over 10 inches on the month's average were common while similar deficits also occurred further north e.g. in the Jaffna peninsula. There was no large area where the average was passed with much to spare. One or two stations did just reach their average and among them may be mentioned Mullaitivu, Kalutara, Matara, Topawewa and Mailapitiya. The distribution during the month was irregular. There was plenty of rain in the first week, as the depression that passed over the island on November 28th to 29th was still having an effect during the first day or two and during the next few days another depression was forming East of the island. This latter ultimately developed into a severe cyclone but fortunately its chief severity occurred after it had got north of Ceylon although it caused some heavy rain here in its early stages (e.g. Rugam and Unichchai both recorded over 8 inches on the 5th 6th).

From the 7th to the 25th the weather over the island was more rain exceptionally clear. From X'mas day onwards there was more rain (Hendon and St. Martin's) Rangalla both recorded 7 inches in a day, but this rain came too late to bring the monthly totals up to average.

The effect of the clear period in the middle of the month shows clearly in the other items of the table above. The low night temperatures were sufficient to bring all the mean temperatures below average and the humidity and amount of cloud were below average too. The mean wind velocities and pressure were slightly above average though their distributions were not markedly abnormal.

A. J. BAMFORD,

Supdt. Observatory.

THE
TROPICAL AGRICULTURIST

VOL. LX.

PERADENIYA, FEBRUARY, 1923.

No. 2.

A YEAR-BOOK OF AGRICULTURAL
INVESTIGATION.

In the present number of the TROPICAL AGRICULTURIST is reproduced the YEAR-BOOK OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE for 1923, embodying some of the principal results of the technical investigations which have been carried out during the year 1922. It is intended to make this YEAR-BOOK an annual publication to be issued free to all subscribers to the Agricultural publications of Ceylon, to all agricultural associations and to the principal estates of the Colony. In future years it will appear as a publication entirely independent of the TROPICAL AGRICULTURIST, but for the present year it has been found necessary to incorporate the YEAR-BOOK with that Journal.

The decision to issue an illustrated report of the technical operations of the Department of Agriculture was made only late in the year, and therefore special preparations in regard to articles and to illustrations could not be made.

It is however hoped that the present attempt to place before agriculturists of Ceylon brief accounts of some of the principal investigations of the previous year will be of value and will warrant the issue of improved volumes in subsequent years. It is also hoped that the issue of these volumes annually will be a means of keeping progressive agriculturists in close touch with the technical investigators and advisors.

There is frequently heard the statement that practical agriculturists and the technical departments of agriculture are

66[FEBRUARY, 1923.

often not in sufficiently close touch with one another. Every effort is made in Ceylon to provide the cultivator with the best technical advice possible. At Meetings of the Committees of the Board of Agriculture free discussion of the results of all investigations take place. Visits are paid by technical officers to estates and gardens. Lectures are given to members of agricultural associations, agricultural instructors are provided for the assistance of village cultivators and courses of instruction are provided at the Agricultural School and in the School Gardens attached to Elementary Schools.

This problem of presenting the results of technical investigations to the agricultural public is one which is being given the most serious attention in all countries at the present time. The organization of extension work for agriculture is being attempted throughout the whole world, and the experience of other countries must be used to guide the shaping of the work in Ceylon.

Extension work generally centres around a central organization. In Ceylon, this central body must necessarily for many years be the headquarters of the Agricultural Department advised by the Board of Agriculture, but as time passes decentralization will become necessary and the establishment of provincial agricultural schools completed. These schools in turn will become central organizations for more limited areas, remaining, as it were, affiliated with a Research Institute at Peradeniya.

The YEAR-BOOK for 1923 includes a considerable amount of information in regard to some of the principal Pests and Diseases of Agricultural crops in Ceylon, and reviews some of the agricultural investigations—the results of which have reached the publication stage. It does not, however, purport to give a review of the whole of the operations of the Department.

Year-book

OF THE

DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE,
Ceylon, 1923.

INTRODUCTION.

BY THE DIRECTOR OF AGRICULTURE.

The presentation of the results of investigations by a Department of Agriculture is a matter of some difficulty—particularly in those countries where an agricultural press has not developed. In the United Kingdom, the Dominions and the United States of America the number of periodicals devoted to agriculture increases yearly, and some of these publications are greatly appreciated by the agricultural communities. In these publications, attention is drawn to the results of scientific investigations carried out by the various Schools of Agriculture and Research Institutes. An increasing number of students are yearly attending courses of instruction at the Universities and Agricultural Colleges or special lectures organized in connexion with Extension work.

In this manner, an increasing number of practical agriculturists are brought into touch with, and are interested in, the Research work which is being carried out for the Agricultural Industries. The value of Research in Agricultural Science is becoming more and more recognised and all progressive agriculturists are insisting that the best investment that agriculture can make is in Research and Instruction.

In Ceylon, a beginning has been made in the provision of research workers for the agricultural industries. Officers are being secured for instruction. Experiment stations have been established and extension work begun. This beginning is but a small one when the importance of the agricultural industries to the Colony are taken into consideration and frequently demands are made upon the Department which at the present time can only be inadequately met.

The Centenary of the Royal Botanic Gardens, Peradeniya, took place in 1922. From the small beginning in the Botanic Gardens, the present Department of Agriculture has evolved. Those who are in touch with the progress of agricultural institutions in America, the United Kingdom, Canada and South Africa, however, realize how slow Ceylon has been to provide the necessary equipment for agricultural research. Some progress is being made but expansion must be anticipated. The Year 1922 has seen the building and equipment of Entomological and Mycological Laboratories at Peradeniya, and

68[FEBRUARY, 1923.

completion of the organization of the Rubber Research Scheme in co-operation with the Rubber Growers' Association and some Ceylon rubber estates. An extension of the work of the Department in all its branches has also taken place.

The programme outlined by the various Committees appointed to consider the Development of the Economic Resources of the Colony, it has, however, been impossible to carry out owing to financial stringency, and urgent building operations have had to be suspended. The building of a Chemical Laboratory is urgently required and the proper equipment of the Central Experiment Station with model buildings for dealing with crops of tea, rubber, coconuts and cacao cultivated there is most desirable. The Experiment Station at Anuradhapura requires capital expenditure. Instruction work in dairying should be begun without delay and further provision made for the adequate provision of Agricultural Schools in the Provinces.

The present illustrated report on the main technical activities of the Department has been prepared in response to requests from the Estates Proprietary Association and the Ceylon Planters' Association. It has been impossible to give lengthy consideration to its production but it is hoped that it will contain details which will be of value to the agricultural interests of the Colony.

This request for the fullest details of the work of the Department from the Planting community is an indication of the value which is placed upon research work for agriculture and it is to be hoped that provision for the full equipment of the Department will be hastened. As this equipment of laboratories takes place, higher courses in agricultural science are to be arranged in order that students of the University College, Colombo, may have the opportunity of qualifying in agricultural science and later specializing in some of its branches.

Ceylon depends for its prosperity upon its agriculture and the development of agricultural industries demands the closest attention. Existing industries require to be safeguarded against the ravages of pests and diseases, new industries require encouragement and investigation, small cultivators require instruction and the village paddy growers assistance. Co-operation, also, demands to be fostered.

Details concerning pests and diseases figure largely in the present YEAR-BOOK. These branches of the Department were the first to be properly organized and equipped, in the belief that the first duty of the Department of Agriculture was to be the vigilant guardian of the health of the Colony's crops.

The blocks for the illustrations have been prepared by the Survey Department and thanks are due to that Department for careful work and prompt delivery.

TEA.

The work of the Department in regard to Tea consisted of a continuation of the manurial experiments at Peradeniya Experiment Station, the testing of green manures for use in tea cultivations, and the continuation of the investigations into the shot-hole borer and other pests and diseases of this crop.

The manurial experiments continue to demonstrate the value of green manures for tea, the dadap and albizzia plots still continuing to give satisfactory yields. Trials have been started with Gliricidia maculata as green manure for tea, and the results have been so satisfactory up to the present time that the demand for cuttings and seed of this plant now exceeds the supply.

Tea tortrix still causes damage, but there is little possibility of this pest being checked until flight breaks are established in the affected areas. Nettle-grub has been under investigation during the year and investigations have been begun on the termites found on tea estates. Details concerning this work is given in the present volume and attention of all planters up-country is directed to the details given of the leaf disease caused by Cercosporrella theæ.

With the prohibition of the importation of tea seed from India in order to safeguard Ceylon against the introduction of leaf blister blight, attention has been paid to the tea-seed bearers in the Colony. There is little doubt that if the present high prices for all grades of tea are maintained new areas will be planted up during the next few years. There will therefore be an increasing demand for good seed, and all estates possessing areas of tea-seed bearers would be advised to pay more careful attention to their cultivation. Most of the tea-seed bearers in Ceylon are too closely planted, and many of them do not receive the cultivation that their importance to the industry demands.

CARE OF TEA-SEED BEARERS.

G. G. AUCHINLECK, M. Sc., A.I.C., F.C.S.,

Divisional Agricultural Officer, Central.

The gradual diminution in the yield of seed from tea-seed bearers, which is taking place on some estates in Ceylon, has recently been under investigation.

Figures at the disposal of the Department of Agriculture shew that in some cases the yield of seed from trees, ranging in age from 25 to 35 years, has been reduced to less than half during the past five to ten years. As the crop is a profitable one, the systems of manuring and cultivation followed by the estates in general leave little to be desired. The tea-plant lives probably for at least three-quarters of a century, so that it is unlikely that the observed diminution in yield of trees of 30 or 40 years of age can be the result of the on-coming of old age.

CLOSE-PLANTING.

Examination of fields of tea-seed bearers shows that in many cases the plants are over-crowded. Normally, tea-plants are set out at distances varying from 3\frac{1}{2} to 4\frac{1}{2} ft. apart, and this space is ample where the plants are

70[FEBRUARY, 1923.

table-pruned to a height of a couple of feet and grown for leaf. Where tea-plants are allowed to grow without pruning, they reach a height of 15 to 20 feet with a corresponding diameter of head, and such plants probably need a space of not less than 12 to 15 feet square. There is very little doubt that several of the fields of bearers in Ceylon were originally planted for leaf, and later allowed to grow up as sources of seed, without attention being paid to removal of surplus plants.

Two effects would be expected from over-crowding, both of which are in evidence in several of the fields of bearers in Ceylon. In the first place, lateral growth being hampered, there would be a compensating increase in vertical growth. Secondly, the production of leaves would take place on the tops only of the plants, all the other parts being shut out from the sunlight. An undue proportion of the vigour of the tree would be wasted on building up necessary wood, and the production of seed, which is dependent on the amount of leaf-surface, would be diminished. The effect of over-crowding on the shape of the tree and on the amount of leaf-production is clearly shown in Plates IV and V.

The harmful effect of over-crowding cannot be overcome by heavy manuring or by improved cultivation. It is probable that harm rather than good will follow. By increasing the vigour and size of the trees, the time is merely hastened when the rates of leaf-surface to woody bulk of the trunk and branches becomes reduced to a minimum. It is no doubt true that a certain number of weaker plants are over-shadowed and eventually killed by their more vigorous neighbours, but the process is a slow and wasteful one.

RENOVATION.

It seems safe to assume that 12 feet square is the minimum distance at which mature tea-seed bearers should be allowed to grow. In a field planted at 4 feet square there are therefore nine times the correct number of plants. It is clearly unwise to make so drastic a reduction as is indicated by these figures in an old field; in the first place, the reduction of crop would be too great and would probably last for several years, while in the second place the remaining plants would suffer severely from the shock of sudden exposure to light and wind.

Old tea-plants which throughout their lives have suffered from over-crowding are abnormally tall and possess a very small area of bearing-surface. If such trees be relieved from over-crowding by removal of their neighbours, it is doubtful whether they would be able to spread laterally, and so increase their leaf-surface, unless some system of topping and pruning be adopted. In addition, therefore, to reducing the number of plants per acre, the planter must pay attention to the question of forcing lateral growth in the case of the remaining plants. Both from the point of view of yield and that of conveniently controlling disease and reaping the crop, tall slender plants are undesirable.

In the majority of cases, where the planter is unwilling to face a heavy loss of crop for several years, a gradual improvement can be effected by annually removing a certain number of plants. In every over-crowded field, there are trees which are slowly being killed by their more vigorous neighbours, and these can be removed year by year with very little loss, or probably an immediate gain, to the yield per acre. If this system be followed, and simultaneously the standard of manuring and cultivation be sustained, the trees which remain should gradually produce more laterals and their production of seed should increase correspondingly. At the same time, more attention should be paid to the individual tree: non-productive wood should be pruned away, the trees should be lightly topped, and every effort made to encourage and preserve new lateral and basal shoots.

The overall scene illustrates the issue of trees being too closely planted, as mentioned in the caption.

Plate V.—TEA SEED-BEARERS IN CEYLON

FEBRUARY, 1923.]71

TRIALS NEEDED.

The gradual removal of weak trees has of course the advantage that there is no sudden and heavy loss of crop, and for this reason it is the method most likely to be adopted by the majority of estates. Where the estate can afford to take the risk of a fairly severe loss, however, it would be of value if systematic trials of more drastic methods of renovation could be instituted.

Two trials which suggest themselves, and which would throw a considerable amount of light on the problems of cultivation of bearers, are as follows. On one acre, carrying 2,700 plants (4 feet square), alternate rows might be removed in one year, and the effect on the yield per acre noted : the space available to each tree would then be 8 \times 4 or 32 square feet. The ordinary cultivation should be carried on, and a special mixture strong in nitrogen given to force vegetative growth. In the second year alternate trees in the remaining rows might be taken out, reducing the number of trees per acre to 680, and increasing the space available to each tree to 8 \times 8 or 64 square feet. In both years, light topping and removal of surplus unproductive branches should be practised, so as to induce lateral growth.

On another acre, a more drastic method might be tried. Alternate rows of plants might be removed and the remaining trees cut back severely. On one half of the acre, all trees should be topped back to 5 feet in height, while on the other half the trees should be collar-pruned to within three or four inches of the soil. From observations on individual trees it seems probable that even old tea-plants would stand such drastic treatment as this ; and there are indications that collar-pruning will in the end produce better results than topping at 5 feet.

It cannot be claimed that these trials are entirely free from risk, not only of loss of crop for two or three years, but even of loss of trees from severe and sudden exposure. The growing of tea-seed bearers is however so different from the cultivation of leaf-tea, and the information concerning the handling of bearers is so scanty, that it is worth while running the risk in order to obtain further information.

NEW PLANTATIONS.

The cultivation of tea-seed bearers is much more akin to fruit culture than it is to the growing of leaf-tea. Hitherto, bearers have been dealt with collectively in the field and very little attention has been paid to the individual plant. Pruning for shape, pruning for seed, replacing unprofitable individuals, are a few of the points which have received no attention. In view of the steady demand for seed of a good jat, and the probable future increase of that demand, the advisability of planting up fresh areas of bearers might well be considered by planters in Ceylon. Growing seed for sale should be a distinct industry and should be no longer hampered by confusing the methods used with those employed in the case of tea grown for leaf.

It is probable that in planting new areas, the planter will be safe in setting the bearers out at intervals of 12 feet, or 300 plants per acre. Were it certain that removal of alternate rows would be punctually carried out, the young plants might be grown at 6 feet apart until the branches of neighbouring plants were in contact. The reluctance of removing large numbers

72[FEBRUARY, 1923.

of healthy trees is however so great, that it is safer to adopt the wider distance once for all in the beginning, and to cover the soil in the wide intervals with inter-crops or green manures until the bearers are large enough to afford their own cover.

From the beginning, attention should be paid to inducing good, shapely growth. The young plants should be pruned to within 3 to 4 inches of the ground, and from 6 to 12 spreading stems allowed on each plant. In later years, branches should be cut back to outside "eyes," so as to produce a good, open, wide-spread head. Eventually, a widely oval shape should be produced. As seed is borne chiefly on the periphery of the head, and is dependent on the area of leaf-surface exposed to air and sunshine, every effort of the planter should be directed towards reducing the amount of large wood and increasing the number of lighter productive branches and leaves.

Once the shape of the tree has been satisfactorily moulded by pruning, the problem of producing an annual crop of new productive wood has to be faced. In other words, pruning for shade has to be succeeded by pruning for seed. On this point it must be frankly confessed that there is little definite information, but observation leads one to conclude that, once a crop of flowers has been produced in the axil of a tea-leaf, the axil becomes sterile. In later years, therefore, the annual crop of flowers must be secured from new branches or from lateral extensions of the existing branches.

In pruning for seed, two points have to be kept in mind; firstly, new and productive branches must be forced annually by cutting back the older laterals, and secondly light and air must be admitted into the head of the tree by pruning away crowded and unproductive branches. Both of these aims can be attained while yet the oval shape of the general framework of the plant is preserved, but a certain amount of skilled supervision will be necessary.
