THE SHOT-HOLE BORER PEST.

N. K. JARDINE, F.E.S.,

Acting Assistant Entomologist.

Shot-hole Borer (Xyleborus fornicatus) was first mentioned in Ceylon in 1868, when EICHOFF described the insect from a specimen collected in Ceylon. GREEN was privately investigating the insect as early as 1892, when it was noticed to be attacking tea on several estates. The first investigation into the life-history, habits, food-plants and control of this insect was therefore undertaken by GREEN some thirty years ago, and the results of his researches were published in a Circular of the Royal Botanic Gardens (No. 9, Vol. 2) in 1903. The concluding remark of this circular is extremely interesting in the light of further investigations by other Entomologists, extending over a period of nineteen years. MR. GREEN says :—"To sum up, keep the tree in a vigorous condition, and it will fight its own battles, provided that it is

FEBRUARY, 1923.]73

relieved from constant reinfection by the systematic destruction of the prunings." In this circular GREEN points out the seriousness of the pest, and suggests that energetic steps be taken to avert its spread.

On the retirement of GREEN in 1913, RUTHERFORD continued the work of investigation. He made the first experiments on the insect under ground, and the results of his experiments proved that the beetle can live, breed and multiply in prunings, buried to any depth consistent with estate conditions. RUTHERFORD was of opinion that the burial of prunings, as a means of control, was useless, and that certain disadvantages would accrue from the concentration of so much decaying organic matter in close proximity to the roots of the plants; and recommended burning of the prunings as the only effective method of control.

In 1914 SPEYER came to Ceylon for the investigation of Shot-hole Borer, and during his five years of service he made a careful study of the problem. His first Bulletin constituted a brief history of the insect, and a list of estates infested with the borer, arranged in their districts to enable planters desiring to purchase tea plants, to distinguish the infected from the uninfected. His next work "Treatment of Prunings on Infested Estates" (Bul. 43) dealt with his experiments to ascertain the effect the disposal of prunings had on the habits and propagation of the beetles; prunings being disposed of in the following ways:—(a) Leaving them on the ground; (b) Burying them to depths varying from four to eighteen inches; (c) Burning the prunings and (d) Burying the leaves and small wood, and burning the large wood. In this work SPEYER bears out the opinion of RUTHERFORD, that the wholesale burial of prunings is not an efficacious measure of control, and he suggests that the soundest method of disposing of prunings is to cut "the leaves and smaller wood up to the thickness of a pencil—immediately after pruning the branches," to bury these and burn the larger prunings at the roadside, and broadcast the ashes over the field. Though this is not a criticism of the investigations, the writer is of opinion that the words "the leaves" should have been omitted as it leads one to infer that the leaves of the prunings are of definite importance to the insect, while this is not the case.

The question of burning prunings was one constantly raised by planters, for it was felt by many that the loss incurred in burning prunings was a serious matter. The results of further experiments by SPEYER are published in a bulletin (No. 44) entitled—"A Control Pruning Scheme, and its Practical Modifications." The scheme was that infected bushes should be pruned between the ordinary pruning periods, and destroyed by fire. For badly infected tea the first round of removing infected branches was to be made at from four to six months, and the second round at from fourteen to eighteen months after the ordinary pruning; and for slightly attacked tea the scheme differed in that the first round for removing infected branches should be made eight to twelve months after pruning. The scheme was to be adopted in conjunction with the application of a mixture of SPEYER'S invention which could be applied to the collars and over branches of the bushes in the form of a paint. It was claimed that this "paint mixture" would kill the borers that came in contact with it. The whole scheme would therefore act as follows:—frequent pruning would prevent undue increase of the insect between the ordinary pruning periods and the application of the "paint" would control the insect in the collars and lower branches.

74[FEBRUARY, 1923.

Innumerable experiments other than those mentioned in this paper were tried by each investigator, but mention is made of only those which have come before the public in the form of publications. The problem of the control of Shot-hole Borer is one bristling with difficulties.

In 1919 JEPSON took over the investigation. His first work was to make trials on the Control Pruning Scheme and SPEYER'S Mixture. The summary of his experiments shows that control pruning results in too severe a mutilation of the bush to warrant its adoption. The paint mixture proved too costly to be used generally, of insufficient benefit, and tending to cause injury to the bushes and promote diebacks. That pruning has a significant effect on the insect is explained by JEPSON in his article "The Restriction of Tea Crop and Shot-hole Borer" (T. A. Dec. 1920). He says: "Instances can be recalled where about every branch on every bush has been riddled by borer and it is usually observed that this heavy degree of infestation has occurred during the six months immediately preceding pruning." This in itself explains why all investigators have first concentrated on the question of pruning as a possible control. JEPSON continues:—"The explanation of this comparatively sudden infestation is that the increase is due, not so much to the exhausted condition of the bushes inviting further attack from outside, as to increase of natural propagation in that particular field, brood succeeding brood, in rapid succession, until checked by pruning." "When it is pointed out that at this period the female progeny of one original female has numbered no less than 10,000,000 individuals, the necessity of taking action to limit the activities of the insect at this period can be readily appreciated."

In "The Treatment of Buried Prunings on Shot-hole Borer infested Estates" (Bull. 54) JEPSON deals further with the problem. His experiments extended over a period of months, and some 11,000 galleries were minutely examined. The object of the experiments was to discover a means of treating the prunings at the time of burial in such a manner that the inmates would be killed. Artificial manures, chemical salts, insecticides and proprietary substances numbering eighteen were used. Neither artificial manures, nor iron or copper sulphates, proved of any benefit. Phenol showed slight effect, while "Kerisol" and "Agrisol" were of material benefit, but the cost of treatment with these substances was high. The cost of materials and the quantities necessary to produce beneficial results prohibit their being used economically, and we are forced to revert back to the method originally suggested, namely, to lop the smaller prunings, bury them and burn the larger branches.

Series of manurial experiments were then instituted. The first consisted of trials with a selection of individual manures to ascertain the effects of nitrogen, potash and phosphoric acid upon Shot-hole Borer. These experiments were completed in February of this year and the results published (Bul. 56). They show that Sulphate of Ammonia and Nitrate of Soda and, to a lesser degree, Lime, have a very beneficial effect in reducing the attack of the borer. The second series, which is still in progress, deals with a general mixture of ordinary estate routine. As these experiments have been left in the hands of the writer during the absence of JEPSON on furlough, he may be permitted to outline the results to date. The object of these experiments is to ascertain what part liberal manuring plays in promoting the process of gallery healing.

FEBRUARY, 1923.]75

Four observations have been made on two similar experiments, and they point to a significant benefit in promoting satisfactory gallery healing. These experiments—though as yet incomplete—are tending to show that a general mixture* of Fish, Nitrolim (or Sulphate of Ammonia) and Muriate of Potash in quantities of 200 lb. at pruning, 350 lb. in the second year, and 550 lb. in the third year is giving very material benefit to the bushes over Shot-hole Borer attack. The results of these observations have not yet been published. So satisfactory are the results however that it is probable that a solution to the problem will be found in good cultivation and the careful destruction of the woody parts of prunings by fire.

From this history of investigation it appears that the greater proportion of work has been concentrated on the question of the disposal of prunings, but the writer has treated of only those investigations which have appeared in publication. Other aspects of the problem which have been carefully investigated may be enumerated as follows:—Soil fumigants; trap trees; food plants; range of flight; immunity of plants at certain elevations; destruction of “Ambrosia” fungus,—the food material of the larvæ and adults in the galleries; crop restriction; insecticides; parasites; predacious enemies; phototropism—the response to the stimulus of light; legislation—to arrest the spread of the insect by the distribution of plants from infected areas; education,—lectures, field demonstrations, distribution of illustrated posters and pamphlets.

* The mixtures used were as follows:—

At pruning—Nitrolim 60 lb., Ephos phosphate 80 lb., and Muriate of Potash 60 lb.

Second and Third years from pruning—Sulphate of Ammonia, 60 lb., fish, 250 lb. and Muriate of Potash 40 lb.

THE EFFECT OF CERTAIN MANURIAL SUBSTANCES ON SHOT-HOLE BORER OF TEA.

C. H. GADD, B.Sc.,

Assistant Mycologist.

It is the expressed opinion of numerous planters that high cultivation and manuring on tea estates exercises a controlling influence upon the activities of Shot-hole borer. Though there is a certain unanimity as to the effects of manures in general, there is a considerable divergence of opinion as to what manurial elements are most effective in bringing about a reduction of borer attack.

Experiments were started by JEPSON in November 1920 in the Badulla district to determine whether a reduction of borer attack follows treatment with certain fertilizers, and if so, to ascertain what manurial elements are the most efficacious.

Sixteen plots in each of three fields were marked out. Each plot consisted of 378 bushes, i.e., 18 rows, each of 21 bushes, and was separated from adjoining plots by guard strips, 4 bushes wide, which were left untreated. By the use of guard strips the risk that a manure applied to one plot would affect the bushes on the boundaries of the adjoining plots was

76[FEBRUARY, 1923.

reduced to a minimum. The bushes in the three fields differed in age, counting from the time of last pruning. In one field they were pruned shortly before the commencement of the experiment; in the second and third fields they were entering their second and third years respectively from last pruning.

The following substances were selected for trial and were applied at the rate of 200 lb. per acre, except where otherwise stated:—

Nitrate of soda, Sulphate of Ammonia, Nitrolim, Nitrate of Potash, Muriate of Potash, Ephos phosphate, Basic Slag, (300 lb.), mixture of equal parts Nitrate of Soda and Ephos phosphate, Dadap loppings (5 tons), Boga medeloa loppings (5 tons), Cattle manure (7 tons), and Lime (5 tons). Each of these fertilizers was applied to one plot in each field and the remaining 4 plots in each field were left untreated as controls.

The final examinations of two fields were made in July 1921, but, as at that time the attack in the field in its first year from pruning was so slight as to be almost negligible, its examination was delayed till February 1922, when the attack, though still small, was considered to be sufficient for a comparison to be made between the various plots.

The following determinations were made for each plot.—

  1. 1. The mean number of open galleries per branch.
  2. 2. The proportion of galleries found empty.
  3. 3. The mean content of occupied galleries.

The mean number of open galleries per branch represents the extent to which branches have been weakened by borers; the proportion of galleries found empty and the mean number of occupants (adults, larvæ and eggs) indicates the rate at which borers are increasing in the respective plots.

The results obtained from the three fields were in some cases inconsistent. For instance, as regards the number of galleries per branch, the nitrolim plot was in one field decidedly better than, the controls, while in the other fields the attack was equal to, or worse than, that in the unmanured plots. The results obtained from these experiments therefore cannot be considered to be conclusive.

A general survey of the experiments, however, shows that of the five treatments which gave better results than the best of the control plots three are nitrogenous manures, viz. sulphate of ammonia, nitrate of soda, and nitrolim, the remaining two being lime and muriate of potash. The best result was obtained with sulphate of ammonia, which gave consistent results in the three fields. Nitrate of soda gave almost equally good results. The results obtained from the other nitrogenous manure, nitrolim, are very little better than those obtained from the best control plots.

The organic and phosphatic manures gave results no better than the unmanured plots.

Though the potassic (muriate of potash) plot gave the fourth best result, yet the nitrate of potash plots gave results on the whole no better than the controls. Similarly where nitrogen was applied in combination with phosphoric acid, as provided by a mixture of nitrate of soda and ephos phosphate, the results were not so good as where a nitrogenous fertilizer alone was used.

FEBRUARY, 1923.]77

Though the above experiments have given no conclusive results, they indicate that certain manurial substances have a beneficial effect in controlling Shot-hole borer. Also they furnish evidence as to the extent to which such experiments are liable to experimental errors, and the information, derived from these experiments should be of great value when designing and carrying out other Shot-hole borer control experiments.

The use of incomplete fertilizers is, in general, not to be recommended. In the above experiments no complete mixture, other than organic manures, was used. Another series of experiments to determine the effect of complete mixtures of artificial fertilizers has been laid out by JEPSON, and, so far as the experiments have progressed, the examinations show that the use of such mixtures is followed by a decisive diminution of Shot-hole borer. Whether this diminution is only temporary or whether it will be maintained, cannot be ascertained till all the examinations are completed.

THE FRINGED NETTLE-GRUB,
NATADA NARARIA, MOORE.

J. C. HUTSON, B.A., Ph.D.,

Entomologist.

The Nettle-grubs, as a group, are probably the best known of the caterpillar pests of tea in Ceylon, since one or more species occur in most districts in the Island and readily make their presence felt, not only on the tea but on anyone who unwillingly walks into an affected area. The term "nettle-grub" is commonly applied to a family of limaciform or slug-like caterpillars, the Limacodidæ, some of which are protectively armed with tufts of urticating or stinging hairs the points of which break off on touching the skin and cause intense irritation.

Some twenty species of this family have been recorded from Ceylon, and seven of these are known to be more or less important pests of tea, while others may possibly occur occasionally in tea areas. The following species have been recorded at various times as tea pests :—

Thosea cana, Wlk., The "Green Nettle-grub;" Thosea recla, Hmpsn., The "Morawak Korale Nettle-grub;" Thosea cervina, Moore, Natada nararia, Moore., The "Fringed Nettle-grub;" Parasa lepida, Cram., The "Blue-striped Nettle-grub;" Spatulicraspeda castaneiceps, Hmpsn., which may be called The "Red-banded nettle-grub;" Belipha laleana, Moore, The "Gelatine grub."

The fringed nettle-grub has been known as a pest of tea in Uva for at least twenty-five years and has become an almost chronic visitation on some estates in that district. Occasional outbreaks of this caterpillar occur at longer intervals in other districts. Attacks of Natada are usually reinforced by small numbers of one or more species of the above mentioned nettle-grubs, but no reports have been received during the last two years of any serious outbreak of these nettle grubs independently of Natada.

78[FEBRUARY, 1923]

At intervals during the past eighteen months Natada nararia has been under investigation both in the field and under insectary conditions, as being one of the most important tea pests during this period, and the following account is based mainly on the results so obtained.

In the tea areas where Natada has become established as a regular pest it probably breeds almost continuously throughout the year, but is usually more prevalent from about August to October, and again in May and June.

HABITS AND LIFE HISTORY.

Moths.—The male and female moths mate soon after emerging from their cocoons and the females may begin egg-laying within a day or two after emergence. As a preliminary experiment to get some idea, among other points, as to the number of eggs which a Natada moth will lay in captivity, it was found possible to insolate ten pairs of these moths in separate breeding cages, one pair to each cage. The females laid respectively the following totals of eggs :—185, 411*, 60, 206*, 305*, 126, 115, 18, 408*, 198*. In the case of the numbers marked with an asterisk (*) the great majority, over 90 per cent., of the eggs hatched, while in the remaining totals not a single egg hatched, indicating that these eggs had not been fertilized. When kept supplied with food in captivity the female moths live for periods varying from 4 to 14 days and the males from 4 to 12 days. There are indications that the majority of the eggs are laid during the first 3 or 4 days after emergence, while the actual oviposition period last from 2 to 10 days. In the insectary, the moths laid most of their eggs scattered about on the sides of the breeding cages, but also deposited them on both the upper and under surfaces of the tea leaves. Under natural conditions in the field the eggs appear to be laid singly on the upper surface of older leaves. Mating takes place mainly at night and most of the eggs are laid during the night. The moths usually rest in the positions shown in Plate VI, figs. 1a and b, the body being held at an acute angle to the twig, usually with the head uppermost. The moths appear to hold on by the second and third pairs of legs, the front pair being folded up close to the body. The wings are often closely applied to the sides of the twig and may serve to steady the moth.

Eggs.—These lie flat on the leaf surface and somewhat resemble a scale insect. The actual egg is pale yellow at first and semi-transparent, and is covered by a thin transparent film which apparently shines with the metallic iridescence mentioned by GREEN. The eggs develop in about 5 or 6 days and before hatching are pale-brown in colour with a semi-transparent centre.

Caterpillars.—These are about 1/25th inch long on hatching and of a dull whitish colour, but become pale green after feeding has begun. The body is fringed with minute tufts of white stinging hairs and there is a double row of still smaller spiniferous tubercles along the back. The young nettle-grubs move to the underside of the leaves soon after hatching and begin eating away small portions of the under-surface, leaving only a thin skin, the upper epidermis. When a number of young caterpillars are feeding on the same leaf this soon becomes marked with numerous small brownish spots. Plate VI., fig. 1f. shows the kind of damage done by the young

FEBRUARY, 1923.]79

nettle-grubs. After about two weeks of feeding the caterpillars are able to eat right through the leaves which very soon assume a notched and ragged appearance. The bushes may sometimes be completely defoliated over an area of several acres. The nettle-grubs are full grown in about 5 to 7 weeks in captivity, but probably take a shorter time in the field.

The Cocoon stage lasts from about 17 to 22 days in the breeding cages, and after the emergence of the moths the life cycle begins all over again.

The complete life cycle of Natada nararia under insectary conditions occupies from about 8½ weeks to about 11 weeks. It has not been possible to ascertain the exact period of development from egg to moth in the field, but it is probably about 7 to 8 weeks under favourable climatic conditions.

FOOD PLANTS.

The fringed nettle-grub has been found to breed freely on dadap (Erythrina lithosperma) which is commonly interplanted with tea as a green manure. The caterpillars also feed on Toona (Cedrela toona) which is sometimes grown along the edges of estate roads and paths running through the tea. This pest is able to develop on Bignonia creepers, and has been found feeding to a slight extent on the following plants:—Eucalyptus robusta; Psidium polycarpon; Castanospermum australe; Tecoma stans; Thunbergia laurifolia; and Rubus ellipticus.

HOW THE PEST SPREADS.

It seems improbable that Natada spreads to new areas to any great extent in the caterpillar stage, since the caterpillars are not naturally very active nor do they habitually drop to the ground or move away to other bushes when disturbed. The spread of the pest seems to take place chiefly in the moth stage, especially at times when there is a strong wind blowing. The emergence of a number of moths in a small area during periods of high winds would lead to a distribution of a certain number of these moths, to more distant uninfested areas of tea and on to any other plants growing across the line of flight. Each fertilized female will be capable of laying at least 200 eggs, perhaps scattered over several bushes, and the next generation of caterpillars will be spread over several acres of tea. Within about 7 to 8 weeks later a still larger number of moths will be emerging to spread the attack further afield. Hence the vital importance of being on the look-out to check the pest at the outset while it is confined to a few bushes.

NATURAL ENEMIES.

The fringed nettle-grub, in common with the other nettle-grubs which feed on the tea plant, is normally controlled by its natural enemies in the shape of small parasitic flies and wasps. A "Wilt disease" is also very effective at certain times. In the absence of its natural enemies, the pest increases very rapidly and at certain times seems likely to go on increasing indefinitely. Then perhaps a sudden change takes place and the attack fades away, and the caterpillars may be seen no more in that particular area for several years. This sudden disappearance of the pest may be due partly to the increase in the parasites and partly to heavy rains, but is often mainly due to the rapid spread of a highly infectious disease. Caterpillars in all stages of development may be affected; the younger specimens become discoloured and shrivel up, while the older nettle-grubs turn brown and become somewhat swollen and glossy. They disintegrate rapidly and

80[FEBRUARY 1923.

a brownish foul-smelling slime oozes out. This spreads over the leaves, especially during rains, and it seems probable that other nettle-grubs get infected by eating the contaminated leaves or merely by crawling over them. This disease seems to be most effective at times when the bushes are heavily infested with the caterpillars, and spreads rapidly in the over-crowded conditions.

ARTIFICIAL CONTROL MEASURES.

These may, for convenience, be considered under preventive measures, which are intended mainly for dealing with small outbreaks of nettle-grub, and remedial measures which are applicable after the pest has got out of hand and are mainly of an emergency nature.

PREVENTIVE MEASURES.

  1. 1. Instruct all kanganies and coolies to keep a look-out for nettle-grub, especially the fringed nettle-grub, on tea and on dadap, and to report the presence of these immediately.
  1. 2. If only a small area is being attacked then put on a gang of coolies to collect and destroy the caterpillars. The infested leaves can be plucked or slashed off with the "grubs" on them, and this should involve only a slight defoliation provided that the outbreak has been taken in hand in time. It may also be necessary to lop the interplanted dadap lightly. The early stages of the nettle grub can often be detected by the spotting of the leaves on both tea and dadap.
  1. 3. All fallen leaves and rubbish under the bushes in and around the infested area should be collected and burnt in order to kill any cocoons. The leaves and twigs of the same bushes should also be searched carefully for any cocoons which may be attached to them and all such cocoons should be removed and destroyed.
  1. 4. Place a few light-traps in and around the infested area or areas, on dark, still nights to catch any moths that may be about. This measure should keep down egg-laying to some extent.

The above measures are all intended for application to small areas up to half an acre at most, and if the pest is detected in time it should only be necessary to treat a few bushes. These measures are not intended for large areas, although they are sometimes carried out on estates where a large labour force is available, and they may do some good. In such cases the caterpillars and cocoons are collected by the bushel.

REMEDIAL MEASURES.

  1. 1. Spray the affected area, or areas, with the lead chromate Rosin compound (No. 2 wash) recommended in Bulletin No. 46 of the Department of Agriculture. This mixture provides a non-arsenical spray which has no harmful effect on the bush and no effect on the made tea. It was primarily recommended for use against tea tortrix, but is effective against all leaf-eating insects. All tea estates which are subject to periodical attacks of nettle-grub and other caterpillar pests should be equipped with at least one modern type of 2 or 3 gallon Knapsack sprayer of the Pneumatic type, and preferably one which is equipped with an internal agitator. Small quantities of insecticides should be kept in stock, so that a sudden outbreak may be dealt with promptly.

2. As an alternative to spraying, or in cases where a large area, say the greater part of a field, is attacked and no sprayer is available, it is usually advisable to prune the whole field, especially if this area is almost due to be pruned. The pruners should start around the edges of the field and gradually work in towards the centre. The prunings should all be burnt immediately, where practicable, and all the dead leaves and rubbish should be collected and burnt also. This is a very drastic method of treatment and should only be adopted in an emergency. The field should be manured after pruning.

In many cases where the outbreak has occurred towards the end of a dry period and rains are expected shortly the planter is inclined to let the pest run on in the expectation that it will be controlled by the wet weather or will be wiped out by disease. This sometimes works out all right in districts where the nettle-grub is only a very occasional pest, but is rather a dangerous experiment in areas where Natada is already an established pest, as there are usually enough survivors to start another big offensive a few weeks later unless preventive measures are adopted after the main attack has died down.

THE TEA LEAF-SKELETONIZER.

A Preliminary Note.

J. C. HUTSON, B.A., Ph.D.,

Entomologist.

Towards the end of July, 1922, a caterpillar pest of tea was reported from two adjoining estates in the Ramboda District and specimens were received from the Superintendent, who stated that the pest was present in small quantities on one estate, while one field on the other estate was covered with it and the bushes had been badly spoilt. About a week later a "tremendous plague of spiders" was reported by the Superintendent in connection with this pest. The same insect has been found recently (December, 1922) by one of the Plant Pest Inspection officers on four tea estates in the Badulla district.

The specimens as received from the Ramboda district were seen to be quite different from any of the usual caterpillar pests of tea and have not previously come under the observation of the Entomological staff, so far as is known. Specimens of the moths were subsequently bred out and are apparently new to the collection at Peradeniya. The moths have been sent to the Imperial Bureau of Entomology for identification, but the scientific name has not been received up to the time of writing.

NATURE OF THE DAMAGE.

The presence of the pest can usually be detected by the small masses of dead leaves near the top and in the middle of the bushes and badly attacked bushes may have a thinned out and ragged appearance due to partial defoliation. The caterpillars eat away small portions of both the upper and under surfaces of a leaf indiscriminately, leaving only a thin skin, so that a badly

82[FEBRUARY, 1923.

attacked leaf may be completely skeletonized with only the ribs and veins remaining. Such leaves are usually more or less covered with frass and loose webbing but this is not shown in the figure. The leaves are loosely webbed together by fine threads to form a sort of "nest" within which the caterpillars feed and pass through the various stages in their development. The damaged leaves sooner or later fall off the twigs, but remain within the general mass. Fresh green leaves are included as required, and these in their turn become skeletonized and dry up. As a rule only the older leaves are attacked. An outbreak of this pest appears to be frequently accompanied by the "tremendous plague of spiders" mentioned above, and bushes may be completely covered with a network of webbing which becomes a nuisance to the pluckers. It is possible that some of the moths may be caught in the spiders' webs as they fly up out of a bush, but this has not been observed so far.

HABITS AND LIFE CYCLE OF THE PEST.

Moths :—The small, slender, dark moths (Plate VII., fig. 1) are not at all conspicuous and probably hide in the tea bushes during the day. They can sometimes be "put up" by beating the bushes in an infested area, but fly only a short distance as a rule and dart back into another bush, where they settle down in the position shown in Plate VII., fig. 2. They are very difficult to detect when at rest, as they may easily be taken for a piece of dry twig or a dead leaf stalk. In captivity the moths begin egg-laying in about a week after emergence and may live for another week or ten days after this.

Eggs :—The eggs are pale yellow when freshly laid and gradually change in colour through orange red to crimson. Before hatching they are seen to be mottled with grey, pink and dirty white. Plate VII., fig. 3 shows the outline of an egg in one position and fig. 4 an egg in outline in another position—further enlarged to show the reticulation on the egg-shell. Under field conditions the eggs have been found on the dead leaves among the grass and debris in a "nest." They can be seen quite easily without a lens when in the crimson stage. In the insectary the eggs hatch in about a week, so far as we have been able to ascertain from preliminary experiments. It is not known at present how many eggs a moth can lay.

Caterpillars.—The newly-hatched caterpillars are about \frac{1}{2} inch long and are orange yellow. Seen under a lens the head and first segment of the body are pale brown and broader than the remaining segments which gradually taper off towards the hinder end. The body is bright yellow and each segment is edged laterally with pinkish markings on each side. These young caterpillars soon begin feeding and cover themselves with a thin webbing of threads over which pellets of grass are soon scattered. The second stage caterpillar has a somewhat mottled appearance with a mixture of pale yellows, browns and blacks while the sides of the body still have a pinkish tinge. The body has become stouter and is broader than the head, except the two last segments which are narrower. In the next two stages the mottled appearance has become more marked, since the colours, yellow, brown and black, with a tinge of green, have deepened and become more contrasty. The full-grown caterpillar is nearly half inch in length and is

FEBRUARY, 1923.]83

mottled with chocolate—brown or reddish-brown and black with a slight tinge of olive green. These caterpillars are quite inconspicuous on the dead leaves among which they usually shelter. The period of larval development takes about 5 to 7 weeks in captivity and probably the shorter period is the more normal one under field conditions. The caterpillars may often be seen in the position shown in Plate VII., fig. 9.

Cocoons. The full grown caterpillars settle down on the leaves, sometimes on the dead leaves, sometimes on the green leaves outside the "nest," and spin a loosely woven cocoon over them. Then they moult for the last time and change into the pupa (see figs. 10 and 11). The pupa is dark brown with shades of lighter brown. In the insectary the pupal stage lasts for about 11 to 12 days, after which the moths emerge to start another brood.

CONTROL MEASURES.

This pest could probably be checked in the early stages of the attack by having the masses of dead and dying leaves cleared out and burnt. This would kill many of the eggs, caterpillars and cocoons. Bushes which are badly webbed over by spiders should receive further attention which may sometimes lead to the detection of this or other caterpillar pests. Nothing more definite can be suggested until the pest has received further investigation. It is requested that all tea planters be on the look-out for this pest and its presence be reported to the Entomologist, with specimens if possible.

NOTES ON TERMITES ATTACKING
TEA IN CEYLON.

J. C. HUTSON, B.A., Ph.D.,

Entomologist.

There are several species of termites (white ants) which are more or less closely associated with the tea bush in Ceylon, and the marked increase of these insects at various elevations has caused much apprehension among tea planters recently. The tea termites, for the most part, may be divided into two main groups according to their nesting habits and nature of their damage to the tea bush, viz :—

A. Termites which form their colonies inside a living tea bush and bore into the heart wood. These are primary pests, and include the well-known Calotermes militaris.

B. Termites which have their nests outside a tea bush, usually underground, and which generally attack the dead or dying bark and wood of various plants, including tea, rubber, dadap, grevillea, and jungle stumps. These include the mound-building termites, and can be regarded mainly as secondary pests and scavengers.

The prevailing anxiety about the tea termites seems to be due mainly to the state of uncertainty as to the actual species of termite concerned in any particular case, and where there is any doubt in the mind of the planter the damage is usually attributed to Calotermes militaris, when in most cases the injury is usually the result of an attack of a fungus disease or of insect injury followed by an invasion of the scavenging termites.

84[FEBRUARY, 1923.

The main object of the following notes is to try and clear up the existing ambiguity by pointing out the essential differences between these two groups of termites in order that the tea planter may, in most cases, be able to diagnose the particular trouble for himself and take measures accordingly.

A. At the present time there are only three species of termites which are known to bore into the heart wood of healthy tea bushes. These are (1) Calotermes militaris, (2) Calotermes dilatatus and (3) Calotermes greeni.

Calotermes militaris is mainly an up-country species, being prevalent mostly in the southern part of the Central Province, but is sometimes found at lower elevations. This termite is intermediate in size between the smaller dilatatus and the larger greeni. It is a fairly serious pest on some up-country estates.

2. Calotermes dilatatus. This is the smallest of these three species of termites. It seems to be mainly a mid to low-country species. RUTHERFORD was of opinion that this termite enters a bush through some old knot-hole or a wound or through a red borer or shot-hole borer gallery and gradually works downwards, sometimes into the roots. The writer has observed this habit in the case of this species in tea seed-bearers, a series of attacked bushes showing progressive stages of injury from top to bottom and even down into the roots. In the case of dilatatus the galleries are distributed throughout the stem and neither RUTHERFORD nor the writer has observed any large cavities formed by dilatatus such as are found in the case of bushes infested with militaris. A complete colony apparently exists in each infested bush and there are indications that dilatatus has winged adults.

3. Calotermes greeni appears to have a wide range of distribution and feeding habits, as it has been recorded from Jaffna ("boring into trees"), Peradeniya ("in dead branch of tree"), Avisawella and Yatiyantota ("from stem of living tea bush") and Ambalangoda ("from stem of living Cashew-nut tree"). In the single instance seen by the writer of a tea bush infested by this species the damage was somewhat similar to that done by dilatatus in that the stem was fairly well riddled by galleries without any large cavity being made. C. greeni is the largest of these three species and has winged adults.

To summarize, it may be said that so far as we know at present, the Calotermes species all have their nests inside living tea bushes, militaris being more prevalent in up-country tea while dilatatus and greeni occur at lower elevations. In cases of injury by militaris, it is usually the lower parts of the bush, from the collar down to the roots which suffer most, but in all the militaris cases noted by RUTHERFORD and in those observed by the writer the injury was so far advanced that it was impossible to say where the termites had originally entered. GREEN was of opinion that these termites apparently enter a bush through the roots and work upwards. It is not improbable that militaris may sometimes gain entry through an injured branch from which the termites may spread in all directions throughout the bush.

Judging from the records of dilatatus injury left by RUTHERFORD and from the present writer's experience of this species in tea seed-bearers and ordinary tea bushes it seems not unlikely that dilatatus may enter a bush

FEBRUARY, 1923.]85

above ground and may tunnel into the lateral branches and later work downwards, although it may possibly sometimes attack a bush from below ground level. Neither dilatatus nor greeni appear to excavate large cavities in the main stem, but have a system of galleries running through the heartwood.

Of the above species of Calotermes, it seems probable that militaris is the most formidable as a pest of tea, since it may escape detection at pruning time and continue its excavations for many years until the bush is reduced to a mere shell. Even in cases where it may enter a bush above the collar, being mainly an up-country species it has a longer time to carry on undisturbed between prunings. On the other hand dilatatus and greeni, probably working for the most part above ground level, would tend to be periodically controlled by pruning, especially by the more frequent prunings at lower elevations. It is possible, however, that were these two species left to their own devices they might eventually bring tea bushes to the condition sometimes produced by militaris in which the bush is completely hollowed out.

None of these three species has been a very serious pest within recent years, only small patches of tea or individual bushes being occasionally attacked. Much of the damage reported as due to Calotermes on further investigation usually turns out to be the work of the scavenging termites following an attack of branch canker or other injury to the bushes.

CONTROL OF THE CALOTERMES SPECIES.

Since these termites have their colonies in individual tea bushes and are not known to nest in the ground or have any main termitarium outside the bushes it follows that the most effective way of reducing their numbers is by treating each infested bush individually on its merits. All completely riddled bushes should be eradicated and burnt immediately, so as to destroy any infesting termites. In cases where the injury is detected in time it should be sufficient to clear out any cavity thoroughly and paint the inside with a liquid wood preservative, such as a Creosote solution, and then fill in the cavity with mortar or cement to prevent water collecting and causing decay. Where there is no cavity but only small galleries the solution can be applied thoroughly to the cut surface and allowed to penetrate into the galleries. This should effectually drive out or kill any termites which are still inside and protect the bush from re-infestation for some time. The presence of the scavenging termites may some times complicate matters and in such cases the use of ordinary tar should be avoided as this seems to afford no protection against the scavengers.

SCAVENGING TERMITES.

B. There are several species of termites which feed on the dead and dying bark and wood of tea bushes, among other plants, and can be regarded mainly as scavengers. It should be understood that these termites are quite distinct from the Calotermes species, as will be indicated below, although they may sometimes be present on Calotermes affected bushes.

The two common species of scavenging termites commonly met with on tea are Termes obscuriceps and Termes redimanni. These are the common mound-building termites, a typical colony of which was described by

86[FEBRUARY, 1923.

GREEN some years ago.* Termes horii is another scavenger which is sometimes found in tea bushes, and probably nests in the ground, but apparently does not construct mounds. Species of Eutermes are also bark-scavengers and a Leucotermes is occasionally found tunnelling in tea bushes which have been killed by root diseases.

These two species, T. obscuriceps and T. redemanni appear to have increased enormously on tea estates within recent years and are doubtless prevalent on most estates in Ceylon, at varying elevations. In the opinion of the writer the prevalence of branch canker on many tea estates has been one of the contributing causes of the marked increase of these termites on tea bushes within recent years. The branch canker fungus usually occurs along the upper surface of lateral branches, invading and killing the cambium layer inside and causing the bark to crack. The disease may also extend down to the main stem and in extreme cases may girdle and kill the bush. The scavenging termites come along and gradually clear away the dead bark and crumbly wood inside, usually working under a screen of earth. Eventually many of the horizontal branches are left with shallow irregular cavities along their upper surfaces and the main stem may also be partially excavated by the termites, which have merely cleaned out the portions of the bush killed by the canker. These injuries are frequently attributed by the planter to the work of Calotermes, especially when there is a fairly deep cavity in the main stem, but in the great majority of cases this particular type of injury is due to branch canker followed by these smaller termites, such as obscuriceps and redemanni.

Incidentally, these termites may also be gradually clearing any old stumps and logs left among the tea and the abundant supply of such food on some estates has encouraged these insects to extend and populate their underground colonies.

It has been claimed that in some cases these smaller termites may help to prevent wounds from healing over and that they sometimes eat away living bark and girdle young tea bushes, but there is no definite evidence that they ever attack healthy living plant tissues. It is true that they usually follow the advance of a disease so closely that it is difficult to say that they do not actually get ahead of it sometimes. In the great majority of cases, however, it is quite evident that they are merely scavengers of dead and diseased bark and wood.

While these termites cannot be regarded as serious pests, their presence in vast numbers on many tea estates is most undesirable and it is strongly urged that vigorous measures be taken to reduce their numbers.

CONTROL MEASURES AGAINST THE SCAVENGING TERMITES.

At the present time experiments are being made by some estates with various paint mixtures applied to the bushes after pruning and a thorough cleaning up with the idea of finding some substance which will protect the bushes from further attack. It is too early to say what effect these paints will have on the bushes and how far and for what length of time they will be effective in keeping away the termites. In most cases the cost of materials and of their application is prohibitive even when used over fairly

* Circular of the Royal Botanic Gardens, Vol. IV., No. 10, 1908, "White Ants."

FEBRUARY, 1923.]87

large areas. These experiments have their value, however, as some substance may be discovered which may be useful in treating individual bushes both for injury by Calotermes species and other termites.

The control measures should be directed against the termites themselves and against their food supply, and may be carried out along three main lines:—

  1. 1. A direct attack should be made on the termites by eradicating their nests, either (a) by using an ant exterminator with sulphur and arsenic or (b) by fumigating with carbon bisulphide or (c) by digging out the nests and destroying the queens and colony.
  1. 2. Their food supply on the tea bush should be reduced by controlling branch canker and other diseases, shot-hole borer, red borer, Calotermes and other insects which injure the frames of the bushes.
  1. 3. Their other sources of food supply should be cut down as far as possible by removing and burning all old stumps and logs which are sometimes found among the tea.

Note. For fuller details see Leaflet of the Department of Agriculture No. 24, now in the Press.

CERCOSPORELLA LEAF DISEASE.

T. PETCH, B.A., B.Sc.,

Botanist and Mycologist.

Attention has previously been called to this disease in the annual reports of the Mycologist. It was first observed in 1909 on young tea plants in the nursery, the plants being defoliated by it. During recent years, it has become generally distributed in up-country districts, more especially in those which are subject to the rains of both monsoons.

The disease appears towards the close of the monsoon rains. Its effect on the tea leaf is very variable, depending to a great extent on the age of the leaf. On the flush it causes minute black or black-brown spots, usually more or less circular, but sometimes extending irregularly from the margin. These spots are sudden and rotten. They resemble in some degree the spots caused by Helopellis, but the latter are generally larger, more angular, and have a reddish tinge. Numbers of these spots may occur on a single small leaf, and if the rains continue they may coalesce so that the whole leaf becomes black and rotten. If, however, the rains cease, the progress of the disease may be arrested, and the young leaf may continue its development. It is then distorted, perforated with holes, and with an irregular margin, the injuries often being bordered by a yellow-green thickened zone (Plate VIII., fig. 1).

On older, but not full-grown, leaves, black circular spots are produced at first, and these subsequently become grey or white, with a well-defined, raised, purple or purple-black margin (Plate VIII., fig. 2.) These spots resemble the common Bird's eye spot caused by Cercospora Theæ; but they are generally larger, up to 5 millimetres in diameter, and they occur on younger leaves than is usual in Cercospora. Many cases, however, occur, in

88[FEBRUARY, 1923.

which it is impossible to distinguish between these two spots without a microscopic examination and identification of the fungus. In such cases, the other symptoms on the younger leaf should be looked for. Reports of the occurrence of Cercospora Theæ for several years without damage to the tea are most probably due to a confusion of this disease with the Bird's-eye spot (Cercospora Theæ).

On the old full-grown leaves, the effect is again different. On these the fungus usually causes large, diffuse, discoloured patches which may extend over the whole leaf. These patches are at first chocolate brown, mottled with yellow brown, and somewhat resemble the spots caused by Brown Blight. When old they turn grey, with a narrow purple black margin about a millimeter wide. In the latter stage, only the more definite margin distinguishes the spot from those of Grey or Brown Blight. (Plate VIII., fig. 4: spot on Acacia Melanoxylon.)

On the larger spots, the fungus may be found as a delicate white film covering the lower surface of the spot and spreading from it over the leaf. It is not so easy to find on the smaller spots, and it would appear that, in general, it does not become superficial until the spot has attained a certain size. The spores are borne on this external mycelium, and are hyaline, long, cylindrical, and septate (Plate VIII., fig. 3). Owing to their large size (up to a two-hundredth of an inch in length), they can often be seen with a hand lens, in minute white tufts, or lying in all directions in a white band at the margin of the spot.

On bushes attacked by this disease, the flush, if not blackened and rotted, is distorted and hard. The bushes may lose most of their leaves, the upper branches being completely defoliated, while the remaining leaves bear large discoloured patches or circular spots. The fungus also attacks the green twigs, on which it causes purple sunken patches.

Indications of a second (perithecial) stage of the fungus have been noted on two occasions. This stage occurs on the old diseased patches, breaking through the epidermis of the leaf in red cushions. It resembles a stromatic Nectria, but has not yet been found sufficiently mature for identification.

In addition to tea, Cercospora Theæ attacks Acacias and various species of Eucalyptus. Indeed, in practically all the recent instances of the occurrence of this disease on tea, it has been found that it originated on Acacia and spread from that tree to the tea. The Acacia concerned is usually Acacia decurrens, but that is only because that species is the one most generally planted. The disease can attack Acacia Melanoxylon and Acacia dealbata.

The first sign of the attack on Acacia decurrens is usually the fall of the leaflets and the partial or total defoliation of the tree. The smaller branches may die back and young plants may be killed, but in general the trees recover and put on new foliage when the rains cease. On the larger leaf of Acacia Melanoxylon, spots are produced similar to those on tea.

The attack on the tea follows the attack on the Acacias, and it is usually worst in the immediate vicinity of the latter. Infection is conveyed from the Acacias to the tea in two ways, viz., in the normal manner by means of spores blown by the wind from one plant to the other, and by the falling

Plate VIII illustrates four figures (1-4) related to leaf diseases of Cercosporaella. Figure 1 shows a leaf with large, irregular necrotic spots. Figure 2 shows a leaf with numerous small, circular necrotic spots. Figure 3 is a microscopic view of a spore with five distinct cells. Figure 4 shows a leaf with a large, irregular necrotic area along the midrib.

PLATE VIII. CERCOSPORELLA LEAF DISEASE

Several vertical wooden stakes are planted in the ground among the bushes. In the background, there are taller trees and a clear sky. The image is framed by a thin black border.

Plate IX.—GLIRICIDIA MACULATA AS A GREEN MANURE FOR TEA

FEBRUARY, 1923.]89

leaflets of the Acacia. The leaflets of Acacia decurrens are small and flat, and during wet weather they adhere to the leaves of the tea, so that the fungus passes from the one to the other. It is quite common to find Acacia leaflets fastened by mycelium to the leaves of the tea bush; indeed, that in many cases affords an easy way of identifying the disease. Naturally, this method of distribution of the disease is less likely to occur in the case of Acacia melanoxylon, which has a large leaf.

This disease has occurred on Acacias in firewood reserves and forest plantations, and has spread from them to Red Gum (Eucalyptus robusta), Karri (E. diversicolor), Grey Iron Bark (E. paniculata), etc. The Assistant Conservator of Forests, Central Division, reports that Red Gum is affected by the fungus to some extent and Grey Iron Bark to a very marked degree. The young Acacias have been killed, but, in general, the Eucalyptus has not suffered so severely. The fungus causes large spots on the Eucalyptus leaves, but they appear to resist the attack better than the leaf of tea. Up to the present, the disease has not been recorded on Red Gums planted alone or in tea.

This disease is a "wet weather" disease, and, as far as has been recorded, it occurs only up-country.

Whether it is advisable to remove Acacias where this disease occurs must depend upon individual circumstances, viz., whether the benefit derived from the Acacias compensates for the periodic damage to the tea.

BLACK ROT OF TEA.

T. PETCH, B.A., B.Sc.,

Botanist and Mycologist.

Black Rot of Tea was described in 1917 in Leaflet No. 2 of the Department of Agriculture. It was there referred to as Hypochnus sp., but in accordance with modern practice, this and similar species should be known as Corticium, and in the list of Ceylon diseases published in Bulletin 52, it was recorded as Corticium Theæ Bernard, a Corticium which attacks tea in Java and Sumatra. Specimens were submitted to PROFESSOR E. A. BURT, who kindly examined them and pronounced them distinct from Corticium koleroga, the species which causes Black Rot of coffee in South India.

During the last year, a comparative examination has been made of Thread Blights on various plants from Ceylon, India, Java, West Africa, and the West Indies. To this collection, DR. C. BERNARD has kindly contributed specimens from Sumatra and Java, including Thread Blights on tea, and from this it is clear that the species which causes Black Rot of tea in Ceylon is not Corticium Theæ. Corticium Theæ is a true Thread Blight, i.e., it forms a definite white cord running along the stem of the host plant. On

90[FEBRUARY, 1923.]

the other hand, the Ceylon Black Rot fungi are not Thread Blights ; their mycelium runs along the stem of the host plant in a very thin hyaline film which is invisible to the naked eye unless it is producing its fructification.

Owing to the difficulty of obtaining mature fructifications of these fungi, it is not easy to distinguish one from another. Investigations during the past year indicate that there are at least two species of Corticium causing Black Rot in Ceylon. One of these occurs on tea, Oxyanthus tubiflorus, Calophyllum Burmanni (Sinh. Gurukina), and Hemidesmus indicus (Sinh. Iramusu), and will probably be found to be a general parasite on jungle shrubs. The other occurs on coca (Erythroxylon Coca).

Black Rot of tea was originally discovered in the low-country, but it has since been found on tea at an elevation of nearly 6,000 ft. It may consequently be expected to be generally distributed.

GLIRICIDIA MACULATA AS A GREEN MANURE FOR TEA.

T. H. HOLLAND, Dip. Agric., Wye,

Acting Divisional Agricultural Officer, Northern.

The interest taken in Gliricidia maculata as a green manure for tea has increased and would appear to be fully justified by results at Peradeniya Experiment Station. Comparative records for a year of the loppings obtained from Gliricidia and Dadaps of the same age both planted 16 x 16 feet show that Gliricidia gave 5 loppings yielding 14.6 tons of green material against 3 loppings yielding 8.7 tons per acre from the dadaps for the same period. The Agricultural Chemist analysed loppings from these trees and found the Gliricidia loppings to be slightly richer in nitrogen. In addition an examination of the roots showed an apparently greater activity in nodule formation on the part of Gliricidia. At suitable elevations therefore the value of this plant as a green manure for tea would appear to be firmly established.

INSPECTION FOR PLANT PESTS AND DISEASES.

N. K. JARDINE, F.E.S.,

Inspector for Plant Pests and Diseases, Central.

The Branch of the Department charged with Plant Pests and Diseases Inspection was founded in 1919. It now consists of two divisions, a Central situated at the Headquarters of the Department of Agriculture, and a Southern at Avisawella.

FEBRUARY, 1923.]91

Since its inauguration, the Central division has inspected the whole of the tea-growing area of Central Province, and the greater portion of that in Uva and Sabaragamuwa east of Balangoda. Special attention has been given to the gardens of small cultivators, for their crops being a miscellany of tea, areca, coconut, jak, kitul, arrowroot, pepper, manioc, pumpkin, beans and other vegetables, insufficient attention is given to the cultivation, with the result that these gardens often become overgrown with weeds, and may become breeding grounds for the major insect pests of the Island crops. It has been a matter of patience to educate the small grower to a realization of the fact that cleanliness of land, and general cultivation will materially improve crop production. In the matter of pests it was an extremely difficult matter to get the small grower to appreciate the loss of crop sustained by insects; he seemed unable to realize that the continued presence of insect pests in the crops restricted their development and production; and the problem of restricting the insects in these semi-abandoned areas had to be tackled—not from an entomological—but from a purely agricultural standpoint. By constantly advocating good cultural methods—not for the control of insects—but for the improvement of crops, the growers became interested in the monetary return of greater production; and by keeping the crops free from weeds, the land clean, well drained, occasionally forked and the surrounding vegetation in check, the insects were automatically restricted. At times the small cultivator was found to be despondent, for he would ask what is the use of his growing garden produce for market when the boutiques, and the stands and stalls of the local markets, were often held and controlled by cliques: it meant though there was a market, he found sales for his produce only at low prices. In the tea-growing area nearly every garden grows a fairly large proportion of tea, and it was the object of the Inspectorate to endeavour to get the gardens cleaned up in order to reduce the predominance of the tea insects—especially Shot-hole Borer—these gardens were producing, and by constantly advocating clean culture many of these tea gardens are now pictures of cleanliness producing quantities of flush which is sold to local factories. Furthermore, the small grower is awake to the fact that there is an added value in possessing a clean tea-garden, he is able to plant nurseries and sell stumps at a profit, and the difficulties he experienced in selling general garden produce are no longer his, for he finds a profitable market for his tea in its place.

Plate X. shows the result after a garden has been cleaned: there are many vacancies requiring supplies. It is a good indication of the smothering effect of an abandoned miscellaneous crop.

92[FEBRUARY, 1923.

Plate XI is indicative of progress : the land has been well cared for : the relations of the owner are assisting in the cultivation of the land, and the plucking of the tea.

Plate XII shows another and smaller garden. It indicates the progress the Inspectorate is making among the small-holders. This particular garden was surrounded by rank vegetation and cheddy ; three years ago it was a mass of weeds, miscellaneous vegetables and abandoned tea. To-day it is well cultivated, well drained, regularly pruned and possesses dadaps evenly planted for shade.

Plate XIII is a view of a nursery in the centre of a large area of small gardens ; it is well laid out, clean weeded, sensibly drained and well cared for. These plants will be sold locally (being in a Shot-hole Borer infected district they cannot be sold outside the infected area) for Rs. 40 to Rs. 60 per thousand, which handsomely repays the owner for the labour expended on the cultivation of the nursery.

The question of tea-garden nurseries has always been one presenting difficulty to the Inspectorate. As stated before, the majority of tea-gardens have been for many years in a semi-abandoned condition and are to-day riddled with Shot-hole Borer, but the owners have found that by raising plants from the seed of their (shot-hole borer infested) bushes, they are able to make a profit by selling these plants before they are large enough to harbour the borer. Though the Inspectorate examines the plants before permits are issued allowing their sale, Shot-hole Borer is not to be found in them because the plants are too small to contain the beetle, but the fact remains that stock raised from perpetually infested bushes must be more liable to the attack of the borer than healthy plants raised from vigorous insect-free bushes. It is therefore pleasing to be able to record that small holders are realizing that clean culture produces greater crop, that with clean crops insects are fewer, and without insects the facilities for the disposal of their crops are easier.

The work of the division of Inspection for Plant Pests and Diseases is (1) educational, (2) advisory and (3) official. It brings to the notice of agriculturists the pests and diseases affecting their crops, the losses that are sustained thereby and encourages them to take remedial measures for their control. It advises as to the remedial and control measures that should be adopted and is responsible for taking steps, where necessary, to enforce the Regulations made for the control of the spread of shot-hole borer of tea and other pests.

RUBBER.

RUBBER.

Tapping and manurial experiments with Rubber at the Experiment Station, Peradeniya, have been continued and new experiments begun. The results of the yields of individual trees, the progeny of Henaratgoda No. 2, have been carefully examined and work carried out in regard to the formation of globular shoots and nodules.

The Rubber Research Scheme has restarted work during the year, particular attention being given to problems connected with the preservation of latex and with the use of disinfectants on tapping cuts as a prevention against bark rot and other diseases.

The first successful results at budding rubber in Ceylon were secured at Peradeniya in September, 1921. During the year 1922 lectures and demonstrations were organized and as the result many estates have a fair number of budded plants. Many others are now recording yields of individual trees for the purpose of selecting suitable mother trees.

BUDDING OF RUBBER IN CEYLON.

BY THE DIRECTOR OF AGRICULTURE.

The first success in budding rubber in Ceylon was secured by the Curator, Peradeniya Gardens in September, 1921. It was thereafter decided to send a student holding the certificate of the School of Agriculture to Java for gaining practical experience. T. V. THAMOTHERAM was selected and upon his return from Java work of budding was begun at Henaratgoda. His earlier efforts were not very successful, but later there was a steady improvement in the number of successes rising in some cases to nearly 90%. Lectures and demonstrations were organized, and coolies trained. Arrangements were made for THAMOTHERAM to visit estates, conduct demonstrations and train coolies in budding. Estates were visited by him in the Kelani Valley, Ratnapura, Kalutara, Kegalle, Matale and Moneragala. The highest recorded total successes were 66% on Alupolla, 60% on Polatagama and 58% on Gwendale.

In addition to this work, a large number of estates have carried out budding work. MR. C. E. A. DIAS sent his Superintendent of Mukalana Estate to Java to study budding, and employed a trained student from the School of Agriculture for this special work.

The following numbers of budded rubber plants are known to the Department:—Mukalana Estate, 4,600; Polatagama, 1,050; Hapugastenne, 600; Nildeniya, 396.

There is therefore no longer any doubt as to the practicability of budding rubber in Ceylon and therefore it is only necessary for estates (1).

94[FEBRUARY, 1923.

to select their mother trees on yield records, (2) plant out good nurseries on which budding may later be carried out, (3) train a subordinate staff officer or some intelligent coolies for the work of budding. No budding will be of value unless the utmost care is given to the selection of mother trees from which the buds are taken. They must be good yielders. Nurseries must also be on good soil and in good vigour if the percentage of successes is to be high. Either the Java method or patch budding may be adopted. They both give good results if the actual operations of budding are carefully carried out and the climatic conditions are favourable. The best results have so far been secured during the months of September to December.

HEVEA SELECTION.

G. BRYCE, B. Sc., Assistant Botanist and Mycologist
and

C. H. GADD, B. Sc., Assistant Mycologist.

In order to ascertain whether any considerable improvement in Hevea yields could be obtained by using seed from high-yielding mother trees when planting up areas with rubber, an investigation of the individual yields records of 161 trees derived from seed from the Henaratgoda No. 2 trees has been carried out. The parent tree is one of the best known heavy-yielding rubber trees, of which records have been published. The seed used was the result of normal pollination, and, as no attempt was made to prevent crosspollination nothing is known of the male parentage of the trees under experiment.

The plot of 161 trees was first tapped in April, 1921, when the trees were 9 years old from planting or ten years from seed. They were all tapped on the same system, viz., one cut, half circumference, sloped at 16° to the left of the vertical channel, alternate days throughout the year. For the first 10 months of tapping, i.e., April 1921 to January 1922, the best tree of the plot yielded 3,044 gms. (about 6\frac{3}{4} lb.) whereas the lowest yielded 1,136 gms.

It is evident that, making due allowance for difference in age, no single tree has a yield approximately the equivalent of the mother tree, which under a more severe tapping system gave from 107 to 234 gms. of dry rubber per tapping and over 390 lb. of dry rubber in 4 years 9 months. Though no single tree has a yield approximately equivalent to that of the mother tree, it does not necessarily follow that yield is not a heritable character.

If yield is a heritable character the influence of the ancestors beyond the immediate parents will still be experienced by the offspring. Though the female parent of the trees under review is known to be a high yielder, nothing is known of the yielding capacity of the male parent nor of that of the ancestors on both sides. It is highly improbable that all the ancestors were high yielders and the effect of these ancestors will therefore be to exert a pull back to lower yields; the greater the number of low-yielding ancestors the greater will be their influence and the greater the pull back.

FEBRUARY, 1923.]95

The test for heredity therefore becomes, not the yield performance of any single tree, but the general performance of the whole generation, and may be stated as the question, "Do the offspring from a high-yielding mother tree give on the whole greater yield, than do the offspring of other trees under the same conditions?" that is—"Are they better than the race?"

To answer this question yield records of experiments at Peradeniya, in which the conditions were similar, were examined. In three experiments suitable for comparison, the mean individual yield varied from 1606 gms. to 1312 gms. whereas the mean individual yield in the plot from selected seed was 1872 gms.

It may therefore be concluded that yield in Hevea is a heritable character and that by the elimination of the influence of low-yielding ancestors a high-yielding strain might be evolved. This would necessitate rigid selection carried on through several generations—a lengthy and expensive process—and, in view of the successful propagation of Hevea by vegetative methods, would probably prove to be an unprofitable undertaking.

From data collected during the course of the experiment an attempt was made to ascertain what characters were closely associated with yield and to what extent they were associated.

Since latex is produced in latex vessels, the yield of a tree is to some extent dependent upon the number of latex vessels in the cortex which are capable of producing latex. To count the actual numbers of latex vessels in the cortex is an impossible task, but, as the vessels are arranged in regular rows the numbers of which may be readily determined (See Plate XV) the number of latex vessel rows may be used to denote the relative number of vessels. The number of latex vessel rows varies with the individual, and the relationship between the number of rows and yield can be readily computed. The co-efficient of correlation between the number of latex vessel rows and yield was found to be .459 + .042. This means that high yields are generally associated with large numbers of rows of latex vessels, but as the correlation is not perfect, though it holds good for groups of trees it does not do so for individual trees.

The average yield of 11 trees each having 7 rows of latex vessels was 1,580 gms.

The average yield of 16 do. 9 do. vessels was 1,702 gms.

The average yield of 18 do. 11 do. vessels was 1,980 gms.

The average yield of 11 do. 13 do. vessels was 2,013 gms.

The average yield of 12 do. 15 do. vessels was 2,171 gms.

The individual tree with the highest yield, however, had only 15 rows, whereas 12 trees with a greater number of rows had smaller yields. Similarly the tree with the lowest yield had 10 rows of latex vessels, whereas there are 44 trees with a smaller number of rows and greater yields.

It has recently been suggested that this relationship between the yield of a tree and the number of latex vessel rows in the cortex might be used in practice, in that the best yielding trees might be selected by bark examination alone without having recourse to the actual measurement of yields.

96FEBRUARY, 1923.

Selection of Hevea trees is made for two purposes (1) to ascertain the poor yielders in order that they may be removed in thinning and (2) to ascertain the highest yielders for the purpose of vegetative propagation.

In the first case, viz., thinning, usually a fairly large number of trees have to be selected for removal. If a stand of 100 trees per acre is to be reduced to 90 trees per acre, this means the removal of 10 per cent. of the trees over the whole area to be thinned. Thus on a large estate a considerable number of trees would have to be removed. It would then be feasible to make the selection by cortex examination alone. The yield of the trees left after selection by cortex examination would approximate so closely to the yield which could be obtained if the selection had been made on individual yield records, that the difference is immaterial. The advantage would always be in favour of thinning by yield and not by cortex examination.

Where the selection is made to ascertain the highest yielders for vegetative propagation the case is very different. Here only a small number of trees are required, but the trees selected must undoubtedly be the very best yielders. As the relationship between the number of latex vessel rows and yield does not hold good for individual trees, it is obvious that bark examination alone is useless for the selection of individual high yielders. As already stated, the highest yielders of the trees of the experiment under consideration is 13th in position with regard to number of latex vessel rows. Consequently, if the selection of a high yielder is made from this plot by bark examination alone, 12 trees would be selected in preference to the actual highest yielder of the plot. The selection of high yielders for propagation purposes must accordingly be made from yield records and not from bark examination.

Characters other than latex vessel rows are also closely associated with yields. Of these girth and cortex thickness appear to be the most important.

Girth affects yield through the length of the tapping cut, the trees having the larger girth obviously having the longer tapping cuts. Girth, however, is also an expression of vegetative activity or vigour of growth, and in this way may be an expression of the influence on yield of this character, the more vigorously growing trees, i.e., those of greater girth, having a greater yielding capacity.

The relationship between yield and cortex thickness may also be due to the same cause, viz. greater vegetative vigour.

It may here be stated that the degrees of correlation between girth and yield, and between cortex thickness and yield, were found to be higher in the present plot than those obtained by workers elsewhere for the same characters. This difference may be due to the fact that all the trees in the present plot are offspring of one parent, whereas other workers were dealing with trees of mixed parentage. Before any recommendations can be made regarding these characters further evidence is required.

Another point of some importance ascertained during this investigation is that the yield is not directly proportionate to the length of the cut, i.e., if the cut is increased to twice its original length the yield does not become twice the original yield but something less. Consequently two cuts on quarters on opposite sides should yield more than one cut on a half.
