GLOBULAR SHOOTS AND NODULES IN HEVEA CORTEX.

G. BRYCE, B. Sc.,

Assistant Botanist and Mycologist.

Globular shoots (Plate XVI, fig. 1) are the spherical woody bodies, which are found in the cortex of Hevea stems, under leaf scars, in the fork of branches and in other places, and do not possess a core of necrotic cortical tissue such as is found in nodules. They have a cambium which produces a small amount of cortical tissue externally and wood elements internally, the latter consisting of twisted tracheids and fibres, occasionally short, tortuous vessels, cubical wood cells and medullary ray tissue, the several elements being interwoven more or less irregularly, but generally becoming more normal in the outer layers. On the inner side toward the stem wood the globular shoot frequently tapers to a point, in which the tissue consists mainly of wood fibres and tracheids; this is evidently the vestige of a former vascular connection with the stem wood. In some cases the point is completely sunk within the tissue of the globular shoot (Fig. 2), while in other cases no trace of any such connection is to be found.

The globular shoots which are found in old leaf scars are, from their position, undoubtedly derived from latent buds. Leaf scars can still be traced on the bark of trees 10 years old, and from them may be frequently obtained globular shoots to the number of 4 or 5, arranged in a horizontal row, and isolated from one another or showing varying degrees of inter-fusion. Such horizontal rows of globular shoots are never found in other portions of the cortex. The leaf scars on any part of the stem indicate the positions of leaves on the leading shoot, when it was of corresponding height, and these in turn indicate the positions on the vegetative point at which leaf primordia were laid down. It appears therefore that in the axil of a leaf primordium several shoot primordia are laid down, one or none of which may develop successfully into lateral branches. That which determines the particular primordium destined to develop successfully is not known, but when once determined its successful growth results in arrest in the development of the other primordia, which then pass into a latent condition. This reciprocal influence of organs upon one another is known as correlation of growth.

The latent primordia may persist in this state for a considerable number of years, and under any favourable change of conditions may resume growth and develop into leafy shoots. In the state of arrest they exhibit a slow growth which is limited to the laying down of wood tissue round the original primordium. GOEBEL states (Organography of Plants) that "arrest may take place earlier or later in one and the same organ, and consequently the construction of arrested organs varies in an extraordinary degree." The various shoot primordia on a vegetative point will develop normally until one primordium gets ahead of the others and causes arrest in their development. The arrested primordia, being of various ages, will also be at different stages of development, and these stages will be found in the cores of the globular shoots derived from the arrested primordia.

98FEBRUARY, 1923.

Two samples of material collected from leaf scars are seen in Figs. 3 and 4. In the former, the globular shoot is seen in section, the apex being directed towards the stem wood and the base towards the outside. The apex is the vestige of the lost connection with the stem, and from it, traversing the globular shoot, runs what may be termed the bud trace or vascular strand, now completely enclosed by layers of wood tissue (see also Fig. 1). On reaching the cortex the bud trace expands into a spherical or conical mass of small-celled meristematic tissue, which may be considered as the vegetative point of the globular shoot (Fig. 5), but in many cases it is completely absent. In fig. 4 the original primordium has not reached as advanced a developmental stage as in Fig. 3. It has, in fact, remained an undifferentiated meristem, until in the course of time, slow growth has transformed it into a globular shoot, consisting of undifferentiated wood tissue enclosing a core of compressed and lignified cells, which represent the original primordium.

Globular shoots collected from the general cortex of the stem, i.e., not from leaf scars, may be actually leaf scar material from cortex which has lost the external marks of its leaf scars, and they would then owe their origin, as in the previous cases, to latent buds. It is also possible that a formation of adventitious buds occurs in the stem cortex, and these buds, under conditions unfavourable to normal development, would also give rise to globular shoots. Globular shoots are therefore to be considered as having arisen from primordia laid down either originally at a vegetative point or later on adventitiously in the cortex.

Sections of globular shoots from the general cortex are seen in Figs. 1, 2 and 6, and 8 to 13. In Fig. 6, a vegetative point is clearly present and the primordia of organs are distinct. It is to be expected that such globular shoots, given conditions favourable to sprouting, would send out a leafy shoot as in the globular shoot in fig. 7. This last exhibited in section, a mass of wood tissue, without vascular connection with the stem and without any internal vascular strand or bud trace, the leafy shoot arising exogenously from the globular woody tissue. Primordia laid down in close proximity to one another frequently unite together, and to such union at an early development stage are to be attributed such double-cored structures as seen in Fig. 8. In some cases the original primordium develops almost completely into wood tissue as in Fig. 8, or it may be small in size as in Fig. 9, or of considerable size as in Figs. 10—13. In Figs. 10 and 11, the cells of the primordium have probably lain dormant for a considerable period, during which time they have been compressed by neighbouring, growing, cortical tissues, and have in addition acquired lignified walls, till some change to more favourable conditions has occurred, and growth has been resumed with the formation of a globular shoot. Other globular shoots exhibit a core of considerable size of more or less unchanged meristematic tissue (Figs. 12, 13). The absence of compression and lignification from the core cells of Fig. 11, would indicate that the primordium did not lie dormant for any considerable period. A similar explanation probably attaches to Fig. 13, the lignification of the core cells being either secondary or primary, i.e., occurring after or before the formation of the globular shoot.

Globular shoots are thus derived from primordia which, when first formed, suffered an arrest in development due to correlation in growth with other and more vigorously growing organs or primordia of organs.

Occasionally the exfoliation of bark results in the exposure and necrosis of the outer portions of the globular shoot. The whole globular shoot may be exfoliated with the bark, but more frequently processes of occlusion result in the covering over of the exposed area of the globular shoot. Deposition of tannin in the wood tissue is abundant around such necrosed areas of the globular shoot (see Fig. 2),

NODES.

The formation of globular shoots is, as we have seen, an example of correlation existing between organs or primordia of organs. It is otherwise with the class of structures which have been described as nodules, whose formation is due to a definite formative stimulus which differs according to the type of nodule. The nodule in Fig. 14 has originated round a mass of necrotic cortical tissue, whose presence in the living cortex has stimulated the cortex to the production of the nodule described. Another type of nodule is seen in Fig. 15 where the infiltration of latex into the adjacent intercellular spaces of the cortex has provided the stimulus to growth. The latex has escaped by the rupture of a latex vessel probably under stress due to cortical growth.

A third type of nodule seen in Fig. 16 has been obtained from wound callus only. Here the cortex has suffered rupture possibly through injury caused at the time the wound occurred, and into the internal lesion thus formed latex has flowed from the damaged latex vessels and has there coagulated. The presence of the coagulated latex in this case provides the stimulus to growth.

In the three foregoing cases the stimulus to growth has emanated from a limited area, and the growth induced has thus been correspondingly limited, being confined in effect to the occlusion of the irritant area and its removal from contact with the living cortex. The process may be regarded as the formation of an internal wound callus and the occlusion of a wound, analogous to the healing processes which occur with external wounds.

In the fourth type of nodule depicted in Fig. 17 the first symptom is a necrosis of the latex vessels, at first local, but spreading gradually from its point of origin along the latex vessel. The stimulus to growth proceeds from the necrotic latex vessel, and as this condition gradually extends along the vessel, so the cortical cells are stimulated to active cell division over an increasing area. This is the type of nodule which develops in the cortex after attacks of Brown Bast.

GENERAL.

The present classification differs somewhat from KRICK's classification of beech nodules (i.e., globular shoots) into (1) bud-, or shoot-possessing, and (2) budless or shootless. He traces his bud-, or shoot-possessing nodules back to latent buds, and states that his budless or shootless nodules are never found on leaf scars, but might from analogy with the former be assumed to be derived from adventitious buds. He argues that against this assumption are the facts that in no case was any trace of a vegetative point found, nor was the development of a shoot or bud ever observed from such a nodule. He concludes then that their method of origin is not the same as in the case of bud-possessing nodules, and that it is still unexplained.

With regard to the non-occurrence of budless nodules on leaf scars it must be pointed out that this does not hold with Hevea, as the budless nodules in Fig. 3, and Fig. 4, were obtained from leaf scars, and must therefore be considered as having originated from latent primordia. The distinction drawn by KRICK between bud-possessing and budless nodules with regard to their origin is therefore not substantiated by the conclusions reached here.

While then some explanation can be afforded for the origin of globular shoots and for the second and third type of nodule, there is as yet no clear explanation of the cause of the two types of phloem necrosis described under the first and fourth types of nodule.

100[FEBRUARY, 1923.

A ROOT DISEASE OF HEVEA.
(XYLARIA THWAITESII COOKE.)

T. PETCH, B.A., B.Sc.,

Botanist and Mycologist.

A root disease of Hevea, apparently caused by a Xylaria, was recorded in 1910, but no further occurrences were observed during the next ten years. In 1921, the same disease was found on two estates, and other instances have occurred in 1922. In all cases, the trees attacked are mature, i.e., over twelve years old.

On the affected roots, the fungus forms black, flat, irregular bands sometimes in a network, and extensive black patches or plates. The bands have not the appearance of being formed by mycelium running along the exterior of the root, as in Fomes lignosus or Rosellinia, but rather of small patches which have fused together into a continuous line. They may be fairly definite, about 2 mm. broad, but are usually broader and irregular. Part of the root may be covered with a network of these bands, the pale cortex of the root being visible in the meshes, while the remaining part is covered with a continuous black sheet. The black bands are smooth, not woolly, sometimes longitudinally ridged, and white internally. They may be up to 1 millimetre thick, but are usually much thinner.

The wood of the roots, in the early stages of the disease, does not show very marked characters. When the tree dies, the wood of the tap root may show diffuse black patches in longitudinal section, especially if split along an annual ring. If kept under suitable conditions, any cut surface of the wood develops a thin covering of white mycelium which soon turns black.

In advanced stages, usually on the lateral roots, the characteristic features of the disease are well marked and quite different from those of any other known root disease of Hevea. When the root is split longitudinally, the central region of the wood is found to be a dark brownish grey and moist, but still hard. Outside this region, the wood is somewhat decayed and drier, and pale brown or yellow brown in colour, the two parts being sometimes separated by a black line. The hardness of the wood, despite its intense discolouration, is a very striking feature. Black lines and ovals may be present in the wood, but they are not a constant feature as in Ustilina.

The inner tissues of the cortex become brown, or yellow brown, and friable, being sometimes represented only by small fragments, united by fine strands of rubber, but the external layer does not show much visible alteration.

The fructification may arise from the dead lateral roots, but in the cases hitherto observed it has generally appeared on the ground near a lateral root or near the collar of the tree. It occurs in clusters, arising from a basal mass in the soil or at ground level. From the basal mass, up to twenty fructifications may arise, forming a cluster four or five inches in diameter. In some cases three or four stout stalks arise from the basal mass, and these divide above into numerous fructifications; in other cases, all the fructifications arise from the same level. The separate fructifications are very variable in shape, either conical, cylindric, club-shaped, ovoid, or sometimes flattened laterally; they may be up to four inches high and an inch in diameter. The outer layer is pale brown or yellowish, but it usually weathers off, leaving the fructification black. The group of fructifications is a cluster of variously-shaped black clubs, not brittle but somewhat corky, and white internally.

The illustrations (Plates XIX and XX) show a cluster of clubs, developed on a diseased Hevea stump in the laboratory. At first the clubs are white, and they change colour gradually from the base upwards. These examples are longer and thinner than usual, probably owing to the conditions under which they were grown.

The fructification appears by the time the tree dies. But in all the cases hitherto found, it has not yet been mature, and, naturally, it has not been thought advisable to leave the tree standing until the fungus matured. Moreover, it is very difficult to cause a Xylaria to grow to maturity under cultivation in the laboratory; the clubs develop, but the perithecia and spores are rarely matured. And the shape of the clubs, under the conditions of laboratory cultivation, is likely to be abnormal. The fungus has, however, been grown to maturity in one case, and there is no doubt that it is a Xylaria.

In the first record of this disease, the fungus was referred to Xylaria zeylanica Berk. Since then, the type specimens of the Ceylon Xylarias in the Kew herbarium have been examined, and an account of them is now in the press. Though the type specimens of the larger Ceylon species are very meagre, and consist, in several cases, of a few fragments only, it would appear that the present species should be referred to Xylaria Thwaitesii Cooke.

THE TOXIC EFFECT OF LIME ON
FOMES LIGNOSUS KLOTZSCH.

G. BRYCE, B.Sc.

Assistant Botanist and Mycologist.

In the treatment of the root disease caused by the fungus Fomes lignosus, applications of quicklime to infected soil have been made in accordance with the general practice of using quicklime as a soil fungicide. Cases were observed where, after such applications of quicklime, the mycelium of the fungus persisted in the soil apparently unharmed. It was desirable therefore to investigate the effect of quicklime on the growth of the fungus, and generally to obtain some information as to the growth of the fungus under acid and alkaline conditions. In the work which was carried out, slaked lime was employed in place of quicklime to obviate the changes which would have occurred in the medium on the hydration of the quicklime to slaked lime. Cultural experiments were therefore carried out in which the fungus was grown on media containing varying quantities of slaked lime and on media of varying degrees of acidity and alkalinity, the effect on the fungus being obtained by measurement of the zone of growth in a given period of time.

In concentrations of less than 0.4% of slaked lime no definite toxic effect on the fungus was observed; above that point the toxic effect increases with increasing quantities of slaked lime till total inhibition of growth occurs at 1.3% of slaked lime.

Where lime was added as a saturated solution of slaked lime (i.e., lime water) a toxic effect was observable at 0.6% of slaked lime.

Carbonate of lime had no observable effect on the fungus.

In media rendered alkaline with caustic soda or caustic potash, no toxic effect was observed at concentrations up to —16 on FULLER'S scale. Beyond

102[FEBRUARY, 1923.

this point there is an increasing toxic effect but growth was still possible at —66 FULLER'S scale, though not beyond that point.

In media rendered acid with hydrochloric acid a toxic effect was observed at +16 on FULLER'S scale, beyond which total inhibition of growth occurred. With sulphuric acid a strong toxic effect was observed at +8 FULLER'S scale, and total inhibition above that point.

The fungus is therefore more sensitive to acid than to alkali; it is sensitive to considerable quantities of slaked lime, and to small quantities of lime in solution. It is indifferent to carbonate of lime.

To obtain the toxic concentration of slaked lime in the soil round one rubber tree would require an application of about 300 lb. of slaked lime. Ceylon quicklime is usually burnt coral of a very low standard of purity containing on the average only 25% of quicklime and 75% of carbonate of lime. The quantity required to produce toxic concentration in the soil would thus have to be correspondingly increased.

Quicklime when applied to soil combines with the soil water to form slaked lime, which in presence of carbon dioxide in the soil is in turn converted to carbonate of lime, which is inactive with regard to the growth of the fungus. The duration of the fungicidal effect of an application of quicklime therefore depends on the rate at which active substances are converted to inactive, i.e., the rate of change from caustic lime to carbonate of lime.

It has recently been demonstrated that caustic lime is rapidly hydrated to slaked lime in a moist atmosphere, small quantities being completely hydrated in one night. Under Ceylon conditions, it follows that quicklime when applied in estate practice, is usually already hydrated to slaked lime. Slaked lime is slightly soluble in water, and thus soil water percolating through the soil may carry slaked lime in solution down to the deeper layers. Such a solution undergoes a rapid diminution in concentration due to the formation of carbonate, and on reaching the fungus mycelium in the deeper layers of the soil would have little, if any, inhibitive effect on the fungus.

Applications of quick lime are made by forking it into the top 6 or 8 inches of soil. It has also been demonstrated recently that the maximum conversion of quicklime to carbonate of lime (or carbonation) in the top 6 inches of soil occurs within 5 days after the application in the case of quicklime (80% caustic lime) in applications of 2 tons per acre. With heavier applications the maximum carbonation takes longer. The process of carbonation, however, occurs in such a way that the fungicidal value of the slaked lime rapidly falls to zero before complete carbonation has taken place. A film of carbonate of lime is formed round the particles or lumps of slaked lime, and this acts as a protective crust which retards the conversion of the interior to carbonate. To all intents and purposes, as regards the fungicidal value of slaked lime on Fomes lignosus, as soon as this crust is formed the lime is equivalent to carbonate of lime and its value accordingly is nil.

Fomes lignosus mycelium is sensitive to acid conditions and is somewhat more resistant to alkaline conditions. The fungicidal value of an application of quicklime depends on the proportion of caustic lime in it, and on the rate of conversion to carbonate. In Ceylon quicklime, the proportion of caustic lime is low, and the fungicidal value with regard to Fomes lignosus is ephemeral owing to rapid carbonation. The after-effects of applications of quicklime are to render the soil more alkaline, and thus to produce, particularly in acid soils, conditions more favourable to the fungus. Under these circumstances the application of quicklime to soil to inhibit growth of Fomes lignosus mycelium is not to be recommended, and attention should be concentrated on the other measures adopted in the treatment of this disease.

See also: BULLETIN OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE, No. 64.

COCONUTS.

The manurial experiments with coconuts at the Chilaw Trial Ground have been continued and work has been begun on the investigation of coconut varieties. A number of distinct varieties have been carefully examined and selected areas of such varieties have been planted out for further investigation.

Insect pests of coconuts have received careful attention throughout the year. Considerable damage has been done in Batticaloa South by the Coconut caterpillar (Nephantis serinopa) and other districts in which this pest has occurred during the past year are warned that it is necessary to prevent any increase if serious damage is to be avoided.

Investigations into the nut fall of coconuts have been made and a comparison study of the grey blights of coconuts and tea carried out.

SOME INSECT PESTS OF THE COCONUT PALM.

J. C. HUTSON, B.A., Ph. D.,

Entomologist.

During the past two years considerable attention has been given to the insect pests of coconuts by the Entomological Division, and information about the three most important pests has been published. The following notes are intended mainly to supplement the information contained in the above publications.

THE COCONUT CATERPILLAR.

Nephantis serinopa.

It was stated in Leaflet No. 20 and in Bulletin No. 58 that so far as was known this caterpillar was a pest of the coastal districts and was not known to occur on inland coconut areas. Since the above was written this pest has been found in small numbers in the Kurunegala District of the North-Western Province and in the Bibile District of the Province of Uva. It is not improbable that further inspection will disclose the presence of this caterpillar in other inland coconut areas. All coconut planters in inland districts should therefore be on the look-out for this pest, and should report its presence immediately to the Department of Agriculture.

In this connection it should be mentioned that there are other species of caterpillars found on coconut leaves which may be mistaken for Nephantis, but none of these can be considered a pest of living healthy palms since they are only known to feed on dead palm leaves and occasionally on cadjans. They appear to be present in most coconut districts

104[FEBRUARY, 1923]

wherever dead leaves are left hanging on the palms or leaves are withering from various causes, such as Nephantis attack, disease or natural decay. The two common species are Herculia nigrivilla and Erechthias pachygramma.

Of these caterpillars Herculia is the one which may be easily taken for Nephantis, since it is usually found in old, dead, rolled up leaflets killed by Nephantis and some times occupies the abandoned Nephantis galleries. The full-grown Herculia larva is about an inch long with a very dark head marked with a red patch in the centre. The body is dark brown mottled with blackish markings along the sides, slender and almost cylindrical and does not taper towards the hinder end, as does the body of a Nephantis larva. The Herculia caterpillars eat holes in the dead leaves and help to produce the almost complete striping of the leaflets which is sometimes noticed after a bad attack of Nephantis. The weathering effects of wind and rain following after attacks by these caterpillars serves to intensify this ragged and tattered appearance of the leaflets.

The Erechthias larva is small, very slender, dirty white with a pale brown head. It is about half an inch long when full-grown, and the alimentary tract is usually visible through the transparent skin as an irregular dark patch along the middle of the body. The caterpillars of both Herculia and Erechthias are very active and move rapidly backwards or forwards when disturbed. Both live under a loosely woven webbing sometimes thinly covered with a few particles of frass, but there is no attempt to make a compact webbed gallery, such as that constructed by Nephantis. They may both be sometimes found occupying old Nephantis galleries. The full-grown Herculia larvæ eat holes in the leaves while the caterpillars of Erechthias rarely do more than nibble away at the leaf surface. It is hoped to publish shortly a fuller account of these and other caterpillars which may be confused with Nephantis, giving illustrations of the different stages and other details which may enable the coconut planter to distinguish them from Nephantis. In all cases where the cultivator is in doubt it is advisable to submit specimens of the affected leaflets to the Entomologist.

NOTES ON CONTROL MEASURES FOR NEPHANTIS.

Cutting and burning of infested leaves:—This measure has had a thorough trial during the past year throughout the infested coconut areas in the Batticaloa district, and a systematic campaign has been carried out under the direction of the local Plant Pest Board and their inspectors, with the assistance of the local Agricultural Instructors of the Department of Agriculture.

It may be said that this is quite an effective means of controlling the pest, provided that it is applied thoroughly during the early stages of an outbreak when the number of infested leaves, or portions of leaves, to be removed and burnt is comparatively small. Even under such simple conditions considerable difficulty has been experienced in getting a certain section of the coconut planters, usually the smaller proprietors, to carry out the prescribed regulations with any degree of regularity and efficiency. There is a dangerous tendency on the part of some estates gardens, which are only moderately infested, to relax their efforts in cutting and burning the infested leaves or portions of leaves for various reasons. Some plead

FEBRUARY, 1923.]105

a shortage of climbing coolies, some complain of the difficulty of cutting and burning the leaves during wet weather, others are convinced that the heavy rains kill off the pest, others have an idea that the partially attacked leaves no longer continue to breed caterpillars, others again are frankly indifferent or are inclined to regard the outbreak of any plant pest or disease as some supernatural visitation which they are fated to undergo and which they are powerless to control.

The cutting and burning of infested leaves may not be practicable during exceptionally heavy rains or on flooded portions of estates, but ordinarily there are fine periods on most days during the monsoon when the control work can be done. Again, a certain number of the immature stages of the pest are doubtless killed off by disease during wet weather or may die after days of continuous rain, but it cannot be expected that the climatic conditions will check an outbreak, since there will usually be enough survivors left to carry on after the rains are over unless control measures are applied until the pest has been reduced to the minimum. With reference to the belief that partially attacked leaves no longer breed the pest it can be asserted that a careful examination of such leaves in many cases reveals the presence of fresh egg-masses and healthy caterpillars and cocoons of Nephantis serinopa. This indicates that partially attacked leaves still serve an attraction for egg-laying Nephantis moths to deposit their eggs among the frass covering the old larval galleries and cocoons. Moreover in the absence of effective parasitic or other natural control, the caterpillar pest can go on feeding and developing so long as there is any green portion of the actual leaf surface remaining. All partially attacked leaves or portions of leaves, therefore, should be removed and burnt.

As stated above, the cutting and burning of infested leaves is quite a practicable and effective method of checking Nephantis in the early stages of an outbreak, but experience has shown that the application of this measure becomes a practical impossibility in cases where the infested area covers hundreds of acres. In certain coconut areas in the Batticaloa district this caterpillar pest has gradually spread over large areas and has continued to be prevalent for considerably over a year. In the opinion of the writer this situation has arisen mainly owing to two factors (1) the steady reduction in the numbers of the local parasites of Nephantis as a result of the attacks of hyperparasites, and (2) the occurrence of unusually long periods of drought during the past two years and the consequent absence of fungoid and other diseases which help to check the caterpillar to some extent during wet weather.

NATURAL ENEMIES OF THE COCONUT CATERPILLAR

It was stated in a previous publication that the Coconut Caterpillar under normal conditions is periodically controlled by its natural enemies, mainly small parasitic wasps and flies. This periodic control has been maintained fairly consistently on the Western side of the Island, and so far as can be ascertained up to the present time this periodic control is due mainly to damp climatic conditions and the presence of a very small parasitic wasp, as yet only partly identified.* This parasite emerges in

* Specimens submitted to the British Museum have been put under the Hymenopterous family Eulophidae, genus incert.

106[FEBRUARY, 1923.

large numbers from the pupæ of Nephantis and is apparently a true parasite of this pest. Other parasites of the caterpillar are also present in smaller numbers, and on the whole the natural control of Nephantis on the Western side of the island seems to be comparatively simple.

In the Batticaloa district of the Eastern Province the relations between the coconut caterpillar and its natural enemies are somewhat more complicated. The whole question of the parasitic control of this pest has received considerable attention in that district during the past eighteen months. The point of greatest interest is the apparent complete absence from the Batticaloa district of the small Eulophid parasite which is so prevalent on the West of Ceylon. The examination of hundreds of Nephantis caterpillars and pupæ has failed to disclose the slightest trace of this parasite. There are, however, no lack of other parasites of Nephantis in the Batticaloa district, but unfortunately in certain localities some of these parasites are themselves attacked by other parasites, known as hyperparasites, with the result that their numbers are reduced and their efficiency, in controlling the caterpillar, is thereby weakened.

Under the circumstances it was thought advisable that an attempt should be made to introduce the Eulophid parasite from the Western side of the island, and therefore during the past year several small consignments of live parasites were sent to the Batticaloa district and liberated on caterpillar infested palms. Recent examinations have indicated that these parasites have probably failed to establish themselves, since no trace of them could be found in any of the various places of liberation.

The whole problem of the parasitic control of Nephantis requires considerable further study and the transference of the small parasites from one side of the island to the other should be carried out under conditions which give the parasites every chance of becoming established. This would probably necessitate the running of a temporary breeding station in some Nephantis area on the Western side of the island from which the parasitised Nephantis pupæ could be forwarded direct to the Batticaloa district for immediate liberation in carefully selected areas.

SPRAYING EXPERIMENTS.

Owing to the kindness of MR. T. S. GREEN of Tirrukovil Estate, Akkaraipattu, Eastern Province, these experiments were carried out on that estate on about half an acre of young palms which were being moderately attacked by the caterpillar. Since no suitable Arsenate of Lead was available it was necessary to use Paris Green. The spray was applied at the rate of 1 cz. Paris Green to 10 gallons of water to which about 3 oz. of lime had been added. The Holder-Harriden 3 gallon Knapsack machine gave fairly good results, but was an old model and had to be shaken up frequently so as to maintain an even distribution of the poison. Care was taken to apply the poison thoroughly to the underside of the leaflet, since Nephantis feeds only on the undersurface and does not eat completely through the leaf. The experiments were carried out by the Senior Agricultural Instructor of the Eastern Province and one of his assistants.

In the first small experiment 7 young infested palms were sprayed thoroughly and the adjacent infested row was left untreated as a control. The spray causes some of the caterpillars to drop to the ground where

they are usually carried off by ants. Complete figures are not available at the present time, but it may be said that the pest was controlled on the treated palms, which remained practically free of re-infestation so long as the poison was present in sufficient quantity. After a time the sprayed palms were slightly attacked, but the pest did not succeed in developing to any extent. The caterpillars developed normally on the controls.

In the second experiment three small blocks each consisting of 10 young moderately infested palms were selected. Block A. was sprayed as in the first experiment, while Block B. was first of all completely cleared of all traces of the pest and then sprayed to ascertain whether spraying would serve as a preventive from fresh attack. Block C. was left untouched and unsprayed as a control to A, though not to B, which apparently had no control. In A the pest was controlled, and in B the palms remained practically free from re-infestation, while in C. the caterpillars developed normally, though not to any serious extent.

While the above experiments are done on too small a scale to be of any real value and complete figures are not available at the present time, still it may be said that they gave positive results in favour of the sprayed trees. Under Ceylon conditions it would only be practicable to spray young palms, say up to 5 or 6 years old, and it so happens that palms of this age are rarely attacked to any serious extent. It is quite a simple matter to have these periodically examined and the caterpillars and webbing removed by hand. Although it is quite possible to spray fairly tall coconut palms further experiments are necessary in order to ascertain if the caterpillar can be controlled economically by this means.

THE RHINOCEROS BEETLE AND THE RED WEEVIL,

These two serious beetle pests continue to be more or less prevalent in all coconut areas, but there is evidence that considerable interest is being taken to reduce their numbers. It is essential that all measures of control should be directed along the right lines, having due regard to the breeding habits of these two pests, otherwise the results may be the exact opposite to what was intended. In this connection the two following cases, out of many which have come under the notice of the writer, may be of interest.

Estate A. had been neglected for many years and had suffered severely from the combined attacks of the coconut caterpillar and the two beetle pests. The result was that many palms had died and had been left standing or had been cut down so as to leave 2 feet of stump above ground. The estate then changed hands and the new manager decided to try and clean up the dead area. The remaining dead trees were cut down in the usual way and the trunks were cut into lengths and left exposed in long shallow trenches to rot and provide humus for the impoverished soil. Incidentally, had the Superintendent decided to go in for breeding Black Beetle he could hardly have chosen a better method. Had all the dead trees and stumps been cut down to ground level and covered over with soil to a depth of 6 or 8 inches and had the logs in the trenches been similarly protected there would have been no exposed decaying material in which the beetle could breed. The most effective method, however, and the safest in the end, would have been to root out all the stumps and burn these along with the piled up logs.

108[FEBRUARY, 1923.

Estate B. had occasion to adopt the practice of collecting all fallen leaves, husks and decayed logs and mulching these at the time of manuring in open trenches or around the bases of the palms. This may be an excellent scheme from the agricultural point of view but entomologically speaking it is a highly dangerous practice. The collection of Black Beetle had been systematically carried out on this estate for some time, and yielded well under 100 beetles a month. Within six months after the adoption of the above system of mulching it was found that the numbers of the beetle were increasing. The monthly toll ran into hundreds and then into thousands. This rapid increase of the Beetle was due mainly to the system of open trenching and mulching of decaying refuse. The result was that thousands of palms were being exposed to attacks in the crowns by the Beetle and the subsequent injury by the Red Weevil. The presence of any young coconut area in the neighbourhood would serve as a further attraction to these two pests and would result in the destruction of hundreds of young palms by Red Weevil following on Black Beetle injury.

It will be seen from the above instances that there are certain estate practices, such as open trenching and mulching, which, however sound agriculturally, may be directly responsible for the breeding of the Black Beetle in thousands and in some cases may lead to a marked increase in the numbers of the Red Weevil.

The method of disposing of dead trees is to have these rooted up, cut up into suitable lengths and burnt in large piles built up over a shallow square or oblong cavity dug in the ground, so that a powerful draught is created.* All old stumps can be added to the pyre. The fallen leaves and other coconut refuse should be collected into small heaps throughout the estate and burnt every two months. This could be done after the picking of nuts.

SOME MINOR INSECT PESTS OF COCONUTS.

The Spotted Locust (Aularches miliaris) has several times during the last two years been reported as partially defoliating young coconut palms. This damage has usually occurred in fields which have been allowed to become overrun with thick grass and weeds, or in gardens where a variety of crops, including coconuts, is being grown on the same plot of land. The young locusts when in the wingless stage usually cluster together in large masses on the ground or on low branches and can be beaten down or collected into sacks and crushed or submerged in water.

In addition to the Coconut caterpillar (Nephantis serinopa) there are at least three other caterpillars which are occasionally found in small numbers eating the green leaves of coconut palms.

The "Bagworm" (Psyche albipes) covers itself with a case formed of small pieces of leaf and eats irregular holes in the leaflets, or sometimes eats away portions of the leaflets until only the midrib remains. The cases should be collected and destroyed.

The "Blue-striped Nettle-grub" (Parasa lepidula) sometimes feeds on the leaflets, at first nibbling away small portions of the leaf surface and later eating right through the leaf. The egg-shaped cocoons are sometimes seen attached to the leaves.

The Hesperid caterpillar, Gangara thysis, occasionally attacks the leaves, but cannot be considered a pest.

Scale insects :—There are several species of scale insects which are found on the leaves of coconut palms, but the only species which calls for any mention here is the "Coconut Scale," sometimes known as the "Transparent Coconut scale" (Aspidiotus destructor). This scale is not the serious pest in Ceylon that it is in some other countries, as it seems to be controlled by parasites and by fungous diseases. The female scale is pale yellow and is usually seen as a minute yellowish spot under a thin papery covering. These scales are sometimes clustered so thickly on the underside of the leaves as to form a complete scurfy layer over the leaf surface. The upper surface of attacked leaves is usually marked with small yellowish spots which coalesce in a bad attack, giving the whole leaf a yellowish appearance, but this yellowing of the leaves may also be due to other causes. Small palms are sometimes attacked on the lower leaves, which can either be sprayed with kerosene emulsion, or removed and burnt. Attention to drainage, cultivation and manuring will maintain the vigour of the palms and help to keep down scale attack.

L. S. BERTUS.

Assistant to the Botanist and Mycologist.

It is well-known that Pestalozzia causes Grey Blight on tea and coconut leaves and a study of the fungus has been made to ascertain the identity of the species that affects each of them.

Typical Pestalozzia spores on tea and coconut are spindle-shaped or fusiform bodies, divided by four septa into a row of five cells of which the three central are pale-brown and the terminal cells hyaline. The apical hyaline cell is crested with hyaline cilia, or thread-like appendages, which vary in number from one to four. To the lower hyaline cell is usually attached a pedicel, or stalk, on which the spore is borne. Abnormalities occur in the size of the spore and the number of coloured cells. (Plate XXIV). The mean dimensions given below were derived from measurements of fifty spores in each case.

PESTALOZZIA ON COCONUT.

Growth in culture.—Spores were grown in pure culture in Maize meal agar, French-bean agar and Quaker Oat agar. The chief feature of growth in all these three media is the collecting together of hyphæ to form tufts. These tufts are originally white in colour and later take on a pinkish tinge. As the fungus advances in age, black pustules of spores are seen to arise from the centre of each of these tufts. In old cultures, the white mycelial growth on the medium was covered with these little black pustules in abundance. In the French-bean and Oat media a stroma is formed in the culture medium, while in the maize meal instead of a stroma a network of loose hyphæ, or a pseudo-stroma is present. In all the three media, spores

110[FEBRUARY, 1923.

that appear to be in pustules are found to originate in distinct pycnidia. Pycnidia are present in large numbers on the loose mycelium growing on the medium and are of diverse shapes and sizes. They are spherical, laterally oval, flask-shaped, rectangular, spheroidal, globose, oval, rectangular-oval, cone-shaped, etc. They consist of a pseudo-parenchymatous wall, yellowish in colour, not possessing ostiolum, and occur singly or in groups very often having common walls. Spores are liberated by a rupture of the wall at any point. In the stroma formed in the French-bean and Oat agar, and in the pseudo stroma in the maize meal, a few spherical or spheroidal pycnidia are seen, embedded partly or completely. Spores were seen liberated from these by a rupture of the wall to the exterior, or into the stroma or culture medium. In the maize meal, a few pycnidia are present, embedded in the culture medium, liberating spores by a break in the wall into the culture medium. Below is a table giving the dimensions of the spores in nature in thousandths of a millimeter and the various culture media.

Media Range of length including terminal hyaline cells Mean Length Range of length of the coloured cells Mean Length Range in width Mean width
Leaves in nature - 15 to 25 20.2 12-16 13.8 5.7 5.7
French-Bean agar - 15 to 22 18.7 10-15 12 5.6 5.4
Oat agar - 15 to 23 18.8 10-15 12 5.7 5.5
Maize Meal agar - 15 to 23 18.5 10-15 12 5.7 5.7

In all the media the cilia are very short, vary in number from 1 to 3, and are not knobbed. They are usually between 2 to 5 thousandths of a millimeter in length, rarely reaching 10 to 12. In some spores the pedicel is not present; when present it is generally between 1 and 3 thousandths of a millimeter long, rarely attaining 4 or 5 in length. Attempts were made to cause the cilia to knob by growing the fungus on tea and coconut leaves, sterilised by boiling, in Roux tubes, but no success was attained. A peculiarity about this Pestalozzia is that the cilia are shorter in culture than in nature, and that although the cilia are knobbed in nature, they are never knobbed in culture.

The base of a coconut petiole suspected to be attached by Phytophthora was incubated, and pustules of Pestalozzia spores were hatched out corresponding in dimensions with the spores in culture, all possessing short cilia and not knobbed. The spores behaved in the various culture media as those obtained from the leaf.

PESTALOZZIA ON TEA,

Growth in culture.—Spores were grown in pure culture in Maize meal agar, French-bean agar and Quaker Oat agar. The chief feature in all the three media is the rich fluffy growth of aerial hyphæ which ultimately forms into a thick, heavy, compact felt of white hyphæ lying on the medium. No formation of tufts of hyphæ occurs. Another feature is the production of spores on loose hyphæ. In the French-bean agar, either a continuous white band of hyphæ, smooth and heavy in appearance, is formed or individual bands of hyphæ occur, the intervening spaces of which become filled up with aerial hyphæ, in time forming a continuous felt. on loose hyphæ on the sides of the glass and on the medium. Small blackish or greyish protuberances appear in the felted layer, giving rise to pustules of spores. Underneath the felt, too, little black bodies are scattered about liberating spores. A stroma was present in the culture medium. In the Maize meal puffs of ærial hyphæ grow out at regular intervals, and with age some of the intervening spaces between the puffs become filled up with ærial hyphæ, so that the whole growth presents a woolly appearance. In time the submerged hyphæ of the woolly puffs appear greyish or blackish, due to the production of a mass of spores on the loose hyphæ. In some tubes black bodies appeared producing pustules of spores. Hyphæ ascended the sides of the glass and bore spores in large quantities. A pseudo-stroma was present in the medium. In the Oat agar growth was fast and vigorous, and the whole surface of the medium was overrun in a few days with ærial woolly hyphæ. Hyphæ ascended the sides of the glass so as to almost choke the tube and bore spores in abundance. In some tubes black masses of spores were seen issuing in pustule form. A stroma was present in the culture. In the French-bean, the blackish protuberances which were present in the felted layer, and the small black bodies which were scattered about underneath this layer are pycnidia and pseudo-parenchymatous stromata containing pycnidial cavities. They are present on the stroma, or embedded in the stroma partly or completely. Few pycnidia were present on the loose felt on the medium. In the Maize meal the black bodies which were seen extruding spores were all pycnidia, on or partly embedded in the pseudo-stroma. The pustules of spores that appeared in the Oat agar were liberated from pycnidia and pseudo-parenchymatous stromata containing pycnidial cavities. The stromatic bodies containing the pycnidial cavities are found on the stroma. The pycnidia are present in the stroma, or on the stroma, a few in the felt of mycelium on the medium, and in the culture medium. In all the three media the pycnidia were mainly present on the stroma or pseudo-stroma and very few in the felt on the medium. They were of various shapes and sizes, completely enclosed by a pseudo-parenchymatous wall, and had no ostiolum, the spores being liberated by a rupture of the wall anywhere. A peculiarity about the pycnidia was the liberation of spores in a large number of cases into the stroma or culture medium by a rupture of the wall at the base, forming a mass of mature spores in a cavity in the stroma or medium as the case may be.

In all the three media the spores possessed very long cilia which varied in length up to 40 thousandths of a millimeter. They varied in number

112[FEBRUARY, 1923.

from 2 to 4. The majority of spores in culture had the cilia knobbed, but many were not knobbed. These spores with unknobbed cilia, when transferred to tea or coconut leaves, sterilized by boiling in a Roux tube, readily formed knobs. The length of the pedicel varied from 3 to 10 thousandths of a millimeter.

MAIN DIFFERENCES BETWEEN THE TWO SPECIES.

The spores of the species on coconut were distinctly smaller than those of the species on tea. In culture the mycelial growth was characterized by the formation of tufts of hyphæ, producing spores from pycnidia in pustule form so as to cover the whole surface of the medium with innumerable small masses of black pustules. Pycnidia were produced in abundance on the loose mycelium on the medium, but in a very poor quantity in the stroma found in the culture medium. The spores which had cilia knobbed in nature, when once taken into culture, could not be made to knob again. The cilia too became short in culture.

The spores of the species on tea were on the average larger than those of the species on coconut. In culture the mycelial growth was characterized by a rich fluffy growth of ærial hyphæ eventually resulting in the formation of a compact, heavy, white felt, lying on the medium. Spores were also produced in large quantities on loose hyphæ. The pustules of spores which were extruded from pycnidia or pseudo-parenchymatous stromata were very much larger than those of the coconut and occurred in much smaller numbers. Pycnidia and pseudo-parenchymatous stromata were mainly found in the stroma formed in the culture medium. Few pycnidia were present on the loose mycelium. The spores which had cilia without knobs in culture could be readily made to produce knobs by growing them on sterilized tea or coconut leaves, whereas the coconut Pestalozzia refused to produce knobs on these substrata. The cilia grew very long in culture. These differences appear to be sufficient to maintain the two species distinct.

There is no doubt that the Ceylon species on the coconut leaf is Pestalozzia palmarum Cooke. The species on tea is Pestalozzia Theæ Sawada.

A POSSIBLE PHYSIOLOGICAL CAUSE OF
"NUT FALL" OF COCONUTS.

C. H. GADD, B.Sc.,

Assistant Mycologist.

The fall of nearly full grown, but immature, nuts from the coconut palm has hitherto been regarded as being primarily due to fungus attacks. The failure to find a causative organism always associated with the disease has given rise to the view that its cause may in some cases be purely mechanical, or due to adverse physiological or environmental conditions.

The discovery that a species of Phytophthora was usually present on fallen nuts led to the suggestion that the disease might be prevented by the application of a fungicide such as Bordeaux mixture. Experiments in 1921 to determine the value of this spray as a preventive of nut fall gave negative results. The number of fallen, but immature, nuts in the sprayed

FEBRUARY, 1923.]113

plot was approximately equal to that in the unsprayed plot. The climatic conditions of that year were unfavourable to the growth of the fungus and the pathogenic organism was not found on any of the fallen nuts examined from either plot. In view of the absence of a pathogenic organism it became evident that causes other than fungus attack might lead to a similar diseased condition.

A serious case of fruit fall of coconuts before maturity is reported from Indo-China, in December, 1920. The appearance of the fruit suggested a parasitic disease, but comparative analyses of the soils of various plots led to the conclusion that the fundamental cause was the insufficient nourishment of the roots, which was remedied by the application of nitrogenous manures. The description of the disease and the presence of certain organisms on the fallen fruits suggests the condition known in Ceylon as "Nut fall." Observations in Ceylon, however, do not lead to the same conclusion, viz., that its cause is an insufficiency of nitrogenous manures. Nut fall in Ceylon is known to occur in plots which are regularly and liberally manured, whereas it is absent from other plots which rarely receive any manurial treatment.

The discovery that the abscission of fruits of Juglans californica quercina is due to water deficit beyond a certain limit, and that a similar cause also leads to the fall of Citrus fruits, may throw some light on the problem of nut fall of coconuts in Ceylon.

A water deficit has already been shown to affect the setting of young coconut fruits in Ceylon. Following a prolonged period of drought, there is an increased fall of the female flowers, or "button nuts," as they are frequently termed. The fall of such "buttons" had previously been attributed mainly to the lack of fertilization, but, undoubtedly, other factors besides fertilization play an important part in bringing this about. The June drop of peaches in Delaware was generally attributed to incomplete fertilization, but an examination of a large amount of cytological material gave conclusive evidence that June drop was not the result of improper fertilization but of other physiological factors. It has also been ascertained that moisture is an important factor in the setting of tomato fruits, and that by an efficient conservation of soil moisture "blossom drop" of tomatoes can be reduced.

The above, together with the fact that an increase of button fall of coconuts follows a period of drought, leads to the conclusion that the abscission of youngest fruits may be caused by a deficit of soil moisture beyond a certain limit. That a similar cause may lead to the abscission of larger grown fruits is worthy of consideration.

114[FEBRUARY, 1923.

Nut fall of coconuts in Ceylon occurs principally during the rains of north-east monsoon. Nut fall therefore occurs, not when there is a deficit of moisture, but during the wettest times of the year. This on the face of it would appear to negative any idea that a deficit of soil water is a contributory cause of nut fall.

The root system of the coconut palm, however, is peculiar in many respects. The roots have no root hairs, and water can be absorbed only through the epidermis of a short region of the root immediately behind the root tip. The remainder of the root is covered by a rigid shell, called a hypodermis, which is impermeable to water. When the growth of the roots is checked by dryness or other unfavourable condition of the soil, the hypodermis is formed nearer to the tip and ultimately no absorbing zone at all is left. Coconut roots are therefore ill adapted to the absorption of large quantities of water. In nature, no roots will grow to any distance into water, nor into a level of soil where water stands, and a rise in the water level ultimately kills the submerged roots.

The hypodermis is impermeable not only to water but also to air. The roots are to a large extent dependent on special breathing organs or Pneumatophores for their air supply. These breathing organs are specialised roots and their structure is such that open ærial communication is maintained through the pneumatophore to the internal tissues of the parent root. Consequently the coconut requires an open, well-ærated soil, and any tendency towards water-logging will interfere with the air supply to the root. An excess of water in the soil may therefore seriously interfere with the vital processes of the roots, leading to a reduced absorption of water and ultimately to the death of the roots. This in effect becomes equivalent to an actual water shortage.

Nut fall of coconuts occurs principally in the Galagedara side of the Kurunegala district, and is there most prevalent during the rains of the north-east monsoon. The soil is a heavy loam which becomes very hard during the dry weather, but is sticky, with a tendency towards water logging, during heavy rains. The soil conditions during heavy rains may become deleterious to the coconut roots and thus lead to the premature dropping of the fruit.

Climatic conditions during the north-east monsoon are favourable for fungus growth, so, at this season, nut fall as caused by pathogenic organisms may be expected to be prevalent. Nut fall, however, frequently occurs at this time even in the absence of any causative fungus. In view of the above it is suggested that heavy rainfall may produce conditions of the soil adverse to the healthy growth of the root system of coconut palms. This, without the intervention of any pathogenic organism, may result in the abscission of immature fruits.

See also: BULLETIN OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE, No. 53.

FEBRUARY, 1923.]115

PADDY.

Selection work so as to provide pure-line seed is being carried out at Anuradhapura and Peradeniya Experiment Stations and the results up to date are most encouraging. Seed of various selected varieties will shortly be available for trial in the different districts of the Colony and arrangements for small preliminary trials have been made for the Maha season 1922-23.

Manurial trials have been carried out in all parts of the Colony, and the benefit that accrue from the applications of green manures and phosphates have been clearly demonstrated.

Transplanting has also been encouraged and competitions arranged to stimulate the improvement of cultivation and the increase of yields from lands already under paddy.

The hulling of paddy by machinery is being carried on at Ambalantota, Anuradhapura Jail and Jaffna. The erection of the Mill by DR. W. A. DE SILVA on Sravasti Estate, Ratmale, was completed during the year and its work should be watched with interest.

SELECTION OF PURE LINE SEED PADDY.

R. O. ILIFFE, M.A.,

Economic Botanist.

During the calendar year the main work has still been confined to the selection and improvement of our Ceylon paddies. Certain important developments have been sanctioned, and these may be treated in brief before describing the main routine.

The range of paddy varieties under test has been increased by the inclusion of types from the North-Central and Central Provinces. The routine samples, on which 2-3 years' work has been done, include, for the Maha season, paddies of the Mawi and Samba groups; for the Yala season, paddies of the Bala Wi, Danahala, Illankalayan, Heenati and Murunkan groups, with more advanced work on certain Suwanda-el, Madoluwa and Kalupanniti types. To these have been added, for Maha, Hatial, Tillanayakam, Illankalayan, Murungan, Anaikodan; for Yala eight types taken from salty or brackish areas, and a large collection of hill paddies.

Arrangements have been made to study certain cultural and growth problems in the field, and, as accommodation is provided, in the laboratory. Experiments with an Indian seed drill, and its connected implements for covering the seed, and for inter-cultivation in the growing crop, are formulated. The possibilities of dry preparation of a seed bed, with, perhaps,

116[FEBRUARY 1923.

light motor traction, are being studied for the drier and flatter areas, but untimely rain has so far prevented an actual trial. Amongst growth problems to be considered are the optimal length of time in the nurseries; the factors affecting tillering, and the results of differences in tillering capacity; the advantages of transplanting, etc. An experiment begun by the late Divisional Agricultural Officer, Northern Division, has been elaborated to show the relative merits of broadcasting, transplanting, sowing germinated seed in drill rows, and broadcasting, but thinning out at an early stage.

Until this year, all work had been carried out at the Experiment Stations at Anuradhapura and Peradeniya. A scheme has been approved and is now in practice for testing pure seed in different districts. Eight stations were selected, and each was to receive 5 varieties in 2 bushel lots. Owing to abnormal drought and other conditions, only 23 Pure Line Selections could be sown. Six trial grounds have been laid out, and this is a beginning of what will become important work. These trials form a link between experiment and practice. They were initiated to test, in the hands of the cultivator, the performance of paddies which gave good results at the Experiment Stations. It is not expected that a variety giving a good yield at Anuradhapura, will necessarily do well at, say, Ratnapura, and before quasi-improved seed is distributed, it is first necessary to know its capabilities in the new district, whilst still in the hands of the Department.

At the same time as the main divisional sowings at Peradeniya, samples of eight pure lines were put down at the School of Tropical Agriculture, Peradeniya. These will serve as a check on those grown at the Experiment Station, and will be used for the instruction of the students. At Anuradhapura, the work has been handicapped by the lack of a suitable place for storage of grain, but the building of a store, a small field laboratory, a threshing floor, and stack yard, have been sanctioned.

At both stations the effects of green, and other, manures are being tried, but it is found difficult to establish a green crop under marshy conditions which do not yield to surface drainage.

Enough has been said to point the general policy adopted and a few general remarks on the methods in use will serve to indicate the relation of policy to practice.

In the first place, it has to be decided whether better results will accrue from improving existing types, or by building up new, or hybrid, plants having a combination of good characters. At first sight, the latter method sounds attractive, but it contains many pitfalls, and results are by no means sure. A large staff, with constant supervision, is required before crossing work on a large scale can effectively be carried out. For other reasons besides, it became obvious that the most good in the shortest time could be effected by the weeding out of the lighter yielding existing paddies, and proper selection amongst the better types. Consequently, a series of Pure Line cultures has been built up, beginning at first with a small number of varieties, which, when sufficiently tested, will give place to others in the order of importance.

To review briefly the theory of work; the progeny of the seed of one parent plant may be uniform, or individuals may vary in certain

characteristics. If it is uniform, it is reasonable to expect, according to observation, that it will remain uniform as long as it is uncontaminated by cross-pollination with other types. If it is tested in the third season and found to agree entirely with its parent and grand-parent, the assumption of the previous year is justified, and a Pure line culture is established. If time is of value, the seed which gives a miscellaneous progeny must be at once discarded, as only a third years' trial, under very careful scrutiny, will reveal those characters which may be said to be fixed. In the case of paddy, as with all other plants which are naturally self-pollinated, the Pure Line culture is easy to establish.

Imagine, then, a plant which is selected from a field, for propagation as a heavy yielder, or as being different from another, or for some other reason. The plant is uprooted. Details are recorded of its botanical features, and, if possible, photographs are taken. Suppose it has 3 ears. One is kept as a herbarium specimen, one is sown, and the other is kept as a reserve in case of failure of germination, etc. Usually the selected plant will bear more than 3 ears, and then the seed is germinated and dropped, one through each hole of a board which is perforated at 3 in. intervals, there being 10 holes in a row, and 10 rows in all. A block of 100 germinated seeds is thus sown, and a space at the corner of the plot should receive 20 or 30 seeds to replace any that subsequently die out. The advantage of this accurate spacing, is to make obvious any plant which comes up out of line. Such a plant becomes a suspect, and is rooted up and destroyed. Thereby, the plots are kept pure. Each plant must be watched throughout its growth, and the features and yields recorded separately. From two or three blocks of 100 plants, only those are selected which give promise of improvement. These are then sown in beds of standard size, and compared with other lines, similarly extracted, comparison being effected either on yield per plant or yield per unit area.

After a further weeding out in the following season, these are transferred to plots each 4 ft. \times 40 ft. with 8 repetitions of each (8 is an arbitrary number which was dictated by the limits of space) as fixed Pure Lines, and the experiment is repeated for at least one season more to corroborate the figures and elucidate environmental or climatic factors. Sufficient seed should then be available for distribution, in order to try the improved seed for other soil, etc., conditions. This part of the proceedings is not entirely under scientific control. Some leading idea can be obtained from the records, and some from observations of growth. But many mistakes will be encountered before the optimal situation is found for all varieties.

In the above experiments, once the seed has passed the "sowing board" season, it is transplanted from the nurseries. Thus we have first the selection of ears in the field; then the sowing of the seed through the "sowing board;" and the next, and subsequent, seasons, the seed is broadcasted into a small nursery plot and afterwards transplanted into the larger plots. At Anuradhapura, each field has been measured to standard, and will accommodate 26 plots of 4 ft. \times 40 ft. It is impossible to standardise the fields at Peradeniya, as they are terraced. The system there has to be modified and plots of 4 ft. 20 ft. have been laid down.

118[FEBRUARY, 1923.

PADDY FLY (LEPTOCORISA VARICORNIS F.)*

G. DOUGLAS AUSTIN,

Assistant to Entomologist.

Paddy Fly is one of the worst pests of paddy in Ceylon since it is prevalent in all the rice districts and is capable of destroying a crop at a very critical stage of its growth.

The popular name Paddy Fly is evidently a literal translation of its Sinhalese name "Goyam messa" ('Goyam' = paddy plant and 'messa' = fly). The other names by which this pest is known in the island are "Paddy Bug," "Rice Bug" and "Rice Sapper." The Tamils do not appear to have given it any particular name because the term "Vandu" which is popularly applied to it, may also be applied to a beetle or any insect with strong wings.

The nature of the damage done to the paddy is characteristic of the pest and consists in both nymphs and adults sucking the sap out of the grain when it is in the milky stage. This type of attack causes the ear to be emptied of its contents and results in the ear putting on a yellowish appearance, while the rest of the plant remains green.

The adult bug is not conspicuous in the field as its general colour varies from a yellowish green to a light brown and harmonises with the grain on which it may be feeding. Adults are not strong fliers and have a tendency to drop down and seek shelter on being disturbed. It has also been observed that the bugs are most active during the cooler parts of the day, that is both during the early morning and in the evening. At Anuradhapura the bugs pass through periods of æstivation during the hottest and dryest seasons of the year. February and May were the driest and hottest months during the investigation. During these periods the bugs sought shelter and concealment in the weedy growth and jungles, showing preference to damp or water-logged fields.

Mating was generally observed in the mornings while periods of copulation were noticed to last from a few minutes to four to five hours. Mating may also occur two or three times before eggs are deposited and may even occur between ovipositions. The difference in the proportion of sexes was not great under natural conditions. From a series of counts made from different habits only a slight excess of males was shown. Under insectary conditions adults lived nearly four months.

The eggs are conspicuous and easily detected in the field. They have a striking resemblance to grass seeds and are laid singly in rows on blades of grass, paddy, or leaves of any plant on which a female may rest. The average number of eggs in a mass is about seven. The actual number of eggs which can be laid by a female was not ascertained. Incubation periods in the insectary lasted from 4 to 9 days; over 80 in every 100 eggs hatch out under field conditions. The nymphs are greenish insects with rather long legs. They begin feeding within an hour of their hatching, and moult five times during a normal nymphal period of about 19 days before they reach the adult stage.

* This note is a summary of the investigations on Paddy Fly made at Anuradhapura from December 1920 to June 1921. See BULLETIN No. 59

FEBRUARY, 1923.]119

A careful search for the natural enemies of this pest resulted in the following being detected :—Proctotrypidae—egg parasites rather rarely ; a predaceous Pentatomid—Asopus malabaricus and two Reduviid predators—Harpactor fuscipes and Irantha sp. The adults and nymphs of these three predaceous bugs were observed to feed freely on both nymphs and adults of Paddy Fly. The predatory habits of the Pentatomid A. malabaricus were hitherto unrecorded.

Host plants :—The bugs were observed to live and breed on 18 varieties of grasses, Panicum colonum and Cyperus polystachys being the two most favoured.

A study was also made of the efficacy of certain methods of control. The veracity of charms and other quaint practices in vogue in the different rice districts was investigated whenever the opportunity arose. Beyond the fact that they are superstitious and something in which the majority of cultivators have great faith, nothing more could be learnt.

Large field nets were not experimented with as they were considered impracticable after trials on a small scale at Peradeniya. Hand nets gave very good results. Winnows smeared with sticky substances made locally and also with Ostico, a sticky substance manufactured by McDougall, gave equally good results. Ropes saturated with kerosene or smeared with Ostico and dragged across affected fields did not give encouraging results.

Crushed sugar cane as suggested by LEFROY in India, placed on buds as a bait, was not found to attract Paddy Fly. Experiments were also made with the Philippine bait which consists of putrid meat hung out in muslin bags. This was reported to be an attractant to Paddy Fly in the Philippines, but gave no results when experimented with at Anuradhapura. It was noticed that flies of various kinds were attracted to the bait in large numbers and were continually buzzing about it. These may have kept away the Paddy Fly.

See also : BULLETIN OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE, No. 59.

GREEN MANURES FOR PADDY.

BY THE DIRECTOR OF AGRICULTURE.

The manurial experiments which have been carried on throughout the Colony during the past two years have demonstrated the value of green manures. In all cases, dressings of green manures produce increased crops—whether they are used alone or are applied with quantities of phosphatic manures.

In some districts leaves and twigs of several plants are used, but in general a sufficiently large quantity is not applied and it is held that this is due to the difficulty of collection and to the cost.

Endeavours are therefore being made to encourage the growth of green manures in the fields themselves or on the high land immediately adjoining many of the paddy fields. Sunn hemp, wild indigo and Daincha are recommended.

Ceylon paddy soils are poor in their powers of water retention and in the finer soil particles. Green manuring should therefore be more generally practised in order that the soil mass may retain more irrigation water and rains.

See also : BULLETIN OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE, No. 57, and FOOD PRODUCTION CIRCULAR, No. 21.

120[FEBRUARY, 1923.

FIBRES.

COTTON CULTIVATION.

'F.' BURNETT, B. AGR.,

Divisional Agricultural Officer, Southern.

In dealing with the above subject I shall confine my observations on the results obtained from the Government experiments conducted at Ambalantota, on 60 acres. The land before planting was of the ordinary low scrub jungle and the soil being a light loam. After clearing and burning the seeds were planted on October the 9th, 10th and 11th, immediately after the first North-east Monsoon rains. The varieties planted were :—

(1) Durango, an American Upland cotton. The seed having been secured from the Department of Agriculture of U. S. A.

(2) Cambodia and (3) Karranganni :—The seed of which was obtained from the Department of Agriculture, Madras.

(4) Sea Island :—The seed of which was obtained from the Imperial Department of Agriculture for the West Indies.

(5) Ashmouni, (6) Assali, and (7) Sakellaridis :—The seed of which was secured from the Ministry of Agriculture for Egypt and,

(8) Cauto :—An American variety of cotton, the seed of which was given to the Department of Agriculture by MR. DENNIS WOOD.

As tillage in land from jungle is difficult during the first year, a seed bed was obtained by mamotying lines in which the cotton seed was sown. After the first sowing, rains did not fall again for 14-15 days, and as the seeds did not germinate field mice became rather troublesome. However, after replanting the vacant places with seeds that had been dipped into a weak solution of Kerosene and water a good stand was obtained. With the late rains, came the weeds, and it was necessary to keep them in check.

It may be mentioned here that it is absolutely essential that a good burn be obtained on newly reclaimed land. In places where a good burn had been obtained, the plants showed a much stronger growth and weeds were not so troublesome. The effect of weeds on the growth of cotton is shown in Plate XXXIV.

The crop was weeded twice. The weeds were placed in the rows of cotton plants and these acted as a mulch, which later proved extremely beneficial owing to the long spell of dry weather which followed.

The first picking commenced in the Durango plot, during the last week of January—3\frac{1}{2} months after planting and continued until June. The acreage of each variety planted and yields were as follows :—

The cotton stumps were pulled up and burnt during July and the whole area was then ploughed and harrowed with a Cletrac tractor placed at the disposal of the Department of Agriculture by MR. S. SEDGWICK the local agent for the Cletrac Company. Considering the number of stumps in the soil and also the stubbornness of the soil, a good seed bed was obtained. Rains were a little late this year and planting was not completed until October 17th. A very good stand was obtained with the exception of Karranganni. It is very noticeable that the plants that came up after re-seeding the vacancies, are not nearly as hardy, and are very backward compared with the main crop planted a week previously. It is also of the utmost importance to plant with the first rains in October in order that the plants may get a good start of the weeds. Weeding of all the plots has been carefully carried out.

Pests had up to this time given very little trouble, but on November 20th an epidemic (of caterpillars)* spread over the whole area, and fed ravenously on the outer leaves—not a single plant being left untouched. Several plants were very badly attacked, the outer leaves being completely shredded. This was particularly noticeable all round by the borders and the question of cutting out the windbelts altogether is under consideration, as it is in these places that cotton pests can breed and subsequently migrate on to the cotton plants. The weed known locally as 'Titta,' † was particularly noticeable in these belts this year, and it was due to this weed that the caterpillar was able to breed in large numbers before coming on to the cotton plant. As soon as the attack was observed remedial measures were immediately taken in hand by spraying and dusting with Paris Green and by hand picking. The latter undoubtedly saved the crop from the first attack.

Dusting by mixing ashes with the Paris Green was partially successful but rains washed off the dust before it could have a lasting effect. Spraying the whole crop was then undertaken by mixing Paris Green 1 oz.—lime 2 lb. and water 60 gallons and this proved very effective. This wash was applied to the leaves by means of small bundles of twigs.

Owing to the success of last year's crop approximately 300 acres are under cultivation in the Hambantota District this year. Manurial and seed selection experiments are also being tried on the Government Experiment Station. Cotton is also being grown in other Districts.
