122FEBRUARY, 1923.

SISAL AND FURCRÆA.

BY THE DIRECTOR OF AGRICULTURE.

The problem of the economic utilization of the dry zone is one that demands most serious consideration. There are vast tracks of available land if only suitable crops can be found and at present the only cultivation consists of paddy under irrigation and the chena cultivation of food grains. The former experiment station at Mahailuppalama demonstrated that sisal would grow in such areas satisfactorily and has led to the formation of a company for the cultivation of this crop.

Can fibres be grown profitably on such a scale than their cultivation can be recommended to the small holder? This is the question that the Experiment Station at Anuradhapura is attempting to solve.

Considerable areas have been planted up in recent years with Sisal Hemp (Agave rigida var. Sisalana) and with a Furcræa, believed to be Mauritius Hemp Furcræa gigantea or a variety of that species. The growth of the plant in these parts has been excellent and during the past year a small decorticating machine has been erected for the extraction of the fibre. It is intended to carry out continuous work during the dry season of 1923, and figures regarding yields will shortly be available. The trial runs have shown that good fibres can be obtained and it is expected that as the labour becomes used to the work better results will be secured.

The Mauritius Hemp should be planted 6 × 6 feet apart and the Sisal either 6 × 6 or 6 × 8 feet apart. The bulbils are first placed in a nursery and when their leaves are 6-9 inches long they are ready for planting out. Weeding should then be attended to, and catch crops of cotton, castor, dhall, etc., may be grown between the rows of plants in the early days of the plantation. When the plants are about 4 years of age leaves are ready for harvest. All leaves of sisal which droop at an angle of more than 45° are ready for harvest and similarly with Mauritius Hemp.

The small machine which has been erected is hand fed and gives a slightly higher industrial loss than the larger machines which have been evolved for use upon large plantations. These small machines however give good results and the fibre turned out from them is generally satisfactory. In the case of Sisal, the cleaned fibre is washed in water and then hung out in the sun to dry. In the case of the Mauritius hemp, the wet fibre, straight from the machine, must be thrown into tanks containing a soap solution for 48 hours and subsequently washed in several changes of water.

The preparation of fibre is not difficult and if the results of the present experiment are successful, there would be no reason why similar machines should not be erected on a co-operative basis for dealing with fibres which might be grown by small holders on high lands in the dry zone which are not at present beneficially utilized.

KAPOK OR SILK COTTON TREE.

(Eriodendron Anfractuosum)

W. MOLAGODE,

Agricultural Instructor, Central Division.

In Ceylon, Kapok known as Kotte (කොට්ට) Up-country and Imbul (ඉම්බුල්) in the Low-country and as Panchamaram in Tamil is a common tree and is widely distributed. It grows from sea level to 2,500 ft. or more. It gives the best results in the low and intermediate elevations only, preferring a warm climate. It withstands a comparatively long period of drought.

PROPAGATION AND CULTIVATION.

The Kapok Tree is propagated either from seeds or cuttings. The planting of cuttings or stumps has been the more commonly practised method of propagation in Ceylon. Nearly every piece of the tree, even

very thick stumps will grow readily. Cuttings should preferably be of a medium size and should be planted as soon as they are cut. Tender branches of the same season's growth should not be planted. Experience has shown that cuttings grow into bearing trees sooner than those raised from seeds, but their life is short and, owing to no tap root being developed, are more liable to be blown down by wind. Raised from seed the tree will begin to give a crop between three and four years. From thence up to the 20th year the crop will gradually increase.

The distance for planting should not exceed 20 \times 20 ft, giving 109 trees to the acre for cuttings or plants. If the soil is poor this distance may be reduced to say even 16 \times 16 ft. As a boundary or roadside tree Kapok is already grown fairly extensively being planted about 8 feet apart.

YIELD.

Though Kapok has been grown in the village gardens and on some estates as a boundary tree there are no reliable data as to yield. The writer has been able to obtain the following figures :—

  1. (1) A full grown tree, probably 20 years old with good spreading branches, gave 780 pods.
  2. (2) A tree of the same size and age within a few yards from (1) gave 448 pods.
  3. (3) A smaller tree of about 8 years gave 360 pods.
  4. (4) A young tree about five years old gave 120 pods.
  5. (5) An isolated tree in an open situation, probably 15 years old, gave 640.

A good average crop per tree has been stated to be 400 pods. 100 pods are required to produce a pound of clean floss. Each tree therefore gives four pounds of clean floss per year and a plantation of an acre of 109 trees will give about 440 pounds of clean Kapok.

HARVESTING.

The first two or three crops are of course small normal crops beginning sixth or seventh year onwards and will gradually increase from year to year until about the 20th year.

It is important that the Kapok crop should be gathered at the proper stage of ripeness. Ordinarily the whole crop of a tree does not ripen at the same time and it may be necessary to make as many as three pickings. It will be noted that before ripening the pods are of a light green colour with a smooth surface. As they ripen the pods turn light brown and the surface assumes a wrinkled appearance. At this stage the pods should be harvested for, if left longer, they burst at the top end and the floss become exposed to rain and dew resulting in a discolouration. If at the time of picking the pods were still closed a few days exposure to sun will open them. If pods not of the right stage of ripeness are gathered, they should be dried in the sun until they show signs of maturity and after the floss is removed from such pods, it should again be well dried. Immature pods even after several days of drying do not open and when forced open the floss will be found to adhere quite strongly to the shell. In unripe pods the floss is not completely developed and the result is that a very inferior grade of floss gets mixed up with the better grade which lowers the value of the bulk. It is therefore necessary that a careful sorting of the crop should be carried out and the floss graded accordingly.

The two very common methods adopted for cleaning the floss are (1) the floss with the seed is spread on a mat, and covered with a jute hessian or a thick cloth and this is beaten with a stick. (2) The floss with the seed is put into boxes or baskets and a bamboo with the lower end split and kept opened with the aid of small cross sticks or a stick or piston to the lower end of which are nailed two pieces of sticks forming a cross is introduced in to the box or basket and spun fast. This causes the curled up floss to open and drop the seed.

The seed is also a product of some importance, containing about 25 % of oil which is edible and is reported to be largely used in the manufacture of soap. The residue is a good cake manure and contains about 5 % of nitrogen.

124[FEBRUARY, 1923.

FODDERS.

By THE DIRECTOR OF AGRICULTURE.

The Department of Agriculture has carried out a series of experiments with fodders at the Experiment Stations at Peradeniya, Anuradhapura and Jaffna.

At Peradeniya, trials were made, and are being continued, with Guinea Grass (Panicum maximum), two varieties, Water or Mauritius Grass (Panicum muticum), Paspalum dilatatum, two varieties, Rhodes Grass (Chloris gayana) and Doob (Cynodon dactylon). The results of these experiments indicate that Guinea Grass is the best grass for the locality of Peradeniya, while Paspalum dilatatum forms a very good pasture giving good quantities of grass of high food value. Subsequent additions to the above trials have been Kikuyu Grass (Pennisetum clandestinum) and Napier Grass (Pennisetum sp.).

The total yields per acre have been as follows for the complete year's growth : Guinea Grass 40.1 tons, Water grass 33.2 tons, Paspalum dilatatum variety A, 27.8 tons and variety B 22.7 tons and Rhodes Grass 22.9 tons.

At Anuradhapura, similar trials on a small scale without irrigation have also been carried out. Here again Guinea grass gave the best results, yielding fair crops of grass in the wet months. In the dry season this grass, as well as others, dried out completely, but Guinea Grass came up afresh with the rains of the following wet season. Doob (Cynodon dactylon) also grows well, but the crops are not heavy. It is however probably the best grass for pasturage in the dry Zone.

At Jaffna, Guinea grass has been grown under irrigation and has yielded satisfactory crops. Extensive trials have also been made with the growing of Fodder cholams, with satisfactory results. The results in 1921, showed that yields of 5 to 8 tons of straw in addition to 850 to 1650 lbs. of grain could be grown per acre and the experiments continued throughout the year 1922 have given equally encouraging results.

In South India, cholam is grown as a rotation crop with cotton. It may be grown for grain but is more usually grown for stock feed and is cut green. If it is not all required green, it is allowed to mature, is then cut, dried and stacked. Afterwards it is used as required.

The fodder question in the Jaffna Peninsula is a difficult one but on the Experiment Station during 1922 no outside fodder was purchased. All the fodder required for the cattle on the Station was grown on the Station and the condition of the animals showed clearly the value of fodder cholam as a cattle food.

MISCELLANEOUS.

WEEDS.

T. PETCH, B.A., B.Sc.,

Botanist and Mycologist

Among the new weeds which have been recorded recently the principal is a native Ceylon plant, Drymaria cordata Willd. This plant occurs on open waste ground in the wet zone above 1,000 ft. and has long been known as a weed in gardens, but it is only during recent years that it has begun to give trouble on estates. One correspondent (Dikoya) states that it was first seen on his estate in 1916, but has now become absolutely rampant, and is gradually spreading to other estates in the neighbourhood. In this case it is chiefly to be found in flats near streams or in low-lying fields.

The plant belongs to the natural order Caryophyllaceæ which also includes the common chickweed of Great Britain, and it is in many respects similar to the chickweed. Its white flower is of the same character, but the plant is larger. It grows to a height of two feet, with many erect slender branches, and may occur in dense masses. Plate XLI shows the upper part of a plant, natural size, with its repeatedly-dividing (dichotomous) inflorescence and heart-shaped (cordate) leaves. The figures to the right show, on a larger scale, part of the inflorescence, the outer envelope of the flower (calyx), and the five incised petals, two stamens, and globular ovary.

The hairs on the inflorescence are sticky. Consequently, when the fruit is ripe, it adheres to the coolies' clothes or tools, etc., and in that way the seed is distributed over the estate. In one case it is said to be more troublesome than Oxalis. It dies down in the dry weather, but "if one leaf is left lying on the ground in wet weather it at once takes root."

MOON recorded the Sinhalese name Kukulu pala for this plant, but that name has not been met with since. Kukulu is a cock, and pala a general term for vegetables, e.g. Sudu-tampala, Amaranthus gangeticus. It has received the name Kadully Pillu on one estate [? Kadalai, Chick Pea].

Eleutheranthera ruderalis (Sw.) Schultz is now established at Henaratgoda. This is an American weed which is becoming generally distributed round the tropics. It is known in Java, but apparently has not been recorded from India. In general appearance it resembles the common Synedrella nodiflora, and it may hitherto have been passed over on that account. But it was found at Henaratgoda after American seed of Chenopodium anthelminticum had been sown there, so that there is some ground for suspicion that it was introduced with that seed, though no seeds of Eleutheranthera are present in the remaining sample.

Among the various specimens sent in as weeds from estates during 1922 were Polygonum punctatum Ham., a common weed in cultivated ground up-country, which was very prevalent among Oxalis on one estate; Schizæa digitata (L.) Sw., a grass-like fern, frequent on damp clayey soil in the low-country; Typhonium Roxburghii Schott., Polon-ala, previously known as a weed in gardens, and now reported as a weed in tea at medium elevations.

Pilea muscosa Lindl., the Gunpowder Plant, was allowed to grow on one estate on steep land to stop wash, and spread at a rapid rate. This species usually flourishes best on a damp gravelly soil. The use of Desmodium triflorum DC., Hin-undu-piyali, for preventing wash appears to be extending.

THE WATER HYACINTH AND ITS ERADI-
CATION IN WEST GIRUWA PATTU.

A. T. REEVE, A.R.C.S.,

Inspector of Plant Pests and Diseases, Southern.

The Water Hyacinth (Eichornia crassipes) is a native of Brazil but has gradually spread over most tropical countries. It was introduced into Ceylon as a garden plant, owing to its beautiful flowers.

In the Tangalle district, it is supposed to have been introduced by a priest at the Mulkirigala temple and from there has been transported by villagers, who had no idea as to how serious a pest this weed could be.

Water Hyacinth was known to be present in the Tangalla district but the seriousness of the infestation of village tanks and water courses was not realized until 1922. A sub-inspector of this division was detailed to proceed to Tangalla and make a preliminary survey as to the extent of the pest in this district and as a result 13 tanks were reported to be infested with this weed. It was arranged that weeding should be started in the dry season and a sub-inspector was sent in June to supervise this work. Owing however to unexpected heavy rains the work had to be postponed until August, only one small tank, Gamage Wewa, being weeded.

On August 15th the sub-inspector was again sent to Tangalle district as conditions were reported to be favorable for weeding and work was commenced from the 18th and lasted until November 10th. The length of time taken with the work was mainly due to the apathy shown by both Velvidanes and cultivators and also to the litigiousness of certain of the cultivators in the Ranna North division. In all 20 tanks and the attendant water ways were clean-weeded and also about 6 miles of the Urubokka Oya. The weed in all cases was pulled out by hand and piled on the banks. The first weeds pulled out were burned but some difficulty was experienced at the end as the North-East rains had set in and some of the piles of weed had to be left unburned. Subsequent inspections have shown that these weeds have rotted and in future burning need not be insisted upon.

This weeding must however only be considered as preliminary. In some of those tanks which were weeded earlier, seedlings were reported one

FEBRUARY, 1923.]127

month after weeding on the banks. It is well known that the germination of Water Hyacinth seeds may be delayed for as long as two years. Apparently the seed needs to be dried for a time and germinates with the application of water. Thus tanks are ideal places for germination to take place. The seed of the plant sinks into the mud of the tank, this, in the dry weather owing to the reduction of water in the tanks, dries up and with the coming of the rains the seeds germinate and the young plants float to the surface of the water.

The Water hyacinth has become a most troublesome pest in many countries and every effort should be made to prevent its spread throughout Ceylon. Its spread may be very rapid and it soon blocks up irrigation channels when it gets into them.

It will be necessary to watch for and remove young plants as fast as they appear for the next two years.

COFFEES ON EXPERIMENT STATION,
PERADENIYA.

T H HOLLAND, Diploma Agr., Wye.

Manager, Experiment Station, Peradeniya.

The interest in the cultivation of the Robusta types of coffee is still maintained. The demand for seed from the Experiment Station abated somewhat. Some 450 lb. of seed were supplied against 537 lb. in 1921. This may be attributed to the fact that several estates are now selling seed. Circulars containing a number of questions on the growth and general progress of these coffees were distributed among growers during the year. The replies received indicate that these coffees can be successfully grown on a considerable variety of soils, under a rainfall of 80 to 100 inches and at elevations between sea level and 3,000 feet. Evidence shows that shade is beneficial if not a necessity and that the health of the coffee usually suffers by its absence. No reliable records of yields were sent in but at the Experiment Station, Peradeniya, yields ranging between 2.09 and 3.70 lb. of berries per tree were obtained for the season 1921-22. This is an improvement on previous years and will probably be exceeded during the season 1922-23. Uganda has been giving the highest average yield in three years. Among diseases, Dieback, is by far the most troublesome at Peradeniya. Spraying with Bordeaux mixture has been unsuccessfully tried and the condition is generally ascribed to physiological causes. Fortnightly picking and burning of dieback branches was continued throughout the year.

Seeds of the strains of Coffee for which disease-resistance is claimed, KENT's Special Arabica and JACKSON's Hybrid, were obtained from South India early in the year. The germination, growth and health of the nursery plants were very satisfactory. A newly opened area of 6 acres was planted with these coffees (three acres of each variety) in the North-East monsoon. The nursery plants were all lifted with a transplanting tool, a method which has proved most satisfactory. The health and appearance of these plants was at the end of the year good.

128[FEBRUARY, 1923.

Gliricidia maculata was planted as shade for this coffee, 96% of the stumps planted were successful, a percentage that is seldom obtained with Dadaps.

In order to supply the constant demand for information with regard to coffee planting the leaflet on the cultivation of Robusta coffees was re-written during the year. This will be issued as Leaflet No. 23.

THE OCCURRENCE OF TELEUTOSPORES
IN HEMILEIA VASTATRIX B. & BR.

C. RAGUNATHAN,

Assistant to Botanist and Mycologist.

The following is a short summary of the work carried out on the occurrence of teleutospores in Hemileia vastatrix on coffee from May 1921 to April 1922.

MARSHALL WARD described the teleutospores of Hemileia vastatrix in his reports on the coffee leaf disease and his papers on the life history and morphology of that fungus. In his second report, written in December, 1880, he stated that the smooth turnip-shaped spores (i.e. teleutospores) were far commoner than he had at first supposed. Subsequent investigators of this disease have, however, failed to find teleutospores, with the exception of Massee in a specimen, from the Berlin Herbarium, which had been assigned to Hemileia Woodii and was said to be on Coffea Ibo. Massee found that the fungus was H. vastatrix and not H. Woodii.

In order to obtain further information concerning the occurrence of teleutospores in Ceylon, periodic observations of leaves of coffee attacked by Hemileia were begun in May 1921 and continued until April 1922. These were carried out at Peradeniya on the following species of Coffee.—Coffea arabica, Coffea robusta, and Coffea liberica.

Teleutospores were found in every month except August and October, 1921, and April 1922. Teleutospores were not found in August 1921 and April 1922, as the bushes were then developing new foliage. It is probable that the absence of teleutospores in October may be due to the retarded progress of the disease owing to unusually heavy rains in August and unfavourable climatic conditions in September, followed by heavy rains in October.

But teleutospores were found in every subsequent month until April 1922. No definite statement can be made regarding their occurrence, except that it is dependent on climatic conditions, as it is subsequent to the uredo stage which in turn is dependent on the same cause. Consequently, the periods at which teleutospores can be found will differ from year to year according to climatic conditions.

A single teleutospore was observed in Hemileia Canthii B & Br. on Canthium campanulatum on February 1st, 1922. This had produced a promycelium in the sorus. The teleutospore is much smaller, and the promycelium is more slender and brighter in colour, than in Hemileia vastatrix.

THE
TROPICAL AGRICULTURIST

VOL. LX.

PERADENIYA, MARCH, 1923.

No. 3.

THE CULTIVATION OF JAK.

Within recent years endeavours have been made to encourage the cultivation of Jak. This has been done with the object of increasing the production of food as well as for the provision of timber.

The Jak (Artocarpus integrifolia) is one of the standard timbers of Ceylon and is being planted by the Forest Department, by lessees on re-afforestation leases and by private individuals. The demand for this timber for building purposes and for furniture is however great and there is little doubt that the villagers who are owners of jak are gradually selling off the timber and allowing their properties to be depleted.

In our present number is included an article relating to the destruction of jak in a section of the Kegalle district. The figures contained therein clearly demonstrate the destruction that is taking place and unless steps are taken to plant up new areas there is little doubt that the increasing scarcity of good jak for timber will become more marked within the next few years.

Nor is this the worst feature of the destruction. The jak in certain parts of the Colony is a most important food of the rural population. With the destruction that is taking place for the purpose of supplying timber, an important food producing asset is being considerably reduced. In years of stress, the jak is often an all-important asset to the rural population, and one cannot view this destruction of a valuable asset without concern.

It has been suggested that the destruction of jak should be controlled by legislation but seeing that most of the trees

132[MARCH, 1923.

are to be found on private lands, it would appear that such a suggestion would be impossible of adoption. It remains therefore to see that the planting of jak shall be at a rate equal to, if not in excess of, the destruction. Encouragements to attain this end must be given.

In the Kalutara district, areas of village forest lands have been leased out for chena cultivation on the understanding that such areas shall be reafforested in jak and other useful timbers. Many of these areas have been successful and there are now a fair number of blocks of good young jak that are making good progress. What can be accomplished in one district might be attempted in others, and there is a possibility that increased quantities of jak could be established fairly easily in those districts of the Island in which jak grows readily.

The encouragement of the cultivation of jak in the Kegalle district of Sabaragamuwa would give satisfactory results and there are sections of the Central Province in which increased areas of jak could be established.

It is satisfactory to note that the Ratmale Colony Committee are proposing to give out to Colonists a number of jak and other food-producing trees during the next North-East Monsoon planting season. Similarly the Government Agent of the Eastern Province is proposing to distribute jak plants for cultivation in the Bintenne Pattu. For the latter division, it is probable that the Department of Agriculture will establish a small nursery at Mahaoya for the provision of these plants in quantities.

The attention of Food Production Committees is drawn to the desirability of encouraging the growth of jak. Such a policy would tend to re-establish an important food-producing tree that is being gradually reduced in number by reason of the increasing demand for its timber.

The experience of large capitalistic food-producing schemes has during the past few years demonstrated that paddy cultivation by capitalists is not likely to be a profitable undertaking at the present prices. Paddy growing in Ceylon is essentially the work of the small holder, be he owner or tenant. The opening up of new areas must necessarily be somewhat slow and if the position of the colony's food supplies is to be improved, one of the matters which must receive attention is the cultivation of jak.

MARCH, 1923.]133

FOOD SUPPLIES.

THE PLANTAIN INDUSTRY OF KEGALLE DISTRICT.

G. G. AUCHINLECK, M.Sc., A.I.C.,

Divisional Officer, Central,

and

C. P. CRISPEYN,

Agricultural Instructor, Kegalle.

There are in Ceylon several agricultural industries which are partly or exclusively in the hands of the peasantry, and in connection with which there have grown up simple but stable methods of handling and marketing. They are for the most part of purely local importance, and do not figure in annual statistics of exports : they are therefore apt to be overshadowed by the great capitalist and export industries of the Colony, such as tea, rubber and copra. The magnitude of some of these industries entitles them to attention, and in addition the methods of cultivation are usually defective, so that they offer good opportunities for the instructional work by the Department of Agriculture.

Village tea, rubber, cacao, cinnamon, citronella and to a certain extent coconuts, depend for their stability on foreign markets. Industries of purely local importance are paddy, the production of sugar, toddy and arrack from coconut or kitul or palmyrah palms, the cultivation of 'wrapper-leaf' tobacco in the Central Province and the 'filler-leaf' in the northern districts, the market-gardens of Nuwara Eliya, the raising of 'black' cattle in the North-Central Province, and the cultivation of plantains, areca-nuts and pine-apples in Kegalle and other districts. In addition to these there are numerous smaller industries such as chillies, betel, dry grains, beans and other vegetables, the sum total of the values of which is considerable.

The diversity of these crops and of the methods of production is surprising. As cases in point we may mention that varieties of paddy number several hundred, and that in a couple of months over 60 named varieties of sweet potatoes were collected in Matara and Galle Districts alone in 1920. Very little accurate information is available as to the yields of these crops or as to the methods of cultivation and marketing used, and it is precisely for this class of work that the instructional staff of the Department of Agriculture exists. A critical and descriptive study of the most important ones is called for, and following on this a systematic campaign directed towards organising and improving each industry in turn is necessary.

PLANTAINS AND BANANAS.

The distinction between a plantain and a banana is not recognised in Ceylon ; all are called plantains. In other countries the banana is a variety which can be eaten without cooking—in other words a table-fruit, while the plantain is a vegetable which must be cooked before it is palatable. The purple cone at the end of the fruit-bunch is usually persistent in the case of the banana, while in the plantain it is shed before the fruit ripens.

The varieties grown in Kegalle may be summed up as follows :—

Kolikuttu. Edible without cooking : sweet, mealy taste : bunches arge.

134[MARCH 1923.

Suwandel. Edible without cooking; sweet: fruits smaller.

Honderawala. Edible without cooking; sub-acid in flavour. Fruits small and straight.

Anamalu. Sometimes cooked as vegetable when green, but also edible uncooked; long, stout fruits, subacid in flavour. Bunches large.

Ash plantain. (Alukehel). Cooked before eating: fruits short, covered with powdery, white wax.

Marathamalu. Cooked before eating. Taste resembles that of Anamalu. Fruits thick and stout.

Rathkehel. Sometimes cooked, usually eaten uncooked. Fruits short, round, sub-acid, red-skinned.

Puwalu. Sometimes cooked, usually eaten uncooked. Fruits thin, sub-acid.

Bingkehel. A dwarf variety of plant; fruits thick. Resembles Anamalu in flavour.

Cananoor. Cooked before eating: Fruits short and stout. This variety is not much relished.

The classification of varieties of plantains and bananas has not yet been satisfactorily carried out in any country, so that it is not possible at this stage to identify the Ceylon types with those of other countries.

VILLAGE FAIRS.

For the most part, agricultural industries which lie in the hands of the peasantry are scattered over large areas of country and are difficult to centralise. The Kegalle plantain industry for example affects the following number of villages in the northern part of the district.

MARCH, 1923.]135
Centre. Contributory Villages.
Rambukkana ... ... ... 153
Aranayake ... ... ... 100
Morontota ... ... ... 89
Alawwa ... ... ... 123
Kadugannawa ... ... ... 140
Total of Villages ... 605

In the smaller centres where Government or Municipal markets are not available, the whole of the village produce is brought into some convenient centre on definite days, and a brisk barter is carried on. The villagers sell their little lots of garden-produce and buy the foodstuffs they need, and traders purchase the products needed in the larger towns and cart them to the nearest railway station for shipment.

Village fairs of this kind are becoming increasingly numerous, and they fill a greater part in the life of the peasantry than is realized by the inattentive onlooker. The Rambukkana fair is restricted entirely to plantains and takes place on Mondays and Thursdays each week; the other fairs in Kegalle deal in all kinds of village produce: at Aranayake, Morontota and Kadugannawa on Sundays and at Alawwa on Tuesdays and Fridays each week.

The control of these village fairs is usually leased out by the Government to influential villagers, a fee varying in amount with the importance of the trade being paid to the lessee, who in turn collects space-fees from each villager wishing to expose and sell produce. The lease appears to be usually a profitable one as may be judged from the following list of fees paid for the chief fairs of Kegalle.

Centre. Annual Lease-fee.
Rambukkana ... ... Rs. 1,500 00
Alawwa ... ... " 1,800 00
Kadugannawa ... ... Free
Morontota ... ... "
Aranayake ... ... " 700 00

In return for the profits derived from his lease, the lessee is responsible to the headman of the division for the order and cleanliness of the fair-ground.

BUNCHY TOP DISEASE.

This disease has been described in the TROPICAL AGRICULTURIST for December, 1921. It has appeared within recent years on every plantation in Kegalle District, and has caused considerable loss in addition to preventing a further extension of the industry.

The cause of the disease is not yet known. An observation plot of one acre is being established by the Department of Agriculture near Rambukkana, on which six of the chief varieties are being planted. Half of the plot is being dressed heavily with lime, and the suckers before being planted are (a) untreated, (b) treated with Bordeaux mixture or (c) treated with Brunolinum. In addition, the effect of dressings of potash is being tried.

The Kolikutu and Suwandel varieties are believed by the villagers to be more susceptible than others to the disease. These two varieties are ranked as the best, and the highest prices are paid for the fruit.

DEFECTS OF VILLAGE AGRICULTURE.

The outstanding characteristic of village agriculture in Ceylon is mixture of crops. The 'mixed gardens' of the villager have always attracted attention and have been defended on the grounds that they best serve the needs of the villager, who wants small quantities of several kinds of vegetables

136[MARCH, 1923.

and also that if one crop fails through disease there will still be some of the others remaining. These arguments may be sound, but the correct method would be to separate the crops into distinct plots : mixed crops mean low yields. The truth appears to be that usually, where the profits on a particular crop are low, the villager will interplant others in the hope of increasing his out-turn per acre. The market-gardens of Nuwara Eliya, and the sugar-cane plots of Galle, in both of which cases profits are usually high, are in their way models of neatness and order, and there is no confusion and mixture of crops.

Plantains should yield high enough profits to induce greater efficiency of cultivation than is the case in Kegalle. An acre yields 300 bunches of fruit annually which at the lowest market-price should be worth Rs 150. Before the fruit reaches the final markets of Kandy or Colombo it has passed through the hands of two, and sometimes three, middlemen. It seems probable that in this way the profits of the villager are reduced considerably, and he therefore is reluctant to rely on this crop alone for his support.

COMPETITION AND CO-OPERATION.

The production of plantains for the local market can be considerably increased without much lowering of prices. Two methods of inducing an increase may be adopted. If the villagers can be persuaded to unite and form a union of growers, it would be possible to eliminate a certain number of middlemen, and so increase the profits of the growers. Co-operative unions of this kind have not yet been tried in Ceylon, but they appear to be a legitimate extension of the functions of existing co-operative credit societies.

Agricultural competitions for substantial prizes have had excellent results in other countries. An annual prize of Rs. 150 for the best small holding of plantains would, if the judging were efficiently carried out and increased in stringency each year, result in a steady extension and improvement of the crop in the district. The problem of increasing the areas under plantains, and at the same time improving the methods of cultivation, by means of the direct stimulus of a substantial money prize is worth the attention of the District Agricultural Committee.

CUTTING DOWN OF JAK TREES (ARTOCARPUS INTEGRIFOLIA) AND ITS RELATION TO THE FOOD SUPPLY OF THE PEOPLE.

P. C. DEDIGAMA,

Ratemahatmaya, Beligal Korale.

The fruit of the Jak tree (Artocarpus integrifolia) as a source of food is recognised throughout the Island. It is well known that during certain portions of the year the jak fruit takes the place of rice and whole families depend on this fruit for their sustenance. It is therefore necessary that steps should be taken to prevent the wholesale cutting down of this tree for use as timber. The following statement shows the number of trees that have been cut down in the Beligal Korale during the last ten years and the probable number of fruits that those trees would have yielded during the period.

It would not be uninteresting to trace the past history of this tree as it shows the importance attached to it at the time as a yielder of food. Mention is made of this tree in a great many old books and old documents "Lekammitiyas" and from them and the fact that this timber is not found in ancient buildings it is apparent that in ancient times the timber of this tree was never used for building purposes and that its yield was utilised as food. From a record which is in my possession of a "Lekammitiya" of Dedigama compiled about 300 years ago I find that the statistics collected are the following,

MARCH, 1923.]137

viz :—Names of each family, extent of mud land possessed by each, number of jak trees and number of buffalos. This clearly indicates the paramount importance placed then on the jak tree as a yielder of food. I have besides heard on good authority that it is on record that during the Dutch period Jak trees were prohibited from being cut down without the sanction of Government. It is a proved fact that the Jak fruit stands only second in importance to rice as the staple food of the people, but this is not so recognised by the Government at present as there is no control or record of the cutting down of jak trees. In point of food value Jak gives more nourishment than rice as it possesses more health-giving properties than the latter. Another advantage is that the produce of the jak tree can be preserved to last throughout the year or even longer. The jak trees standing now have been planted by past generations and those of the present day make no effort to plant new ones to replace those that are being cut down. The trees of spontaneous growth are not looked after by the people and are being destroyed by stray cattle. Under these circumstances this food-producing tree is menaced with reduction to a very great extent in some districts and the remaining trees being those that are not fit to be utilised for timber which will be about 10%.

There are whole families living solely on this food so long as the season lasts. The preservation of the jak tree is more incumbent on the people now than it was 5 or 10 years ago owing to the fact that consequent on the sale of high land to estates by villagers there is very little land for producing other food grains to supplement the staple food of the people. This want will be even greater in the future when with the increase of the population and the available land is planted up with permanent products a very much larger number than at present will have to be dependent on the produce of the jak tree. The timber of the jak tree is both strong and good and there is a large demand for it for building purposes and for making household furniture, etc. This has given rise to an influx of traders from outside who with a very small sum of money purchase this valuable food-producing tree and there are instances where trees have been sold at only a few cents a cubic foot, the villager being forced to accept it by his poverty as such traders come in large numbers during the lean months, i.e., from middle of September, to middle of February every year.

There is legislation to prevent the removal of buffalos outside a District and this was provided to increase the number required for agricultural purposes. I am strongly of opinion that the necessity for prevention of jak trees being cut down is greater inasmuch as manual labour for agricultural purposes can supplant the work got out of buffalos. If the buffalos in a village like Dedigama, by some mishap, is totally destroyed and their labour is not available the paddy fields are not going to be abandoned because out of a population of 2283 in this village a thousand five hundred or more men, women and children can turn out and cultivate the fields. Taking for granted that all the jak trees are cut down in this village there is no possibility by any means of replacing the food lost thereby for at least ten or more years to come. Another point of vital importance which has to be taken into consideration is the fact that the area available for paddy cultivation is limited as almost all irrigable lands have been asweddumised while on the other hand the population is increasing and creates a demand for an enhanced supply of the staple food.

On the above grounds I would suggest that immediate steps be taken to protect the jak tree by law. No jak trees may be cut down without due enquiry by a Government officer and authority obtained from Government after proving to its satisfaction that the owner has one or more plants growing in his garden, free from cattle, to replace the trees that are sold or cut down for his own purposes.

138[MARCH, 1923.

A complete list of jak trees in each Wasama should be made and a register should be kept by each aracci for periodical inspection by an authority. Experiments should also be carried out by the Agricultural Department to find out means to make the existing trees more productive and villagers, through Agricultural Societies, should be made to improve their own trees. By experimenting on a few trees I find that those that are kept free from shade yield more than those that are neglected. Very old trees do not usually yield many fruits but by pollarding a certain number of the branches and roots and also by digging round them and spreading a certain amount of common manure the trees get a new lease of life and begin to yield as any good tree.

It is several years since the statistics in the following statement were collected and since then a very large number of jak trees have been cut and removed. Having visited such localities as the borders of the Gurugoda Oya, Alauwa Ferry and Ambepussa Railway Station I have found large numbers of jak trees lying in those places awaiting removal. The majority of these trees were young ones of about 20 to 30 years of growth and this is evidence of the fact that trees of older growth have almost been utilised. The eagerness to sell even young trees is accounted for by the fact that the price of jak timber has doubled or even trebled itself recently.

In this Division there are Crown lands leased for food production and as a further measure if extensions of the lease of these lands be applied for a condition might with advantage be added that a given number of jak trees should be planted in them before they are delivered over to Government. As regards the existing Crown lands small portions of them ranging from even half an acre to one or more in a village may be given out for planting jak trees. It is inadvisable to give out one large acreage in one locality for this purpose as it is necessary to plant this food-producing tree in small areas in every village so that all may be benefited.

If each family has 5 jak trees, two bread-fruit trees and a very small extent of paddy land this Division can be self-supporting as regards its food supply.

COCONUTS.

SELECTION OF COCONUTS.

H. W. JACK, B.Sc., B.A.,

Economic Botanist, Department of Agriculture, F.M.S. & S.S.

The days when rubber estates paid big dividends being now in the past, the thoughts of Agriculturists have turned to crops other than rubber, and coconuts, already well established in the country, are gaining more attention than heretofore. Coconut oil and vegetable oils in general, have sprung to a position of considerable importance in the world's economy during the last decade and the position has been decidedly enhanced since the war which, more than any other factor, proved the utility of vegetable oils.

The following figures clearly indicate the growth of the coconut industry in the Federated Malay States and similar increases occur in the Straits Settlements :—

COPRA EXPORTS IN THE FEDERATED MALAY STATES.
