TROPICAL AGRICULTURIST

VOL. LX.

PERADENIYA, APRIL, 1923.

No. 4.

TOBACCO EXPERIMENTS.

Experiments with tobacco were begun in 1914 at Jaffna with a view to ascertaining if a tobacco suitable for export to Europe could be grown in the North. The principal tobacco crop of the Island is grown at Jaffna and much of this is exported to Travancore. From time to time the import duties in Travancore on Ceylon tobacco have been raised and the export business from Jaffna made difficult. With the view of solving these difficulties and with the hope of growing a variety suitable for a wider market, experimental work was begun.

A large number of varieties were grown experimentally but with the exception of the White Burley none was found to be suitable for the district. The burning qualities of the majority were found to be poor, and the European market was prepared to accept only the White Burley. Since then a certain quantity of this tobacco has been grown regularly on the Jaffna Experiment Station and a purchase scheme for privately grown White Burley inaugurated.

With the further raising of the duty on Jaffna tobacco by the State of Travancore in 1922, greater interest was taken in the possibilities of White Burley cultivation and requests were received at the Jaffna Agricultural Conference for a further extension of the purchase scheme. It is hoped that this may be possible as the prospects before its cultivation appear to be promising.

The cultivation of White Burley tobacco for the European market has made marked progress in India during the past few years and there would appear to be no reason why the tobacco-growing districts of Ceylon should not grow a suitable export

196[APRIL, 1923.

product. It is stated that the Ceylon White Burley has a distinctive red colour of its own, but that its quality is not quite as good as some of the tobacco now being produced in India.

In the Dumbara district and in Matale the object of the experiments has been to discover if a cigar tobacco of better quality than the local variety can be grown. A large number of cigar tobaccos have been experimented with, as well as a number of other types. A few of these appear to be promising but their flavour and aroma still requires, if possible, improvement. These experiments are now being carried out at the Nalanda Experiment Station and a number of the most promising varieties are still under experiment.

It has also been suggested that flue curing should be attempted in order to ascertain if a tobacco suitable for cigarettes could be prepared. A few experiments have been carried out privately in the Dumbara Valley since the original experiments at Jaffna, and it is possible that arrangements may be made with tobacco experts in India to carry out a further trial during the forthcoming season.

Recently Ceylon has been visited by representatives of the British and American tobacco manufacturing industries. These gentlemen have carefully investigated the experiments that have been carried out in the past and have visited the Dumbara and Matale tobacco growing areas. They consider that work in connexion with White Burley in Jaffna and possibly elsewhere should be continued, that attempts should continue to be made to grow, if possible, a thin cigar wrapper leaf in the Dumbara area and that experiments should be made with flue curing.

They recognised that the locally grown tobacco commands a good price in the local market and therefore it is probable that only high grade tobaccos could be grown for export with any chance of competing economically with the existing industry. Further experiments are necessary—especially in regard to the finer grades of cigar tobaccos and with flue curing.

This visit from recognised authorities in the Tobacco world has been of considerable value and should enable the Department to continue its experiments along those lines which offer the greatest element of success.

APRIL, 1923.]197

TOBACCO.

WHITE BURLEY CULTIVATION IN THE JAFFNA DISTRICT.

Department of Agriculture, Ceylon.—Leaflet No. 26.

It is estimated that more than 7,000 acres are under tobacco cultivation, and more than half the population of this district are directly engaged in this industry. The prosperity of the whole district depends largely on tobacco cultivation and trade. Jaffna exports a little over 4 million pounds of manufactured chewing tobacco to the value of 2 million rupees to the State of Travancore, and also supplies to a great extent the needs of other districts of Ceylon. The inland trade and the prosperity of the cultivators is governed by the market rate of the export tobacco. The State of Travancore imports tobacco from Jaffna and Coimbatore. The Government of this State has twice placed difficulties in the way of import of Jaffna tobacco, and encouraged the import of Coimbatore tobacco by imposing differential import duty unfavourable to Jaffna. On both these occasions the Ceylon Government succeeded in inducing the Travancore Government to alter the duty and equalize the rates of import duty from both countries. On the last occasion, in the year 1910, an arrangement was made with the State of Travancore for Jaffna to export a fixed quantity of 5,745 candies per year.

INTRODUCTION OF WHITE BURLEY TO JAFFNA.

Shortly after the above arrangement in the year 1910, at the request of Jaffna people, the Government decided to help the people by obtaining the services of a tobacco expert. In 1914 ten acres of land at Tirunelveli were placed at the disposal of the Government by the Jaffna Tobacco Committee, and the work of finding a variety suitable for Jaffna and one that could be marketed in Europe was started. Nearly forty varieties brought by Mr. B. F. SCHERFIUS, a tobacco planter, from America were tried. Out of these the White Burley tobacco introduced from the blue grass region of the Kentucky lime soil area was found to be suitable. Favourable reports were received on samples submitted to the Imperial Institute in London. The crops were annually shipped to London, and were sold at prices ranging from one shilling and four pence to one shilling and ten pence per pound. This tobacco is used mainly as a pipe and cigarette tobacco. As a pipe tobacco it is highly valued, as it has a very great absorptive quality and is easy to flavour.

LOCAL CULTIVATION OF WHITE BURLEY.

From 1919 when the suitability of White Burley to Jaffna had passed the experimental stage, the cultivators were encouraged by the Department of Agriculture to grow this variety and deliver the plants, green, at the Experiment Station at Tirunelveli at prices ranging from 5 cents to 20 cents per plant. The following figures show the extent to which White Burley has so far been cultivated by Jaffna cultivators :—

Plants. Value.
Rs. c.
1920 ... Two cultivators ... 1,095 ... 177 10
1921 ... Seven cultivators ... 2,687 ... 466 80
1922 ... Seven cultivators ... 4,611 ... 646 80

Last year the State of Travancore raised the duty on Jaffna tobacco by Rs. 20, and Rs. 10 on Coimbatore tobacco, thus imposing a differential duty of Rs. 10 unfavourable to Jaffna. The new duty has affected the local

198[APRIL, 1923.

prices, and has reduced the average price to 20-25 cents from about 30-35 cents. There is thus a demand now for White Burley seed, and the cultivators are even prepared to pay for seed. The Department sold in 1922 one-ounce packets at 25 cents per packet to 39 cultivators from nine villages.

PECULIARITIES IN THE METHOD OF WHITE BURLEY CULTIVATION.

Tobacco is a special crop, and requires expert treatment. In Jaffna the nursery stage and the establishment of the plants in the field presents great difficulty. Fine distinctions are noted in tobacco cultivation in the slightly varying garden soil conditions of the district. Early cultivation is suitable in lighter soils and later cultivation in the heavier soil, so that a definite date cannot be fixed to suit all villages. Each village has its own season, and the seed must be sown at the right time.

Nursery.—The selection of site is of utmost importance. A well-drained soft friable virgin soil, rich in organic matter, is to be preferred. In hard heavy clay soils the seedlings become stunted, owing to the roots being unable to penetrate into the soil, with the result that the roots lie on the surface and are curved and bent. The tap root must be straight, and must run deep into the bed. In other respects the preparation and treatment of the bed is the same as for local tobacco.

Diseases in the Nursery.—White Burley is very susceptible to disease and beds where plants were known to have suffered from disease should be discarded. The damping-off disease appears when the seedlings are crowded and the bed is too damp. Watering should be stopped till the beds get dry, and later water should be applied very sparingly. The bed should be thinned out, and the healthy plants transplanted into a new bed.

An Eelworm attacks the roots. This prevents the absorption of moisture, and the plants are stunted. This trouble is not likely to occur if the plants are kept in vigorous growth. The beds should be well manured and watered, and the seed sown at the right season. Black Stem is a more dangerous disease than the above two. The disease often escapes notice in the early stages, and only appears at the transplanting season. The disease is attributed by farmers to the application of dung of cattle which were fed with Italian millet, whether this is so or not, the manure applied to the bed should be well rotted. There is no remedy for this disease, and plants grown on affected beds should not be used for planting without careful examination.

Special Treatment of Nursery to economize Irrigation.—In watering the beds a rule-of-thumb method should not be followed. Water should only be sprinkled when the soil gets dry. If the surface be continually kept moist, there is no chance for proper root development. The surface moisture dries up sooner than the deeper layers. By encouraging deep rooting the frequency of watering can be reduced to a minimum, with a corresponding amount of saving in labour and expense. The roots are made to go deep by reducing the watering to a minimum without injuring the plants.

Transplanting and Watering.—The right size to transplant is when the biggest leaf is about 4 inches long while planting. The tap root should be kept straight, and the leaf raised upright to cover and protect the bud. Plants of this size do not require extra shade immediately after transplanting. The opportunity to encourage an enlarged root system at this period of its life should not be missed. An experiment was tried in 1916 to determine what method and intervals were best for watering. The results show that plants watered once in four days by digging a hole about 4 inches deep alternately on either side of the plant, filling it with water, and loosely refilling with soil after the water is absorbed, did the best. Surface watering as practised by cultivators hardens and bakes the surface soil, encourages a shallow root system, and hastens evaporation. By the new method the water is applied close to the roots, soil is loosely filled in, serves as a mulch,

APRIL, 1923.]199

minimizes evaporation, keeps the soil cool, and encourages deep rooting. Plants thus treated require only seven waterings during the first month. The whole plot should at this time be loosely cultivated to keep the soil in good tilth which will conserve moisture. During the second month, narrow channels are opened on one side of each row. For the second watering, channels are opened on the opposite side. Gradually these channels are made broader until one channel serves to water two rows. Three days after each watering, the soil is cultivated crosswise with a cultivator. By this time the leaves attain their full size, serve as shade, and no further cultivation is necessary, and irrigation may be reduced to once in ten days. The topping and suckering is the same as practised for local tobacco.

Seed Plants.—The best plant with desirable characters should not be topped, but allowed to go to seed. Just before the flowers open, the seed head should be bagged to prevent cross-fertilizing. Mature seed should be graded before use.

Harvesting and Curing.—Ripeness of plant is judged from the colour and appearance of leaves and stalks. The leaf should break when folded and pressed between the fingers in the mornings. The stalk should crack when split with a sharp knife. The stalk is split from the top with a tobacco cutting knife to 4 inches from the base. It is then cut across the base, and the harvested plants are hung in a sheltered room on lathes. Four to five plants are put on one lathe. The harvesting should be done in the morning after the dew has dried off. The presence of dew on the leaf causes a dark colour in the cured leaf. In order to facilitate handling, the plants are allowed to wilt in the sun a few minutes before transporting. The air curing method is applied to White Burley. This is a slow process and requires about three weeks. The leaf undergoes two stages in curing which should be intelligently followed. In the first stage the leaf turns yellow. At this stage the leaf is still alive, and any injury interferes with the proper curing. The leaf utilizes the stored plant food, converting starch and other carbohydrates into the other compounds, and eliminating water. The chlorophyll disappears and the leaf yellows. At this stage the most favourable condition for curing is humid warmth. Absence of moisture cures the leaf green, and excess of moisture darkens the colour and the leaf begins to rot. This stage lasts four to five days, when the leaf assumes a golden yellow colour, begins to die, and turns brown. This is the second stage. In order to fix the bright colour, the leaf should be rapidly killed and dried by opening ventilators. The drying process takes about fifteen days.

Stripping and Grading.—When the plants are cured and well dried, the leaf is stripped from the stalk. The morning is suitable for this work, as the leaf is soft and pliable, but dries and crumbles in the afternoon. The leaf is graded according to colour, texture, and size. The leaves are divided into five grades in the following order starting from top to bottom :—

(1) Red, (2) Lug, (3) Bright, (4) Trash, and (5) Flyings. The Red leaf is dark red and thick. This grade is used for wrapping chewing tobacco. The Lugs are lighter and bigger and used for pipe tobacco. The Bright is the largest leaf in the plant, and is very bright. This grade is used for pipe and cigarettes. The Trash and Flyings are the lowest leaves, very light and bright and smaller in size than the others. These grades are used for cigarettes. About ten to fifteen leaves of each grade are tied into bundles which are called "Hands." The "Hands" are bulked and allowed to age; while ageing the leaf attains flavour, burn, and other desirable qualities. This takes about six to eight months. After ageing the tobacco is ready for shipping.

Jaffna, February 21, 1923.W. P. A. COOKE,
Farm School Officer. 200[APRIL, 1923]

FIBRE.

ROSELLE FIBRE.

HIBISCUS SABDARIFFA VAR. ALTISSIMA.

G. E. HENNING,

The factors of primary importance in the cultivation of roselle are those of climate and soil. It is urged that no success with this crop can be obtained in really dry weather, although on the other hand excessive rain is liable to do injury by beating down the plants in their young stage. Planting should be carried out if possible at the commencement of the rainy season.

Soil.—It has not yet been determined what particular type of soil will yield the highest returns of fibre but roselle is known to thrive on loam soils which are capable of retaining a good supply of moisture, and on any other good friable soil. Laterite soils are, however, unsuitable; as is also a light soil deficient in humus. Steep hills should be avoided as Roselle has a small tap root; consequently heavy rains are liable to uproot the plants; in addition to this, the crop is more likely to be damaged by wind storms. Well drained flat land, and gently undulating ground, are suitable.

Planting.—The area to be planted, which must be thoroughly clean and free from weeds, should be chankolled, or forked, to a depth of about 4-6 inches, and after being exposed for a few days to the action of the atmosphere, any surface lumps of soil should be broken up so as to form a fairly even seed-bed. When the climatic conditions are favourable, the seed is drilled in rows about 3 inches apart and the soil slightly raked over; the rate of sowing being about 25 lb. of seed per acre. By planting close, one avoids side branches which break the continuity of the fibre, and thus one obtains better yields per acre,—as there is considerable waste in cultivating for branch fibre. A safe estimate on this system of planting is half a ton of combed fibre, per acre. On Sweet Kamiri Estate, up to 1,400 lb. of fibre per acre from one harvest have been obtained. The cost of upkeep after planting is practically nil as weeding is discontinued after sowing, any weeds that do appear during the early stages of growth being soon shaded out. It will be seen from this that it is very necessary to have the land free from weeds prior to sowing. On Sweet Kamiri Estate two consecutive crops have been obtained over 12 acres without material decline in yield.

Stripping and Retting.—The best time for cutting is just after the plant has flowered i.e. at about three months from planting. When the time comes for harvesting all fibre should be stripped from the wood in the field before retting, as this is more economical.

An effective method of stripping is to have about six pegs of hard wood fitted tightly into a good beam, say three feet long on uprights of about 4 feet in order to allow it to be fixed firmly in the ground. The method of

APRIL, 1923.]201

stripping the fibre is to give the butt end of the stalk three or four sharp taps until the fibre at the butt-end is freed from the stick,—the ends being gathered in the hands; placing the fibre round the peg and pulling, when the whole of the fibre will strip from the stick. It is important not to harvest more fibre than can be stripped on the day of cutting, otherwise the material becomes dry and it is then extremely difficult to separate the fibre from the stick. It would appear that the best time for harvesting is after rain, as the fibre comes away more easily from the stick than it does during a dry period. The retting tanks should be near a stream to facilitate the washing of the fibre after retting. Retting takes from eight to ten days. The material should be inspected on the eighth day and removed from the tank if sufficiently retted, but if not, left for another day or so until the process is complete. The cultivator is warned of the danger of over retting, which causes the fibre to be weak and brittle. A recent report by a London broker on one sample of fibre submitted indicates this danger. The broker in question stated.....“but part rather weak caused probably by being over-retted.” The fibre while in the tank is kept submerged in the water; this is easily done by placing heavy jungle timber over the fibre. The fibre after being removed from the tank is thoroughly washed in running water, if possible, and care taken to see that all foreign matter is removed during the process of washing. The next operation is sundrying, after which the fibre is combed and baled, when it is ready for shipment. It is not essential to comb the material but it is to be recommended as a very much higher price is obtained.

Costs.—The following costs are based on Roselle being grown as a catch crop with a yield of half a ton per acre, per crop.

Retting - - - - - 2.00 ,,
Baling - - - - - 0.10 ,,

i.e. $106.40 per ton.

The report received from London on samples of fibre submitted are distinctly encouraging. The following abstracts from reports may be cited as typical:—

(a) London, 29th September 21. "Material is of a jute nature but stronger." We value samples as follows:—

"A" Sample uncombed valued about £20 per ton
"B" Sample combed about £30 ,,

(b) "The value of this fibre on the 8th February was about £28 per ton as against the value of jute at £24 or so per ton, and you will remember that the sample you supplied was not of first quality."

The amount of combings is very small, not exceeding 2-3 per cent. of the total crop. Preliminary advice from London of the first ton shipment (sent on 4th June) states that the firm price would be about £35 per ton.

The profit therefore amounts to £133 per ton or about 75 per cent.

In further explanation of market price, it should be pointed out that the price of jute has varied in the last year from £24 to £38 per ton, the price having shewn a steady rise during the year under review.—MALAYAN AGRIC. JOURNAL, Vol. X, No. 8.

NOTES ON ROSELLE FIBRE.

An enquiry for 7000 tons at £30-0-0 per ton has recently been received in Malaya. The Firm of MESSRS. DUREGE AND THOMAS, LTD., Penang, has erected a baling press and are prepared to receive parcels for baling and exporting and hold out a price of £28-£29 per ton c.i.f. London.

It has been found that groundnuts as a rotation crop for Roselle is a very profitable investment as well as putting nitrogen into the soil.

Latest experiments have shown that the present practice of retting in stagnant water can be more effectively and cheaply done in a running stream provided the water is clean.

It is believed that Roselle sown on lalang land dug over only once will by its shade practically kill out the remaining lalang roots. Experiments in this connection are now being carried out.

Excellent reports are now being received of rope made from Roselle fibre in Malaya.

The cultivation of Roselle on young rubber clearings holds out a profitable employment for spare labour while restriction lasts.

One advantage the cultivation of Roselle holds over other fibres is the fact that no machinery is required in its preparation for export except baling.

Roselle fibre is said to be an improved substitute for jute and to contain almost double the strength.

The range for uses for jute are wide.

(1) Making cloths of different qualities ranging from substitutes for silk to shirtings—curtains, carpets and gunnies.

(2) For making paper from waste.

(3) In making cordage from the coarser qualities

In 1913 (Pre war) India exported over 768,451 tons of jute of which the United Kingdom took 350,000 valued at nine and a quarter million sterling. In addition India exported 3683/4 million gunny bags valued at four and a half million.—MALAYAN TIN AND RUBBER JOURNAL, Vol. XII, No. 2.

FRUITS.

FRUIT CULTURE IN FLORIDA.

The following extract is taken from Kew Bulletin of Miscellaneous Information, No. 8, 1922 :—

Fruit-growing is a subject of importance in tropical countries, not only from the point of supplying markets for local consumption, but also in the hope of establishing an export trade to markets in temperate and more densely populated countries. The accompanying résumé of a paper by DR. J. C. TH. UPHOF, in which he gives his experiences of fruit-growing in tropical and sub-tropical Florida, should be of interest to those similarly engaged in other tropical countries.

Fruit-growing in Florida has become an important industry during recent years, and has been developed through the introduction of modern systems of orchard management, the use of machinery, the latest methods in combating insect pests and plant diseases, and in organising a sound system of marketing. These results have been largely possible through the enterprise of American and European financiers, the work of the United States Agricultural Experiment Stations and the Department of Agriculture, and the lessons learnt from the study of similar industries in the neighbouring State of California.

Oranges, grape fruit, tangerines and pecans are already on the markets as crops of first importance, whilst the cultivation of avocados, mangos, and other tropical fruits is being prosecuted with energy. It is hoped that the pine-apple industry, which during the last eight years has steadily declined, will also be revived.

CITRUS FRUITS.

Nurseries.—Oranges are budded on to sour orange or grape fruit stock when it is three to four years old. Satsuma oranges are generally budded on to Citrus trifoliata, as this stock can stand the cold better in the northern part of Florida.

Seeds of the stock are sown in nurseries in December and January, that of Citrus trifoliata in September and October. Sowings are made in rows 2 ft. apart, and the seedlings transplanted when one year old to rows 4 ft. apart, where for one or two years they remain to get established. They are then budded, wax cloth being used to fasten the bud, and, provided the bark easily separates from the stem, the operation may be carried out at any time of the year. In the spring seedlings are topped, but the shoot from the introduced bud is staked if necessary and only pinched back when it is some 30 in. long.

Planting.—The land is first cleared, broken, and prepared, and the young trees planted out in December and February during their resting period. They must not be planted too deep as their roots are surface-feeders, and care must be taken not to expose the roots before planting.

204[APRIL, 1923.

The best plan is to have the holes opened only just ahead of the planters who bring the seedlings in boxes from the nurseries. It is advisable to mix about 1 lb. of chemical fertiliser with the soil of each plant before filling in the hole : fresh manure is not recommended. A thorough watering must be given after planting and repeated every ten days for some time, each plant receiving 5 to 10 gallons. The usual planting distances are, for oranges and grape fruit, 25 by 25 ft., or in the best soils 30 by 30 ft., for Satsuma oranges, 20 by 20 ft., for lemons 20 by 25 ft.. for limes 15 by 20 ft., for kumquat oranges 10 by 15. ft.

A most important fact to be borne in mind is that Citrus fruits must have good drainage. In Florida, where the land is usually very sandy, a hard pan is occasionally found a few feet below the surface, and this is generally broken by dynamite, so as to lower the water level of the soil.

Manures.—The supply of organic matter must receive careful attention by way of green manures and in regular applications of chemical fertilisers.

As green manures, leguminous plants are generally grown, and of these preference is given to Velvet Beans (Stizolobium Deeringianum, Bort., and S. niveum, Roxb.) and the Iron and Brabham varieties of the Cow Pea (vigna sinensis, L.). In the matter of chemical fertilisers the number of applications and composition of the fertiliser require to be varied according to the age of the crop. Young trees receive three or four applications a year, in the spring, once or twice in the summer, and finally in September. The spring and summer fertilisers contain 5 per cent. nitrates, 6-8 per cent. phosphates and 2-3 per cent, potash, but in the autumn the nitrates are reduced to 2-3 per cent. The first application is 1 to 2 lb. a tree, and is increased by 1 lb. a tree until the trees are five to six years old and are in full bearing. Fertiliser is then given three times a year with a percentage of 3 to 4 of nitrates, 7 to 8 of phosphates and 3 to 4 of potash, until the trees are some ten years old when the amount per tree is 15 to 30 lb. yearly, whilst large, old trees may require as much as 30 to 70 lb.

Catch crops and honey.—Catch crops of cabbage, lettuce, beans and strawberries, and even peaches are grown for the first three or four years, but should then be cut out.

Bee-keeping provides a useful side crop, besides being important to the trees for pollination purposes. Excellent honey is obtained from the Citrus flowers, and the light-coloured Italian bee, which is common in the United States, is the one usually kept. When the flowers are over, however, the bees may be removed.

Pruning.—This is confined to thinning out unnecessary branches and shaping the tree and is generally done in summer.

The Crop.—The trees flower in March and April and occasionally again in the early summer. The fruit is gathered from November to the following April.

FUNGUS AND INSECT PESTS.

The following are the principal diseases encountered :—

Root Disease.—“Foot Rot,” caused by Phytophthora terrestris. Chiefly attack old sweet-seedling groves, and is rarely found where the sour orange stock has been raised, as this appears very resistant to attacks. It first appears in the collar or in the main roots, just below the surface of the soil. The decaying bark has the appearance of being water-soaked and a watery gum is found beneath it. Diseased parts are cut out and the wounds painted with an antiseptic. The use of seedlings of the sour orange stock is the best way to prevent the appearance of this disease.

APRIL, 1923.]205

Stem Diseases.—"Withertip," caused by Colletotrichum gloeosporioides, attacks the twigs and branches, especially of lime and lemon varieties. It appears as a withering and dying back of the twigs and branches. Pruning is recommended, and some growers spray with Bordeaux Mixture (4-4-50.) directly after winter pruning.

"Gummosis," cause at present unknown. Appears generally on sweet oranges and grapefruit varieties. Appears as an exudation of gum and the formation of characteristic spots on the trunk and large branches. The treatment recommended is the removal of the dead and diseased bark down to the healthy wood; treat with an antiseptic and cover with tar or whitelead paint.

"Dieback." At present the cause of this disease is not known.

"Scaly Bark" is caused by Cladosporium herbarum, var. citricolum. Spraying with Bordeaux Mixture (5-5-20) is recommended.

Leaf Disease.—"Melanose" is caused by Phomopsis citri.

Fruit Diseases.—"Fruit Rot," caused by Colletotrichum glaucesporioides. Causes an anthracnose-like spotting of the fruit. An ammoniacal solution of copper carbonate is recommended and must be applied every ten days until the disease is under control.

"Fruit Canker," caused by Pseudomonas citri, was generally reported but has been got under control by a well-organised State campaign and quarantine. It appears on the fruit and young twigs as characteristic light brown spots 1/16th-1/4 in. in diameter, occurring singly or in groups and coalescing. On the leaves it appears as watery spots. All attacked trees must be destroyed.

"Citrus Scab" is caused by Cladosporium citri.

Of insect pests the following are the commonest: Citrus White Fly (Dialeurodes citri), Purple Scale (Lepidosophes Beckii), Rust Mite (Eriophyes oleivorus), Florida Red Scale (Chrysomphalus aonidum), and Cloudy-winded White Fly (Dialeurodes citrifolia). Spraying is recommended with a mixture of soap \frac{1}{2} lb., paraffin oil 2 gallons, water 1 gallon, diluted to 10 to 50 times with water.

Biological control by the introduction of entomogenous fungi has received considerable attention and is assisted by the Florida State Plant Board, who distribute fungi culture for this purpose.

THE SETTING OF FRUIT.

Investigations undertaken by MR. D. CASELLA* prove that fungicidal and insecticidal preparations are all most decidedly injurious to the setting of fruits if they come in contact with the pollen. All the specifics he tested were harmful, including sulphur, to which some persons attribute a beneficial action in the setting of fruits. Water also proved injurious; it intensified the harmful effects of previously applied fungicides on the germinative power of the pollen. These conclusions confirm the contentions of many growers that it is harmful to use either insecticides or fungicides at the time when the blossoms of fruit trees are expanding.—GARDENERS' CHRONICLE, Vol. LXXIII, No. 1889.

*"Study on the Pollen of Fruit Trees" by D. CASELLA (Cattedra di Arboricoltura ella R. Scuola sup. di Agricoltura in Portici pp. 24, 4 pl. Cosenza, 1922.

COFFEE.

COFFEE CULTURE.*

J. HAGEN.

(Translated from the Dutch by H. L. LUDOWYK, Librarian, Department of Agriculture.)

CHAPTER VI.—Continued from March Issue.

HARVESTING AND MANUFACTURE,

After a period of from seven to ten months, the duration depending upon the species planted as well as on the climate in which it grows, the coffee berries begin to ripen. Arabian coffee puts forth blossom four times, of which one flowering, by its noticeable profuseness, may well be marked out as being the great or principal flowering.

Liberian coffee, Quillou and the other flower regularly throughout the year, although at one special time the bloom is more copious than at others.

On a coffee estate the harvest season is really the most enjoyable time of the year. Many people come to lend a helping hand—who, by the way, seek recompense too—and then the whole estate is awake with life and animation. Women and children are principally employed to do the plucking, but, if necessary, men are also hired. Armed with empty sacks, empty baskets and light bamboo ladders too, if necessary, the pluckers make their way to the gardens. Each cooly is allotted a row of trees of which he has to pick the berries. Careful supervision should be maintained over the picking so that no unripe berries are allowed to be picked, and that the workmen do not, through carelessness, injure the trees. As soon as the ripe berries are picked, those fallen on the ground, some of which may perhaps be unripe, ought to be picked up. These should be separated and marked out as inferior.

At about 3 o'clock in the afternoon, the pickers return with their sacks quite full, and the clerk receives the berries and pays the labourers. Here and there on the plantation, the small beast of prey, the "loewak" leaves traces of the damage it has done to the crop. These remnants too should be gathered. Good tasters prefer this coffee to any other; and the fact that these animals attack only the ripest berries may account for this preference. On receipt, the coffee is first measured, and then weighed. This helps the people in the factory to ascertain approximately what output of manufactured coffee would be available for the market. Generally what is done is this: A basin which holds just a picul (1.17 cwt.) of red coffee is taken and the coffee is measured off with it. Five of these basins go to make up one picul (1.17 cwt.) of manufactured coffee. This is the case with Arabian coffee.

* ONZE KOLONIALE LANDBOUW VII, DIE KOFFICULTUUR, DOOR J. HAGEN, and Planter, TWEED DRUK-HAARLEM, 1917, H. D. THEIME EN ZOON PRIJS £2.2s.

APRIL, 1923.]207

The raw product of both Liberian and Arabian coffee can be prepared in two ways : the ordinarily adopted dry method, or the wet West Indian method.

If the common method be adopted, the coffee should at once be brought to the drying pans where they should lie heaped up for about 24 hours. After this the silvery film will be noticed to get loose, so that with little effort it can be separated from the bean. Some are under the impression that this process is detrimental to the quality of the coffee ; but I know from experience that it is not so. The berries should then be spread in the sun or in a desiccating chamber taking care to see that it is regularly stirred. When the coffee has reached the stage of dryness required—when it has become “glass-hard,” so hard that like a piece of glass it cracks and flies in smithereens when it is struck with a hammer—then the other parts of the process of manufacture that are the same as those of the West Indian method can follow. For the present, the dry method should be employed in the case of inferior coffee, and every estate should provide itself with a factory in which the superior types of coffee should be prepared according to the wet method. The coffee prepared according to the latter method, on account of the finer nature of the product and the uniformity in colour, fetches higher prices ; and what is more, it has the advantage of being less expensive than the other. These points surely show the superiority of the wet method over the dry one.

In a factory of the British West Indies, the coffee, when brought just after plucking is emptied into a trough of masonry work through which a stream of water is kept running. This stream brings the coffee to the pulpers by which the pulp is removed. There are two sorts of pulpers commonly in use—the Walker pulper and the Lidgerwood Pulper. The latter being larger and of greater capacity are dearer.

The coffee is brought up by the water into the Walker Pulper between a turning disc and a pair of fastened iron blocks. The discs have a rubbed surface of copper. Sometimes it is of iron completely and I, for my part, prefer the latter since the iron plate would not as fast lose from use the rubbed nature of its surface. The blocks of iron—the knives—are set at a little distance from the disc. When the disc turns, the coffee is directed against it by the blocks. This wears and tears away the peel, and the beans, free of peel, are directed out.

The Lidgerwood pulpers are worked on the same principle, except that the disc is replaced by two cylinders, also with rubbed surfaces as in the case of the disc. The coffee is brought up by the stream of water to the first cylinder which lies just next to, and nearly touching, a block of rubber. The coffee gets caught in between the rotating cylinder and the block of rubber and the rubbed surface of the cylinder causes the rind to peel off. Berries that have escaped pulping come in with the stream of pulped coffee that flows into revolving drum which is perforated. The pulped coffee escapes through the perforation and the rest comes to the second cylinder where the same process as has been described takes place.

The floor of a receiving trough of a coffee factory slopes sharply from the base of the walls towards the middle of the floor causing an angular

208[APRIL, 1923.

depression. The trough is in its length given a slope of from 3 to 5 in 100. The coffee then lies in a cumulated triangular heap in the trough, and the stream of water that is directed down it bears away the berries. By regulating the flow of water down the trough, the amount of berries washed down can also be regulated. This is a great convenience, for the influx of a larger supply of berries than the pulper can deal with can be prevented.

Liberian coffee cannot be prepared in any way other than by that of the wet method, since the peel when dry gets hard, tough and leathery and difficult to remove. Furthermore, when this species is prepared according to the dry process, it does not have a good appearance and regularity in colour. The pulper above described cannot be used for Liberian coffee. The size of the berries vary so much, and the peel is so thick and leathery that the process of improving upon the already existing pulpers to suit this species took rather a long time. The pulpers that are suitable are those of SCHAPP and those of RIEMSDIJK.

The pulped coffee is again washed down by a stream of water to the fermenting basins where they remain for from 36 to 40 hours, the duration depending on the climate. Fermentation which sets in pretty fast is retarded or prevented by heat. For this reason the heaps of coffee are covered with sacks.

The fermenting basins are also of masonry work. They are about 3\frac{1}{3} feet deep. The other measurements, of course, depend on the quantity of coffee that one intends them to receive. The floor of the basin is sloped away so that all water can be excluded through a sluice with a sheet of perforated corrugated iron.

Fermentation so changes the nature of the glucose layer that after the fermenting process is over, the layer can easily be washed off. This is done in the wash basin in which the coffee is stirred and washed in fresh streaming water till it is quite clean. The beans now, without the adhering pulpy matter become hard to the touch.

In the meantime, the men have the opportunity of gathering together the floating beans and those that are not of a superior quality, and putting them among the inferior coffees. On large estates there is used a washing machine—a drum or cylinder which keeps turning round fast on an axle provided with a number of pegs.

When the washing is over, the coffee is brought into the drying pans either getting coolies to transfer it, or, if the factory has facilities for the purpose, by means of a stream of water. We see now that the choice of a site for a factory is not a very simple matter. If possible such land should be chosen as would allow water to be got to it easily, and which would also allow all the transferring of the coffee during the different stages of manufacture to be effected by means of a current of water. This at once cuts out a great part of the expense on labour that will have daily to be incurred otherwise. If water power can further be utilised by means of a water-wheel, so much the better.

Drying pans are generally large trays made of interlaced bamboo and supported on wooden trestles. The bottom of the pan too is of bamboo and it is almost entirely covered with coir mats in order to prevent the beans from falling through the interstices which occur as the bamboo is not closely interlaced. These pans are also provided with lids fixed to them—these can be turned open in order to dry the coffee when the sun shines bright. Better equipped factories, however, have their drying pans of masonry structure, the floor of which, as it is also a hard one and impervious, is made high along the middle and sloped away towards the sides of

APRIL, 1923.]209

the base, so that the water that strains out of the beans can easily flow out of the pan. The pans are also provided with an iron roofing just above it. This is fixed on a frame that can be moved on rails, so that it can be pushed away or pulled on, as required, easily.

In the drying pans the coffee is thinly spread out and regularly and repeatedly dried in the sun. If there is a very large harvest, sun-drying alone becomes a very heavy task and impracticable, even though much labour be employed; and in wet seasons this process of drying would take a very long time. On this account, nearly every estate goes in now for desiccators. The coffee, first wind dried, is brought into the desiccating chamber and dried by letting into the chamber currents of heated air. Three or four days are taken up in this process. It is possible to dry the coffee faster by raising the temperature, but this is injurious to the colour of the product.

The desiccating chambers used in India are of quite different type—according to the old system, the air is heated under a perforated iron floor by means of hot tubes. Later an improved method was devised for transmitting the warmed air through the coffee from generators, or by means of a ventilator, placed above the coffee, drawing the hot air through it. In some cases double bottomed desiccating chambers have been introduced and also many other improvements. During the drying process in the desiccating chamber, the coffee should regularly be moved about, stirred and spread by the coolies. It is important that the beans be thinly spread and not allowed to be in heaps.

When the coffee gets glass-hard, then, the next step in the process of manufacture, hulling, can take place. This is done by pounding the coffee in small baskets, and can be done by women; or the whole process can be carried out by machinery specially adapted to the purpose. If the former means be employed, the coffee is returned by the labourers free from all loose shell and quite clean and only the sorting remains to be done.

The oldest machines for this purpose were mills with wooden or iron wheels turning in a hollow or gutter. The wheel had to be prevented from touching the sides of the gutter in order to avoid injury to beans. This will render good service, but demands much labour. Later, hulling machines were constructed specially for the purpose; and of these, the "Engelberg" is one of the best. Here the coffee is brought between two cylinders, the inner one of which rotates swiftly while the outer one is fixed. The machine is so constructed that it crushes only the horny shell of the bean. By means of an exhauster, a great part of the crushed shell is separated at the same time, so that the coffee comes out clean or very nearly so, and but little winnowing is required.

Then follows the next step of the process, the sorting which is done first by machine and then by hand. The sorting machine is constructed as described below. There is a long cylinder with perforations of different sizes which keeps on turning slowly. A spiral introduced within it keeps on continually forcing the beans out. In this manner sorting according to the sizes of the beans is effected since the beans have to pass successively from the smallest perforations on one side to the largest on the other. In most cases there are four different dimensions for the perforations. The round beans being the largest remain to the last in the cylinder, and find their place in the sort in the largest beans—the extraordinary large beans, or the "elephant beans," giant beans. After this comes the hand sorting. The women pick out of the five different sorts all the broken and discoloured beans.

As mentioned before, in the case of Liberian coffee the wet process only has to be adopted. The colour desired in this case is a straw-yellow. The bean should also be entirely free from the silvery film.

210[APRIL, 1923.

For Robusta both methods can be employed ; but for obtaining the favourable colour and for separating the whole of the silvery film from the bean the British West Indies method is preferable. As the rind in the case of Robusta is soft and thin, the commonly used pulping machines, with the plates slightly adjusted to suit its needs, suffice. The coffee is left to ferment then for 36 hours and is brought dripping into the desiccating chamber and dried as fast as possible at a pretty high temperature. Coffee so prepared will seldom fail to have as good a colour as would guarantee the fineness of the flavour it would then possess. There should be only 2 sortings: 1st quality and pickings.

When the coffee has been put into sacks having the stamp and name of the estate, and weighing one picul (1.17 cwt.) when filled, it is ready for export.

When shipping and exporting is difficult planters might find it necessary to store their coffee. It can be stored either in unhulled beans or after hulling and sorting. In both cases care should be taken that the coffee is dried glass hard before putting it in sacks. The coffee ought regularly to be taken out of their sacks and put into other sacks, so that by so doing, it can regularly be brought to view and examined. The bluish-gray colour now gradually disappears as the coffee absorbs moisture ; and the weight increases.

Care should be taken to see that the coffee is kept free from the attacks of the beetle. Most beetles, especially the larvae of Araecurus fasciculatus feast on stored coffee and once they get access to it the coffee will lose a considerable percentage of its weight. As a trap for these, there should be left in the store rooms here and there, some dishes with infused coffee in them. The beetles come to it and while many of them are occupied in drinking off the dish, they can all be captured.

CHAPTER VII.

COFFEE AS CATCH CROP.

Of late coffee has become considerably important as a catch crop. This is especially the case in rubber estates.

The necessary conditions that a catch crop should fulfil are these :—

  • (I) The interplanting should in no way be prejudicial to the main crop.
  • (II) It should come soon into bearing.
  • (III) It should not demand too much labour and attention.

We too, as the case of those who plant rubber—having planted far apart and there being much empty ground from which no benefit is derived, and more space than is necessary for the soil to profit by from the play of the sun upon it—have been anxious to hit upon the plant that would best satisfy the above enumerated conditions. And in the quest we have not been unsuccessful. As far as my experience and observation goes, I feel that all catch crops are injurious to the main culture. In the case of Robusta and also of Quillou coffee I must make an exception, at least when it is planted in districts where the species thrive well, as for instance in the damp regions of East Java.

These coffee species have the advantage of giving in a short time a good harvest, and they do not injure the Hevea at all. In the five years during which Robusta is grown as a catch crop it yields about 35 cwt. per acre. After the five years it has to be uprooted in consideration of the development of the Hevea plants. It is obvious that the yield of Robusta will go a great way to defray the expenses of the rubber estate. Especially now, when there has been such a drop in the price of rubber, it will be found very advisable to cultivate both Hevea and Robusta together.

APRIL, 1923.]211

SPICES.

PEPPER IN SARAWAK.

The following information is published by the Committee for Agricultural and Forest Exhibits, Malaya-Borneo Exhibition, in "Notes on Sarawak Trade."

Pepper-growing, which used to be one of the chief industries of Sarawak, is gradually dying out, chiefly on account of a disease for which no cure has yet been found,

It is grown on red loamy soil, and will not flourish in clay or sand.

The pepper vine was cultivated in the Upper Sarawak district and at Lundu and Simatan; these are the old plantations. Large quantities are now grown in the Batang Lupar and Rejang districts, but the plantations are not sufficient to replace the large districts which have died out in the Upper Sarawak district.

The amount exported in 1911 was about 2,800 tons, as compared with just over 1,000 tons in 1920.

PLANTATION.

There are two kinds of vines grown in Sarawak, the broad leaf vine and the small leaf vine.

Vines are planted from cuttings in soil prepared with burnt earth in the months of August and September; the cuttings are planted four to five feet apart, and they require shading until they begin to shoot.

When they have been planted about eight months, a belian post (tuat), about 16 feet long, is put in the ground near the plants, leaving some 12 feet above ground for the vines to grow around. Burnt earth is applied to the growing vine three times a year until it bears, which is about two years after planting; while the vine is maturing, the flowers appearing on the growing shoots are plucked.

After two years' growth, when the vine is considered mature, flowers are left to seed, but the young shoots are thinned out continually; the stronger shoots are tied to the post by means of a jungle twine made from "kulit slaut." At this period the vines are manured with prawn refuse abok (sessar), about six tahils being applied to each vine.

The crop is harvested about 10 months after flowering, in the months of July to September. If the crop is weak, quantities of berries drop to the ground; these are gathered up to be marketed as black pepper.

This is the more usual method of cultivating pepper at the present time; in the old days, however, the method of cultivation took longer, the method being as follows:—

When the shoots from the young plants had reached a height of about six feet up the post, they were pulled down and curled around the foot of the post; three or four of these shoots were layered, the rest being cut off, these layered shoots being again thinned out as the vine grew up the post until the vine was considered mature, about three years after planting, when the followers were left to seed.

Although by this method the vine did not come into bearing until three years after planting, it continued to bear heavier crops for some 20 years, as against 10 to 15 years by the present method.

212[APRIL, 1923.

To continue the description of the growth and care of the pepper vine : When vines approach the bearing season they are sprayed with a mixture of rotten tobacco and tuba, prepared with water ; but even this spraying does not appear to prevent the spread of the fatal disease of black berries, known amongst Chinese as " Voo Choon."

It is this disease which had done such damage to the gardens of Upper Sarawak district that the industry is dying out.

PREPARATION.

White pepper is produced from the plucked berries which are gathered during the harvest, packed in gunny bags and immersed in water for about one week, or until the outer skin of the berries has rotted off.

After immersion the berries are put into baskets and washed ; during the process the baskets are rotated by hand, when the rotted outer skin rubs off and is easily separated from the clean berries remaining.

The washed seeds are then sun dried, after which they are shaken up in large open baskets, the stalks being separated from the seeds during this winnowing process.

The dried seeds are now ready for the market ; only 5 per cent. moisture is allowed to be contained in the finished product ; this standard is maintained by Government regulations, and inspectors are appointed to control this.

Black pepper.—There are three methods of preparing black pepper.

(1) The plucked berries are piled in heaps in the house of the planter where they are left for three days, after which they are sun dried for another three days.

(2) The plucked berries are poured into boiling water, after which they are sun dried.

(3) The berries are smoked over a fire, being placed on mats made of small sticks and twigs until dry.—INDIAN SCIENTIFIC AGRICULTURIST, Vol. 4. No. 1.

VANILLA.

Another interesting cultivation which does not receive all the attention that it deserves is vanilla growing. This is not a cultivation that could be generally recommended in the absence of an expert in the curing of the beans, but such an expert has been present in the island for some years, and there is, at the proper season a market for uncured vanilla beans which have been picked in the right condition.

There are so many opportunities of growing vanilla vines on suitable trees in a small way, or in the case of properly laid out cultivation, on tutors especially grown for this purpose, that it is rather remarkable so little has been done in this direction. Possibly the difficulty of getting healthy vines to flower sufficiently, and the need of pollinating the flowers, have proved a drawback, but how to overcome the former and how to effect the latter could be easily demonstrated at the Botanic Gardens to interested persons in the course of a few minutes.

Dominica possesses the advantage of a suitable climate for growing Vanilla together with the very great benefit of a resident expert in curing this product. Clearly now is the time to make an effort to lay the foundations of a vanilla industry.

In this connexion it may be mentioned that a large vanilla nursery has been maintained at the Botanic Gardens for many years past, and cuttings are available at any time in large quantities at merely nominal charges.—

Report on the Agri. Dept., Dominica, 1921-22.

APRIL, 1923.]213

SOILS AND MANURES.

THE MANURING OF COFFEE.

It appears probable that the effect of the manuring of Coffee with chemical fertilisers has not been watched for a period long enough to justify advising their general use. There can be no doubt that the ordinary chemical manures (Sulphate of Ammonia, Sulphate of Potash, Nitrate of Soda, Superphosphate) have a useful effect on annual crops in so far as the immediate result is concerned and that the after-effects have but a secondary importance, but for Coffee and for other plants, a slower and more durable action being desirable, the value of these manures has yet to be established. In fact, SIR JOHN LAWES has gone so far as to affirm that chemical manures are decidedly unsuitable for Coffee and there seems generally to be contradictory views in every country where this plant is cultivated.

Manures, however, which can nevertheless be confidently recommended are those of organic nature, including the prunings of the plant itself, weeds, the pulp and other residues of the preparation of the bean, as well as dung, green manure, bones, dried blood, oil cakes, natural guano, fish guano, and, among the mineral matters, ashes and lime. Cattle manure and green dressings however are not always available; but the system of breaking down straw and using it in the place of cattle manure has some chance of success and as the humification of straw cannot be obtained by simple humectation but requires the presence of nitrogen, the latter can be added in the form of cattle urine, or by filtration of sewage water on a bed of straw.

It is not possible to choose a manure from those quoted above without a knowledge of local conditions, and after experimentation, particularly regarding the economic advantages.

A manure of notable value can be obtained by mixing the pulp of the berry with bone meal, in the proportion of 1 part of Bone Meal to 20 parts of pulp, to which should be added a generous amount of ordinary estate rubbish. The mass should be buried or sheltered from the sun and rain for several months. When sufficient decomposition has taken place, the mixture should be buried around the plant without, however, damaging the roots, or it may be applied as a mulch. The pulp, the husk and the other residues of the preparation of the bean have their value in nitrogen, phosphoric anhydride, potassium and lime; whilst the bone meal furnishes phosphoric anhydride, nitrogen and lime. The percentage of these constituents in the pulp is much higher in the fresh material than when the pulp has been exposed to the sun and rain; it is very necessary therefore to keep it under cover as is outlined above. Any ash obtained by burning the various bits of rubbish which collect on the estate may be added to the mass, thus improving the potassium content. When considered necessary (and tropical soils are often deficient in lime) it is as well to broadcast slack lime over the ground some months before applying the above or other manure, at the rate of 1775 kg. per hectare. This is equivalent to 3,900 lb., per hectare which equals 2.47 acres [Say 1600 lb. per acre: Ed. P.C.] or if the bushes, are planted as widely as 3 metres by 3 metres (roughly 9\frac{3}{4} ft. by 9\frac{3}{4} ft.—Ed. P.C.) at the rate of 1 kg., 36 (approximately 3 lb. Ed. P.C.) per plant.
