SOIL TEMPERATURE.

Everyone concerned with the cultivation of plants is aware that the temperature of the soil plays an important part in determining the rate of growth and ripening of crops. It is a commonplace of horticultural knowledge that some soils are early and others late, and it is recognised that early soils owe their property of precocious crop production not only to their situation in sunny districts, and to their aspect, but also to their texture. For a heavy soil, even if well drained, will hold more water than a light soil, and will in consequence warm up less rapidly in the spring. It is no less well known that the temperature of the soil has a remarkable effect on root action. If it falls below a certain minimum absorption of water it is checked and growth is retarded. It does not matter whether there is or is not ample water present in the soil, for as the temperature falls roots become less and less efficient at absorbing it. Temperature, therefore, determines the availability of water in the soil. Although knowledge of effects of soil temperature on plant growth is fairly satisfactory, it has many gaps and as a first step towards the filling of these gaps, Messrs. KEEN and RUSSELL have carried out a very complete series of observations* at Rothamsted on the daily fluctuations of soil temperature throughout the year. The results of their records are of great value both to the botanist and to the horticulturist. They show that the roots of plants enjoy a more congenial climate than do the aerial parts, for the soil is on the average both warmer

* The Factors Determining Soil Temperature, JOURNAL OF AGRICULTURAL SCIENCE, XI, 3 July, 1921.

216[APRIL, 1923.

and moister than the air above it. As would be expected, the soil-temperature shows a daily periodicity. At a depth of six inches it begins to rise at about 9'30 a. m. and reaches a maximum at about 4'30 in the afternoon. From that time the soil temperature falls slowly and is at its minimum at about 8'30 a. m., so that the roots of a plant remaining at six inches below the surface enjoy a rising temperature for about 7-8 hours and have to submit to a falling temperature for the rest of the twenty-four hours. The soil reaches its daily maximum temperature some three hours later than the air. The maximum in summer is about 22°C. (71½°F.), though this figure is occasionally surpassed. The summer minimum ranges from 18-21°C. (64-69½°F.). In both summer and winter the minimum soil temperature is well above that of the air ; so much as 6-8°C. (43-46½°F.) in summer and about 3°C. (37-40°F.) in winter. It is not surprising, therefore, that root growth of many plants should continue throughout the winter months when stem growth is entirely or almost entirely arrested. An interesting fact brought out by the records made by MESSRS. KEEN and RUSSELL is that maximal soil temperature on a given day is not closely correlated with the number of hours of sunshine on that day. When, however, instead of a sunshine recorder, an instrument for measuring the total solar radiations is employed, the observations show a close connection between maximum soil temperature and the amount of solar radiation. Rain reduces the maximum but wind apparently does not. Another observation of great interest is that the transition from winter to summer values is generally quick—a quickness which is reflected in the growth of plants in spring. The rapid rise in soil temperature is to be ascribed in part to the increased solar radiations and in part to the drying of the soil. Similarly the cooling of the soil in early winter is rapid, and is attributable to clear October nights when the amount of radiation of heat from the soil becomes considerable. The transition from summer to winter state which our plants exhibit is a complex one, beginning early in the summer and extending over a long period of time. The first sign of the approaching change—this going into winter quarters—is, perhaps, the formation of cork in the stems. This is known to begin well before summer is past. Other changes follow in due course and order ; the vessels of the wood become thick-walled with narrow cavities, in sharp contrast with the thin-walled, wide vessels of early spring. Growth of tree vegetation also slows down early, while summer is still here : later, the winter buds make their appearance and the leaves prepare themselves for their fall by forming a layer of corky tissue in their stalks. Only too little is known of the immediate causes of these advance preparations for the winter state—though the significance of the changes is evidently the need of the aerial parts to prevent a loss of water which the roots, also becoming less active, could not make good. It is not unlikely that the signal to the plant to set going in the hey-day of summer the work of preparing for winter consists in the change of soil temperature. As each day in spring and early summer brings a somewhat higher soil temperature, the plant's activities wax, but the moment the change comes, slight though it be, when to morrow's soil temperature is a little lower than to-day's, the growth of the plant wanes and the orderly and leisurely preparation for winter rest begin.

—GARDENERS' CHRONICLE, VOL. LXXII, No. 1872.

APRIL, 1923,]217

INFLUENCE OF IRRIGATION ON THE COMPOSITION OF THE SOIL.

J. E. CREAVER,

Department of Chemistry and Bacteriology, Utah Agricultural Experiment Station, Logan.

Water has a double action on the soil. It assists or hinders the normal development of the processes in the soil, and its most manifest influence is over the process of nitrification, of which the maximum is attained when the soil contains 60% of its water-holding capacity. Above or below this concentration, there is a decrease; and nitrification ceases when the quantity of water reaches or exceeds 90%. As regards nitrification, therefore, an excess of water is more detrimental than an insufficiency. Under good moisture conditions, from 50 to 100 lb. of nitric acid may be produced in an acre of soil during a season; it is a well-known fact that this acid is of great assistance in the liberation of phosphorus and potassium. The moisture content acts similarly, but in a less degree, on ammonification, the maximum production of which is also reached when the soil contains 60% of its total water-holding capacity. All the other processes which take place in the soil are also dependent on its water content; for instance, the production of carbonic acid gas, which may be as much as 60.1 per acre per day; it also plays an important part in the solution of tricalcium phosphate. Finally, it influences the production of lactic, acetic, butyric, sulphuric, and other acids, which help to dissolve potassium, etc.

The other fundamental action of irrigation water is that it brings or carries away plant food; it impoverishes or enriches the soil. To gain an idea of the enormous quantities of substances that water may carry off from the soil, it is only necessary to consider the constituents of river water. The substances in solution such as for instance, sodium chloride are not generally of any importance in agriculture, but useful substances, such as potassium, nitrogen and phosphorus are not lacking. The writer describes certain analyses on the question. Some irrigation drain waters are still richer; certain of them contained as much as 133 pounds per acre foot.

When irrigation is carried out properly, the water as it evaporates, deposits the substances it contains, as in the case of the Nile. Thus, in Utah, the waters used for irrigation contain 0.79 to 59.0 parts of potassium per million, or an average of 5 parts which may be used by the soil. Irrigation waters contain besides potassium, nitrogen and other useful soluble substances; they are therefore capable of improving the soil. The great point is to irrigate in moderation in order not to wash out the soil. Irrigation may transform the desert into a garden or render the most productive fields barren, according as it is well or ill done.—INTERNATIONAL REVIEW OF SCIENCE AND PRACTICE OF AGRICULTURE, Year XIII—No. 9,

218[APRIL, 1923.

DEEP-ROOTING PLANTS AND SOIL FERTILITY.

A fertile soil is a "live" soil, and one with a generous supply of decomposed organic matter and humus. A soil can only be fertile or highly productive when it is filled with teeming millions of bacteria. Only life can beget life. The bigger the life within the soil the larger the life it is capable of producing above ground in the form of fruit, etc. In soils with faulty substrata one foot from the surface there is life only in a thin or shallow zone of a few inches. A small life can only beget a small life. A Shetland pony cannot produce a draught horse. To breed big trees and huge crops the parent must be there.

The parent should consist of the 6,000 tons of fertile soil, four feet deep over every acre. Never forget that the amount of fertility underneath determines the amount of productivity on top. It is one of the natural laws in the balance of nature.

The most efficient and valuable chemical agency in disintegrating "hard pans" and loosening up faulty substrata is the root system of deeply penetrating tap-rooted plants. By reason of the killing and decomposition of a suitable root system in situ in the soil certain organic changes are effected in the roots through bacterial agency, whereby nitric acid is produced in addition to other chemical compounds which have a valuable flocculating effect on the soil colloids, and by further chemical interaction convert basic nutrients into available plant-food. Decomposing organic matter in the soil is nature's cure for her faulty soil formations.

Decaying organic or vegetable material means a veritable chemical factory within the soil, incessantly manufacturing carbonic acid, ammonia, nitric acid, etc. The bigger the factory the larger the output of these chemicals, therefore the more roots and vegetative materials incorporated the more nitric acid, etc., produced, and the more completely will faulty substrata be converted into mellow congenial soil.—SOUTH AFRICAN SUGAR JOURNAL, Vol. 6, No. 11.

STRAW FOR MANURE.

Investigations carried out recently at Rothamsted (England) Experiment Station have demonstrated the value of adding a soluble nitrogenous fertiliser, such as sulphate of ammonia, for the purpose of accelerating the decomposition of vegetable matter to be used as manure. The process has been used with great success in the treatment of straw, which is first wetted thoroughly and allowed to lie until it has become damped through. The sulphate of ammonia is then spread over the surface (at the rate of \frac{3}{4} cwt. to 1 cwt. per ton of straw) and conveyed in solution into the heap by applying water to the surface. It is necessary that the heap be kept in a moist condition throughout the period of decomposition.—AGRIC., GAZ. of N. S. W. Vol. XXXIII, Part 3.

APRIL, 1923.]219

PESTS AND DISEASES.

SOME INSECTS NOTED AS PESTS OF FRUIT TREES IN SOUTH INDIA.

In the AGRICULTURAL JOURNAL OF INDIA, Vol. XVIII, Part I is reproduced a Paper, on the above subject, read before the NINTH INDIAN SCIENCE CONGRESS, MADRAS, 1922, by T. V. RAMAKRISHNA AYYAR, B.A., F.E.S., F.Z.S., Assistant Entomologist, Madras, from which the following summary is taken :—

Mango.—Insect injury to the mango plant is chiefly caused by four or five kinds of pests, viz., the mango hoppers, the stem-borers, fruit flies, leaf-eaters and scale insects. The mango hoppers (Idiocerus spp.) are very small active creatures appearing in swarms on tender shoots and flower-heads of the mango plant during the cold weather. They suck up the nutrition from the tender parts and often produce serious damage by causing the blossoms and buds to drop down, thereby preventing fruit formation. The stem-borers, of which the commonest one is that popularly known as the mango stem-borer (Balocera rubus), are stout fleshy larvæ of longicorn beetles which enter the stem and burrow through the interior, feeding on the internal tissue of the stem. The borer is often found to kill the branches of trees or even at times the whole tree. The presence of the pest on the tree is indicated by the heap of powdery wood dust and excrement that is seen on the ground below the affected branch, and also by a gallery-like structure of the same materials on the bark of the infested stem. Fruit flies (Chaetodacus spp.) of two or three kinds sometimes cause severe damage to mango fruits. The wriggling whitish maggots of these flies are found inside infested fruits; the latter appear more or less healthy outwardly in the initial stages of infestation, but when cut open will show numerous white maggots burrowing through the pulp and making the fruit unfit for consumption. What happens is that the adult flies thrust their eggs just under the soft skin of the ripening fruits and these eggs become the maggots which, after feeding on the pulp, drop to the soil and become flies after passing the pupal stage. A good percentage of some of the valuable varieties of mango suffers from this kind of injury. Of the leaf-eating pests of mango mention is made of the common nettle grub (Parasa lepidula) of South India, an apple green slug-like spiny caterpillar very irritating to the touch. Young plants suffer more than grown up trees; in the former case the plants are often completely defoliated by hundreds of these slug-caterpillars. Weevils of different kinds often do appreciable damage to the foliage, the leaf-twisting species (Apoderus tranquebaricus) being the chief. The Mango weevil (Cryptorrhynchus mangiferoe) is not an important pest. Scale insects and mealy bugs (Chionaspis, Pulvinaria, Lecanium, Pseudococcus, etc.), are also occasionally found doing damage to the mango plant.

220[APRIL, 1923.

Citrus.—The different varieties of citrus, such as sour and sweet limes, lemons, oranges, pomelos, etc., have been so far found to suffer chiefly from attacks of stem-borers, leaf-eaters, plant lice and fruit-sucking moth. The stem-borers do damage exactly as in mango but the specific insects are not the same in this case though the habits of the larvæ are similar. The orange borer beetles, of which two species (Chloridolum alcemene and Chelidonium cinctum) have been noted, are often bad pests in Coorg and Mysore. Of the leaf-eaters the first place should be given to the orange butterfly (Papilio demoleus), a black and yellow insect found very commonly all over South India. The dark green caterpillar of this butterfly eats the leaves, and sometimes young plants and tender foliage suffer badly. Besides the orange butterfly there is another tiny caterpillar, the larvæ of a very small moth (Phyllocnistis citrella), which sometimes causes injury to the citrus leaves by mining through the leaf tissue and making the leaves wrinkle and curl up. Plant lice (Toxoptera aurantis) of the dark purple brown kind are found now and then in colonies on the fresh shoots of citrus plants, sucking the nutrition and affecting the vigorous growth of the plants : often the affected shoots fade and die. The fruit-sucking moth (Ophidocres fullonica) is an interesting and rare example of an adult lepidopterous insect causing direct damage to a crop. The moth which is stout and beautifully coloured flies about at night in the orange gardens ; a number of these moths settle on the ripening citrus fruits, pierce them by means of their long proboscis, which is supplied with sharp spines, and suck up the fruit juice. As a result the fruits begin to rot and drop down before they ripen fully.

Pomegranate.—The specific pest of this delicious fruit is the fruit-boring caterpillar of a butterfly popularly known as the pomegranate butterfly (Virachola isocrates). The butterfly is one with coppery blue wings and is found fairly common all over South India. The larva is a fleshy dirty brown caterpillar found inside infested fruits, which generally show a hole on the surface through which excrementitious matter is thrown out by the boring larva. An infested fruit when cut open shows many seeds completely spoiled and rotting mixed with excreta of the borer. A hairy caterpillar (Euproctis fraterna) sometimes appears on this plant and does some damage to the foliage, but is not as serious as the fruit borer.

Jak.—Similar to mango and citrus, the jak tree also suffers from stem-boring grubs ; often the mango stem-borer is itself found on the jak tree. Sometimes the shoots and tender leaves are profusely covered with colonies of mealy bugs (Icerya and Pseudococcus) visited by swarms of ants. These mealy bugs drain the sap and affect the vigorous growth of the shoots. At the time when buds and fruits begin to form, a shoot-boring caterpillar (Clyphodes coesalis) and a fruit-borer weevil are seen to do some damage.

Bananas.—The banana plant is not subject to any serious pest. The foliage is occasionally found eaten by caterpillars of sorts—chiefly by a black hairy caterpillar (Pericallia ricini), a spiny slug-caterpillar (Parasa lepidula), and a smooth dark brown caterpillar (Prodenia litura). The well known stem-borer of banana (Cosmopolites sordidus), a small black weevil which has recently become a serious pest of this plant in Australia, Fiji, etc., though found in a few places in South India, has not yet assumed the status of a serious pest. Lace-wing bugs, plant lice and scale insects are also occasionally noted as minor pests.

APRIL, 1923.]221

Grape.—The only insect that might be called a specific pest of grape in South India so far is the grape-vine flea-beetle (Scelodonta strigicollis). It is a very small active coppery brown beetle which appear in numbers on the vines and bites holes on the leaves and tender parts of the plant. Cockchafer beetles are occasionally found feeding on the tender foliage at night, and now and then sphinx caterpillars (Hippotion spp.) also do some damage as leaf-eaters.

Guava.—As a rule this plant suffers chiefly from the attacks of a mealy scale (Pulvinaria psidii), colonies of which sometimes cover the whole foliage as white mealy masses which are visited by swarms of black ants, the ants often doing greater harm as carriers of the pest; as an after effect a sort of sickly black blight appears on the plant. The fruits are invariably subject to fruit flies, often the same as found on mango. Now and then stem-boring beetle grubs are also found as on the mango tree.

Melons.—Fruit flies constitute the main pest of melons of different kinds though now and then a leaf caterpillar (Glyphodes indica) and leaf beetles (Aulacophora spp.) do some substantial damage.

Tamarind.—Though this is not an edible fruit as those mentioned above, it is extremely important as an essential material for culinary purposes. The fruit and shoots of this tree suffer from hard scales (Aspidiotus spp.) and mealy bugs.

Of the other fruit trees which are of minor importance mention is made of fig, pine-apples, custard-apple, wood-apple, cashew, sapota, papaya, zizyphus and the bread-fruit tree. Of these, the papaya, sapota, custard apple and breadfruit tree have not so far been found to be attacked by any serious insect pests. On pine-apple was found a mealy bug (Pseudococcus bromelioe) which is believed to be an introduced pest. The edible fig has been found subject to the attacks of stem-boring longicorn beetles of which there is one (Olenecamptus bilobus) special to fig in the same way as in mango and jak. On the foliage a slender ashy grey caterpillar (Ocinara varians) and some greyish weevils are noticed frequently. Mealy bugs and scales also occasionally appear on the fruit and tender shoots. Zizyphus suffers chiefly from the attacks of a fruit fly (Carpomyia vesuviana) and one or two caterpillars infesting the fruit. Some of the main principles upon which control measures should be based are briefly indicated. All insect pests of fruit trees can be brought together under two main groups according to their feeding habits, viz., those that damage the plant tissue by biting and chewing, called biting insects, and secondly those that affect the plant by sucking up the plant sap from the tender portions, known by the name of sucking insects. Under the first category is included the different kinds of stem and fruit-boring larvæ and leaf-eating caterpillars and beetles. In the latter group are the mango hoppers, the citrus plant lice, scale insects, mealy bugs, the fruit-sucking moths and other bugs sucking the sap from the tender portions of the fruit trees. Except in certain special cases, all control measures depend a good deal on the above grouping, which, of course, pre-suppose a knowledge of the food habits of each pest. And this is particularly so when insecticidal methods are concerned. For all borers inside the stem, shoot and fruit, a direct curative measure like the application of insecticides is impracticable in most cases, as the creatures are internal feeders; so, only such preventive methods as will check the multiplication of the pest are practicable in such cases—such as pruning the affected branches, cutting down and burning dead and dying stems, and destroying infested fruits. In some cases where

222[APRIL, 1923.

beetle or moth larvæ bore into thick stems of trees, they may be pulled out by a hooked wire, or killed by injecting a poisonous mixture by means of a syringe. For fruit flies, however, the only possible methods as far as we know at present are destroying infested fruit and trapping the adult flies by poisoned syrup. In the case of leaf-eaters like caterpillars and beetles, they can be easily collected and destroyed by simple mechanical means, or if insecticidal methods are demanded, a poisonous mixture can be dusted or sprayed on the foliage on which the insects feed. The particular class of insecticides used in such cases is called a stomach poison and this is the kind generally used against biting insects; the poison mixes with food and poisons the insect. The common stomach poisons known are Paris green, lead arsenate, zinc arsenate, etc. For the other class of insects in which are included the mango hoppers, mealy bugs, scales, plant lice, etc., insecticidal methods will be found more practicable and effective. The kind of insecticide used in the case of most of these insects which are sucking in habit is called a contact poison; contact poisons generally affect the insects by external irritation and closure of the respiratory holes; such an insecticide does not mix with the food of the creature. Among the well-known contact washes used are fish-oil soap, crude oil emulsion and tobacco decoction. Spraying experiments carried on against the mango hopper pest with such washes in different parts of India have been found effective, and this method is becoming popular. For plant lice, mealy bugs and scales also such an application will be found effective. As stated before, peculiar pests like the fruit-sucking moth and bugs might require special methods based on common sense and experience, such as covering the fruits, trapping the insects, etc., etc. There is little doubt that insecticidal methods of pest control always play an important part in orchards, since some of the most destructive of fruit tree pests appear to be sucking insects—scales, mealy bugs, hoppers, plant lice, etc. Every fruit-grower who wishes to carry on his work on scientific and successful lines will do well to stock some of the important appliances and materials necessary for carrying on insecticidal methods of pest control whenever wanted. Among these may be mentioned a knapsack spraying outfit, a brass syringe with a long spout for treating borers in stems, one or two hand nets, and a small stock of insecticides like Paris green, lead arsenate, fish-oil soap and crude oil emulsion. These may be considered as essential things for a gardener in the same manner as are his garden implements.

BANANA BUNCHY TOP DISEASE.

DR. DARNELL SMITH, Vegetable Pathologist of the New South Wales
Department of Agriculture

and

HENRY TRYON, Vegetable Pathologist and Government Entomologist,
Queensland.

Theories relating to the following possible agencies in promoting plant sickness were investigated:—

1. Soil Depletion, by the Loss—to Some Extent Absence—of Essential
Banana Plant Food Constituents in it.

Fertiliser field experiments have rendered it evident that the use of complete fertilisers of varying constitution, as well as fertilisers providing a single essential plant food requirement, do not prevent the occurrence of the disease, either in soils relatively rich or in ones relatively poor, as ordinarily understood.

APRIL, 1923.]223

(Note.—These experiments, which have been conducted on proper lines, have, however, not so far related to humus-producing fertilisers nor covered the entire range of soil-types).

2. Loss of Vigour in Banana Plants—e.g., by the Continuous use of Banana Plants of a Single Origin.

Although the general habit of the plants in which the disease may manifest itself, including such plants as receive fertilisers as a field routine procedure, and although the high quality of the banana fruit that the district generally yields, would appear to be conclusive as to the "strain" of plants generally grown not having developed weakness, and so disease, this factor—hypothetical impairment of stamina—has not been lost sight of. It has now been shown experimentally to be non-operative by the manifestation of the Bunchy Top disease in plants introduced into the affected area from remote districts in which there has been no history of the occurrence of the malady, equally with those of local origin. One of these experiments, in which banana corms were obtained from north of Cairns, Queensland, covered no less than ten distinct field plots in the Tweed District.

3. Soil Acidity.

The factor of soil acidity, which might be presumed to operate in promoting the occurrence of disease, has been the object of test experiments with so far negative results. Antacids applied to the soil, whether in the form of lime or basic phosphates, having failed to protect plants from the disease occurrence—even ones introduced from "clear areas."

4. Soil Contagion.

Field experiments have again shown that the disinfection—by one or other fungicides—of suckers in planting, and simultaneously that of the soil with which they are brought in contact, does not prevent the occurrence of the disease in plants derived from such suckers.

5. Definite Parasite Action.

Again, investigations have so far failed to reveal the presence of a fungus-organism or of fungus-organisms capable of originating Bunchy Top under experimental conditions, although certain ones, included in groups in which undoubted plant parasites occur, have been met with by one of us. (The inquiry, however, is still in progress.)

6. Animal Parasites.

A nematode causing plant injury that we have commonly found in connection with the roots of Bunchy Top affected plants, not being invariably found to occur in this association, cannot be the exclusive cause of the malady. That any insect is inculpated has not been shown definitely to be the case.

(Note. Some notoriety has attached to the pronouncement that a particular insect—the Banana Aphid (Pentalonia nervosa)—serves as the communicator of the disease between one plant and another, or even is its prime cause in healthy plants, and although general observations do not favour the explanation a remedy involving this insect theory is being tested in the New South Wales portion of the infected area.)

224[APRIL, 1923.

7. Climatic Factors.

The prejudicial effects of meteorological conditions unfavourable to the growth of the banana plant, those only gradually manifested in the course of years, cannot be settled by direct experiment. It appears, however, to be interdicted by what is known regarding the geographical range of the Cavan-dish and of other banana varieties, not only in the Tweed area but elsewhere. In regard to the former, there is evidence that in the past an abundant yield of good fruit has been raised from healthy plants for eight or ten successive years.

8. Climatically Injured Soil Conditions.

No evidence as to the nature of the change spontaneously produced in the soil under banana crops, since its adaptation from its original condition as a scrub or forest soil to this cultural use was obtained. This is a matter amongst others that it is proposed to be inquired into.

9. Prevention and Cure.

Both these are dependent on a knowledge of the cause of Bunchy Top disease or must have relation therewith. Not knowing the cause they cannot be predicted, and moreover we have not sought to discover them by empirical procedures conducted in this respect in the dark.

10. Further Research.

Further scientific inquiry on the cause, prevention, and cure of Bunchy Top disease is still called for. This inquiry should embrace both field and laboratory experiments and research. The bestowal of the fullest measure of scientific thought and endeavour in respect to the disease is urgently necessary.—QUEENSLAND AGRIC. JOURN. VOL. XIX., PART 1.

CITRUS SCAB.

W. V. TOWER.

Citrus scab is the worst pest that the grower of citrus fruit has to contend with in Porto Rico. This disease during the first years of the citrus industry only attacked young trees, the old being immune. During the past few years this does not hold and many old trees that once bore fine fruit are now producing crops practically worthless for shipping that must be sold for canning purposes.

A co-operative spraying experiment for citrus scab was started with one of our largest growers. The results of the first season's work is very encouraging. The season was exceptionally wet and the bloom extended over a prolonged period. Four applications of Bordeaux oil were made. The results obtained from the first four applications have been so conclusive that owners have sprayed two other groves.

Four applications of Bordeaux oil were made to 3,000 trees which were being prepared for early fruit. This comes from blossomings in December, January and February. These blossomings are not often heavy and as they come during our cold winter rains the fruit is liable to be very scabby. This year the first blossoms came out on the 15th of December, but as they were few in number, spraying was not started until December, 29th. The

APRIL, 1923.]225

second spray was applied on January 27th, the third on February 13th, and the fourth on March, 9th. No definite spraying program could be held to on account of the very unsettled weather and the small amount of fruit set from the first bloom. Just prior to January, 27th a second blossom appeared which set well. Following the February and March sprayings there was a flush and a blossom. The fruit which appeared after the last spraying with Bordeaux was sprayed with lime and sulphur on March 25th. By this time the rust mites had made their appearances.

The results in the six groves of 3,000 trees are as follows: clean fruit, 94.4 per cent; just a trace of scab, 5.2 per cent; slightly spotted with scabby areas, 0.4 per cent.

Check trees were selected in one of the worst infested groves on this property. These are at the foot of a cliff and do not get the early morning sun. The scab infection in the check trees was as follows; clean fruit, 10 per cent; just a trace of scab, 44.7 per cent.; slightly spotted with scabby areas, 27.5 per cent.; very badly scabbed but not knotted, 17.5 per cent.; knotted and literally covered with scab, 0.3 per cent.

Sprayed trees in the same grove showed the following: clean fruit, 90.6 per cent; just a trace of scab, 9.3 per cent.; slightly spotted with scabby areas 0.1 per cent.

Groves in the same vicinity showed a very high scab infection. On one grove, not sprayed, the following figures were found: clean fruit, 3.5 per cent. just a trace of scab, 17.3 per cent.; slightly spotted with scabby areas, 24.4 per cent; very badly scabbed but not knotted, 50.3 per cent.; knotted and literally covered with scab, 4.5 per cent.

Another grove on the same property was divided into three sections. One part was sprayed four times, another part two times, and the remainder not sprayed. The results were as follows:

A grove of 900 trees was sprayed on January 13th with Bordeaux 3-4-50 and 1.2 per cent. oil and again with the same formula on April 12th. These two applications were made before the spring blossom which occurred in May. The blossom was very heavy on May 11th and the grove was sprayed with lime and sulphur 1-30. The results were as follows: clean fruit, 97.3 per cent.; just a trace of scab, 2.4 per cent.; slightly spotted with scabby areas, 0.3 per cent.

Another grove of 800 trees which also blossomed late was treated as follows: sprayed on April 5th with Bordeaux 3-4-50 with 1/2 per cent of oil and again on May 8th with the same formula. The blossoms commenced to come out on April 29th and on May 9th was heavy. The results showed: clean fruit, 93.8 per cent.; just a trace of scab, 6. per cent; slightly spotted with scabby areas, 0.2 per cent.

226[APRIL, 1923.

The results obtained are very encouraging but Bordeaux oil spray for scab must not be used unless the planter is willing to fight the scale which will surely follow, for all beneficial fungi, moss and lichen are killed. This spray if applied haphazard will give poor results. Only the best spray materials should be used. A well planned campaign should be made and carried out. Be on the constant lookout for scale and rust mites as these two pests come in very quickly after spraying with Bordeaux oil. Plenty of material for fighting them should be on hand.

Recent tests with the oil emulsion have been made at the station on grapefruit trees with fruits six months old. The solution has been used at the following strengths: 1, 1\frac{1}{2}, 2-2\frac{1}{2}, and 3 per cent. of oil emulsion. There has been no dropping of leaves or burning of leaves or fruit.

In all the tests made with Bordeaux oil using 3-4-50 Bordeaux with 1/2 per cent. of oil there was a little burning of the young tender shoots. No small fruit or open blossoms were injured by this strength of spray. A few unopened blossoms buds were burnt and dropped, but no serious loss of leaves or blossoms was apparent.

Directions for making Bordeaux-oil and a plan for spraying campaign may be found in Extension Note, 42.

For convenience in handling this spray a two stage loading platform is recommended, the upper capable of holding a 400 to 600 gallon water tank. the lower two 200 gallon tanks for diluted lime and copper sulphate and two 60 gallon barrels for stock lime and copper sulphate in solution. The platform should be made so that the water in the large storage tank will run by gravity into the two diluting tanks for the lime and copper sulphate. The lime and copper sulphate tanks should have a capacity equal to the spraying outfit. They should have outlets of the same size brought together so that the two liquids may flow down a trough mixing on the way to the spray tank. The agitator should be running while the two liquids are entering the spray tank. After the Bordeaux has been well mixed, and tested with potassium ferrocyanide, the stock oil solution is added.

In the work described there were employed a foreman, two men for preparing materials, two spray men and a cart man. The spray wagon made seven loadings at the mixing tank and sprayings through the grove in a day.—AGRIC. EXTENSION NOTE No. 53 OF THE PORTO RICO AGRIC. EXPT-STATION.

CEYLON AGRICULTURE.

ESTATE PRODUCTS COMMITTEE OF THE
BOARD OF AGRICULTURE.

Minutes of the 13th Meeting of the Estate Products Committee of the Board of Agriculture held at the Experiment Station, Peradeniya, at 2-30 p.m. on Thursday, March 8th, 1923.

Present.—The Director of Agriculture (Chairman), the Government Botanist and Mycologist, the Government Entomologist, the Government Agricultural Chemist, the Assistant Botanist and Mycologist, the Acting Assistant Entomologist, Major J. W. Oldfield, O.B.E., M.C., Messrs. R. G. Coombe, J. S. Patterson, A. P. Waldock, S. R. Hamer, C. E. A. Dias, John Horsfall, H. D. Garrick, F. R. Senanayake, N. G. Campbell, A. P. Goonatilleka, L. H. S. Peiris, A. J. Austin Dickson and H. A. Deutrom (Acting Secretary).

Letters and telegrams regretting inability to attend were received from the Hon'ble the Government Agent, W.P., Colombo, the Hon'ble the Controller of Revenue, the Government Agent, S.P., Lieut-Col. T. Y. Wright, Mr. A. W. Beven, Mr. J. B. Coles, Sir Solomon Dias Bandaranaike, C.M.G., Mr. Geo. Brown, Mr. W. R. Matthew, Mr. R. Garnier, Gate Mudaliyar A. E. Rajapakse, Dr. C. A. Hewavitarne, Mr. N. D. Stephen Silva, the Hon'ble Mr. H. L. De Mel, C.B.E., and Mr. Thomas A. de Mel.

The CHAIRMAN said that there was no time to print and circulate the minutes of the previous meeting and enquired whether the members would like it read.

MR. GARRICK proposed that the minutes be taken as read and confirmed.

MR. HORSFALL seconded.

Before proceeding with the business on the Agenda the CHAIRMAN read a letter from Government with regard to the protection of Cabaragoya. He said in conclusion that the matter will come before Council shortly.

The CHAIRMAN said that in accordance with the decision taken at the last meeting HIS EXCELLENCY THE GOVERNOR has approved of the following gentlemen being re-appointed :—SIR SOLOMON DIAS BANDARANAIKE and MR. R. GARNIER as members of the Estates Products Committee of the Board of Agriculture.

He also announced the following new appointments to the Committee :—

MR. JOHN HORSFALL in place of LIEUT. L. BAYLY.

MR. A. M. C. DIAS and MR. W. C. DIAS BANDARANAYAKE.

Agenda Item 1. Progress Report of the Experiment Station, Peradeniya.

In dealing with this report the CHAIRMAN stated that it was only a brief record owing to the period it covered being limited to one month in dry weather. He mentioned that the dadaps and cacao were in the course of pruning and commented generally on other items of interest in the report.

228[APRIL, 1923.Agenda Item 2. Results of Manurial Experiments with Tea.

The CHAIRMAN said that the figures in regard to the results of the manurial experiments in tea were in the hands of the members as they had already been submitted to the members at the last meeting. He asked MR. BAMBER to briefly review the reports.

MR. KELWAY BAMBER said that the results showed that the change of pruning in 1919 had greatly affected the yield. The average yield in 1921 was 610 lb. of tea per acre and for 1922, 710 lb., the average for the last three years being 950 lb. per acre. The bushes were an extra month before coming into bearing owing to the low pruning given in October last year.

In regard to manuring MR. BAMBER said there was little difference between the effect of Groundnut cake and Sulphate of Potash and Groundnut cake only, but jat influenced the yield of plot 146 to the extent of 50 % per cwt. Similarly there had been little difference in effect between Groundnut cake and Superphosphate and Groundnut cake alone, but in this case too, a larger yield was apparent in the plot of better jat. Comparing the difference between two plots one manured with Superphosphate and Sulphate of Potash and the other with a complete mixture containing Groundnut cake with Superphosphate and Potash, the complete mixture showed 30 lb. made tea per acre in its favour on the Hybrid plots.

On the Manipuri jat plots, the Potash and Phosphoric acid only gave about 21 lb. of tea per acre more than the complete manure.

Calculated to 2,722 bushes per acre all the manured and green manured plots showed an increase over the control plots, the Nitrogen and Phosphoric acid plots showed an excess of 250 lb. and 310 lb. of tea per acre.

The Nitrogen and Potash plots showed 60 lb. and 290 lb. increase, the larger increase being with the Manipuri Indigenous jat.

With regard to the green manure plots the original Dadap plot had an increase of 395 lb. of tea per acre and Albizzia plot 320 lb. while the cattle manure plot showed an increase of 345 lb. per acre and the Dadap plot planted in 1912, 245 lb. of tea per acre.

MR. BAMBER said he thought it would be better to alter the pruning period from October to December. He said that the average rainfall at Peradeniya had been 87 inches a year. In 1920 which had been a record year for crop the rainfall was 101.5.

The CHAIRMAN said that the pruning in October had resulted in the loss of many bushes. He suggested for the consideration of the members that the plots be pruned in December instead.

MR. COOMBE enquired whether all the plots were to be pruned in December.

MR. BAMBER said that the committee thought for comparative tests they should all be pruned in one month.

The CHAIRMAN enquired whether they would prefer to postpone decision as to whether the pruning period should be altered until the full rainfall figures were before them.

MR. A. J. AUSTIN DICKSON said it would be well if they had these figures which would show exactly the dry months.

APRIL, 1923.]229

The CHAIRMAN said that February was usually a dry month. He added that there had been abnormally dry weather for 4 months following the pruning in October 1922.

MR. COOMBE remarked that in 1921-22 there was a marked difference in yield in plots 144 and 149. One gave 500 lb. and the other 760 lb.

MR. BAMBER said it was due to very heavy pruning.

MR. CAMPBELL said his experience of the Low-country was that pruning in December was more risky than pruning in October.

MR. GARRICK agreed with MR. CAMPBELL and enquired whether it would be better to antidate the pruning.

MR. AUSTIN DICKSON said that it was generally agreed that pruning a plot 3 or 4 months before the dry weather helped to carry it over the drought, but on the other hand, if it was pruned in the dry weather the bearing was delayed. A pruned field must be "in tipping" before the drought came on.

MR. J. SHERIDAN PATTERSON said it used to be the rule in Kalutara and the Kelany Valley never to prune after Christmas. The 25th December was looked upon as the very latest date it was safe to prune up to.

The CHAIRMAN—I take it that the Committee are rather in favour of the adherence to the month of October.

The Committee agreed to this.

The Committee confirmed the Chairman's proposal that the final publication of the yields in connection with the experiments should be delayed till the end of the present season, that is, the end of September.

MR. R. G. COOMBE said that he understood that these experiments were being carried out from the point of yield and not quality.

The CHAIRMAN said we have not taken any data with regard to quality at all.

MR. HAMER asked whether all the plots were mulched with Dadaps.

MR. BAMBER said only plots 144 and 149.

He explained that the various mixtures used were not intended to give large results of crop. They had to be continued for a series of years to find out the effect of Potash, Nitrogen and Phosphoric acid. There had been very little difference in the yields so far, and the only marked contrast between Potash and Phosphoric acid was in the appearance of the bushes.

Agenda Item 3—Results of Manurial Experiments with Rubber.

The CHAIRMAN said that the experiments this year consisted of two series, the old and the new which was begun in April last year and the records of which had been kept for nine months. He asked MR. M. KELWAY BAMBER to analyse the experiments.

MR. BAMBER said that the old experiments consisted of applying general mixtures with an excess of nitrogen, an excess of phosphoric acid and an excess of potash respectively on various plots. The potash plot showed the lowest yield in comparison with the control plot. The only plot that equalled the control plot was that to which was applied an excess of phosphoric acid.

The new experiments had been conducted in the Avenue rubber which had been manured for some years, tapping commencing nine months ago. It was yet too early to draw any deduction from the experiment, but it seemed

230[APRIL, 1923.

that the omission of potash had the effect of reducing the yield more than had been the case with the old rubber. The control plot treated with lime only gave the highest yield. He thought that these experiments would be very useful in time to come as long as they would be continued on the same lines as originally laid down. The mixtures used were entirely mineral manures without any organic element in their composition. The results of the experiments over a series of years would teach them the actual effect of Nitrogen Phosphoric acid and Potash independent of organic matter.

The CHAIRMAN explained that with regard to the older experiments he would like to mention that the plot treated with an excess of potash and which continued to give the poorest yield of rubber was the last thinned. The small yield may not entirely be a question of manuring.

He also wished to draw members' attention to a point on which it might be advisable to make further investigation. They would notice that the control plot gave an average of 2573 cubic centimeters of rubber per tree, equivalent to 998.91 grams of 2 lb. 3 ozs. rubber. Plot No. 2 (lime and mixture without potash) also gave an average of 2570 cubic centimeters, but in this case the yield was 820.60 grams or 1 lb. 12 ozs. of rubber per tree. In other words the percentage of rubber in the first instance was 38, which is very high. Before, therefore, accepting the figures as final, he would like to have the difference investigated.

MAJOR OLDFIELD asked whether there had been a secondary leaf fall during the experiments.

The CHAIRMAN replied there had not been one.

The CHAIRMAN said that it was not proposed to publish the figures in the TROPICAL AGRICULTURIST since the experiments had only been conducted for a period of nine months, and was by no means final.

In regard to the figures for the old series he stated that, as had been remarked before, the experiments had been carried out on very good, flat, alluvial land and he would not like rubber planters consider them as conclusively proving that manures in rubber are of no value. The figures certainly indicated that they were getting no increased yields at the Experiment Station.

MR. R. G. COOMBE asked whether the soils of the different plots had been analysed.

The CHAIRMAN replied that the soil on the plots had been analysed and that no material differences between the different plots were to be noticed.

MR. BAMBER remarked that the plots with excess of nitrogen always seemed to have a healthier leaf appearance than the phosphoric acid plot, though in the latter the yield was best of the three.

MR. C. E. A. DIAS suggested an exchange of the manures, i.e., that in the present potash plot the potash be removed and phosphoric acid substituted and vice versa.

MR. BAMBER said he would certainly like to see other experiments conducted on these lines, but, was the period of the present experiment long enough to confirm the results? However, he did not think there was any objection.

The CHAIRMAN said he would not be able to give effect to such a decision until next year, since the manures had already been applied.

APRIL, 1923.]231

The meeting approved the proposal and the Chairman announced that he would give it effect as soon as practicable.

MR. DIAS then asked whether manuring experiments in rubber could not be started in important planting centres, say Kalutara. He thought that Government might well consider such a question.

The CHAIRMAN : It is a question of finance, MR. DIAS.

MR. DIAS : I don't think there is any difficulty about finance.

The CHAIRMAN replied : Can we expect the co-operation of rubber planters, on the same lines as in the coconut experiments ? He added that it would be necessary to employ a man to keep the records.

MR. DIAS : If this Committee is willing to do that I will offer you 20 acres of land in Horana planted with rubber.

The CHAIRMAN : I will go into that with MR. BAMBER and submit the matter for the consideration of the Committee at the next meeting. I thought I heard MR. OLDFIELD say that the Rubber Research Scheme might be willing to help.

MAJOR OLDFIELD : The officers of that scheme might be able to supervise the work.

MR. COOMBE enquired whether an officer of the Rubber Research Scheme had not reported against the manuring of rubber.

The CHAIRMAN replied that this was not precisely the case. The officer had stated that so far, he had not seen increased yields from manuring. The general health of the trees, might be improved.

MR. SHERIDAN PATTERSON : His experience is like that of the Experiment Station. No results are obtained from the application of manures.

MR. COOMBE said that the proposed experiments need not necessarily be limited to the Kalutara district but should be carried out in other areas as well.

The CHAIRMAN : That is a question of cost, MR. COOMBE.

MR. COOMBE : It raises the old question again, Sir, the starvation of the Agricultural Department in an Agricultural country.

Agenda Item 4. Results of Tapping Experiments with Rubber.

The CHAIRMAN said it would be advisable to take these experiments one at a time, the older experiments first which consisted of the two and three-day tapping trials on Experiment Station, Peradeniya. This consisted of Series I in triplicate, started in 1919 consisting of three blocks of trees tapped on alternate days and Series II every third day.

He called upon MR. PETCH to give a short review on the experiments.

MR. PETCH said that two and three-day tapping experiments (old series), both cuts are started at the same height 27 in. from the ground. This gives the advantage at first to the two-day tapping because it reaches the lower part of the stem earlier than the three-day tapping. The ratios of the yields expressing the three-day yield as a percentage of the two-day yield have been 73% in 1919 ; 71% in 1920 ; 70% in 1921 and 80% in 1922.

According to previous experiments the three-day yield should have been about 75% of the two-day yield. In this case the result has been slightly below that for the first three years and above that in the fourth

232[APRIL, 1923.

year. The two-day tapping has been handicapped to some extent. In the first place the change was made to a new panel at the beginning of 1922, according to the schedule, though some bark still remained untapped at the base of the stem. In the second place the two-day tapping in 1922 lost six tappings for some reason or other.

Theoretically the number of tappings should have been 181, whereas it only got 175. The increase of ratio in 1922 is due to the fact that the two-day tapping is now at the top of a panel whereas the three-day tapping is at the base of a panel.

After discussion it was decided to change the three-day tapping to a new panel as soon as the panel tapped out was equal to that tapped out in the two-day tapping.

TWO AND THREE-DAY TAPPING EXPERIMENTS (NEW SERIES).

In the new series of two versus three-day tapping the cut in the two-day tapping is at 24 inches from the ground, while the cut in the three-day tapping is at 16 inches. This gives the advantage to the three-day tapping. The ratios of the yields, however, are 100 to 76, that is, the three-day tapping yield is 76% of the two-day tapping yield, so that putting the three-day tapping lower does not appear to have made any difference.

SINGLE "V" AND ONE CUT TO THE LEFT.

In the experiments on tapping with a single "V" as compared with tapping on the single cut to the left, the yield obtained by "V" tapping was practically the same as the yield obtained by the single cut. This experiment was carried out in duplicate and the same results were obtained in both series. It was previously held that the single cut to the left yielded up to 14 per cent. more than the single cut to the right, the precise amount depending on the angle of the cut. That was based upon the supposed fact that the latex vessels in the tree always sloped to the right. That appears to be the case in young trees but it has since been found that the slope of the latex vessels changes with the age of the tree and if the slope is at first to the right it gradually changes over until the latex vessels slope to the left, and then in a few more years changes over the right again. The difference obtained by tapping with the "V" and the single cut is due to the slope of the latex vessels at any given time and this will vary according to the age of the trees. Consequently, the result in an experiment of this kind will not be always the same, and in estate practice there can be no constant difference as regards yield between tapping to the right and tapping to the left.

INDIVIDUAL YIELD EXPERIMENTS.

The CHAIRMAN suggested that the Committee should postpone discussion on the results of the "Individual tree yield experiments" till MR. BRYCE and MR. GADD had completed their further investigations.

This was agreed to.

ALTERNATE DAY AND DAILY IN ALTERNATE MONTH EXPERIMENTS.

MR. PETCH said that the fourth series of experiments was planned to determine the difference in yield between tapping on alternate days throughout the year, and tapping daily in alternate months. An experiment of this character was begun in 1912, but it was found that the plan of the experiment was faulty owing to a circumstance which had not been foreseen.

APRIL, 1923.]233

In tapping on alternate days throughout the year the tapping experiences good seasons and bad seasons alike, but in tapping during alternate months, it may happen that the trees are not tapped in the best yielding months, but in the worst yielding months or vice versa. In the present series this has been avoided by taking two groups of trees tapped in alternate months, the one group tapped in January, March, May, etc., and the other in February, April, June, etc. This will be in accordance with estate practice where it would be expected that different blocks would be tapped in alternate months. In estimating the results, therefore, it is necessary to take the average of the two sets or groups of trees tapped in different series of alternate months. As far as this experiment has gone the results show no difference. The yield obtained by tapping on alternate days throughout the year is the same as the yield obtained by tapping daily in alternate months.

Experiments on tapping and resting periods of various lengths have been carried out for some years in Cochin China. Trees have been tapped one month and rested the next month or tapped three months and rested three months. The results are said to be highly favourable to prolonged resting periods, but the different factors of the experiment have been varied to such an extent that it is not possible to draw any definite conclusion.

The CHAIRMAN said he wished to report to the Committee that there were 93 rubber trees at Henaratgoda ready for tapping and asked MR. PETCH to explain the proposed experiments to be started in April.

MR. PETCH said that as regards yield, there were only three fundamental factors in tapping, viz. the time interval, the size of the panel, and the height of the cut from the ground. If the effects of these three were determined separately, it should be possible by combining the results to estimate the relative yields of any two tapping systems. Several experiments have been carried out on the time interval, but very few on the other two factors. There was only one published experiment on the relative yields from halves, thirds and quarters, tapped in the same way, and none that he knew of on the height of the cut. MR. PETCH gave a brief outline of the plan of an experiment to determine the relative yields from cuts at different heights. It was agreed that the simpler experiment to determine the relative yields from halves, thirds, and quarters on trees of the same age and same average girth, should be begun at Henaratgoda.

MR. PATTERSON enquired the age of the trees.

The CHAIRMAN said they were 10 years.

MAJOR OLDFIELD enquired whether it was intended to leave the plot under grass, or to have it clean weeded.

The CHAIRMAN stated that it was not proposed to clean weed the area.

Among the exhibits at the meeting were some horsehair blight on Hevea sent in by MAJOR OLDFIELD and two bags of fibre (Sisal and Mauritius) from the Dry Zone Experiment Station, Anuradhapura.

With regard to the horsehair blight MR. PETCH stated that he considered that the dead leaves attached to the specimen were last year's leaves. Horsehair blight had been under observation for several years, and had never been found to be other than epiphytic. It did not do any damage.

234[APRIL, 1923.

The CHAIRMAN passed round a rough proof copy of the "YEAR BOOK OF THE AGRICULTURAL DEPARTMENT, CEYLON." He said that sanction had been obtained for the printing of 3,000 copies annually and it is proposed to issue these copies gratis to all members of the Planters' Association, Low-Country Products Association and Ceylon Estates Proprietary Association. He would be glad of suggestions in regard to distribution. After discussion it was decided to send 100 copies to the Ceylon Association in London, and single copies to all Government Agents and Assistant Government Agents and members of the Legislative Council.

H. A. DEUTROM,

Acting Secretary, Estate Products Committee.

ANURADHAPURA FOOD PRODUCTION AND AGRICULTURAL COMMITTEE.

Minutes of a meeting of the Anuradhapura Food Production and Agricultural Committee held at the Kachcheri on Saturday, the 3rd March, 1923.

Present.—Mr. G. F. R. Browning, Govt. Agent, N. C. P. (in the Chair), Mr. H. R. Freeman, Mr. T. H. Holland, Acting Divisional Agricultural Officer, N. D., Mr. B. W. G. Tennekoon, Kachcheri Mudaliyar, and Mr. C. C. Woolley, Secretary.

1. The minutes of the previous meeting held on the 6th January, 1923, were read and confirmed.

2. The committee was informed that a sum of Rs. 177/- had been advanced (from "Profits on Food Control" funds) for seed paddy for maha cultivation of the fields damaged by floods under Bassawakulam.

3. The Director of Agriculture's letter No. 303 of the 9th February, 1923, stating that suitable arrangements regarding the appointment of an Agricultural Instructor for this Province would be made as soon as possible, was read (vide resolution No. 13 passed at the last meeting).

4. The report of the judges giving marks awarded to the various competitors for prizes for the last best cultivated plots in the Ratmale Colony during the maha cultivation (vide resolution No. 7 (b) passed at the last meeting) was read. It was decided to award the following prizes:—

1st Prize—Rs. 35.00—to Ausadhahamy who scored 80 marks

2nd Prize—Rs. 25.00—to Sittiya who scored 78 marks

3rd Prize—Rs. 15.00—to Punchirala who scored 70 marks

5. The rules suggested by the Divisional Agricultural Officer, N. D., for prizes for competitions for paddy cultivation (vide resolution No. 10 passed at the last meeting) were read. It was decided that the present rules were quite sufficient. As regards the present rules, however, it was decided that the Headmen in giving their reports on the cultivation should assign marks for each of the points mentioned in rule 4 (vide notice circulated to the Chief Headmen with Circular No. 23 of 27th January, 1923).

APRIL, 1923.]235

6. The lists of competitors forwarded by the Ratemahatmayas, Nuwaragam and Hurulu Palatas, and the Revenue Officer, Tammankaduwa, for prizes for paddy cultivation during the coming Yala harvest were submitted.

7. The Divisional Agricultural Officer, N. D., in moving his resolution "that the question of introducing 'Kapok' and 'Akund' or Silk Cotton as village industries be considered," read correspondence on the subject, submitted samples of 'Kapok' and 'Akund' for inspection by the Committee, and stated that he would collect samples and obtain quotations as to the commercial value of these products which grow wild in Ceylon. It was understood that pamphlets on the subject were being published by the Director of Agriculture. It was decided that these pamphlets be distributed to the villagers through the Headmen and that the Divisional Agricultural Officer, N. D., should report further on the matter.

8. On MR. FREEMAN'S motion, the following resolution was passed:—"The Committee condemns the proposal of SIR P. RAMANATHAN to shoot buffalos on the Northern Railways, as being undesirable from an agricultural standpoint."

9. MR. FREEMAN moved that the Agricultural Department be asked if it would take over an ordinary village abandoned chena and see if, by green manuring or other means, additional fine grain crops could be raised. The Divisional Agricultural Officer, N. D., undertook to report on the subject at the next meeting.

10. MR. FREEMAN moved that it be suggested to Government that, under DR. W. A. DE SILVA'S scheme for Colonization in small lots under Nachchaduwa, irrigation rate, if reimposed, be limited to Rs. 2'00 per acre per annum, as a variable rate from Rs. 4'00 to Rs. 8'00 or over would prevent people taking up land. The CHAIRMAN said that he would bring the matter up at the conference of the Heads of Departments to be held in Colombo next week in connection with this scheme.

11. MR. FREEMAN moved that the Agricultural Department be asked if some jak and breadfruit plants could be supplied for villages. The Divisional Agricultural Officer, N.D., undertook to communicate with the Director of Agriculture on the subject.

12. On MR. FREEMAN'S motion, it was resolved to ask the Headmen to encourage the growing of sugar canes in suitable villages.

13. On MR. FREEMAN'S motion, resolved that "it is desirable that the close season for teal in the North-Central Province should be abolished as they destroy quantities of sown grain."

14. On MR. FREEMAN'S motion, resolved that "it is desirable that the export of dried meat (wild boar flesh) from Tammankaduwa be allowed on permit, as the number is becoming excessive and as there is a danger to inhabitants and crops thereby."

15. MR. FREEMAN withdrew his motion "that it be suggested to the Director of Agriculture that the produce of the Experiment Station, Puliyankulam, that is not used, be given away weekly to villagers at the entrance gate."

16. It was resolved that the Ratemahatmaya, Hurulu Palata, be authorised to supply seed paddy for Uttimaduwa (10 amunams) and Habarana (5 amunams), the advance being made from "Profits on Food Control" funds.

17. On MR. FREEMAN'S enquiry, a statement furnished by the Chief Accountant, Railway Department, showing that 4,750 tons of paddy and 137 tons of kurakkan were exported from the North-Central Province during 1922, was tabled.

PROGRESS REPORT OF THE EXPERIMENT STATION, PERADENIYA.

From 1st February 1923 to 28th February, 1923.

TEA.

Crop has been poor, 3,818 lb. green leaf was plucked from 11 acres against 4,378 lb. in January. The two Dadap and Albizzia plots gave the highest yields.

The young supplies have been mulched.

Light Leaf Manipuri Indigenous tea seed obtained from Kotiyagala Estate have been planted in nursery beds and supply baskets for filling up the existing vacancies.

Seed of Dark Leaf Manipuri Indigenous has been booked to be supplied in March or April from Mousakande Estate.

RUBBER.

The various green manures in the young rubber which have died out have been uprooted and the land is being ploughed.

130 stumps were budded according to the Java method on 10th January of which 106 were successful or 81.53% ; the Patch method 6 out of 10 or 60% and the Diamond 7 out of 14 or 50%, the average percentage on the whole being 77.27%.

CACAO.

A light pruning accompanied by a partial lopping of shade is in progress.

A round of excision of bark canker has been completed.

The autumn crop is nearly finished and the spring crop is expected to be a light one.

APRIL, 1923.]237

COCONUTS.

The whole area under coconuts have been ploughed and disc-harrowing is in progress.

COFFEE.

Die-backs and superfluous suckers have been removed.

The six-acre plot of young plants of JACKSON'S Hybrid and KENT'S Arabica have been forked and mulched round with green material close at hand.

PADDY.

The Panchikawatte fields are being ploughed and will be sown with Daincha seed. The outer drains in the Totadeniya area has been cleaned and deepened.

ECONOMIC COLLECTION PLOTS.

All the young plants in this area have been mulched round and the plots clean weeded. Plants for supplying the vacancies during the S.-W. monsoon have been ordered.

FOOD PRODUCTS.

The following 8 varieties of Tannia yams have been replanted in plot 18—2 feet in the rows and 6 feet apart :—

Dasei-ala, Kandala, Thadala, Thumas-ala, West Indies A, West Indies B, West Indies C and Trinidad.
