238[APRIL, 1923.

POULTRY.

RAISING TURKEYS FOR PROFIT.

There is no branch of the poultry industry that offers greater opportunities for money-making than turkey culture.

The turkey is distinctly an American bird. It was found by the colonists widely distributed throughout the American continent, and was domesticated by the Indians long before Columbus sailed on his westward voyage. The year 1585 found the English using the turkey as an article in the Christmas feast.

This great fowl has continued to be the leading meat for Thanksgiving Christmas and most all other festivities.

Prohibitive prices have prevented many people from indulging in regular feasts of this "King of all meats."

The past few years has found a greater demand for the medium-sized bird. When you take into consideration the cost of a bird weighing 20 to 30 pounds, and selling retail at from 6d. to 1/- per pound, it is readily apparent why the middle class of people do not serve this delicious food more frequently.

While the supply of poultry products has increased wonderfully during the past few years, the demand has, more or less, fully kept pace. The price also has steadily advanced, until poultry raising has become one of the greatest and one of the most profitable industries of the country. Not many years back poultry raising was looked upon with a good deal of misapprehension and rather lightly, perhaps by many, but it is now given its rightful place with other industries, and is generally recognised as one of the greatest wealth-producing factors of the country.

The one branch of the industry that does not seem to have made as rapid strides, is that of turkey raising. Apparently at least, the supply has not increased as rapidly, in the same proportion to the demand, as chickens. There is no time of the year when this is more apparent than at the holiday season—the period of greatest demand. Many are unable to get turkey for love or money—they must be satisfied with goose, duck, or just common chicken.

There are several breeds of turkeys, and all have their points of excellence. The largest, and perhaps the most popular is the Mammoth Bronze. Nearly everyone is familiar with this breed. Then there is the Narragansett, not quite as large as the Bronze, but said to be equally as hardy. The Bourbon Reds, White Hollands, Blacks and Slates are all good, and nearly of an equal size.

The standard weight of mature birds of the different breeds are as follows:—Bronze, male, 36 pounds, female 25 pounds; Narragansett, male 30 pounds, female 18 pounds; White Holland, male 26 pounds, female 16 pounds; Reds, Slates and Blacks, male 27 pounds, female 18 pounds. Greater weights than these have been recorded, one Giant Bronze in West Virginia having reached 60 pounds. These heavy weights

APRIL, 1923]239

are not common; the general average runs well below the standard weight, which shows, in many cases, that the birds have not received the care and feed required. Turkey raising is something of a speciality, and requires a little different system from that of raising ordinary domestic fowls, but the important differences are few and easily mastered. Turkeys adapt themselves easily to various climates, and can be raised successfully in any part of the country. You can raise them anywhere if you start with the right stock and give the right care. The principal thing to avoid is inbreeding; if this is practised, the turkey quickly deteriorates, loses vitality, and for this reason new blood should be introduced at least every other year. The vitality of the flock should be looked after with the greatest care. Strong vitality is one of the prime factors of insuring success. Don't try to economise in this particular. A pound or two spent in getting new blood from a healthy vigorous flock will be money well invested.

Turkey raising cannot be engaged in as generally as that of chickens, for the reason that turkeys do not thrive in confinement, hence it must be confined to those who can give them range. People living in the rural districts, therefore, are the ones to whom we must look and upon whom we must depend for our Thanksgiving and holiday turkeys. It is probably for this reason that turkey raising is not so well understood as that of chickens. This is not to say that people of the rural districts are not as progressive, but being limited to the rural district, turkey raising does not offer the opportunities to the many that chickens do, therefore, interest cannot be so great and development is consequently less rapid.

Unlike the majority of our domestic fowls the turkey retains many of its natural instincts. Especially is this true in its desire to roam the fields. Nothing delights the turkey more than to roam through the fields and over the meadow in search of grasshoppers and other insects. During the summer and autumn until frost kills the insects turkeys will thrive on them alone, with but little grain. It seems to be a diet especially suited to their needs, and the exercise the birds get in hunting them develops large, muscular frames that will quickly put on flesh, when the proper time arrives later in the autumn.

The orchard fenced off makes an ideal place for a turkey ranch. If the old birds persist in flying over the fence, one of the wings can be clipped the same as chickens. After the young get old enough so they are out of danger, the flock can be given the range of the fields. They will do but little damage and will pick up insects without number that would do great damage to growing crops. A stretch of timber land, if free from destructive animals, will make an excellent run for turkeys, and I know of no place that would suit them better, after the young get old enough to be given this liberty.

As the birds are great foragers they sometimes get to roaming too far from home, and in order to keep them from straying away and becoming some neighbour's turkeys they should be fed every night shortly before roosting time, and near the roosting quarters. In this way they are taught to work toward home as evening draws near.

Turkeys like to roost in the open and, as a rule, they do better than where attempts are made to confine them. They like high roosts, and it is often they can be seen on the highest limb of the highest trees. The turkey is largely an open air bird, and for this reason its inclinations in this direction should be catered for as much as possible. Do not attempt to make them roost in close quarters nor should they be allowed or compelled to

240[APRIL, 1923.

roost with the chickens. An old shed with but a roof, and that roof high up, will make good winter roosting quarters for a flock of turkeys. On most any farm suitable roosting quarters can be easily and cheaply provided. They should be partially protected from severe storms and the roofs should be up reasonably high from the ground, or difficulty will be experienced in getting the turkeys to take to them. But don't attempt to enclose them at night as you would chickens. Turkeys are not built that way.

The selection of breeders may seem to some a matter of little importance, yet nobody taking thought, will fail to see that this is one of the most important matters relative to any kind of reproduction and upon recalling experiences you may be able to explain a number of past failures. You may realise the importance of using good parent stock, but it is seldom that this matter is given due consideration.

It is too often the custom to discard only the extremely inferior birds and retain as breeders all that are fair, although some of these do not come close enough to the standard to retain the breed characteristics in their offspring, or even to produce high-class market birds.

One male bird to ten or twelve females is about the right proportion, although good results have been secured with a greater number of females to one male. However, it is best not to have too many; better too few than too many. A single mating of the male and female fertilises all the eggs for a single hatch. The hen turkey may be allowed to sit on her eggs, or they may be placed under a common chicken, as is often done with the best results. This is simply a matter to be decided by the individual. Where the intention is to let the hen turkey sit on the eggs it is a good plan to remove the eggs from the nest, with the exception of one or two, until she is entirely through laying, when they can be returned. Do not take all the eggs away and try to deceive the bird with china eggs. Generally they are not fooled and may take another nest.

Keep the brood coops clean and free from vermin and be sure to go over the little fellows, also the old bird, at least once a week with some good insect powder. Do not allow them in the cold, wet grass early in the morning until they are two or three weeks old.

For the first feed good results may be had with bread soaked in sweet milk and fed rather more dry than wet. Gradually follow this with a small amount of good chick feed, always remembering to feed sparingly at all times. After a short time small grain may be added.

Scalded milk, commonly called Dutch cheese, is one of the very best feeds after the poults get to be a few weeks old.

One of the very best ways to prevent disease among turkeys is by disinfecting. The prevailing disease is black head. This trouble generally occurs about the time when the birds reach the size of a quail. This is largely due to an excess of grasshoppers and insects found on the range. The liver becomes diseased, abscesses form and the birds die. Epsom salts is the very best thing to keep the livers of turkeys normal, and a small amount in the drinking water once a week will save many of the young birds.

Turkeys to be fattened for market should be confined for three weeks to a roomy, open front shed and one that is free from draughts. A very good

APRIL, 1923.]241

fattening food consists of a mixture of ground oats, corn meal and barley meal, worked up into a wet mash by the addition of boiled potatos and some skim or diluted milk. The food should be fed in troughs placed sufficiently high off the ground to prevent the birds from treading in them. Two feeds daily of this food and a mid-day feed of green stuff will put the birds in good, heavy condition.

It is folly of the greatest degree to inbreed in this line of fowls, and the one who becomes so careless as to fail in introducing new blood into his flock each succeeding year would best leave this branch of the poultry industry alone.—SOUTH AFRICAN POULTRY MAGAZINE AND SMALL-HOLDER, Vol. XV., No. 132.

FATTENING POULTRY FOR TABLE PURPOSES.

RESULTS OF EXPERIMENTS AT GROOTFONTEIN.

S. W. NASH,

Asst. in Poultry, Grootfontein School of Agriculture, Middelburg, Cape Province.

(Abstracted)

Most farmers when they require a bird for the table seize the first fowl they can catch in their poultry run, cook it within an hour of killing and generally disappointed to find the bird thin and not tender. If this bird had been kept in a coop for two or three weeks and fed on soft food its weight could have been increased, the flesh made soft and the flavour improved at an extra cost of 1d.

A fattening coop can be made out of any old packing case, with a few slats at the bottom and in front. A dish for the food should be placed within easy reach of the birds.

The experiment at Grootfontein covered eighteen days. The cockerels used were poor specimens and were unsuitable for sale as breeding stock. Each bird received, while in the fattening coop, 3\frac{1}{2} oz. of common mealie meal and pollard (three parts mealie meal and one part pollard) mixed with enough separated milk to make a thin paste.

The cost of feeding was 6d. per bird for the eighteen days or one penny more than that spent on those in the runs which cost 5d. per bird.

The birds selected for the experiment were carefully weighed at the commencement of the experiment and placed in the coop. They were fed thrice daily. Drinking water and green food was withheld. To serve as a check two White Leghorns one each Black and Brown Leghorns and one White Orpington were marked and put back in the runs and fed with the flock in the ordinary manner. At the end of the experiment it was found that the light breeds had gained 1 lb. 3 oz. in weight, while the heavy breeds had gained 1 lb. 12 oz. There was a marked difference in the appearance of the birds when dressed for cooking. The flesh of the fattened birds was succulent and tender while that of the check birds was stringy and rather tough.—JOURNAL OF THE DEPT. OF AGRIC., U.S., AFRICA.

242[APRIL, 1923.

CO-OPERATION.

CO-OPERATIVE ASSOCIATIONS IN
CANADA.

The agricultural co-operation movement is of comparatively recent origin in Canada, and its progress is due, amongst other causes, to the active encouragement given to it by the Federal and Provincial Departments of Agriculture and to the conditions arising out of the War. Canada being a comparatively new country, the development of agricultural co-operation has necessarily proceeded on somewhat different lines from those which it follows in older countries. Perhaps the most striking differences are the early application of co-operation to the sale of the staple agricultural products of the country, and the more rapid development of this form of co-operation in comparison with co-operative credit and the co-operative purchase of farm requisites.

Grain.—The grain industry is the most important branch of agriculture in Canada and was the first to which co-operation was applied on a large scale. The chief provinces devoting their energies to grain growing are the three prairie provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. In these provinces Grain Growers' Associations and Co-operative Elevator Companies have been formed under Acts of the Provincial Legislatures, and the Governments have made loans in aid of organisation and of the acquisition and erection of elevators up to 85 per cent. of the estimated cost.

In 1920, on the discontinuance of the Canadian Wheat Board, a Wheat Markets Committee representing the provincial farmers and grain growers' associations was formed for the purpose of establishing a wheat marketing agency as a non-profit undertaking, and a draft agreement was drawn up by which it was proposed to bind the growers to deliver to the agency (to be known as the UNITED FARMERS' GRAIN CORPORATION, with its principal office in Winnipeg) all the wheat grown by them in Canada for five years. The Corporation, on the other hand, was to agree to sell the wheat at the best prices obtainable and to pay the whole amount received less handling, grading and selling charges. The Corporation was to be authorised to establish selling, statistical or other agencies in any city in the world and was to be given power to borrow money on the wheat delivered to it for sale, and to exercise all the rights of ownership without limitation. It was not found possible, however, to bring the scheme into operation in time to deal with the 1921 wheat crop, and at the end of the year the Canadian Council of Agriculture decided not to proceed with the project but to ask the Federal Government to reappoint the Wheat Board.

Live Stock.—The principal centres of the live stock industry of Canada are the provinces of Quebec, Ontario and Saskatchewan, and it is in these three provinces that the co-operative organisation of shipping, grading, stock-yarding and marketing has been most largely developed. It has also

APRIL, 1923.]243

been organised, however, in the Maritime Provinces (Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island) and recently an export cattle-pool covering the whole of Canada has been formed by the United Grain Growers, Ltd.

In Ontario the Provincial Department of Agriculture has issued elaborate suggestions, rules and regulations for the co-operative shipping and marketing of live stock in the province, with a model of a shipping statement. In Saskatchewan the first step towards the organisation of co-operative marketing was taken by the local Department of Agriculture, which issued a bulletin in 1912 explaining the method of co-operative marketing and the benefits to be obtained therefrom. As a result, 9 incorporated co-operative stock-marketing associations were formed in 1914, and this number had increased to 54 by 1920, exclusive of the unincorporated branches of the Saskatchewan Grain Growers' Association. To encourage the organisation of live stock marketing the Co-operative Organisation Branch of the Department supplies each new association, free of charge, with a set of receipts and account forms sufficient to record their marketing for one year, together with a bulletin explaining how the accounts should be kept.

In Quebec several of the sheep breeders' and wool producers' co-operative associations sell sheep co-operatively, their managing secretaries often being the agricultural representatives of the Department of Agriculture. In order to introduce co-operative live stock marketing in the Maritime Provinces, the Dominion Department of Agriculture in 1919 entered into an agreement with the farmers of a district near Bathurst, New Brunswick, to prepare and arrange for the co-operative sale of their sheep in the open market in the autumn of that year. Very good results were obtained from the sale and in the next year the scope of the work was extended to include cattle and hogs.

Following a visit to Great Britain in 1921 of a director and the treasurer of the United Grain Growers, Ltd., to study the live stock marketing conditions, an Export Cattle Pool was formed by the association, under which co-operative shipments were to be collected at country points and sent to Montreal where the accepted cattle would be graded and initial cash payments made according to weight and quality. After grading and payment shippers would be given participation certificates indicating the weight and quality supplied and the amount of cash advanced, Steers, heifers, cows and bulls would then be separately pooled and the gross selling price in each pool, minus cash advances, and expenses would be divided equally amongst contributors on the basis of live weight supplied. The Pool was not formed in time for the 1921 season.

Dairying.—Quebec and Ontario are the two chief dairying provinces. In Quebec a large amount of the co-operative dairying is in the hands of the Quebec Farmers' Central Co-operative Association, all the transactions of which are under the supervision of the Minister of Agriculture, who may take part at meetings of directors, appoint auditors and require the products to be graded by graders appointed by him if the interests of agriculture so require. Besides dairy products the association handles poultry, eggs, live stock, pressed meats, game, wool, vegetables, honey, apple, sugar, and syrup

244[APRIL, 1923.

and farm requisites. The export trade of the association is facilitated by the removal of restrictions on borrowing powers applied to other co-operative associations.

The co-operative sale of dairy products in Ontario is chiefly undertaken by the United Dairymen Co-operative, Ltd., which acts as the central selling agency for its patrons, either individuals or creameries or cheese factories, whether co-operative or otherwise. At first the company met with strenuous opposition from the local dealers and other interested persons, but it is becoming more and more the central selling agency for local cheese factories and other dairy enterprises.

Co-operative dairying in Prince Edward Island was started in 1891 when the Dominion Commissioner of Dairying visited the island and on behalf of the Dominion Government offered to supply the plant and operate a factory at a fixed charge and to market the butter and cheese, the farmers themselves erecting the necessary buildings. The success of the factory soon led to the formation of other co-operative factories.

In Saskatchewan, following the establishment of the Dairy Branch of the Department of Agriculture, an arrangement was made in 1907 whereby all the co-operative creameries voluntarily placed themselves under the supervision and direction of the Provincial Dairy Commissioner. By this arrangement the Dairy Branch engaged the managers, purchased all supplies, kept the accounts, marketed the produce and paid the patrons.

In Alberta there are about 53 co-operative creameries receiving cream according to grade and selling butter on the grades of the Dairy Commissioner of the Provincial Government. If desired, the Butter Marketing Service of the Department will act as a central selling agency, 250,000 dollars being allotted to the Department with which to make advances on butter sold. This is generally done to the amount of 80 per cent.

Wool.—The co-operative marketing of wool in Canada was started in 1914, and owes its growth almost entirely to the activity and initiative of the Dominion and Provincial Departments of Agriculture. In those early days the Departments supplied expert graders free of charge and undertook to act as central marketing agencies for any associations which might care to sell their wool in this manner. From the first the project was a success, 4 to 8 cents more per pound being obtained than could be secured by non-co-operative sellers. It was not, however, collective marketing alone that brought improvement, but the education of farmers in improving their flocks and wool and in grading and packing their produce for market. In 1917 a great step forward was made by the Dominion Government when it arranged for the proper storage in Toronto of the western wool clip and also negotiated with the banks for advances to wool growers. In 1918 the aim of the Government was achieved when the local associations all over Canada met together and formed their own central marketing association under the name of the Canadian Co-operative Wool Growers, Ltd., with headquarters in Toronto (chosen for its transport facilities and its conveniences for the buyers of Great Britain and the United States) and with warehouses and branches in the different provinces of Canada. In 1920 the company

APRIL, 1923.]245

marketed the wool of about 12,000 farmers, the amount received being about one-third of the total Canadian clip, of which 51 per cent. was sold to the American trader, 45 per cent. to the Canadian, and 4 per cent. to the English.

Eggs and Poultry.—Co-operative marketing of eggs is now being undertaken fairly generally throughout the Dominion. Its development has been made possible by the assistance given by the Dominion Poultry Division, and not only are the amalgamated producers' associations in some instances supplying a considerable proportion of the eggs for local consumption on certain markets, but one co-operative company (the United Farmers' Co-operative Co., Ltd., of Ontario) has become one of the largest exporters in the Dominion. In all, during 1920, rather more than 3,000,000 dozens of eggs were marketed co-operatively.

In Prince Edward Island the main marketing medium is the Co-operative Egg and Poultry Association, the members of which are grouped in separate branches known as Egg and Poultry Selling Associations or "Circles," each of which is designated by a number, the individual members in each circle being likewise designated by numbers which are stamped on their eggs. Each egg circle employs a collector who has charge of the collection of all eggs, ships them to the central candling station (at Charlotte Town, where there is also a poultry killing station and a central hatchery) and apportions the return to the members according to quantity and quality received. The remuneration of the collector may be either by way of salary or commission. The produce is not bought by the Association, but is consigned to it and sold by the business manager. A stated sum per unit is advanced on all produce received by the Association, some members being paid weekly and some monthly. The balance of the return often provides for all expenses and the reserve fund is distributed to members according to the net value of the produce marketed through the Association. This Association has served as a model for the development of co-operative egg and poultry marketing associations in various other provinces of the Dominion, but in Nova Scotia, where the conditions are different, the Poultry Department of the N.S. Agricultural College undertook to act as a central marketing agency for the local co-operative associations, taking 4 cents per dozen eggs of the proceeds of the sales for the handling and marketing expenses, the balance being paid to the managers of the local associations immediately the eggs were sold. The Department assumed no financial responsibility; it agreed to provide the outlet and assist in organising the circles, all other work devolving on the local managers.

Fruit and Vegetables.—The co-operative marketing of fruit and vegetables is most in evidence in the provinces of Ontario, Nova Scotia and British Columbia. In Ontario, which produces nearly 70 per cent. of the total fruit crop of Canada, there is no central selling organisation, and in

246[APRIL, 1923.

recent years the need for the formation of such an organisation has been strongly pressed. In Nova Scotia an Act was passed in 1912 to facilitate the incorporation of Farmers' Fruit, Produce and Warehouses Associations. Under this Act, the United Fruit Companies of Nova Scotia, Ltd., was formed, primarily for the handling of apples. The central company has representatives in Havana and London, these being the two chief markets, and also an intelligence system which keeps them informed every day from all the principal markets. When a big order is received the local companies are notified to have cars ready for shipment on a certain date from the local warehouses, where the fruit is stored and inspected by the company's inspectors to ensure a uniform and high standard.

In 1915 the Annapolis Valley associations subscribed 5,000 barrels of apples for the purpose of an advertising campaign carried out by the Nova Scotia Fruit Growers' Association. In addition, the Provincial Government gave a cash contribution, and an experienced representative was sent to England to advertise Nova Scotia fruit in the principal cities.

In British Columbia an amendment to the Agricultural Associations Act was passed in 1913, whereby duly incorporated associations might secure a Government loan amounting to 80 per cent. of the subscribed capital. The work of these associations was to assemble, grade and pack according to standard rules all fruit and vegetables grown by the respective shareholders, and otherwise to prepare them for market. At the same time a united selling and buying organisation was established under the name of the Okanagan United Growers' which in the first year handled sixty-five per cent. of the crop grown in the district and is now the price-setting factor in British Columbia.

The British Columbia Fruit Growers' Association, working in conjunction with the Provincial Department of Agriculture, advertises the fruit and vegetable products of the province in the markets of Alberta and Saskatchewan. Window cards are distributed free to the dealers, bulletins are inserted in the prairie newspapers, and a free booklet of eighty pages giving recipes and methods of canning is sent to all interested. Circulars referring to the fruits in season are also issued to all retailers every few weeks.

Fruit Preserving.—In 1917 the Ontario Department of Agriculture was instrumental in equipping a small community Canning Centre at Parkhill in which some thousands of pounds of fruit and vegetables and also chickens were canned, and sent to the Canadian Forces during the war. This centre was very successful and resulted in the formation of several other centres in the province. With the cessation of hostilities, however, all the canning centres were disbanded with the exception of that at Parkhill, which is now run as a co-operative community centre.—JOURNAL OF MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE, VOL. XXIX., No. II,

APRIL, 1923.]247

GENERAL.

KITCHEN GARDENING.

The following is an extract from a Paper on "Kitchen Gardening with Special Reference to Cabbage, Tomatoes and Beans" read at a meeting of the Agricultural Society of Trinidad and Tobago, by R. O. WILLIAMS, Superintendent, Royal Botanic Gardens, and taken from PROCEEDINGS OF THE AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY OF TRINIDAD AND TOBAGO, Vol. XXII, Part 11.

CHOICE OF SITUATION AND SOIL.

Provided other conditions such as soil, rainfall, etc., are favourable, the greater the elevation, the more successful is the cultivation of vegetables likely to be. It is often the case that one has no choice and only low-lying land is available. This need not be an obstacle provided other necessary conditions of cultivation are adhered to.

Most vegetable crops grow best in a medium soil, that is to say neither too sandy nor too clayey a nature. Old pasture land composed of good loamy soil is very suitable. A very stony soil, or shallow soil overlying rock stones or gravel is not recommended, as it quickly becomes impoverished by drought, and the action of the sun.

Much can be done to improve soil conditions by trenching and by applications of plenty of pen manure, but it is preferable in the first instance that a good site with suitable soil be chosen that the crops may derive a maximum amount of benefit from work put into the land.

DRAINAGE.

Good drainage is an absolute necessity as it is essential that water does not lie upon the land even for a short time. The system adopted must depend entirely on local conditions. It is generally necessary to grow vegetables on beds, and provided these are raised sufficiently the paths between serve to carry surplus water to the main drains. On sloping land these beds should be laid according to the contour of the land and not straight down the slopes, so that surface washing during heavy rains may be avoided.

CULTIVATION.

This must be very thorough and it should be remembered that vegetables are remunerative crops giving high returns per acre, but to get good crops intensive cultivation requiring a large amount of labour and consequent proportionate expenditure is necessary.

Supposing a piece of old pasture is the site selected for the vegetable garden, mere forking of this is not sufficient.

The plot to be planted should first be thickly spread with manure and a trench two spits deep opened at one end. Into this must be turned the sods and manure which are then covered with the second spit of soil. This should be done in such a manner that a perfect trench is kept in front of the

248[APRIL, 1923.

worker, and the whole of the soil is turned or mixed to a depth twice that of the tool being used, all grass and manure being completely buried. If it is decided to make the land into beds the top soil with the weeds, etc., from the paths may also be turned into the trench. Beds should not be made wider than four or five feet, otherwise it is difficult to plant or weed without treading on them. Made of this width they can be easily reached from the paths on either side. During the wet season beds are recommended for practically all soils except the very light ones, and even on these the plants will be found to thrive better if the land be ridged in a similar manner as practised for sweet potatoes and the plants put in on the ridges. It is not necessary to form raised beds during the dry season.

SELECTION OF SEED.

This is an important matter and it is only by actual trials under local conditions that it is possible to make recommendations. If one might venture to speak generally it is better to choose those varieties listed by English and American seedsmen as "summer" varieties rather than choose "spring" or "autumn" kinds. Seeds must be purchased from a reliable nurseryman and for shipment to the tropics it is necessary to ensure that they be packed in sealed tins. When exposed to the moist warm air of our climate chemical changes rapidly take place within the seeds and after a few days or weeks according to the nature of the seed they will not germinate. If seeds are not sown immediately on arrival they should be put into air tight jars. The best for the purpose are glass desiccators. Some substance such as unslaked lime or calcium chloride should be placed at the bottom for the purpose of absorbing moisture, from the air contained in the jar. Over this place a piece of perforated zinc and then the seeds on top. Only remove the cover when necessary. I find seeds after two months give almost as high germination percentage as when freshly received and have had onion seed give 30-50 percentage vitality thirteen months after storage in this way in Grenada.

SOWING SEED.

The greatest trouble probably with which one has to contend, when raising seedlings in Trinidad is the destruction of the seeds by small ants and practically all small seeds should be sown in such a manner that the beds or boxes may be isolated from their ravages by water, oil, tar, etc. The method adopted at the gardens is to make a bamboo staging about 2\frac{1}{2} feet high on which is placed about two inches of soil in which the seeds are sown. It is better that this soil be baked before sowing as it not only kills weed seeds, but also minimises the losses from the "damping off" fungus. The uprights of the staging are smeared with crude oil at the time of sowing. The seeds are sown thinly and covered with a thin layer of soil, a useful recommendation is to cover to their own depth. Leaves are then spread over the staging till germination commences when they are immediately removed and the seedlings allowed full exposure to the sun throughout the day; careful attention must of course be paid to see that they are not allowed to get dry at this stage as this would be fatal. It is my experience that more seedlings are lost in Trinidad by coddling than by exposure to the sun and it is common to see weakly, drawn seedlings the result of raising under too shady conditions. The losses amongst such seedlings are great and even those which survive are not so sturdy as seedlings raised in the sun. In their young stages they are

APRIL, 1923.]249

also very much more susceptible to the damping off fungus than are those raised under more exposed conditions.

When only a small quantity of plants are required seeds may be sown in boxes and pots and isolated from ants in some such manner as I have described. With some root crops such as beetroot and carrots it is necessary to sow them direct in beds. The former seeds which are somewhat large are not often troubled by ants and damage to the latter can be controlled to some extent by mixing the seeds with a little soil which has been moistened with kerosene.

TRANSPLANTING SEEDLINGS.

As soon as the first true leaves begin to form the seedlings should be pricked off into either tiny pots, boxes or beds. They can be put into pots quite easily and cheaply; simply spread the pots in a batch, fill with soil by means of a shovel and press the soil when inserting the seedlings. The advantage of this method is that seedlings suffer less check when transplanting.

Seedling Tomatoes, Cabbages, etc., can remain in small pots two or three weeks exposed to the sun except that protection for a day or two might be given at the time of transfer from seed beds to pots or beds. By this time they will have grown into hard, sturdy plants capable of being transferred to their permanent position in the garden.

PLANTING OUT.

Planting should of course be done preferably during showery weather—but if this is not possible watering must be done and some protection given from sun for a day or two, a stiff fair sized leaf inserted close beside each plant serves the latter purpose well.

After planting there is little to be done for some time except weed and water, and drier the weather the more necessary it is to keep the surface soil well stirred to prevent caking and cracking the cause of rapid evaporation. Stirring the surface soil also admits free percolation of rainfall or the water supplied. When the plants are in full growth it is advisable to give a second application of pen manure stirring the surface soil so as to cover it as much as possible. Avoid putting the manure in actual contact with the stem of the plants. If grass or other material is also available at the same time for application in the form of a surface mulch this is very desirable. Under our conditions of climate the sun's action quickly impoverishes the soil and it is very necessary if good crops are to be gathered to constantly replenish the soil in food material and when possible protect by mulching from the direct rays of the sun.

REAPING.

Little need be said as regards reaping the crops but owing to their perishable nature it is best to gather either in the early morning or late evening, preferably the latter if they have to be packed for transport to market, to ensure the produce being dry. Cleanliness of course and careful handling are also necessary. After reaping, all refuse of the crop must be buried or burnt otherwise this forms congenial breeding grounds for the numerous pests and diseases to which vegetables are liable.

In this connection as well as from a manurial standpoint the rotation of crops is strongly advised.

250[APRIL, 1923.]

SEASON.

The best season for growing vegetables in most places in Trinidad is undoubtedly from the end of the wet season and the first two or three months of the dry. The best time to commence sowing seed is during November, making successional sowings till the end of January. Most of the crops take from three to four months to mature, so that reaping should commence from February onwards. They can also be grown of course throughout the year, but at the end of the dry season conditions are usually too dry unless one has special means for irrigation, and during the wet season the losses amongst the young plants are so great that it could scarcely be reckoned a paying proposition.

The exception to this is to be found at Gasparee where MR. and MRS. G. LAMOTTE have for some time past been engaged in growing tomatos and vegetables. There, owing to the absence of a sufficient water supply cultivation in the dry season is impossible but owing to the precipitation being so much less during the wet season than we experience here growth of these crops can be successfully undertaken.

WATER SUPPLY.

As may be gathered from these remarks a plentiful water supply is a necessary factor towards the success of the kitchen garden. If a definite system of irrigation can be arranged so much the better but where one is not so fortunate resource will have to be made to the hose or water pot.

The application of water requires to be carefully and thoroughly undertaken. It should be done in early morning or late evening and a thorough soaking given even though by this means a portion of the garden only may receive treatment every few days. If frequent sprinklings are given instead of thorough soakings the young tender roots are brought to the surface where they will require still more frequent waterings or they become scorched and the plants die.

PAPER MULCHING OF PINE-APPLES.

A. T. LONGLEY,

Board of Agriculture, Honolulu.

A few years ago MR. C. F. ECKART introduced a paper mulch for use in the production of sugar-cane, which is being used with great success in Hawaii. MR. ECKART'S patent rights covering paper mulch also include its use in the production of pine-apples and various other crops. No experiments had been made with pine-apples, however, until 1919, when an experiment was planted in roofing paper by the Hawaiian Pine-apple Company, Ltd., after MR. WHITMORE had seen the mulch in use on cane in Olaa. As a result of the excellent showing made by paper mulch in this and more recent experiments on both upper and lower lands, the Hawaiian Pine-apple Company has acquired an option on all patent rights for growing pine-apples in paper mulch. It is estimated that there are at present 461 acres planted in paper, 68 acres of which will fruit in 1922. The Hawaiian Pine-apple Company has 431 acres, LIBBY McNEILL, and LIBBY 25 acres, and the California Packing Corporation 5 acres.

APRIL, 1923.]251

The first yields were obtained from paper-mulch plantings during the past season. These yields and the appearance of all paper-covered plantings, ranging from a few months to two years old, leave little doubt as to the value of the paper. Plants in paper grow uniformly larger, greener, and healthier, and produce larger fruit than plants grown without paper. The fruit maturing on paper mulch last season was very carefully weighed, as was that on adjoining check lines, and the results showed an average weight of 4 lb. 8'24 oz. for the fruit grown with paper, while that grown without paper averaged only 3 lb. 8'66 oz.; a difference of nearly 1 lb. Allowing 7,300 fruiting plants to the acre, this shows an increase of 7,107'2 lb., or a little over 3½ tons in favour of the paper.

As the plants on paper were in much better condition after the fruit was harvested than those grown without paper, it is believed that the first ratoon crop will show at least as great an increase as the plant crop, and that the second ratoon crop will also show a substantial gain. It is not improbable that the total increase will amount to 8 or 9 tons for the three crops, and that an additional ratoon may be grown at a good profit in many fields. Had the entire field in which the experiment was conducted been planted with paper mulch and yielded at the same rate as the experiment, the production would have been 23'3 per cent. greater. From the appearance of plants in paper mulch on the better lands which will bear next year, there is reason to believe that this high percentage of increase will be maintained or even bettered. The experiments being conducted by the California Packing Corporation (LIBBY McNEILL, and LIBBY) and the Hawaiian Pine-apple Company cover a wide range of soil and climatic conditions, and in every case show a decided improvement from the use of paper. In all experiments where the plants have been growing a few months, the exact boundaries of the paper-covered lines can be established from a great distance by the increased growth and healthier colour of the plants.

While the greatly increased yield is the most important benefit derived from the use of paper mulch, it has many good points that recommend it. While no account has been kept of weeding costs, it is conservatively estimated that paper mulch will save two-thirds of this expense. The space around the plants which ordinarily takes the most time needs no hoeing, and the weeds between the lines can be fairly well controlled by cultivating. In addition to cutting labour costs to a minimum, it prevents the growth of weeds between the plants during long wet spells. Fertilising costs are also lowered, as it is not necessary to feed the weeds. It is expected that the saving in weeds costs for two years will pay for the greater part of the material and labour for applying the paper.

Paper mulch also prevents hard rains from packing the soil around the roots of young plants, and in dry weather keep the plant-food more available by holding the moisture in the soil, where under ordinary conditions it would dry out and bake. Tests made during the hot, dry weather showed approximately double the amount of moisture in soil under paper as in soil without paper. At the same time, temperature tests were made with and without paper mulch, which showed the soil under paper to be warmer by from 2 to 5 degrees, depending on the quality of the paper, and also showed a minimum ranging from 2 to 6 degrees higher at night. The temperatures were taken under several different makes of paper with recording thermometers such as are used in the canneries.

252[APRIL, 1923.

After successful experiments had been carried on by the Hawaiian Pine-apple Company and others at Wahiawa, the Hawaiian Pine-apple Association's experiment station planted an experiment in April of this year (1921) at Kailua, Oahu, which shows conclusively that paper mulch is far better for that section than any of the other fifty plots which were treated with various chemicals. The plant growth on the paper mulch is at least three times greater in weight and much healthier than other plots, only two plants out of 129 showing the least signs of weakness. Practically all plants in the chemically treated and check plots are small, weak, and of poor colour. There has been practically no rain at the experiment since it was planted, yet the soil under the paper has been kept in a moist and friable condition throughout, even when no signs of moisture could be found to a depth of 18 inches in other plots. Especially interesting is the fact that a plot of approximately 10 by 15 feet entirely covered with roofing paper shows even better plants than the adjoining plot, where only the lines were covered. The soil under the middle of this plot was apparently as moist and loamy as under the other. It is evident that it would be impracticable to put paper over a whole field, even though it were not necessary to cultivate. Space must be left for drainage and for the men in harvesting. If it is true that the control of moisture and temperature are factors in checking what is known as wilt, paper mulch may be the remedy.

The best and cheapest method of applying the paper, so far as known, is by hand. After the land has been properly prepared for planting, a sled is dragged along the slightly raised line, breaking lumps, smoothing the surface, and bevelling the sides slightly. The paper, which comes in rolls of about 500 square feet each, is fastened at the end of the line by putting some soil on it. A man; with an adjustable handle which fits in both ends of the roll, backs along the line, unrolling the paper. As the paper is unrolled a man on either side of the paper puts on enough soil with a hoe to keep the wind from tearing it until a small plow can throw a small amount of soil along both edges. Care should be taken, however, not to get too much soil on the paper, and it is sometimes desirable to have a man follow the plough with a broom to sweep off any excess. There should be a gentle slope from the centre of the line towards the edges of the paper in order that the water may run off quickly instead of standing in depressions between the plants. A crew of four experienced men can lay paper for $3.00 an acre or less. This figure will be reduced somewhat when the paper is cut in 300 feet lengths to fit the standard lines, instead of the 110 to 170 feet lengths, as at present, which necessitate an extra man in the laying crew to carry the rolls of paper from the field road towards the centre of the line.

An ideal paper mulch for pine-apples should have the following qualities:—It should be 300 feet long, at least 36 inches wide for double lines, strong enough to withstand the weather for at least two years without, shrinking or tearing, or rotting out on the edges where it is necessary to put the soil to hold it in place. It should also be waterproof and of good insulating qualities to hold the heat and moisture around the roots. In order to determine the relative values of different makes and qualities of paper for use in the production of pine-apples, a comparative experiment was planted by the Hawaiian Pine-apple Company on 3rd September, 1921, containing

APRIL, 1923.]253

ten kinds of building, insulating, and specially made papers. The papers being tested are all 36 inches wide, but vary in length from 110 to 300 feet to the roll, in weight from 5 to 14 lb. per 100 square feet, and range in cost from $40.00 to $244.00 per acre. A close check is being kept on these different papers to see how they stand the weather, and careful records will be kept of the yields. At this early date it would appear that one of the cheaper papers will be the best adapted for pine-apple culture.—QUEENSLAND AGRIC. JOURN., VOL. XVIII., PART 4.

A GLOSSARY OF AGRICULTURAL TERMS AND PHRASES WITH NOTES.

T. B. P. KEHELPANNALA.

The following glossary of agricultural terms and phrases, occurring in official correspondence, documents and current colloquial intercourse are published for general information:

1. Adipalla.—The bottom layer of the stacked paddy in a threshing-floor, which is sometimes set apart as a perquisite to the Andé cultivator by generously inclined wealthy paddy land owners. Also called "Warupalla" or "Warupatula."

2. Agaraya.—A washaway; depressions caused by the erosion of flood water.

(In the district of Anuradhapura the term is used for "drainage or water supply in a tank.")* CLOUGH interprets it as "a house." Sans "Agaraya"=a house. In the Glossary of native words published by Government the term "Agarè" is called "A Valley; also a tributary stream."*

3. Agas.—First fruits of a harvest.

4. Agamata.—The smaller or narrower and of a liyadda a terraced bed of a field divided by a niyara=ridge, (b) the terminal liyadda of a paddy field, (c) the lower end of a range of paddy fields derived from aga end, ata direction. Called also Patupota.

5. Ahàwana-ata.—The reservation bordering a paddy field next to a high land. There is no Wana-ata for fields situated in the middle of a range of tract of paddy fields. (b) Called also Aswana-ata Pillàwa and Wana-ata are synonymous terms. The first step in the cultivation of a paddy field consists in the clearing of the reservation of its jungle growth.

6. Akawanawa.—To turn water to a paddy field: term used in Walapane, Nuwara Eliya District. Ordinary colloquial term in other districts is Watura-Harawanawa: Watura=water, harawanawa=turn.

7. Akyàla.—Remuneration of a laha of paddy to the Kapurala (lay-priest) for his invoking the gods for the protection of the crop from insect pests. Called also Deyange laha (god's share) or Akyàla-laha.

8. Alut-Sal-Mangalle.—Literally festival of the new rice; the annual thanks-giving feast of the harvest home held in January. In Kandy, the first ripened crops are brought from a field at Gurudeniya—a field allotted for the

* Manual, North-Central Province, p. 264.

254[APRIL, 1923.

particular purpose from ancient times, when the first ripened sheaves of paddy are brought in procession on elephants and in decorated pingos covered with white cloth, the rest of the service—tenants and villagers—meet at Dalada Maligawa from all the neighbouring districts on full moon day, where a big feast is prepared and partaken of after the dedication to the gods.

9. Aluwanwudanawa.—To describe with ashes mystic symbols and harvesting implements on the threshing floor to increase the crop and avert evil influence.

10. Amuna.—Is a dam raised across a stream or river to obstruct the current of water and direct it to the irrigating channel. In colloquial language the term Amuna is also used for the Irrigating channel properly the Ela. The two words Ela Amuna mean dam and “Channel” and “Dam.”
(b) A measure of capacity, which varies in different districts from 4, 4\frac{1}{2} to 5 bushels; (c) The extent of high or mud land sown by the said measure.

11. Andaherapanawa.—To loudly intone Uve ! Uve !! Uve ! ! ! whilst levelling, ploughing and thrashing, to incite the animals to quicker action, the sound is considered pleasant to the animals.

12. Anda-mulletuwa.—A field sown by a tenant on condition of delivering half the crops to the proprietor as an acknowledgment of ownership.

13. Anda-kumbure.—A field cultivated by another with the express permission of the land-owner on the agreement to deliver to the proprietor half the crop and straw as rent. The inviolable customs governing Anda-kumbura (fields let out for half share) are that the cultivator cannot on any pretence whatever reap the field without first informing the land owner and permission obtained. The cultivator must inform the land-owner of the reaping with the invariable present of the betel and a box of dressed provisions. The cultivator must repeat his visit on the day of thrashing, and operations cannot begin without the presence of the land-owner, his deputy, or Kankanama (supervisor).*

14. Anda-paraveniya.—A field let out by a land owner to an individual to cultivate in perpetuity, the former to receive a divided half of the crop as royalty, the cultivator considering it as his permanent holding.

15. Ande.—An equal share or any part thereof received by the proprietor from the cultivator of a high or low land. The term Ande has several applications : viz. (a) Hariande=equal share; (b) Gankara Ande=The land owner's ground share. (c) Karuande=One-fourth share appertaining to the co-cultivator. (d) Kuttu Karaya=A co-cultivator. (e) Kuttu Ande=The co-cultivator's one-fourth share. (f) Acdakaraya=A co-cultivator, one who cultivates a land on the footing to give half share of the proceeds to the land-owner.

* In the case of low-caste cultivators, they must visit the Gowivanse land owners with undressed foodstuff—five neliyas of rice, a bunch of plantains and vegetables with a dry-fish.

APRIL, 1923.]255

FOOD PRODUCTION.

Until quite recently almost the whole of the food crop farming done in the Colony has been carried on by women. Even now the majority of food farms are made by women. The planting is done by them, the produce marketed and sold by them.

Food crop farming had very little interest for men, and was even looked on as women's work and something beneath the men's dignity. It is good to see, however, that young men in the district are becoming interested in food crop farming, and are also anxious to learn something about poultry farming. Until this kind of work is taken up more generally and more scientifically by the young farmers, the cost of foodstuffs will remain high. In the past, practically the whole of the work has been left to the women, who have had to work hard, and when labour, transport and the time spent in the market are taken into consideration the profits are only small.

Encouragement towards the production of more foodstuffs and better crops could be given by good demonstration work in the Agricultural Stations throughout the Colony, and by the distribution of more plants and seeds from these stations. Better varieties of yams, cassava, tannias or coco-yam, and other vegetables essential to the native could be raised for distribution, and the same with fruits :—oranges, limes, pine-apples, avocado-pears, tomates, etc.

Other methods of increasing the quantity of food would include (1) Prize Competitions for Foodcrop Farms, run on similar lines as the present Cacao Farm Competitions, and (2) local Agricultural Shows. By holding Farm Competitions, lively interest in the production of foodstuffs would be roused, and more particularly if all the competitions were placed on an equal footing by distributing plants, seeds or sets to them from the Agricultural Stations—free of charge, or at a very low rate—just sufficient to cover expenses incurred in raising the plants, etc.

The farms could be classed according to size and prizes given for the highest number of marks awarded for general cultivation, draining, weeding, spacing when planting, and staking in the case of yams, tomates, etc. The produce of the farms could either be judged on the farms or samples entered for the local Shows and prizes awarded in the usual way.

By holding food farm competitions, Agricultural Officers would visit the farms regularly, and would see for themselves, if the farmers made good use of the plants, etc., distributed to them.

Transport as it affects Foodstuff by road or lorries is at present very expensive. Owners and drivers of lorries do not appear to have a special rate of charges for mileage, or weight, and growers of food crops have no standard of weight, or measure. Usually an agreement is struck between the growers and the lorry man according to the weight, and particularly to the bulk of the load—the lorry man always being well on the right side of the deal.

Owing to the high charges made by lorry men for the conveyance of foodstuff to the railway, and markets, much produce, which would tend to bring down prices if it could be marketed, is now left to waste.

256[APRIL, 1923.

It should be possible to adopt a system whereby a number of foodcrop collecting centres* could be formed on roads, and near the railway in some instances, and that a lorry system could be run, to convey these foodstuffs to the railway or direct to markets, and so tap the food growing districts, which have hitherto been more or less in the background, owing to the difficulties of transportation. Such stations might be worked by young officers of the Department who are now in training and the whole supervised by a District Officer.

The whole scheme is to form a system of "clearing stations" so that farmers can bring in their produce, have it weighed, and consigned to any place at a cheaper rate.

It may be possible to find some form of standard crates for the easier handling of the produce, and thus do away with the bulky package one sees on lorries and trains.—JOUR. OF THE GOLD COAST AGRIC. AND COMMERCIAL SOCIETY.—Vol. 1, No. 4.

The pressure distribution throughout March was of the singularly even type that is associated with local thunderstorms. In the daily reports the code figures for "thunderstorm" and "distant thunder and lightning" were consequently very frequent while the contours on the rainfall charts for the month's total are correspondingly irregular. The rainfall totals were above their average rather more often than below. The sixteen stations given in the table show this ratio as thirteen to three which is rather an overestimate for the Island as a whole, while at quite half the stations the totals, whether above or below, were within a couple of inches of their averages.

The list of stations at which averages were passed by 5 inches or more is also very informative. The chief areas concerned were in the extreme north and part of the North Western Province and the extreme south—if we may stretch the latter term to include Deniyaya—but even more significant is the distribution of such stations round the hills. They do not show windward and lee sides but seem scattered all round e.g. Bulugahapitiya, Kurunduoya, Keenagabaella, Carney, & Kenilworth with an outer fringe in the north of the Kelani Valley including Kanaangama & Digalla.

As regards distribution in time, the 13th and 14th stand out as the days on which there was the nearest approach to a definite depression, and it was about then that the most widespread rain occurred.

In the northern half of the island temperatures have been appreciably below average, in the southern and western parts there has been more variation than the offsets in the table indicate, as the maximum temperatures have been consistently above their averages and the minimum ones as consistently below theirs. Ratnapura with mean maximum for the month 93.2 and absolute maximum 97.2 usurped an unenviable position at the head of the list of temperatures that has been more often held in March by Kurunegala.

THE
TROPICAL AGRICULTURIST

VOL. LX.

PERADENIYA, MAY, 1923.

No. 5.

AGRICULTURAL CONFERENCES.

The report of the Agricultural Conference at Jaffna which is published in our present number should be of interest to agriculturists generally. It was organized in order that the agriculturists of the North should have an opportunity of placing before the Department of Agriculture some of their requirements, of hearing the results of the experiments which are being carried out at the Jaffna Experiment Station and of discussing these results freely.

In conjunction with the Conference, visits to farms were arranged as well as visits to the Experiment Station, lectures to farmers, and training classes for office-bearers of Co-operative Credit Societies.

There is no doubt that the discussion of the work of the Department of Agriculture with those agriculturists for whom the work is being carried out is productive of useful results. The Department is thereby placed in intimate touch with the requirements of the various industries, and the results of research work and of investigations are placed before agriculturists as soon as they become available.

The establishment of the Experiment Station at Jaffna is of recent date and already valuable results have been secured from experiments with tobacco and with fodder cholams. The work that is being carried on with Kurakkan varieties and with different types of chillies is becoming of interest and may lead to valuable results in the course of the next few years.

The plans for the Agricultural School in conjunction with the Experiment Station are maturing and regular courses in the agricultural practices of the North will be started next year. Visitors to the Station were enabled to see the work that was being carried on and to learn something of the plans for the future.

260[MAY, 1923.

The lectures to farmers in Tamil were greatly appreciated by those present and it is hoped to make such lectures an annual feature of the work of the Station. The number who attended these lectures was estimated to be seventy, but it is expected that in future years this number will be considerably increased.

Similarly the lectures to office-bearers of Co-operative Credit Societies were well attended, and this course should prove valuable to those who are interested in the fostering of the co-operative movement in the North.

The general impression of the whole Conference was most encouraging and it would appear to indicate that further conferences should be organised not only in Jaffna but in other parts of Ceylon.

There is a great need for rural development throughout the whole Colony and the organization of the industries of the small grower is essential if an improvement of the economic condition of the country is to be secured. The Department of Agriculture is charged with the duty of fostering and of assisting in this development. By Conferences in various districts it is possible to secure valuable information of the actual needs of those districts and to place before workers definite data based upon scientific investigation which should be of assistance in their industries.

The subjects dealt with at Jaffna consisted of White Burley Tobacco, Fodder Cholams and Well Irrigation—subjects of prime importance in the agriculture of the North. If the present export trade of tobacco with Travancore were to find itself in insuperable difficulties the prosperity of the Jaffna peninsula would be materially reduced unless another money crop could be found for tobacco or unless another variety of tobacco could be grown for export to a wider market. The fodder question is equally as important to the Jaffna cultivator and a proper solution of this is necessary in the interests of agriculture of the North. Similarly data in regard to the relative costs of well irrigation by different forms of lifts is necessary if the most economical method is to be adopted.

It was problems of this character that were tackled and fully discussed. This exchange of views cannot but be of material benefit to the Jaffna cultivators and to those interested in the welfare and development of agriculture in the North and in Ceylon generally.

MAY, 1923.]261

COCONUTS.

CEYLON'S COCONUT CROPS.

(H. K. RUTHERFORD.)

It is now possible to complete the comparisons of output of Coconut products for the four pre-war years 1911-14, the war years 1915-18 and the post-war years 1919-22.

It may be remembered that in my previous notes on this subject in the TROPICAL AGRICULTURIST I selected four year periods in order to average the good and bad yielding years.

The object in view in compiling the figures herewith given, was to elucidate to what extent the Coconut industry in Ceylon was increasing its production, and this could only be ascertained by the conversion of all the products to a nut basis.

The conclusion arrived at is that production has increased by 60% in the last 12 years. This result is based on the average of 3 years 1911-13 as compared with 1920-22. I have eliminated 1914 as the exports in the latter part of the year were probably affected by the war, and I have also discarded the year 1919 as exports for the year may have been abnormally increased owing to the clearing out of stocks accumulated during the war.

The increase in production is probably due to two causes, viz., a steady coming into bearing of young plantations and to a higher state of cultivation of the palms.

There is no evidence to shew that there has been any extensive development of area planted under coconuts. MR. L. J. B. TURNER, Director of Statistics, in his census of Ceylon Coconuts 1921 gives the total planted area as 820,000 acres, although he admits that in the detailed returns comprising this acreage there are several discrepancies calling for investigation. In 1915, the acreage given in Ferguson's Directory was 800,000 acres.

As MR. TURNER's census was the first ever attempted it is reasonable to assume that the next time it is undertaken the native headmen will have become more accustomed to the work of collecting the statistics required and thus lead to greater accuracy.

The production has been increasing at the rate of 5% per annum for the last 12 years, and no doubt this progress can be maintained if a more liberal cultivation of the palm were more general throughout the Coconut growing districts.

A study of the subjoined figures shews that within recent years the greatest increase in Tonnage of exported produce has been in desiccated coconuts.

262[MAY, 1923.

The increases in exports (taking the averages of 1911-14 as compared with averages of 1919-22) are as under :—

No progress has been made in enabling one to arrive at the actual total output of the coconut growing in the Island, as there is no data available whereby the local consumption can be even approximately ascertained.

COFFEE.

HINTS ABOUT THE GROWING OF COFFEE.

(Translated from the Spanish of "La Hacienda")

Before the young coffee plants are transplanted to their permanent site during the first season, they should be allowed to remain in the nursery until they have 5 or 6 pairs of leaves; younger plants should not be removed. The transplanting can be done with a digging fork, care being taken not to damage the roots. The plants should be carefully examined and any that are lacking in vigour or have poor root development should be rejected. The other should have the tip of the principal root cut off by a clean knife cut to prevent the root turning upwards on being transplanted. To prevent the young plants from dying out they should be wrapped in wet sacking and care should be taken to avoid exposing them to the sun.

The ground having been well prepared beforehand by removing all stumps, digging and levelling the surface, we can now proceed to make the holes of a size suitable for the plants—the hole should be sufficiently large to allow the roots to be fully extended. The plants should be placed at the same depth as it was in the nursery with the roots in a normal position. The surrounding soil should then be beaten down firmly, but not backed tightly.

If the transplanting is done with the roots in a ball of soil, the season is a less important factor than in the preceding case.

A number of shallow boxes, bamboo trays or baskets, will be required. Nurseries are frequently constructed as a raised bed with an enclosing frame work; in transplanting the frame can be removed; then, commencing with the first row, cut the ground in squares in such a way that each plant will be in the centre of each square block of earth. Any projecting roots may be cut.

It the soil is of a suitable consistency it can be moulded by gentle pressure with the hands and if clayey may easily be kept in position with large leaves. When the first row is finished the same operation can be repeated with each successive row.

The plant with its ball of earth should be placed in the boxes or trays, avoiding handling as much as possible. They are then carried to the holes previously prepared beforehand and planted in the manner described.

If the coffee plants are transplanted in the first season, that is, when they have 5 or 6 pairs of leaves, the result will be as satisfactory to transplant them with the roots bare as if the slower, more laborious and therefore more costly method of transplanting them with the soil surrounding the roots is adopted.

When the plants are allowed to remain in the nursery till the second season, that is, when they are 18 or 20 months old, great economy is effected because the care of a nursery in good condition is a small matter compared with the expense of caring for a plantation. If this method is adopted it will be better to place the plants 8 inches apart instead of 6, thus giving the roots and stems more room for development. By leaving the plants in the nursery until the second season they will be stronger and better able to resist unfavourable conditions.

266[MAY, 1923.]

The process of transplanting is the same as indicated for the younger plants.

In a trial plot of plants that were left in the nursery till the second season, two rows were planted under exactly equal conditions with the exception that for the first row the plants were transplanted with their roots bare while for the other row they were taken up with a ball of soil. In the following season the first row did not produce any coffee but 25 % of the trees in the second row produced some berries. The average height of the plants in the second row was 10 inches more than those of the first row. We can see, therefore, that with plants 18 to 20 months old it is preferable to transplant them with a ball of soil. Nevertheless this does not mean that good results may not be obtained by the other method if care is exercised. If the method of transplanting with bared roots adopted, a dull day should be chosen and the evaporating surface of the plant should be reduced by cutting the leaves in half.

Some authorities recommend that the plants should be cut down to six inches from the ground immediately before transplanting if the stem is of the diameter of a pencil. If the plants are not very strong and especially if the conditions are not very favourable, the little tree will have difficulty in recovering from this severe pruning. Frequent weedings will be necessary because the small plants would otherwise be smothered by the rapidly growing weeds. Moreover if the plants are hidden by weeds they are easily trodden down by the labourers. From this will be seen the advisability of inspecting the young renewals several times, removing the unsuitable ones and leaving only the more vigorous plants.

CARE OF YOUNG COFFEE BUSHES AFTER TRANSPLANTING.

The most convenient time for cultivation is at the end of the rainy season or at the beginning of the dry weather, before the soil has become quite dry. By keeping the ground around the tree in cultivation a larger amount of moisture will be retained which would otherwise evaporate. If it be possible to cultivate several times at the commencement of the dry season, so much the better.

A similar effect will result from cultivations given after a shower of rain in the dry season. Cultivation benefits the plants in other ways besides conserving moisture. The small roots are better able to penetrate the soil and chemical changes are accelerated which render more food available to the plant.

In cultivating the soil around the tree, special care should be taken to avoid damaging the roots.

WEEDING.

During the rainy season the vegetation on slopes prevents the surface soil from washing away, but all the growth should be cut at the beginning of the dry season, not only to reduce to the minimum the evaporating surface but also that it may serve as a means of conserving the moisture for the tree.

The construction of trenches at right angles to the slope of the ground will diminish the loss of surface soil. These trenches catch the leaves and any soil loosened during weedings which would otherwise be washed down the slopes by the rains.

Where weeds are very abundant frequent forking or cultivation is necessary to avoid weed seeds spreading all over the plantation. The number of weedings depends naturally, on local circumstances.

Where the coffee has little shade and weeds are most troublesome it is an excellent plan to sow a leguminous crop at the commencement of the rains, to be cut when the dry season begins. It is best to have a crop that does not reach a great size. The donkey turnip, Canavalia ensiformis, is of rapid growth and, considering all the circumstances, it would perhaps be difficult to find a leguminous plant more suitable than this one for coffee.

MAY, 1923.]267

PRUNING.

As the plants develop it becomes necessary to prune them. Most coffee planters have their own particular ideas about this work, but this does not prevent us making one or two suggestions which may be useful. Generally pruning is done with a machete (chopping knife) and this leaves nothing to be desired if the instrument is well sharpened and is used by a person who can properly use it, and make a clean and precise cut. Notwithstanding, it frequently happens that the branch is not given a complete cut and consequently it breaks, leaving numerous splinters projecting. These small openings are filled with water during the first shower and this continues in subsequent rains till the water rots the branch at a place lower than the point of fracture. If a clean cut has not been effected such fracture can be avoided by finishing off the cutting of the branch with a saw. The part that has been cut with the saw can afterwards be smoothed off with a sharp knife, so that the cut may be left clean and without projections. In pruning, the cut should be made obliquely, so that water will run off and will not filter into the cavities. To make large cuts waterproof a coat of paint is sufficient.

At all times the cutting off the tops should be practised to prevent the trees growing too high. This operation stimulates the tree to throw out more stems, with the consequent production of new lateral branches.

PLANTATION MANURES.

In considering future attentions to the coffee plantation we should not forget to collect and make use of manures at hand.

The method of preparing coffee in the Great Antilles allows the return to the soil of the coffee pulp, quite fresh. But most of the manure that this produces is lost through not knowing how to apply it. The following partial analysis, which gives us the quantity of nitrogen, phosphoric acid and potash contained in 3,880 kilos of coffee in husk is of considerable instructive value.
