From this it can be clearly seen that if it were possible to return to the ground all the manure (plant food) except the amount taken by the berry, then more than a quarter of the phosphoric acid, nearly half the potash and much more than a quarter of the nitrogen that the crop extracts could be returned to the soil. Of course a part of the plant food must be lost, but this loss should be reduced as far as possible by returning to the soil the husk as soon as it has been removed from the coffee. In many plantations

268[MAY, 1923.

great heaps of fermenting husks exposed to the intense rays of the sun and to the inclemency of the rains may be seen behind the shelling house, thus losing a large quantity of nitrogen and soluble potash.

Again, many plantations have large numbers of animals and consequently quantities of animal manure. From this as from the coffee husks, large quantities of soluble ammonia and potash compounds are frequently lost through carelessness. We should not pile manure up in heaps exposed to sun and rain as is generally done. The sooner the soil receives it the less loss there will be. If it is not possible to apply it as soon as it is made it should be conserved in a well covered pit, from which there is no outlet. It would be also convenient, where circumstances permit, to store the manure in a place where liquid manure should be collected. The value of this is not generally appreciated.

Although the composition of animal manure varies according to the food of the animal, and its age, the following figures will give an average to serve for comparison.

Composition of the Urine and Excrement of Horses :—

Excrement Water Nitrogen Phosphoric Acid Potash
Solid 75.0 0.56 0.35 0.1
Liquid 90.0 0.52 A Trace 0.92

If the coffee is planted in raised banks or terraces the manure should be spread uniformly around the tree and mixed with the covering vegetation. If there are no banks then holes or small trenches should be made a little above the trees and the manure placed therein.

SHADE.

To obtain good results, it seems to be indispensable in many places to use shade trees—their mission of wind-breaks is of no small importance. In the first preparation of the ground all places, which by their position are exposed to strong winds, should be left covered with trees and at least one row on the highest ground. It is also convenient to leave some alongside the principal drains in such way that their roots will protect the soil against washing away. The trees are of great utility in coffee plantations, breaking the force of heavy rains with their foliage and in preventing wash and in holding the soil in its place with their roots. Moreover, the falling leaves increase the supply of humus. As coffee leaves do not fall and as the humus content of some clay soils is very poor, this is an important mission that the shade trees fulfil.

Care should be taken that the shade is not very dense. This is a fault easily incurred because beneath dense shade the coffee tree appears to grow vigorously, but appearances are deceptive and the crop is liable to be a very small one. If, then, the shade is dense, we should lighten it.

LEGUMINOUS TREES FOR SHADE.

Leguminous trees should be used as shade for coffee because they possess the property of obtaining part of their nitrogen from the air and do not depend only on the soil for obtaining this element.

Amongst the more important leguminous trees for shade we may mention the following :—

Guava, Inga vera.—This is a tree much used for shade and there is good reason for its popularity. Its form is open and spreading and it gives a moderate and well distributed shade. Its development is rapid and it may be planted simultaneously with the coffee, in which case the shade trees would have to be planted close together. It is best to place them at twice or three times the distance apart which separates the coffee trees,

MAY, 1923.]

269

always arranging for the shade tree to be in the centre of a square formed by four coffee trees. When the plantation is ready to give a good crop the shade obtained by this method will be amply sufficient, but we must be on the alert because, owing to the small distance between the trees, the shade may become very dense. If that does take place it can be rectified easily by first cutting off branches and later removing alternate trees.

Guama, Inga laurina.—In some places this tree is much used, but its shade is very dense and less spreading than that of the Guava; it is more popular as a wind break than as a shade tree; another drawback is that it affords food for an ant which does much damage to coffee. If in any districts it is observed that the coffee trees or the guama trees are infested by this ant great vigilance should be exercised and as few as possible of this variety of tree be planted.

Bucare, Erythrina sp.—This tree grows rapidly; it is easily propagated by seeds or cuttings and is seen in many places as shade for coffee. It has the bad property of letting the branches fall, thus causing damage. Also its large protuberances and superficial roots take up much more space, in proportion to the extension of its branches, than other trees used for this purpose.

Moca, Andira inermis.—This tree is of slow development and if it is to be used for shade, other trees of more rapid growth should be planted to shade the coffee beforehand, until the moca develops. Its form is frequently unsuitable as it is more inclined to grow flat and spreading. As however, the wood is strong there is no fear of its damaging the coffee by falling branches.

TEMPORARY SHADE.

Sometimes a planter wishes to grow coffee on a piece of land that has no shade. For this it is necessary to plant something of more rapid growth than the permanent shade trees, and which will afford protection and shade until they are in condition to do so. The Agati gaudiflora is a small leguminous tree of rapid growth. The guineo, however, is better for protection against winds as it gives a denser shade and assists in extirpating weeds and produces something whilst the coffee is developing. But the system which is often followed in planting guineos leaves much to be desired, because they are seen so close to the young coffee that the result is an unequal struggle for existence between the slow-growing and the fast-growing plants, and this can only have prejudicial effects on the coffee.

The following plan is recommended when the guineo is decided upon for provisional shade. In case the Agati is used, one or two may be placed in the centre of each square formed by four coffee trees, because the Agati gives less dense shade than the guineo and many more would be required.

270[MAY, 1923.

COTTON.

COTTON EXPERIMENTS IN MALAYA.

In the MALAYAN AGRICULTURAL JOURNAL, Vol. X. Nos. 10, 11 & 12, is published an article on "Cotton Experiments in Malaya" by H. W. JACK, B.Sc., B. A., Economic Botanist and W. M. SANDS, F. L. S., Assistant Economic Botanist, from which the following abstract is taken.

Cotton of long-staple grades is not likely to be over-produced in the sub-tropical and tropical countries of the world. Moreover, strenuous efforts, with large financial backing, are now being made by the recently formed Empire Cotton Growing Corporation to extend the culture of cotton in British Colonies and Protectorates in order that the cotton spinners of Great Britain may obtain adequate supplies of the raw material for their mills. Production of long-staple cotton is in danger of being restricted below normal requirements on account of the ravages of insect pests, and further the quantity available for British factories is steadily diminishing owing to the increased consumption of this class of cotton by American manufacturers.

Long-staple cotton of a high grade is required by the rubber and motor industries. Next to rubber, long-staple cotton is the most important raw material used by these and the outlook for the future is unsatisfactory because there is not enough of the best grades produced to meet the demand.

About 1914, trials were made with Egyptian, American Upland and Caravonica cottons, but the crop records of these experiments were not available. A comparatively good return, however, was reported. In 1921 a plot of Sea Island cotton was grown at the Kuala Kangsar Government Plantation. Owing chiefly to late planting, the yield obtained from it was small, but the Superintendent considers that the prospects of cotton-growing in the district are favourable.

At the Serdang Government Plantation, Egyptian and Sea Island were planted last season, but the results were unsatisfactory, apparently on account of unsuitable soil conditions.

In other parts of the Peninsula the 'kidney' or 'chain' cotton (Gossypium prasiliense), Caravonica, Egyptian, Assam Indigenous, Garo Hill, Dwarf Patani, and other varieties have been grown on a small scale by planters. With the exception of selected strains of Egyptian and Caravonica cotton all of these have coarse short staples, and are therefore of low value.

Although the prospects of cultivating the more valuable long staple cotton in Malaya cannot as yet be estimated, still recent trials indicate that a fair measure of success may be anticipated in average seasons.

The writers are of opinion that it would be wiser to confine initial experiments to Egyptian and Sea Island types. These cottons produce the finest, longest and strongest staples; they command the highest market-prices and further, they are derived from the same species, Gossypium barbadense.

As the market for the finest Sea Island cotton is very limited, types producing moderately fine grades of this class of cotton should be grown; these together with selected Egyptian varieties are required in large quantities in Great Britain. The plants can be grown as annuals, that is, they

MAY, 1923.]271

would only occupy the land for about seven or eight months of each year ; this is a great advantage because pests can be better controlled. Again the danger of natural hybridization and mixing of seed of long and short staple varieties would be avoided. Cotton from mixed, or hybridized seed is hardly saleable.

Should experiments with Egyptian and Sea Island cottons not prove satisfactory, then some of the best long staple American Upland or other varieties might be tried, but it is doubtful whether the market value in Europe of the lint from these would be sufficiently high to make the crop remunerative, unless the yield per acre was heavy and the cost of production low.

Three varieties of Egyptian and five varieties of Sea Island cottons have been experimented on a small scale by the Botanic Division of the Department during the past two seasons, chiefly with the object of obtaining a supply of pure seed of selected Egyptian and Sea Island varieties for larger trials. The Egyptian varieties were obtained from the Department of Agriculture at Cairo and the Sea Island from St. Vincent, British West Indies.

TIME OF PLANTING AND RAINFALL.

Cotton-growing when dependent on rainfall is usually a rather speculative undertaking. The plant succeeds best in places where the rainfall is good, but well distributed, during the first four months of its growth and then gradually decreases in the following three months when the bolls are maturing. Cotton, once it is established, can withstand fairly dry conditions if they are not too prolonged. It is a mistake to suppose that absolutely dry weather is essential at harvest. Good crops can be obtained even if the weather is showery, provided the rains are not continuous and spells of sunshine intervene.

SOIL.

As a rule light soils of good fertility are better than heavy ones. Provided the rainfall is not excessive, some of the heavier lands may also prove quite suitable. On poor soils the growth is stunted and the yield low. On the other hand, very rich soils often induce rank vegetative growth which leads to poor crops. Good drainage of the land is essential.

The soils on which the experiments were made were light and recently cleared of "blaha." The land selected for the crop should be worked up some time before planting is started, or preferably the cotton should be grown on land previously cultivated. When a considerable quantity of green dressing is present this material should be allowed to dry thoroughly before it is buried under the soil. There would be no danger in using well-rotted pen manure on poor soils.

PREPARATION OF LAND.

The methods of preparing land for cotton vary a great deal. In Malaya with the ample rainfall, and the unlikely occurrence of long periods of drought, provided the season for planting is well chosen, the ridge system appears to be one which should be adopted. For this method the land should first of all be clean-weeded and the weeds allowed to dry after being ranged in lines 4 or 5 feet apart. Ridges should then be thrown up either by plough or "changkol," covering the weeds completely. The ridges may be high or low, but preferably not less than 1 foot high at the centre. On good soils the ridges may be 4 or 5 feet apart : four feet is usually sufficient and on poor soils three feet. In dry districts the cotton may be planted on the flat. An advantage of the ridge method is that less cotton on the lower branches is damaged by rain and the root-system of the plants is better aerated. A water-soaked condition of the soil often leads to loss of

272[MAY, 1923.

crop because it checks the elaboration of food owing to root-asphyxiation, with the result that immature bolls are shed. Any factors, however, which tend to limit elaboration of food, such as periods of rain, low rate of evaporation, or little direct solar radiation, are precursors of augmented rates of shedding.

The ridge system answered well in the experiments, and damage due to rain and soil-water was almost negligible. The ridges, however, were about 15 inches high and 5 feet apart. This spacing was too wide, a width of 4 feet would have given better results because the plants did not cover the ground well between the five-foot ridges. With ridges spaced at 4 feet, there would have been a larger number of plants per acre which would have given a larger yield and the weeding costs would have been reduced.

In one plot a large shade tree was allowed to remain and this seriously affected the growth of the plants over a considerable area surrounding it. Cotton cannot be grown successfully under shade, or near large trees.

PLANTING.

The usual distance of planting the seed on ridges is two feet where the soil is of average fertility, but closer spacing may be given on poor land. Three or four seeds are placed in small depressions about 1 inch deep, made with a stick and lightly covered with loose soil. After a period of seven days has elapsed, provided the weather is favourable, the young seedlings will be seen. Should vacancies occur, the holes where no seedlings are seen should be resown. The supplying of "dead holes" as early as possible is desirable. The seedling should be thinned out when about six inches high leaving the two strongest in each hole. The young plants must be kept scrupulously clean-weeded. Shallow cultivation should be practised to avoid injuring the roots. Weeding may be continued until bolls are formed, or the plants have covered the ground, but it should not be unduly prolonged as it may damage the plants.

This practice was followed in the local trials. The spacing distance of 2 feet proved sufficient on the better portions of the land, but was too wide on the poorer sandy areas; in other respects the methods were found to be satisfactory.

FLOWERING AND BOLLING.

The plants grow to a height of 4 feet or more in suitable soil. The first flowers appear in two months from the time of planting and about seven weeks later, if all goes well the bolls which develop from them open. Flowers appear in rapid succession after the plants have reached the age of two months. About the 14th week the largest number of flowers is produced, with the result that the maximum number of bolls matures about the 21st week. This number gradually decreases up to the seventh month. Should a second crop be obtained from the basal lateral branches which develop later than the primary branches the picking season may be prolonged by one to two months.

The cotton produced on the first-formed branches is, as a rule, better in quality than that from the basal laterals.

In our experiments the growth and bolling of the Egyptian and Sea Island plants in areas with suitable soil was quite up to the average of rain-grown cotton of these varieties in other countries and a yield of 200-250 lb. of lint per acre was indicated.

MAY, 1923.]273

The following important pests, identified by the Government Entomologist, were recorded as causing damage to the stem, leaves or bolls:—

Cotton-stainer Dysdercus cingulatus
Leaf-roller Sylepta derogata
Hairy caterpillar Euproctis scintillans
Swarming caterpillar Spodoptera pecten
Boll-worm Earias insulana

The damage caused by the cotton-stainer is puncturing of young and unopened bolls in its efforts to reach the enclosed seeds. The punctures allow deleterious bacteria and fungi to enter the soft tissues and destroy or stain the enclosed lint.

The details of the various methods which can be successfully employed to keep cotton-stainer under control cannot be given here but they may be classed under the following heads:—

  1. 1. A close season three or four months.
  2. 2. Trapping by means of cotton seed in the close season.
  3. 3. Hand-collecting.
  4. 4. Destruction of all known food-plants in the vicinity of cotton fields.
  5. 5. Spraying with "tuba" mixture and other sprays.

The hairy caterpillar (Euproctis scintillans) damages the growing shoots and leaves by feeding on them, and boring into the stem thus causing a severe setback. Where damaged shoots are seen they should be cut out and the insect killed. Quite a number of shoots may be injured by the pest in the early part of the season.

The leaf-roller (Sylepta derogata) is a pest which often causes extensive damage and nearly all the leaves on the plants may be damaged or destroyed and development completely arrested. Dusting or Spraying with Paris Green or Lead Arsenate are effective remedies. All attacks must be dealt with as soon as observed.

The boll-worm (Earias insulana) is a rather serious pest as it feeds on the seed-cotton inside the boll and is difficult to control. So far, the attacks have not assumed large proportions, but the pest is capable of causing extensive damage. As an aid to the control of this insect a close season, during which all the old cotton plants are destroyed by burning or burying, is beneficial.

As mentioned above, these are the chief pests observed so far but there are others of less importance which were noted and should be treated. Cotton is a crop that requires careful watching throughout the entire period of its growth, and the success of its cultivation will largely depend on the recognition of attacks of pests, and the energetic application of approved early methods for their control.

PICKING.

The cotton must be picked when the bolls are fully open and at frequent intervals especially in showery weather as prolonged exposure to moisture causes the seed to germinate and thereby renders it useless for planting purposes. Again if the seed-cotton is left too long it may drop from the boll to the ground and be soiled. It was found desirable to pick the cotton at least once in every three days in the local trials.

PADDY.

CALCULATION OF THE PROBABLE SOIL ERROR IN PADDY TRIALS.

G. G. AUCHINLECK, M. Sc., F.I.C., F.C.S.,

J. C. DRIEBERG, DIP. AGR. (POONA),

R. D. KADRAMER (Student, Peradeniya Agricultural School),

Department of Agriculture, Peradeniya, Ceylon.

Comparative trials of varieties of paddy, or of the effects of manures on paddy, are marred by errors some of which can be determined and taken into account, while others can be diminished by exercising greater care in the work of planting, manuring, threshing and measuring; even under the most scrupulous control, the chances of obtaining identical yields from two or more plots of the same variety, treated in the same manner, are so small that they must be regarded as practically impossible.

An important source of error is the initial differences of productiveness which exist between parts of the same field. To avoid this, it is necessary to precede any comparative experiments by determining the variations which exist in the field when the whole is treated in a uniform manner. This cannot conveniently be done in every case, and we therefore must determine the average error on several different fields and use the results for the purpose of criticising results obtained elsewhere.

The trial described in this paper was made at the Farm School at Peradeniya during the season August 1922 to February 1923.

The results are strictly applicable only to this season, this field and the variety of paddy used. They afford a guide, however, both to the methods of determining errors and to the degree of accuracy which may be expected from comparative trials elsewhere.

EXPERIMENTAL FIELD.

The field upon a part of which these trials were made is the levelled bottom of a narrow ravine, with steep high banks, irrigation-water being led in at the upper end and trickled down through successive bunds to the outlet below. This conformation is typical of many of the paddy fields in uplands of Ceylon and usually results in greater fertility at the lower end and lessened fertility near the banks of the ravine.

During this season the field was divided into four sections.

It is obvious that no deductions can be drawn from these figures concerning the relative value of the two manures used. It is also doubtful whether the higher yields of sections C and D are due to closer transplanting or to their position at the lower end of the ravine. The results therefore serve as an example of the improbability of obtaining reliable comparative results when only one plot is used for each method of treatment.

The mean yield of the whole field is 1447 pounds per acre of paddy in the husk (36 bushels approximately), a figure above that for the computed average yield of Ceylon, but comparable with yields obtained on village fields of good fertility. The unusually wide transplanting on half of the field combined with the good yield is an incidental point of interest. Hatiel is a long-term variety of strong growth and it is doubtful whether similar wide planting would be successful in the case of smaller short-term paddies.

UNIFORMITY OF THE EXPERIMENTAL AREA.

A block of land in Section A was chosen for experiment and was divided into 56 square plots each of 100 square feet area (10' x 10'). The yield of grain and of straw and the number of plants in each plot were recorded separately. The total yield from the block was found to be 1430 pounds per acre of paddy in the husk, so that the fertility of the block is closely comparable with that of the average of the whole field (1477 pounds per acre).

In order to avoid the errors which accompany the usual method of measuring the crop by volume, each lot of grain was weighed on laboratory balances. Threshing was done by hand in the laboratory, so that the losses on this score are negligible. In general the records of weights of grain in these trials are of a higher degree of accuracy than those of the weights of straw, the difficulty of reaping, drying, and weighing straw being considerably greater.

AVERAGE DEVIATION OF INDIVIDUAL PLOTS.

There is considerable variation in the yields of single plots. The averages are 68.4 ounces of grain, 137.3 ounces of straw and 88.2 plants. The average deviation is obtained by adding together all deviations (whether plus or minus) from the mean and dividing by the number of plots. If the average deviations of grain, straw and plants are divided by the mean, 100 comparable percentages result.

PLOTS CONSIDERED IN GROUPS.

In other words, we may lessen the errors in comparative trials either by increasing the number of plots, or the size of plots, or both simultaneously. These results indicate that on land of this class, under careful methods of control, plots used for comparative trials should be not smaller than 700 square feet. Quadruplicate plots, each of 1000 square feet would probably differ from one another by not more than about 6 % of their mean.

STANDARD DEVIATIONS AND PROBABLE ERRORS.

The "average deviation" used in a previous section is not the usual means of expressing variations, the customary method being to calculate the "standard deviation" and the "probable error."

\text{Standard deviation} = \frac{\sqrt{\text{sum of squares of all deviations}}}{\text{number of plots}}

MAY, 1923.]279

It is obvious that the average and standard deviations bear a definite relation to one another, and that they must give parallel though not identical results. The probable error is obtained by multiplying the standard deviation by '6745.

The significance of the factor '6745 is as follows :—

If the frequency-curve shown in the graph in a previous section of this paper were a perfect or ideal one, a vertical line drawn from the topmost point of the curve to the base-line would divide the area within the curve into two equal parts and any further deviation would have an even chance of falling on either side. Two vertical lines one on each side of the middle line and the same distance from it, may be drawn which will also enclose half the area within the curve. For an ideal curve it is found that these two lines when so drawn fall at a distance from the middle line equal to '6745 times the length of the middle line, this proportion being almost constant.

Any determination (in this case deviation) has therefore an even chance of falling within or without the space between the two lines. Hence the probable error is the figure which affords an even chance for any determination to fall within the middle half of the curve, and it has been adopted as a convenient and reasonable estimate of allowable error.

CONCLUSION.

In this paper an attempt has been made to determine the errors which arise from initial differences in fertility of various parts of a field. Errors which arise from irregularities in water supply, incorrect measurement of plots, popular methods of measuring the crops, of sowing and of threshing have been as far as possible avoided.

In future seasons it is proposed to repeat these trials on the same block of land, employing the same variety of paddy in the major season and a short-term variety (Heenati) in the minor season. Seasonal effects due to fluctuations in rainfall are to a large extent absent in the case of an irrigated crop such as paddy, and it should be possible to obtain closely similar results each season and to perfect the table of corrections.

On land of moderate uniformity elsewhere in Ceylon, such a correction-table should be applicable with a fair degree of accuracy. Repetitions of these trials on other land would however make this point more certain,

280[MAY, 1923.

PADDY MANURING EXPERIMENTS.

This present summary is a continuation of that previously placed before the Food Products Committee of the Board of Agriculture and contains results which have been secured up to date. The records of the present Maha crops are not yet available as harvesting is not yet complete. The results now recorded relate to the Northern, North-Centra, Southern, Western and Uva Provinces.

NORTHERN PROVINCE.

With but one exception, all manured plots gave an increased yield over the plots which received no manure. Applications of green manures alone gave increased yields of from 4\frac{1}{2} to 10 bushels per acre, whilst the addition of Superphosphate to an application of green manure further increased the yields by 2\frac{1}{2} to 5 bushels per acre, whilst the further addition of Sulphate of Ammonia gave further increased crops. The Fish Guano plots gave yields of 6 to 12 bushels in excess of the no-manure plots. The yields of straw were also materially increased, an increase of 20 cwt. per acre being recorded in one instance from the plot receiving green leaf, Superphosphate and Sulphate of Ammonia over the no-manure plot.

The experiments clearly demonstrate the value of manuring, and particularly the value of the application of green manures and phosphates. The experiments will be repeated in order to ascertain if the results obtained up-to-date are confirmed and in order that further data of the economies of manuring may be secured.

NORTH-CENTRAL PROVINCE.

Increased yields were secured by the application of manures. Applications of Superphosphate have given increased yields. In some cases the yields from applications of green leaf have been satisfactory—ranging from 3 to 5 bushels per acre increase. An addition of Sulphate of Ammonia, to the application of green leaf and Superphosphate has given the largest crops both of paddy and of straw, but the increase has not been sufficient to pay for the cost of the manure. In this province, the indications are that applications of phosphatic manures will give profitable increases of crops and further trials in this direction will be made.

SOUTHERN PROVINCE.

The results of the experiments in this Province have been very variable and it is difficult to arrive at definite conclusions until a further series of results have been secured. Although increases of yield have resulted from the applications of manures, the cost of the manures have in several instances been in excess of the value of the increased yields secured. The results show that the best results are to be secured by the application of green leaf or green manures, provided that the application is made in sufficient quantity. In Wellabodda Pattu, the applications of manures have been markedly profitable, the best results having been secured by a complete mixture of Fish Guano, Ephos Phosphate and Bone Meal. In Morawak Korale applications of Crushed bones at the rate of 150 lb. per acre have given highly satisfactory and profitable results.

MAY, 1923.]281

The experiments in the Southern Province have demonstrated that Cyanamide is a manure which should be used in paddy cultivation with caution. It cannot be recommended at the present time. The use of Basic slag on boggy lands is being experimented with, but the results up to date are not conclusive.

COLOMBO DISTRICT OF WESTERN PROVINCE.

The best yields have been secured by the plots which received animal-meal, the second best from the plots which received green leaf and bone dust and the third best from the plots which received Fish Guano. The yields were 35 bushels, 28 bushels, 22 bushels respectively against an average yield of 15 bushels from the no-manure plots. The yield of straw was likewise increased by manuring.

KALUTARA DISTRICT OF WESTERN PROVINCE.

The application of green leaves and phosphatic manures (Ephos phosphate in this instance) has given increased and profitable yields whilst the applications of Ephos-phosphate alone, of animal meal and of Fish Guano have also been profitable. In some cases the increases in the yields have not been sufficient to cover the cost of the manures.

Applications of phosphatic manures, of green manures and of such manures as Fish Guano and animal meal are recommended for this district.

UVA.

In the Badulupitiya range the best yields were obtained from the application of green manure and Ephos phosphate whilst in the Viharagoda range of fields the highest yield was given by the plot which received a mixture of sterilized animal meal and bone meal.

F. A. STOCKDALE,
Director of Agriculture,

Peradeniya, 17th March, 1923.

STUDIES IN RICE.

K. V. JOSHI.

Observations are reported on the influence of seed preparation, seeding methods, and soil conditions on rice intended for transplanting together with a description of the growth of rice seedlings.

Where sprouted seed was submerged, the plants survived but developed thin, tall, and weak, while with shallow applications they were shorter and sturdier and with a broader leaf. Seed planted 0.5 to 1.3 and 4 in. in depth required 117 to 120, 140 to 150, and 170 hours respectively, for emergence of shoots. Seedlings from depths greater than 1 in. were weaker and easily broken in uprooting for transplanting.—EXPT. STN. RECORD, Vol. 46, No. 7.

282[MAY, 1923.

CEYLON AGRICULTURE.

AGRICULTURAL CONFERENCE AT JAFFNA.

MARCH 1923.

T. H. HOLLAND, Dip. Agr., Wye,

Acting Divisional Agricultural Officer, Northern.

On Monday, March 19th, a meeting of the Food Products Committee of the Board of Agriculture was held at the Jaffna Kachcheri. This meeting was followed by a general conference of agriculturists of the Northern Province.

The Government Agent MR. B. CONSTANTINE took the chair. In opening the conference, the CHAIRMAN said that they were very pleased to see the Director of Agriculture in Jaffna. It was fortunate that the running of night trains had been resumed in time. He hoped that further conferences of this nature would be held in the future.

The DIRECTOR OF AGRICULTURE said he had first of all a pleasant duty to perform in the presentation of the BRITO BABAPULLE gold medal for paddy cultivation. This medal which was kindly presented by DR. C. BRITO BABAPULLE of Colombo was open to members of Co-operative Societies and had this year been allotted for competition in the Northern Province. He then presented the medal to the winner MR. N. SWAMINATHAN of Chetty-kurichi, Poonakari, who had secured the fine yield of 99 bushels from 28\frac{1}{2} lachams, an average yield of 83 bushels per acre.

SIR PONNAMBALAM RAMANATHAN asked the winner a number of questions on the methods of cultivation and manuring he had adopted on this occasion.

MR. R. SENIOR WHITE suggested that an account of the cultivation of the plot in question should be inserted in the Tamil Magazine. MR. BEDDEWELA said that Ceylon was not self-supporting in paddy, the only way to solve this problem was for Government to give land almost free for paddy cultivation.

MR. CONSTANTINE said that was exactly what was being done in the Northern Province. Considerable areas were being taken up under Iranaimadu Tank. He gave figures of the total area that would be available under the Tank.

SIR P. RAMANATHAN said that land should be given at not too prohibitive a price.

MR. CONSTANTINE replied that such was now the case. Land was being given at from Rs. 30. to Rs. 50. per acre and rent free for 3 years. He thought that those who were taking up this land would probably spend about Rs. 200 per acre in bringing it under cultivation and would be able in 6 or 7 years to sell the land at about Rs. 500, per acre.

PROFESSOR MUTTUKUMARU said that a great deal of money had already been lost on these lands and the price of paddy had now fallen. He detailed the difficulties due to lack of labour, the absence of drinking water, etc., etc.

MAY, 1923.]283

He thought that the rate for land should be reduced to Rs. 30. per acre. Many people were already throwing up their lands. He spoke on behalf of a Company the Directors of which were already contemplating approaching Government on the subject.

SIR P. RAMANATHAN urged that permits for issue of railway tickets at reduced rates should be issuable by managers of lands as they were by Superintendents of Estates. At present these permits had to be obtained from the Government Agent.

The Government Agent said he saw no reason against this if the railway authorities were agreeable.

MR. A. SABAPATHY spoke of the hardships endured by his coolies through illness. After some further discussion it was proposed by SIR P. RAMANATHAN and seconded by MR. A. SABAPATHY that the following requests be forwarded to Government :—

  1. 1. That a goods shed be erected at Kilinochchi and that pending its completion temporary accommodation for goods be arranged.
  2. 2. That the local train which now runs from Kankesanturai to Pallai be run on to Kilinochchi.
  3. 3. That freight for goods be charged as from Kilinochchi and not as from Mankulam as at present.
  4. 4. That a receiving Post Office and a telephone service be established at Kilinochchi.

A further discussion followed on the various difficulties to be overcome in food production efforts in these new lands.

The conference was resumed at 2.30 p.m. when lectures and discussions on Tobacco, Well Irrigation and Fodders had been arranged.

TOBACCO.

The DIRECTOR OF AGRICULTURE opened the subject of tobacco. He mentioned the difficulties encountered in the past in the export of Jaffna tobacco and the attempts that had been made to solve those difficulties. Efforts had been made to find a tobacco suitable for Jaffna conditions which would not be dependent on the South Indian Market. The services of MR. B. F. SCHERFFIUS, an American Tobacco Planter, had been obtained and after a number of experiments he had established the fact that White Burley tobacco alone of the varieties tried would suit local conditions and be acceptable to the London Market. Agents in England had stated that they could take any quantity of the White Burley Tobacco.

The local tobacco situation had been easier of late and in consequence the cultivation of White Burley had not extended very much. MR. W. P. A. COOKE had been associated with Mr. SCHERFFIUS throughout his experiments and he would now ask him to speak on the matter. MR. COOKE then spoke on his experience with White Burley tobacco when working with MR. SCHERFFIUS. He laid special emphasis on the unnecessary amount of watering which was commonly given to young plants but complained that to prepare plants for such altered treatment it was necessary to encourage deep rooting in the nursery. This could be achieved by avoiding watering the beds as long as any moisture existed in the top inch of soil. Cultivators were now keenly interested in the cultivation of White Burley,

284[MAY, 1923.]

he attributed this mainly to the fact that they could sell their crops direct to the Department of Agriculture without the medium of a middleman. The curing and grading moreover were simple operations and could easily be done by the cultivator himself. MR. COOKE commented further on the contents of a leaflet on the subject which had been distributed to the meeting.

The DIRECTOR OF AGRICULTURE then asked MR. SABAPATHY to give his views on the subject.

MR. SABAPATHY said that he had been instrumental in starting the tobacco trial ground. He gave some details of the history of the various crises the Jaffna tobacco industry had gone through. He thought that the cultivation of White Burley could be largely extended by suitable propaganda. The villagers were mainly ignorant on the subject.

The DIRECTOR OF AGRICULTURE asked MR. SABAPATHY to give an estimate of the number of plants which cultivators would produce if propaganda were carried out. The Government could not of course indefinitely continue the practice of buying plants, some machinery would eventually have to be evolved for the disposal of the crops.

MR. SABAPATHY said that he would safely estimate a production of 50,000 plants of White Burley. He then referred to the memorial presented by the people of Jaffna last July asking Government to take steps to endeavour to get the preferential duty imposed by the Government of Travancore reduced to the same level as the duty imposed on Coimbatore tobacco. No reply had as yet been received to that memorial and he would ask the Government Agent or the DIRECTOR OF AGRICULTURE to ascertain the present position.

MUDALIYAR RAMALINGAM, Kachcheri Mudaliyar, Jaffna, then made a few remarks. He had been a member of the old tobacco committee and had been associated with the experiments for a number of years. Various Government Agents had carried out fairly extensive propaganda on the subject of White Burley but until quite recently cultivators had taken no interest.

The DIRECTOR OF AGRICULTURE concluded by thanking those who had contributed; information he would he said ascertain what provision could be made for the future purchase of White Burley plants. He was convinced that there was a future for White Burley and the London Market alone would gladly take all that Jaffna could grow.

FODDER SORGHUMS.

The DIRECTOR OF AGRICULTURE then asked Mr. N. SENATHIRAJA to speak on the subject of Fodder Sorghums—a paper on which subject had been laid on the table.

MR. SENATHIRAJA said that cattle were necessary for every agricultural operation. Where waste and forest lands were abundant the question of fodder was of less importance. In Jaffna such lands were not available, cattle were often half starved and the fodder question was one of paramount importance. The area available for cultivation of fodder crops was very small and fodder had of late years become very scarce and dear.

The time had come to find new fodder crops and improved methods of cultivation. The introduction of Fodder Sorghums or Cholams had to a

MAY, 1923.]285

large extent filled this need. He then gave details of the results of the trials with Sorghums carried out on the Jaffna Experiment Station.

MR. A. M. RICHARDS, Veterinary Surgeon, remarked that he had some knowledge of the crop in India. He had tried it at Kilinochchi where it had done well. Cholam stood high as a cattle fodder and this view had been borne out at Coimbatore Agricultural College.

MR. RICHARDS related that he had first taken up some land at Elephant Pass for dairy farming. Though the soil was suitable water failure had rendered the growing of fodder too difficult and he had transported his venture to Kilinochchi where his cattle were doing well. The growth of cholam practically solved the food and fodder question. MR. RICHARDS then embarked on the question of branding cattle and the consequent loss of value to the hides. According to last year's census there were 94,222 cattle in Jaffna and he calculated that about 2 lakhs of rupees were lost annually by the practice of branding. There were two brands—the communal brand and the registration brand ; the registration brand could easily be put upon the neck.

The discussion then reverted to Sorghums. PROFESSOR MUTTUKUMARU endorsed the good opinion held of this crop. He thought that a chaff cutter was necessary to chop up the straw and suggested that the Department of Agriculture should get a machine up for exhibition. It was at present the custom for people to sell their cattle for slaughter at the beginning of January or send them away to the wannu for grazing.

The DIRECTOR OF AGRICULTURE again emphasised the importance of the fodder question. He mentioned its connection with the question of irrigation and asked MR. COOKE to speak on the water lift figures recently obtained by him.

WELL IRRIGATION.

MR. COOKE said that the time available since the final rains for obtaining these figures has been short. He apologised for certain omissions. He then read and commented on the figures. His deductions were that for shallow wells the Persian wheel was the most suitable form of lift while for a deep well the double Mhote was more suitable. Local users of the double Mhote were well pleased with them. He emphasised the importance of co-operation as a means of producing the capital necessary for the purchase of such machines.

MR. SINGAM, an Engineer, then gave his views. He contended that so many small holdings existed that the demand was not so much for these large machines as for a cheap water lift that could be used by one man and his family. Such a lift he claimed to have evolved after much work and long experiment.

The DIRECTOR OF AGRICULTURE agreed that there was a future for a one-man water lift if a satisfactory lift could be found but he still believed in the double Mhote and the Persian wheel and until MR. SINGAM had completed his experiments he would ask the public to reserve their judgment in regard to the smaller lifts.

MR. A. SABAPATHY said he would like to mention his practical experience. Some of his tenants had followed his example and gone in for Persian

286[MAY, 1923.

wheels. They had come to him for advances for buying cattle and for fodder, then cattle had died and yet more advances were required; finally in some cases the tenants had abandoned these lifts and gone back to well sweeps.

MR. COOKE said that in some cases Persian wheels were installed in places where only tobacco was grown. In such cases they were unwilling to displace tobacco for fodder for cattle. He maintained however that they would in any case keep cattle for the sake of the manure and recommended them to start growing fodder.

The conference then terminated with a vote of thanks to the chair.

VISITS TO THE JAFFNA EXPERIMENT STATION.

On Tuesday March 20th the majority of the visitors paid a visit to the Government Experiment Station at Tinnevelly. A representative collection of improved ploughs, cultivators and other implements were laid out for exhibition and demonstration was given in the use of Economy Straw Trusser. Specimens of the produce of the Experiment Station were laid out in a shed for inspection.

Later in the morning a few of the visitors went on to MUDALIYAR W. MUTTUVELUPILLAI's farm where the working of the Hellice elevator was inspected with interest.

LECTURES TO FARMERS.

On Wednesday morning March 21st lectures to farmers had been arranged at the Experiment Station at Tinnevelly. Between 70 and 80 cultivators were present. The Acting Divisional Agricultural Officer MR. T. H. HOLLAND welcomed those present. He would he said have liked to have seen a larger gathering but hoped that those who had shown their interest in such matters by their presence would pass on to their fellow cultivators anything of interest or utility they heard that day.

MUDALIYAR V. M. MUTTUKUMARU, Maniagar of Jaffna town, then spoke a few words impressing on cultivators the importance of the work being done by the Department of Agriculture.

MR. W. P. A. COOKE then delivered a lecture. He dwelt first with Well Irrigation and White Burley Tobacco. He then described the uses and advantages of the various agricultural implements which were laid out for exhibition.

MR. N. SENATHIRAJA then lectured on the work of the Department of Agriculture and kindred subjects. A large collection of Tamil leaflets were distributed.

FOOD PRODUCTS COMMITTEE OF THE BOARD OF AGRICULTURE.

PROTECTION OF KABARAGOYA.

The CHAIRMAN said that Kegalla raised the question of protecting the Kabaragoya from destruction and the Department of Agriculture took up the matter and certain representation was made to Government after careful enquiries were made and having obtained the opinion of agriculturists as regards the usefulness of the Kabaragoya in the protection of paddy crops from being destroyed by crabs, field mice and several classes of insects. The Government approved the recommendation and steps have been taken to prepare a draft Ordinance prohibiting the destruction of the Kabaragoya. He further said that the matter could not have been brought before the Committee as immediate action appeared desirable. The Committee approved the action by the Director of Agriculture.

Agenda Item 2. Representation of Food Production Committees or District Agricultural Committees on the Board of Agriculture.

The CHAIRMAN stated that the Matale Agricultural Committee raised the question of representation of the Food Production Committees or District Agricultural Committees on the Board of Agriculture and asked Mr. SENIOR WHITE the member representing the Matale Committee to speak on the subject. Mr. SENIOR WHITE explained how it was necessary to obtain a clear understanding on the question of whether a member nominated to the Board of Agriculture by a Food Production Committee was the representative of the District or whether he was nominated in his individual capacity.

The CHAIRMAN, the Divisional Agricultural Officer, Central Division and SIR PONNAMBALAM RAMANATHAN joined in the discussion. It was decided that members representing Food Production Committees were members of the Food Products Committee of the Board of Agriculture as delegates of the District Committees, who nominated them.

Agenda Item 3. Freight Charges on Manures on the Railway.

GATE MUDALIYAR C. H. A. SAMARAKKODY moved for discussion the desirability of obtaining concession for the paddy cultivators on the transport of manure by the Railway on reduced rates on smaller quantities. He said that the matter was also discussed at the conference of representatives of Co-operative Societies held in 1919. The price of bone manure is at present exorbitantly high and the smaller paddy cultivators cannot afford to manure their fields. On a question from SIR PONNAMBALAM RAMANATHAN, the CHAIRMAN explained the rates charged at present.

MR. SENIOR WHITE thought that the concession should be allowed to other products as well. MR. BANDARA BEDDEWELA supported MUDALIYAR SAMARAKKODDY. MUDALIYAR GUNATHILAKE suggested that the concession should be allowed to Co-operative Societies.

The CHAIRMAN explained the present concession allowed to Co-operative Societies and said that he was prepared to recommend further concession to help cultivators through Societies. After further discussion the following resolution proposed by the mover and seconded by GATE MUDALIYAR RAJAPAKSE was finally carried.—

288[MAY, 1923.

"That in reference to rule 10 (c) of the Railway regulations this Committee is of opinion that the concession granted to 10 tons lots should be extended so as to include 4 tons lots and over on manure consigned to Co-operative Societies."

It was agreed that the Director of Agriculture be requested to approach the Government with a view to obtaining the concession asked for by this resolution.

SIR PONNAMBALAM RAMANATHAN said that those who are engaged in cultivation of paddy at Karachi experience great difficulties in the transport of their produce in that they require facilities such as construction of roads and a Railway Station at Kilinochchi. The Government Agent said that the construction of the road has already been sanctioned and the Irrigation Engineer has reported that the road would be completed shortly.

The CHAIRMAN suggested that the matter be brought before the next meeting if the road in question was not completed, or it might be left in the hands of the Government Agent. This latter proposal was agreed to.

MR. SABAPATHY enquired what action had been taken as regards his motion at the last meeting with regard to facilities for travelling by Railway to persons engaged in the cultivation of paddy under Irranamadu Scheme and the CHAIRMAN explained that the matter is under the consideration of the COLONIAL SECRETARY. MR. SABAPATHY also drew attention of the Committee to the motion agreed upon at a meeting of the Committee with regard to the reduction of the rail freight on straw and the proposed experiments in baling of straw.

The CHAIRMAN explained that a baling press was procured and trials were made and results have been fairly satisfactory. For demonstration purposes the press was brought to Jaffna and would be exhibited at the Tinnevally Farm. Further trials would also be made with another type of press.

A discussion followed in regard to the issue of tickets to coolies from Jaffna to Paranthan, Kilinochchi, etc., in which the Government Agent, the CHAIRMAN, MR. SABAPATHY, SIR PONNAMBALAM RAMANATHAN took part. It was agreed that the matter is one for the Government Agent to look into.

Agenda Item 4. Further Results of Manurial Trials with Paddy.

The CHAIRMAN read a summary of further reports of results of paddy manurial trials in the various provinces. He said that it was a continuation of the results placed before the Committee at a previous meeting. He remarked that complete mixtures gave increased yields but these increases in several instances were not sufficient to pay costs. In the discussion, which followed, MESSRS. SENIOR WHITE, MUDALIYAR MUTTUKUMARU, SABAPATHY, MUDALIYAR RAJAPAKSE, BANDARA BEDDEWELA AND SIR PONNAMBALAM RAMANATHAN took part. At the discussion it was elicited that the average yield of paddy per acre per crop was 40 bushels in Matara, Kandy, and Kegalle, and the fields of very small sizes produced a crop averaging 100 to 120 bushels per acre in Jaffna under intensive cultivation.

MR. BANDARA BEDDEWELA suggested the exchange of seeds but the CHAIRMAN pointed out that his experience was that such a procedure should be adopted with caution. It was preferable to attempt to improve local varieties by selection.

GATE MUDALIYAR RAJAPAKSE suggested that the results of paddy manuring experiments should be published, with the actual cost of manure applied.

MUDALIYAR MUTTUKUMARU said that in Jaffna Margosa poonac gave very good results but this poonac is not available in large quantities. It was agreed to continue the trials.

MAY, 1923.]289

MR SABAPATHY asked whether the proposed model farm at Kilinochchi has been abandoned and the CHAIRMAN said that the proposal has not been abandoned but that the work could not be taken in hand until funds were available.

Agenda Item 5. Results of Trials with Coix Lachryma.

The CHAIRMAN tabled the statement showing results obtained at the Peradeniya Experiment Station with trials of Coix Lachryma (Job's tears). This variety is soft shelled and is recommended for cultivation in the Philippines from where seeds were originally secured. Seeds are available at the Experiment Station, Peradeniya.

Agenda Item 6. Results of Variety Trials with Food Crops at the Experiment Station, Peradeniya.

In tabling the results of variety trials with food crops such as maize, dioscorea yams, manioc, sweet potatoes and tannias and colocasias at the Peradeniya Experiment Station, the CHAIRMAN said that little attention is paid by the village cultivator to varieties grown and their relative yields. These trials have shown that there were marked differences of yield given by the different varieties and that it would be possible to eliminate bad varieties and to encourage the cultivation of only the good types. The trials will be continued on all Experiment Stations.

Agenda Item 7. Results of Experiments with Kurakkan (Ragi) at the Experiment Station, Jaffna.

The CHAIRMAN next tabled the results of trials with Kurakkan at the Experiment Station at Jaffna and said that the varieties would be compared in the next season for conclusive results and that the Mysore varieties have given heavy yields in grain and straw in the second season.

MUDALIYAR MUTTUKUMARU said that the local variety takes three months while the Mysore variety takes five months to ripen; Kurakkan is cultivated after the paddy or tobacco crop and that the cultivators cannot find time to grow the Mysore variety though it gives a better yield. The statement submitted showed however that there was practically no difference in the rate of maturity of the local and Mysore varieties tried on the Experiment Station, Jaffna.

MR. BEDDEWELA suggested that analysis should be made to find out the food value of different varieties. The CHAIRMAN agreed to have this done.

Results of Experiments with the use of Tank Silt at Experiment Station, Jaffna.

The CHAIRMAN said that the cultivators use tank silt for improving the land and this experiment was carried out to ascertain the value of tank silt in improving lands brought under cultivation newly.

The land manured with tank silt yielded nearly double the quantity ordinarily obtained. In the discussion which followed it was pointed out that tank silt is not available in sufficient quantities. Its value is recognised, but it is difficult to secure.

N. WICKREMARATNE,
Secretary,
Food Products Committee.

PESTS AND DISEASES.

NOTES ON TERMITES ATTACKING TEA
IN CEYLON.

Department of Agriculture Leaflet No. 24.

There are several species of termites (white ants) which are more or less closely associated with the tea bush in Ceylon, and the marked increase of these insects at various elevations has caused much apprehension among tea planters within recent years. The tea termites, for the most part, may be divided into two main groups according to their nesting habits and the nature of their damage to the tea bush, viz. :—

(a) Termites which form their colonies inside a living tea bush and bore into the heartwood. These are primary pests, and include the well-known Calotermes militaris.

(b) Termites which have their nests outside a tea bush, usually underground, and which generally attack the dead or dying bark and wood of various plants, including tea, rubber, dadap, grevillea, and jungle stumps. These include the mound-building termites, and can be regarded mainly as secondary pests and scavengers.

The prevailing anxiety about the tea termites seems to be due mainly to the state of uncertainty as to the actual species of termite concerned in any particular case, and where there is any doubt in the mind of the planter, the damage is usually attributed to Calotermes militaris, when, in most cases the injury is usually the result of an attack of a fungous disease or of insect injury followed by an invasion of the scavenging termites.

The main object of the following notes is to try and clear up the existing ambiguity by pointing out the essential differences between these two groups of termites, in order that the tea planter may, in most cases, be able to diagnose the particular trouble for himself and take measures accordingly :—

(a) At the present time there are only three species of termites which are known to bore into the heartwood of healthy tea bushes. These are (1) Calotermes militaris, (2) Calotermes dilatatus, and (3) Calotermes greeni :—

(1) Calotermes militaris.—This termite was investigated some fifteen years ago by MR. E. E. GREEN (then Government Entomologist), and the results of his observations were published in the TROPICAL AGRICULTURIST for March, 1907. GREEN found that this termite works entirely in the heartwood of the bush, and that the branches, the main stem, and even the roots may be completely hollowed out, leaving merely a hollow shell. He observed that in spite of this extensive damage the bushes continued to flush well and showed no external signs of injury, the reason for this being that only the heartwood is devoured, while the sapwood remains intact and carries on the functions of the plant. "The devoured tissues," he continues, "are replaced by earthy matter into which adventitious roots are thrown out apparently from the inner walls and evidently obtain much nourishment from the earthy matter." GREEN further observed in digging out infested tea bushes that there were no signs of any extension of the termite galleries into the surrounding soil, nor were any of the insects found in the excavated soil. GREEN found nothing resembling a specialized queen,

292[MAY, 1923.]

such as are found in some of the mound-building species, nor any indications of special brood cells or honey-combed nest. The adult termites, or Kings and Queens, are wingless,* and the eggs are laid inside the bush. GREEN concludes that each colony is self-contained, and that the removal and destruction of the infested tea bush should destroy the complete colony. The presence of the pest can seldom be recognised until the bush has been pruned, when sections of the galleries are exposed. GREEN was of opinion that in recently attacked bushes only collar pruning can disclose the infection, as the insects apparently effect their entrance through the roots, working up first into the stem and later into branches.

Neither the late MR. RUTHERFORD (MR. GREEN'S successor) nor the present writer have been able to confirm this last observation. It is possible that in some cases the militaris termites may enter the bush below ground, but it seems probable that another method of entry is through some weak spot above ground, such as a decayed knot-hole or old borings of the shot-hole borer, or else of the red borer as in the case of C. dilatatus.

A typical colony of Calotermes may be developed somewhat as follows:—A royal couple, resembling each other in size and external appearance, on emerging from an infested tea bush, may find their way to a neighbouring uninfested bush into which they gain entry either below ground or through some weak spot above ground, as mentioned previously. It is possible that the royal pair may be attended by workers from the parent colony, but the queen lays her eggs probably in a small cavity in the tea bush. These eggs develop into workers, and probably a few soldiers, which are at the first looked after by the queen and by any attendant workers. All the work connected with the building up of the colony is done by the workers, which are blind and work entirely under cover inside the tea bush. Eventually, a complete colony consisting of different castes is developed within a bush. There are the workers of various ages, the younger ones being whitish with small rounded whitish heads while the older ones are mottled white and brownish with pale brown heads and stout blackish, toothed mandibles or jaws. The workers usually form the majority of the inhabitants of a Calotermes colony, and at first are sexless, but are probably developed into fertile males and females, either winged or wingless, as required by the needs of the Colony. The soldiers are conspicuous by reason of their large, elongate brown heads armed with rather long, curved black jaws. They have pale spots on the head representing eyes, but it is not known how far these are functional. The soldiers are few in number as compared with the workers, and it is their duty to protect the colony from invaders.

Calotermes militaris is mainly an up-country species, being prevalent mostly in the southern part of the Central Province but is sometimes found at lower elevations. This termite is intermediate in size between the smaller dilatatus and the larger greeni. It is a fairly serious pest on some up-country estates.

(2) Calotermes dilatatus.—This is the smallest of these three species of termites. It seems to be mainly a mid-to low-country species. RUTHERFORD was of opinion that this termite enters a bush through some old knot hole or a wound, or through a red borer or shot-hole borer gallery, and gradually works downwards, sometimes into the roots. The writer has observed this habit in the case of this species in tea seed-bearers a series of attacked bushes showing progressive stages of injury from top to bottom and even down into the roots. In the case of dilatatus the galleries are distributed throughout the stem, and neither RUTHERFORD nor the writer

* Winged adults were found in 1909.

MAY, 1923.]293

have observed any large cavities formed by dilatatus, such as are found in the case of bushes infested with militaris. A complete colony apparently exists in each infested bush, and this species is known to have winged adults.

(3) Calotermes greeni appears to have a wide range of distribution and feeding habits, as it has been recorded from Jaffna ("boring into trees"), Peradeniya ("in dead branches of tree"), Avissawela and Yatiyantota ("from stem of living tea bush"), and Ambalangoda ("from stem of living Cashew-nut tree"). In the single instance seen by the writer of a tea bush infested by this species, the damage was somewhat similar to that done by dilatatus, in that the stem was fairly well riddled by galleries without any large cavity being made. C. greeni is the largest of these three species, and has winged adults.

To summarize, it may be said that, so far as we know at present, the Calotermes species all have their nests inside living tea bushes, militaris being more prevalent in up-country tea, while dilatatus and greeni occur at lower elevations. In case of injury by militaris, it is usually the lower parts of the bush, from the collar down to the roots which suffer most; but in all the militaris cases noted by RUTHERFORD, and in those observed by the writer the injury was so far advanced that it was impossible to say where the termites had originally entered. GREEN was of opinion that these termites apparently enter a bush through the roots and work upwards. It is not improbable that militaris may sometimes gain entry through an injured branch from which the termites may spread in all directions throughout the bush.

Judging from the records of dilatatus injury left by RUTHERFORD and from the present writer's experience of this species in tea seed-bearers and ordinary tea bushes, it seems not unlikely that dilatatus may enter a bush above ground and may tunnel into the lateral branches and later work downwards, although it may possibly sometimes attack a bush from below ground level. Neither dilatatus nor greeni appear to excavate large cavities in the main stem, but have a system of galleries running through the heartwood.

Of the above species of Calotermes it seems probable that militaris is the most formidable as a pest of tea, since it may escape detection at pruning time and continue its excavations for many years until the bush is reduced to a mere shell. Even in cases where it may enter above the collar, being mainly an upcountry species, it has a longer time to carry on undisturbed between prunings. On the other hand, dilatatus and greeni, probably working for the most part above ground level, would tend to be periodically controlled by pruning, especially by the more frequent prunings at lower elevations.

None of these three species has been a really serious pest within recent years, only small patches of tea or individual bushes being occasionally attacked.* Much of the damage reported as due to Calotermes on further investigation usually turns out to be the work of the scavenging termites following an attack of branch canker or other injury to the bushes.

CONTROL OF THE CALOTERMES SPECIES.

Since these termites have their colonies in individual tea bushes, and are not known to nest in the ground or have any main termitarium outside the bushes, it follows that the most effective way of reducing their numbers is by treating each infested bush individually on its merits. All completely riddled bushes should be eradicated and burnt immediately, so as to destroy

* Recent reports indicate that Calotermes species are on the increase in some districts.

294[MAY, 1923,

any infesting termites. In cases where the injury is detected in time, it should be sufficient to clear out any cavity thoroughly and paint the inside with a liquid wood preservative, such as a creosote solution, and then fill in the cavity with mortar or cement to prevent water collecting and causing decay. Where there is no cavity, but only small galleries, the solution can be applied thoroughly to the cut surface and allowed to penetrate into the galleries. This should effectually drive out or kill any termites which are still inside, and protect the bush from re-infestation for some time. The presence of the scavenging termites may sometimes complicate matters, and in such cases the use of ordinary tar should be avoided, as this seems to afford no protection against the scavengers.

(b) There are several species of termites which feed on the dead and dying bark and wood of tea bushes, among other plants, and can be regarded mainly as scavengers. It should be understood that these termites are quite distinct from the Calotermes species, as will be indicated below, although they may sometimes be present on Calotermes bushes.

The two common species of scavenging termites commonly met with on tea are Termes obscuriceps and Termes redmanni. These are the common mound-building termites, a typical colony of which was described by GREEN some years ago.* Termes horni is another scavenger which is sometimes found in tea bushes, and probably nests in the ground, but apparently does not construct mounds. Species of Eutermes are also bark-scavengers, and a Leucotermes is occasionally found tunnelling in tea bushes which have been killed by root diseases.

A brief summary of GREEN'S observations on a mound-building colony may be of interest. He says: "The large cone-shaped mounds of several species of termites are common features in the landscape in Ceylon up to an elevation of 3,000 feet or more. It is interesting to note that though the same species occur at still higher elevations, they usually conceal their nests entirely below ground level." He continues: "The adult males and females are the well-known flying ants that sometimes invade our bungalows, attracted by the light of the lamps. The flights usually occur after a shower of rain." GREEN then goes on to describe how a single pair of these winged termites may found a colony. They drop their wings and find their way into some crevice in the soil, and the female lays a batch of eggs. This initial family may possibly be tended by the parents, or more probably by some stray workers from another nest. Soon the original parents are imprisoned in a special earthen cell underground, and are surrounded by an army of workers who pass in and out of the royal cell through minute galleries. The original female or queen gradually increases in size until she may measure more than three inches in length, and becomes what is practically an elongated bag full of millions of eggs. These eggs are carried away by a constant stream of workers as they are laid, and are placed in special nurseries where the young termites are tended until they are able to forage around for themselves. "As the colony increases, fresh galleries and nurseries are excavated. The soil that is removed is laboriously piled up above ground level, forming the conspicuous castellated mounds that one knows so well." Ventilation shafts may be opened down into the depths of the nests, and around such a shaft "are grouped large cavities which are more or less filled up by sponge-like mosses, within the cells of which the young are reared. These cellular masses are known as the 'fungus gardens,' and have been built up of pellets of digested vegetable matter." GREEN then describes the various castes in the nest of one of these mound-building termites, the small white workers with their rounded reddish heads, the soldiers with their larger and more elongate heads, armed with prominent
