jaws. Both the workers and soldiers are sexless. "Then there are some larger pallid individuals, with rudimentary wings, which will eventually appear as the mature winged sexual insects. There are in addition certain half-developed females that are apparently kept in reserve as potential supplementary queens, in case of any accident to the original mother of the colony." GREEN further points out that the workers of most species of termites are blind and always work under cover.

It is the workers of these mound-building termites, among others, which may often be found eating away the dead bark and wood on the outside of tea bushes under cover of a film of earth which they have previously built over the portions of the bush to be consumed. So long as there is any dead bark or wood available, these termites will frequent a bush, provided there is sufficient moisture. During periods of dry weather they may retire down to the underground nests, but come up after rains and resume their feeding and their construction of the earthen screens over the bushes.

These two species.—T. obscuriceps and T. redemanni—appear to have increased enormously on tea estates within recent years, and are, doubtless, prevalent on most estates in Ceylon at varying elevations. In the opinion of the writer the prevalence of branch canker on many tea estates has been one of the contributing causes of the marked increase of these termites on tea bushes within recent years. The branch canker fungus usually occurs along the upper surface on lateral branches, invading and killing the cambium layer inside and causing the bark to crack. The disease may also extend down to the main stem and in extreme cases may girdle and kill the bush. The scavenging termites come along and gradually clear away the dead bark and crumbly wood inside, usually working under a screen of earth. Eventually, many of the horizontal branches are left with shallow irregular cavities along their upper surface, and the main stem may also be partially excavated by the termites, which have merely cleaned out the portions of the bush killed by the canker. These injuries are frequently attributed by the planter to the work of Calotermes, especially when there is a fairly deep cavity in the main stem, but in the case of great majority of cases this particular type of injury is due to branch canker followed by these smaller termites, such as obscuriceps and redemanni.

Incidentally, these termites may also be gradually clearing any old stumps and logs left among the tea, and the abundant supply of such food on some estates has encouraged these insects to extend and populate their underground colonies.

It has been claimed that in some cases these smaller termites may help to prevent wounds from healing over, and that they sometimes eat away living bark and girdle young tea bushes, but there is no definite evidence that they ever attack healthy living plant tissues. It is true that they usually follow the advance of a disease so closely that it is difficult to say that they do not actually get ahead of it sometimes. In the great majority of cases, however, it is quite evident that they are merely scavengers of dead and diseased bark and wood.

While these termites cannot be regarded as serious pests, still their presence in vast numbers on many tea estates is most undesirable, and it is strongly urged that vigorous measures be taken to reduce their numbers.

CONTROL MEASURES AGAINST THE SCAVENGING TERMITES.

At the present time experiments are being made by some estates with various paint mixtures applied to the bushes after pruning and a thorough cleaning up, with the idea of finding some substance which will protect the bushes from further attack. It is too early to say what effect these paints

296[MAY, 1923.

will have on the bushes and how far and for what length of time they will be effective in keeping away the termites. In most cases the cost of materials and of their application is prohibitive even when used over fairly large areas. These experiments have their value, however, as some substance may be discovered which may be useful in treating individual bushes, both for injury by Calotermes species and other termites.

The control measures should be directed against the termites themselves and against their food supply, and may be carried out along three main lines:—

(1) A direct attack should be made on the termites by eradicating their nests.

(2) Their food supply on the tea bush should be reduced by controlling branch canker and other diseases, shot-hole borer, red borer Calotermes, and other insects which injure the frames of the bushes.

(3) Their other sources of food supply should be cut down as far as possible by removing and burning all old stumps and logs which are sometimes found among the tea.

1. There are three ways of destroying the nests of the underground termites: (a) by using a white ant machine with sulphur and arsenic, (b) by fumigation with carbon bisulphide, and (c) by digging out the nests.

(a) It is sometimes a difficult matter to find a termite nest, termitarium, especially at higher elevations where very often no definite mounds are built, and sometimes the only indications are a few small inconspicuous holes in the ground. The method of using the white ant machine, sometimes called the "Universal" Ant Exterminator, has been described by GREEN in the Circular mentioned above, and the information is given here for easy reference: "The machine consists of a small charcoal furnace in connection with an air pump. Some glowing charcoal is placed in the furnace; a spoonful of the mixture (composed of white arsenic 85 per cent. and sulphur 15 per cent.) is thrown on to the charcoal and the lid firmly clamped into position. A flexible nozzle is pushed into the main entrance of the nest, and all supplementary holes are plugged with clay. The pump is then worked, and drives the vapour into the nests, forcing it into all the ramifications of the galleries. Little jets of smoke will soon arise from crevices and unsuspected openings for several yards round the main entrance. These should be immediately stopped with clay or pounded earth. After a few minutes of vigorous pumping, the nozzle may be withdrawn and the hole plugged with clay. The nest should remain undisturbed for a week, when the mound may be levelled. If opened immediately after the application, some of the insects will revive. In some few cases there may be feeble signs of renewed activity, in which case a second application will complete the work of destruction; but this is seldom necessary."

The present writer has some experience of the Ant Exterminator, but with varying success. The best times for the application of the poison appear to be when the colony is in full activity, and galleries and nurseries are being excavated. The termites are poisoned in the process of clearing away the arsenic deposited on the walls of the galleries, and they may also be affected to some extent by the sulphurous fumes. In older and well-established nests, where the termites are concentrated mainly in and around the royal chamber and in the fungus gardens and rarely come to the surface, especially in dry weather, the poison seems to have practically no effect. The presence of several large nests within a comparatively small area will involve the treatment of all the nests in the group if the termites are to be eradicated from that area.

MAY, 1923.]297

(b) Fumigation with carbon bisulphide (CS_2). This is a colourless liquid which gives off a very deadly gas on exposure to air. This gas is also highly inflammable, and should only be used under competent supervision. The smaller openings in a nest are first of all plugged with clay or damp earth. Then the mouth of the main opening is stopped with tow or cotton waste soaked with carbon bisulphide, or the liquid can be poured down through the opening which is then plugged with clay. Use from one to two ounces of the fumigant according to the size of the nest. The vapour, being heavier than air, sinks downwards and gradually penetrates to all parts of the nest, killing all the inhabitants. The writer has found this method to be more effective than the sulphur and arsenic treatment, but the difficulty of obtaining this fumigant in sufficient quantity at the present time and the dangerous nature of the gas rule it out as a practicable method of control for general use.

(c) Probably the most effective method which can be recommended for adoption by estates is the eradication of the nests by digging them out and destroying all the queens and the fungus gardens with their population of eggs and workers in various stages of development. The estate coolies can be turned on to this work as part of the estate routine in conjunction with the removal of old stumps and the general cleaning up of the tea bushes.

2. The systematic eradication of termite nests on an estate should cause an appreciable decrease in the termite population, but this will necessarily be a long and tedious process, and meanwhile the tea bushes will continue to attract the scavengers, unless measures are taken to improve the general health of the bushes. Considerable injury is sometimes done to the frame of a tea bush by the fungus commonly known as branch canker, as was indicated elsewhere in these notes. This disease has been prevalent for many years in various districts, but no special efforts have been made to control it. It should be realized by tea planters that quite a fair amount of the dead bark and wood on their bushes is the result of the old branch canker wounds which are subsequently cleaned up by the termites. The control of this fungus will do much to improve the general condition of the frames of tea bushes and incidentally will deprive the scavengers of an important source of their food supply on such bushes.

The Mycologist recommends that as much of the diseased wood as possible should be removed at pruning time, and that the bushes should then be thoroughly sprayed with Bordeaux mixture immediately after pruning. This treatment will kill off the fungus on the old wood, and will indirectly protect the new wood from serious attack. It cannot be expected that spraying will eradicate the disease or that the old wounds will immediately heal over, but it should reduce the prevalence of the disease in the treated area and enable the bushes to carry on until next pruning with increased vigour. This treatment must be repeated at each pruning as part of the estate routine.

All "diebacks" due to shot-hole borer injury or other causes should be removed periodically, as these only serve to attract the smaller termites.

3. There is yet another important source of food supply on many estates for Termes obscuriceps and other termites with similar feeding habits. This supply consists mainly of the numerous old jungle stumps and dead stumps of grevillea, dadap, coconut, etc., which are only too common on termite-infested estates. Incidentally, many of these stumps are foci of

298[MAY, 1923.

root diseases which kill off the surrounding tea bushes. It is strongly urged that all such stumps should be removed gradually, as opportunity occurs, and burnt, since their removal and destruction will at the same time eradicate many flourishing colonies of termites or portions of colonies. These termites are usually to be found invading the surrounding tea.

A campaign such as the one outlined in the above suggestions for control work will necessarily extend over many years, but a start should certainly be made, and, in fact, is being made on some estates. It should be borne in mind that a campaign of this nature, if systematically and thoroughly carried out year by year, will result in the control not only of the various species of termites, but of some of the more important tea pests and diseases as well, and will tend towards the production of vigorous bushes with plenty of sound wood on them. Good cultivation, drainage, manuring, and judicious pruning and "tree surgery" will also contribute towards the development of better yielding tea.

SUMMARY.

The termites, or white ants, attacking the tea bush may be divided into two classes, viz :—

(a) Those which bore into the heartwood of living bushes and form a complete colony in each infested bush. There are three species of Calotermes, namely, C. militaris, C. dilatatus, and C. greeni. Of these, militaris is mainly an up-country species, and is sometimes a serious pest, since it works chiefly inside the lower part of a bush, and its injury is often not detected until the bush is completely hollowed out and reduced to a shell. The other two species occur at middle and lower elevations, but are not serious at the present time, since they attack mostly the upper portions of bushes and are probably controlled at pruning time.

Control.—Dig out and burn all badly riddled bushes. In cases where the attack is detected in time, the bush may be saved by cleaning out the cavity and treating with a solution of creosote, or other wood preservative.

(b) The smaller scavenging termites which feed only on dead and diseased bark and wood, have their nests outside the bush, usually underground. These are mainly Termes obscuriceps and Termes redemanni, while Termes horii and species of Euterms also have much the same habits.

Control.—(1) Destroy the termite nests, either (a) by using an Ant Exterminator with sulphur and arsenic, or (b) by fumigating with carbon bisulphide, or (c) by digging out the nests and destroying the queens and colony. The last method is probably the cheapest and most effective for general use.

(2) Clear the tea bushes at pruning time of all branches badly affected by branch canker, and then spray with Bordeaux mixture immediately after pruning to control this disease. Repeat this treatment after each pruning. Remove all diebacks periodically.

(3) Gradually eradicate all old jungle stumps and other dead stumps in or near tea areas and destroy all such stumps by fire, where possible.

J. C. HUTSON,

January 20, 1923.

Government Entomologist.

MAY, 1923.]299

THE CONTROL OF SHOT-HOLE BORER IN TEA BY THE USE OF GENERAL MANURES.

PRELIMINARY REPORT,

C. H. GADD, B. Sc.,

Assistant Mycologist

and

N. K. JARDINE, F.E.S.,

Acting Assistant Entomologist.

Introduction.—The presence of Shot-hole Borer was first recorded from Sarnia Estate, Badulla, in February 1917 on 60 acres of four-year-old tea in the Mahattenne Division. A few years ago it was the practice of this estate to give the fields a pruning mixture at the rate of 200 lb. per acre, followed by 350 lb. of general mixture a year after pruning, and a further 350 lb. of the same mixture the second year after pruning. Since 1919 the application of general mixture two years after pruning was increased from 350 to 550 lb. per acre, and a decrease of borer in all third-year fields so treated has been observed since the practice was adopted. It has also been noticed that gallery entrance healing has been prevalent in these fields, many of the galleries being completely occluded, and those galleries which had not healed contained few inmates.

Objects of the present investigation :—The objects of the present investigation are :—

  1. (1) To check the above general observations.
  2. (2) To ascertain experimentally the effect of a complete manure at varying quantities per acre on shot-hole borer attack.
  3. (3) To ascertain to what extent manuring promotes healing of shot-hole borer galleries.

Scheme of Investigation :—In August, 1921, twenty-five small plots were marked out in a field at Sarnia estate. Each plot consisted of approximately 200 bushes which were entering their second year from pruning. The plots were separated, one from another, by guard strips of two rows of untreated bushes. The object of these guard strips was to ensure that the manures applied to one plot would not affect the bushes in the neighbouring plots. Five small scattered plots or unit plots were treated alike and constitute one main plot A. Plot A therefore comprises 5 unit plots each of 200 bushes, in different parts of the experimental area. Similarly plots B, C, D. and E. each consists of five scattered units. By using small scattered plots any error due to lack of uniformity of shot-hole borer attack over the experimental area will, to a large extent, be eliminated.

When the bushes were pruned in 1920 the whole area received a pruning mixture at the rate of 200 lb. per acre consisting of :—

Nitrolim ... ... ... 60 lb.
Ephos Phosphate ... ... ... 80 lb.
Muriate of Potash ... ... ... 60 lb.

The control plot E. as well as the treated plots therefore received this mixture, but will receive no other manurial treatment during the experiment. Plots A. B. C. and D. in addition to the pruning mixture have received a general mixture in varying rates. The general mixture consists of :—

Fish Manure ... ... ... 250 lb.
Sulphate of Ammonia ... ... ... 60 lb.
Muriate of Potash ... ... ... 40 lb.

Examinations of the plots are made twice each year at approximately six months' interval.

Data Collected.—In order to make accurate comparisons between the plots certain data were collected, by means of which the intensity of the attack and the rate of healing of galleries could be measured, in order that conclusions could be based on definite ascertained details. Without a means of measuring shot-hole borer attack a comparison of the plots would be mainly a matter of opinion, which in the absence of definite demonstrable facts would be of little value.

The following data were therefore collected for each plot :—

  1. (1) The number of branches on each bush.
  2. (2) The number of galleries, opened and healed, on each bush.
  3. (3) The proportion of empty and occupied galleries.
  4. (4) The number of occupants, adults, pupæ, larvæ, and eggs in the occupied galleries.

It will be evident that the above details could not be obtained for each bush in the plots or for each gallery in the bush. Consequently the data for each plot was obtained from representative samples from each plot.

Previous work on shot-hole borer had led to the conclusion that 125 bushes would form a representative sample for each plot. Therefore twenty-five bushes were taken as a sample from each unit, so making 125 for each plot. The selection of the bushes was made in a definite pre-arranged manner and was carried out similarly in each unit. In this way the personal element in selection was eliminated.

Twenty-five open galleries from each unit making 125 for each plot were dissected and the contents counted in order to ascertain the proportion of empty galleries and the mean content of the occupied ones.

Method of Determining Results.—(a) Healing. The numbers of healed and opened galleries were recorded separately for each bush. It was therefore an easy matter to determine for each bush what percentage of the total galleries had healed. From these results a mean for the 125 bushes from each plot was obtained. This mean percentage fairly represents the rate of healing for each plot.

(b) Number of open galleries.—It has been shown elsewhere* that where

* DEPT. AGRIC., CEYLON, BULL. 56.

MAY, 1923.]301

shot-hole borer attack is uniform the number of galleries in a bush will depend upon the size of the bush, larger bushes having the greater number of galleries, but the number of galleries in a branch will be more or less constant whatever the size of the bush may be. By a branch is here meant a branch arising from the old frame of sufficient diameter to allow the entry of the insect. Consequently the number of open galleries per branch has been used as a measure of the number of open galleries present in each plot. By dividing the number of open galleries by the number of branches of each bush and averaging the 125 results for each plot a value representative of each plot has been obtained.

(c) Gallery contents.—The rate of increase of shot-hole borer attack will to some extent depend upon the number of individuals raised in the galleries. If large broods are present in the galleries then it is to be expected that in the near future shot-hole borer attack will rapidly increase. If on the other hand, the galleries contain but few insects at some stage of their development, it follows that in the near future the attack will not be so severe as in the previous case.

An estimation of the number of insects present in the galleries has been obtained by examination of 150 galleries from each plot, i.e., 25 galleries from each unit. These galleries are carefully opened and the number of inmates including adults, pupæ, larvæ and eggs, recorded for each gallery.

(1) Proportion of empty galleries.—Of the 125 galleries of each plot a certain proportion were found to be empty. This proportion has been determined for each plot. Significant differences between plot results, i.e., differences too great to be accounted for as being due to random sampling, would indicate that some factor is at work which causes the galleries to be vacated prematurely.

(2) Mean content of occupied galleries.—The number of inmates, including adults, pupæ, larvæ and eggs was recorded for each gallery found to be occupied, and from these determinations the average content of an occupied gallery was obtained for each plot. Significant differences between these results would indicate that in a plot having a large mean content, conditions are more favourable for raising large broods than is the case in plots having smaller mean contents.

By comparing the plots according to the above data, reliable conclusions can be formed regarding the effect of treatment on the intensity of shot-hole borer attack and upon the rate of healing of borer galleries.

1st Examination.—At the commencement of the experiment (August, 1921) all the bushes of all plots had been treated alike and it may be fairly assumed, owing to the scattered arrangement of the unit plots, that the attack and the rate of healing in all main plots, were equal. The first examination of the plots, was made in May 1922, nine months after treatment and the commencement of the experiment. The results of this examination are given in Table 1.

Table 1. First Examination.

Plot Percentage of galleries healed Mean number of open galleries per branch Number of open galleries found to be empty (of 125 examined) Number of occupied galleries examined Mean content of occupied galleries
A 49.9 ± .72 .299 ± .012 24 ± 2.9 101 4.62 ± .32
B 49.2 ± 1.17 .315 ± .012 27 ± 3.1 98 4.65 ± .26
C 42.7 ± 1.22 .372 ± .013 20 ± 2.8 105 4.70 ± .32
D 45.3 ± 1.27 .345 ± .013 26 ± 3.1 99 4.90 ± .39
E Control 28.8 ± .89 .534 ± .017 15 ± 2.4 110 5.28 ± .35
302MAY, 1923.

It will be seen from Table I that all the manured plots are better than the control plot in every respect. They have a greater percentage of galleries healed, and a smaller number of open galleries per branch, a larger proportion of empty galleries and a smaller number of inmates in the occupied galleries.

(a) Percentage of Galleries Healed.—It must, however, be remembered that these determinations have been made by sampling and consequently the results are liable to error due to sampling. It remains to ascertain therefore whether the observed differences are of such a size that they are likely to have arisen as a result of sampling alone, or whether they are of such a magnitude that is improbable that they are solely due to this cause. The probable error of each result is given in Table I. From this it can be calculated that the difference between the control plot E. and the manured plot C., which gives the worst result of the manured plots in the percentage of galleries healed is 13.9 \pm 1.51 i.e. the difference is 9.2 times as great as its probable error. It may be taken as a rule that where the difference between two results is as much as 5 to 10 times its probable error, the probability of such a difference occurring solely as a result of random sampling is so small that we are justified in saying that the difference is significant; and that a difference 10 times its probable error is certainly significant in so far as there is certainty in human affairs. Consequently the difference between the plots C. and E. is of such a size that it is very improbable that it has occurred as a result of sampling and that it is highly probable that it has arisen as a result of the differential treatment the plots have received. Since the other manured plots A., B., and D., show greater differences from the control plot than does plot C. it may be concluded that these differences must also have arisen as a result of differential treatment.

(b) Mean Number of Open Galleries per Branch.—If we examine the difference between the results shown by the manured plots and that of the control plot as regards the number of open galleries per branch in a way similar to that used for the percentage of galleries healed we find that plot C, the worst of the manured plots has 162 \pm 0.21 fewer galleries per branch than has control plot E. This difference is 7.7 times as great as its probable error and may be considered to be significant. Similarly the differences shown by the other manured plots may be shown to arise not so much as a result of sampling but as a result of differential treatment.

From the facts that all the manured plots have a greater proportion of healed galleries, and fewer open galleries we may conclude that healing has proceeded more rapidly in the manured plots than it has in the control plot.

(c) Proportion of Empty Galleries.—Turning now to the examination of the open galleries we see from Table I that of the 125 galleries examined from plot B., which has given the best result in this respect, 27 \pm 3.1 were found to be empty whereas the control plot had only 15 \pm 2.4 empty of the 125 examined. The difference between these two results is therefore 12 \pm 3.9 which is only 3.1 times as great as its probable error. This difference may have arisen solely as a result of random sampling and we are not justified in concluding that the observed difference is real or due to the differential treatment. The observed differences between the other manured plots and the control plot are also small compared with their probable errors.

(d) Mean Content of Occupied Galleries—Plot A. has the smallest mean number of inmates in its occupied galleries, viz. 4.62 \pm .32 whereas the control plot E. has the greatest number 5.28 \pm .35. The difference between these results is .66 \pm .474, the difference being only 1.4 times as great as its probable error. It is therefore very probable that the differences observed between the manured plots and the control plots as regards the mean content of their occupied galleries has arisen as a result of random sampling and is not due to the differential treatment of the plots.

MAY, 1923.]303

We are not therefore justified in concluding as a result of the first examination that the manures applied have had any influence on the proportion of open galleries found empty or on the mean content of the occupied galleries. It is more probable that the observed differences in these respects between the manured and the control plots are due to sampling and not to the effect of the manures applied.

Second examination.—The second examination was made in September, 1922, 12 months after the commencement of experiments and 4 months after the first examination. The results of the examination are given in Table 2.

Table 2:—Second Examination.

Plot Percentage of galleries healed Mean No. of open galleries per branch No. of open galleries found to be empty of 125 examined No. of occupied galleries Mean content of occupied galleries
A 69.1 ± .99 .399 ± .021 71 ± 3.74 54 2.52 ± .23
B 63.5 ± 1.18 .430 ± .022 68 ± 3.76 57 3.70 ± .33
C 65.4 ± 1.05 .456 ± .023 69 ± 3.75 56 2.38 ± .26
D 65.8 ± 1.18 .470 ± .033 57 ± 3.76 68 3.13 ± .27

The results obtained from the second examination are in many respects very similar to those obtained from the first examination. Each of the manured plots has given results better than the control from every point of view. The treated plots have greater percentages of healed galleries, smaller numbers of open galleries per branch, larger proportions of empty galleries and smaller mean contents of occupied galleries.

If the difference between the observed results of each manured plot and the control plot are compared with their probable errors in a manner similar to that carried out for the first examination, we find that we are justified in concluding that the manured plots have given results significantly better than the control as regards the percentage of galleries healed and the mean number of open galleries per branch. The differences observed between the manured plots and the control as regards the proportion of empty galleries and the mean content of occupied galleries are, however, insignificant. The fact that the proportion of empty galleries is again lower and the mean content of occupied galleries again higher than in any of the treated plots is however of importance and would indicate that there is a real difference in these respects, but that the error of experimentation is sufficiently large to mask these real differences. Further examinations will bring more light on this point, but at present it is inadvisable to state definitely that complete manuring results in an increase in the proportion of empty galleries or a decrease in the mean content of the occupied galleries.

350 lb. application v. 550 lb. application.—It will be noticed that for the first two examinations plots A. and C. had been treated alike i.e., they had received 350 lb. of mixture per acre at the commencement of the second year from pruning, and plots B. and D. had each received 550 lb. We may therefore combine plots A. and C. and regard them as one plot of 10 units. Similarly plots B. and D. may be combined as one plot of 10 units. By comparing these combined plots we shall be able to determine whether the heavier application of manure has resulted in greater benefit as regards Shot-hole Borer attack than has the smaller application.

It will be readily seen from Table 3 that results obtained from the plots A. & C. for the first examination are very slightly different from those of plots B. & D. The differences are so small compared with their probable errors that they must be considered to be insignificant. The results of the second examination show that plots A. & C. which received manurial mixture at the rate of 350 lb. per acre have on the whole given slightly better results than plots B. & D. which received a heavier dressing. When however the differences observed between these plots are compared with the probable error of these differences they are found to be too small to be significant and we are justified in concluding that these differences have arisen as an error of random sampling. There is therefore no significant difference between the 350 lb. plot and 550 lb. plot at either examination.

Conclusions.—The following conclusions have been drawn from the experiments so far as they have progressed. The experiments are not yet complete, two further examinations at six months' interval have to be made of each plot. Final conclusions cannot be formulated until all the examinations are completed so that the following are offered tentatively.

1. The application of a complete manurial mixture at the rate of 350 lb. or 550 lb. per acre at the end of the first year resulted in an increase in the rate of healing of the shot-hole galleries and a corresponding diminution in the number of open galleries.

2. The proportion of empty galleries and the mean number of inmates of the occupied galleries were not definitely affected by the application of the manures.

3. The application at the rate 550 lb. of general mixture per acre gave no better results than the smaller application of 350 lb. per acre.

4. The application of manures has little if any direct effect on the Shot-hole Borer insect itself. It however increases the vigour of the bushes which are thereby enabled to repair more rapidly the damage done by the insect. Consequently where the intensity of the Shot hole Borer attack is judged by the damage done to the bushes it would appear that a reduction in the Shot-hole Borer attack follows the application of manures.

"BUNCHY TOP" DISEASE IN BANANAS:
INTERESTING EXPERIMENTS.

MR. T. BROOKS, of Highfield, Murwillumbah, claims to have discovered a cure for the "bunchy top" disease in bananas. In 1920, MR. BROOKS treated portion of his plantation with sulphur, but this did not have the effect desired. In May last, root rot set in, and in December it appeared as if the whole plantation was "settled." MR. BROOKS now contends that the sulphur applied last year, at the rate of about 8 cwt. per acre, together with island fertiliser, plays an important part in the treatment he is now applying. He has started with a mixture which he calls basic super, which contains 45 per cent. lime and 17 per cent. phosphoric acid. This was applied in some cases around the stools to a radius of 3 feet or 4 feet, in two plots. The whole surface was treated with from 8 cwt. to 10 cwt. per acre, and the suckers before being planted were well dusted with the mixture. All suckers planted were taken from "bunchy top" stock, but of the 800 planted since April not one, so far, appears to be affected with the disease. On the contrary, every leaf shows splendid colour, and the stems are strong and vigorous, while the growth for this time of the year is exceptional. Old stalks up to 5 feet high, which obviously were badly affected with the disease, are not throwing out vigorous centre leaves and evidencing fullness of sap.

Although the experiments are only in part developed, and a whole season is necessary to stamp them as conclusive, the hearty growth of every plant treated, and the unusual crop of peas, beans, and other vegetables, demonstrate that MR. BROOKS has developed a wonderful growth force in his soil.

MR. BROOKS is making his discovery public in order that it might form a base for further experiment should it fall short of expectations. His line of reasoning is that the application of the sulphur renders the phosphates soluble, so that they can be readily taken up by the plant, hence the rapid growth following the sulphur treatment. But this also allowed the heavy autumn rains to wash the phosphates out of the soil, which accounts for the return of the disease after the rain last year. The sulphur remaining in the soil acts as a fungicide, and connecting with the basic super, assists the restoration of the lost sulphates. The lime contents give a warmth and sweetness and stimulate the root growth.

Discussing the matter recently, the Minister for Agriculture and Stock (HON. W. N. GILLIES) remarked that developments in this connection were being closely watched, and that his Department is in communication with the New South Wales authorities on the subject. From departmental information there is very little evidence of "bunchy top" in Queensland.

—QUEENSLAND AGRIC. JOURN., Vol. XVIII, Pt. 4.

SOILS AND MANURES.

THE SELECTION OF MANURES.

Much has been written in days gone by in the CHRONICLE of the various methods of valuing and selecting Manures and it may not be out of place to deal with the subject again, as the price of manures is a thing of continual interest to the planter and also to the manure supplying Firms.

The Planter's problem is something like this :—

One Firm offers a mixed manure with some such guarantee as

Nitrogen 3\frac{1}{2}—4\frac{1}{2} per cent.

Phosphoric Acid 9\frac{1}{2}—11 per cent.

Potash 3—4 per cent.

Lime 11—13 per cent.

@ Rs. 105/- per ton.

Another offers Nitrogen 4—5 per cent.

Phosphoric Acid 7—8 per cent. and

Potash 5 per cent.

@ Rs. 125/- per ton.

Which is the better value ?

Just at present the most expensive ingredient in a fertiliser is the Nitrogen and reference to a recent manure price list gives the following prices for nitrogenous fertiliser.

Name Per Cent. of Nitrogen Price per ton Value of each per cent. of unit.
Rs. Rs.
Groundnut Poonac 7—8 125/- 18/-
Castor do 4—5 120/- 30/-
Pungai do 4—5 105/- 26/4
Sulphate of Ammonia 20—21 330/- 16/8
Nitrate of Soda 15—16 280/- 18/10
Fish Guano 6—7 75/- 12/8
Blood Meal 11—22 260/- 23/10
Nitrolim 18 330/- 18/5

In the manufacture therefore of a mixed manure, the manufacturer has at his disposal, Nitrogen, whose cost per unit varies from Rs. 12/8 per unit in Fish Guano to Rs. 30 per unit in Castor Poonac which is to say that in a mixture guaranteed to contain 4 per cent. Nitrogen the Nitrogen if derived from Fish Guano would be worth Rs. 50 and if derived from Castor Poonac would be worth Rs. 120. This last, however, is an extreme case as it is not possible using Castor only to give a mixture containing Phosphates and Potash with 4 per cent. Nitrogen and a better example to take would be Blood at Rs. 23/10 per unit. If the Nitrogen in a mixture were to be derived from Blood alone it would represent a value of Rs. 94/8.

MAY, 1923.]307

The Fertiliser Manufacturer has two things to consider to provide the cheapest possible mixture and to provide the best possible mixture. In the making up of a mixed fertiliser, he will not as a rule draw all his Nitrogen from one source, but will as far as possible derive it from as many sources as possible, so that the plant may at all times of its growth be able to get some Nitrogen from the mixture. One kind of Nitrogen in a mixture means that this Nitrogen will be available all at the same time with the result that at one time, the plant may have more Nitrogen than it wants and the next time may be starved. The selection of the various forms of Nitrogen is found only by years of experience and is known as balancing the fertiliser.

In a well balanced fertiliser then the Nitrogen may be derived from such sources as say—one-third from easily available sources e.g., Nitrate of Soda or Sulphate of Ammonia, one-third from sources less easily available, such as Fish or Poonac and the remaining third from say Blood. Assuming that this may be the case, the valuation of a mixed manure may be on some such basis as follows:—

One unit from Nitrate of Soda ... Rs. 18 10 0
" " " Fish ... " 12 8 0
" " " Groundnut ... " 18 0 0
" " " Blood ... " 23 10 0
or Four Units Nitrogen ... Rs. 72 12 0

Coming now to Phosphoric Acid, the forms as before and the cost per unit from which this may be derived are as follows:—

Name Price per ton Per cent. P_2O_5 Price per unit
Superphosphate Rs. 105 14/15 Rs. 7/8
Conc. Superphosphate " 270 42/45 " 6/6
Basic Slag " 110 20/21 " 5/8

These are purely phosphatic manures and in the case of Bone Meal and Basic Bone Super, the value of the phosphate may be found as follows:—

In Bone Meal the usual guarantee is 4 per cent. Nitrogen and 22 per cent. Phosphoric Acid. The Nitrogen may be assumed to be equal in value to that of Groundnut and hence worth Rs. 72 per ton (18 \times 4) leaving for 22 units of P_2O_5 Rs. 110.72 or Rs. 38 per ton, in round figures Rs. 2 per unit. Similarly in the case of Basic Bone Super, with 2\frac{1}{2} per cent. Nitrogen and 12/13 per cent. Phosphoric Acid soluble in Citric Acid 15/17 per cent. total P_2O_5 @ Rs. 125 per ton we arrive at a value for the Phosphoric Acid taking 3 units of insoluble P_2O_5 at Rs. 2 per unit as shown in Bone Meal above, Rs. 6—3—0 per unit of Citric soluble Phosphoric Acid.

Phosphoric Acid in Mixtures may then have a value of Rs. 2 per unit if it is insoluble Phosphoric Acid and say Rs. 6—8—0 per unit if soluble in Citric Acid. Phosphate which is guaranteed to be soluble in Citric Acid is more readily available than insoluble while of course the most readily available of all is superphosphate at from Rs. 6.6 to Rs. 7.8 per unit. The Phosphoric Acid in a mixture then may be worth Rs. 7 per unit for water soluble P_2O_5, Rs. 5.8 per unit for citric soluble e.g., in Basic Slag or Basic Bone Superphosphate or Rs. 2 per unit in Bone Meal or Mineral Rock Phosphate.

A good mixture then will contain its P_2O_5 balanced from the above various kinds or at least from citric soluble and insoluble so that in a mixture guaranteed to contain 8 per cent. Phosphoric Acid we should have

8 ,, Total value Rs. 30

With regard to Potash, prices of Sulphate and Muriate show that Rs. 4/- per unit represent fair value.

We are now in a position to compare the two manures.

(1) Nitrogen ... ... 3\frac{1}{2}—4\frac{1}{2} per cent.
Phosphoric Acid ... ... 9\frac{1}{2}—11 „
Potash ... .. 3—4 „
Nitrogen ... ... 3\frac{1}{2} \times 18 = Rs. 63
Potash ... ... 3 \times 4 = ,, 12
Rs. 75

Leaving Rs. 30 for 9\frac{1}{2}—11 units of Phosphoric Acid or say Rs. 3 per unit of Phosphoric Acid. This shows that the bulk of the Phosphoric Acid is in all probability derived from insoluble or not very readily available forms.

(2) Nitrogen ... ... 4—5 per cent.
Phosphoric Acid ... ... 7—8 „
Potash ... ... 5 „
Nitrogen ... ... 4 \times 18 = Rs. 72

Rs. 92

Leaving Rs. 33 for 7 units of Phosphoric Acid or Rs. 4—12—0 per unit.

This would seem to indicate that the bulk of the P_2O_5 in this case is derived from water or citric soluble P_2O_5 and as a consequence is more readily available than the P_2O_5 in the first manure.

It is hoped that these notes may be of assistance in helping Planters to arrive at the value of mixtures offered them, while they should always insist on being supplied with a guarantee of the citric or water soluble Phosphoric Acid contents of a mixture which is a true guide to the availability of the Phosphoric Acid.

While on this subject, the increasing cost of transport both by rail and by cart is day by day worthy of more serious consideration. 21 cwt. of Sulphate of Ammonia will give exactly the same amount of Nitrogen as 60 cwt. of Groundnut Poonac while the transport charges will be slightly more than one-third of the cost of transporting the poonac. It is urged that the value of the poonac is increased by the value of its organic matter but if one considers that the top 9 inches of soil contains 2,500,000 lb. per acre, the addition of 5 cwt. or 560 lb. of Groundnut per acre is not going to increase the percentage of organic matter in the soil by any appreciable extent, while the cost of application is increased.

Sulphate of Ammonia, Nitrate of Soda and Nitrolim all supply Nitrogen in concentrated form and Phosphoric Acid can be supplied in the form of concentrated Super containing 42-45 per cent. Phosphoric Acid twice as much as is contained in Bone Meal or the best Basic Slag.

Potash Salts fortunately are already in a concentrated form.—PLANTERS' CHRONICLE, Vol. XVIII, No. II.

POULTRY.

POULTRY FEEDING.

[Interim Report on an Experiment.]

A. OWEN-JOHN F. B. S. A.,

Lecturer in Poultry Culture, Grootsfontein School of Agriculture.

General.—This feeding experiment commenced on the 8th of August, 1921, with the object of determining the value of dry-mash feeding as against wet mash for egg production.

The first test was completed on 7th August, 1922. Two uniform lots, each consisting of fourteen South African Utility White Leghorn pullets, nine to ten months old, were used. The birds were not specially selected, but were those left over after all birds required for breeding, testing, etc., had been selected. They were accommodated in a run 50 ft. by 40 ft. with a house 8 ft. by 6 ft., the floor area of which was covered with six to eight inches of litter to provide scratching crib (and the necessary exercise) in which the grain was fed. A careful record was kept of the number and weight of the eggs produced daily from each of the birds.

Feeding.—The mash used consisted of equal parts by weight of wheaten bran and pollard, with 20 per cent. of meatmeal and a little fine charcoal, added with \frac{1}{2} lb. of salt to each 100 lb. of mash. This was fed to the "wet mash" lot in the morning, moistened with water to a friable consistency, allowing 2 oz. per bird. To the "dry mash" lot the mixture was fed in a self-feeding hopper which was open all day, the birds being allowed to help themselves. The grain feed given to both lots consisted of two parts of oats to one part of yellow cracked maize, by weight; this was fed in the afternoon, scattered in litter as above mentioned, allowing 2 oz. per bird.

The reason why oats and maize were used was that both are available to almost any farmer and in any part of the country. Green food was given at midday, consisting of lucerne, when available, otherwise cabbage leaves, feeding as much as the birds would consume.

The following is a table of the results obtained :—

310[MAY, 1923.

Conclusions.—From the foregoing results the following conclusions are drawn:—

1. Dry mash produced 430 eggs more than wet mash, or an average of 30.71 eggs per hen.

2. Dry mash feeding produced 287 eggs more than wet mash during the winter months when prices are highest, or an average of 20.5 eggs per hen.

3. Dry mash produced a superior average weight of egg.

4. Dry mash entails much less labour in feeding, at the same time giving in superior results.

5. The birds came through the moult in much better condition and a much shorter time on dry mash.

6. The size of egg was well maintained during the hot summer months on dry mash, the wet mash lot showing a decrease in size of egg during this time.

7. On the basis of 1s. 6d. per doz. the dry mash lot laid eggs to the value of £15. 16s. 1½d., and wet mash £13. 2s. 4½d., a balance of £2. 13s. 9d. in favour of the former.

8. Periodically during the year an equal quantity of mash was weighed out to each lot of birds to ascertain whether one consumed more food than the other. In this connection it was found that the dry mash lot consumed on an average for the year 2 lb. per month more (per 14 birds) than the wet mash lot. Taking into consideration the cost of the extra 24 lb. of mash consumed in dry mash feeding, the evidence thus far is still decidedly in favour of dry mash feeding as against wet mash.

9. In June, 1922, a male bird was introduced into each pen with a view to ascertaining any difference in the hatchability of the eggs of each lot. Here again there was marked difference, the eggs from the dry mash lot showing a superior hatchability to those from the wet mash pen, even with changing the male birds periodically. This was observed during the months of June and July.

This test is being continued for a further period of twelve months with each lot of birds changed, i.e., wet mash lot put on dry mash and the dry mash on wet mash. Careful records of results are being kept, and after the completion of the test on the 7th of August next, a final report will be issued,—JOURN. OF DEPT. AGRIC. UNION S. A.—Vol. VI., No. 2.

A CURE FOR CRAMP.

A contributor to an overseas journal gives the following method of treatment for fowls suffering from cramp: The affected bird is separated from the remainder of the flock and placed in a convenient coop or small house.

A perch is fitted to this coop or house, made 12 in. long, 3 in. wide and raised slightly off the floor. A piece of flannel is tacked on to this perch and is then saturated with embrocation. On this the bird roosts all right, and it is claimed that in a couple of days it will have recovered.

If the bird is so bad that it cannot perch, a piece of flannel can be laid on the ground, saturated in embrocation, and the bird placed thereon. In both cases the heat of the bird's body will render it possible for the embrocation to be absorbed.—SOUTH AFRICAN POULTRY MAG. AND SMALL-HOLDER, VOL. XV., No. 134

MAY, 1923.]311

CO-OPERATION.

AGRICULTURAL AND INDUSTRIAL CO-OPERATION IN MYSORE.

K. H. RAMAYYA, B. A.,

Barrister-at-law, Registrar of Co-operative Societies in Mysore.

Agriculture is the chief occupation of the people in the Mysore State and nearly 52\frac{3}{4} lakhs or 90 per cent. of the population of the State subsist on this industry. With a view to improving the economic condition of agriculturists and their earning capacity, Government have been devoting special attention to the development of agriculture. They have granted concessions to ryots for bringing more lands under cultivation. They have instituted a special Department of Agriculture to advise and help the ryots about the best methods of cultivating various kinds of crops, by providing them with improved implements, such as ploughs, harrows, seed-drills, and also with good varieties of seeds, manure, etc., at cheap rates of cost. This department gives them technical advice about the methods of raising crops and preventing diseases of them by frequent inspections. There is also a Department of Sericulture with a Special Officer who pays special attention to the development of that industry. There is a Veterinary Department with branches at all the district head-quarters whose officers, by providing medical aid and advice, prevent the mortality of cattle which are a great asset to the ryot in Mysore. With all these facilities provided to our ryots, they have not utilized the beneficent measures adopted by Government to their best advantage.

There are now 1,233 co-operative societies in the Mysore State started chiefly for the benefit of the agriculturists. They have a membership of 51,377 with a working capital of Rs. 2,512,000 and are serving about 5,000 villages in the State. There are over 17,000 villages in the State and the co-operative movement has not brought all of them under its beneficent influence. Thus, there is ample scope for starting many more co-operative societies for the benefit of these agriculturists.

It is admitted on all hands that the Co-operative Movement has vast potentialities for raising not only the economic standard of the people but their moral and social standards also. Agricultural Co-operation means for the peasant better farming, better business and better living; better farming, because more capital will be applied to the land, better seeds, manure, implements and livestock will be obtained and expert advice will be available; better business, because the small ryot by combining with others gains all the advantages of wholesale dealers; better living, because economic prosperity and combination for better business purposes bring in their train well ordered social life. Agricultural Co-operation can help the

312[MAY, 1923.

agriculturists in the following ways :—

(1) It provides him with the capital that he requires for carrying on his occupation, at a cheap rate of interest,

(2) It enables him to utilize it most profitably and

(3) It enables him to sell his produce to the best advantage possible.

The first object is served by the credit co-operative society. The second is achieved by the formation of various kinds of societies, such as, societies for the supply of improved varieties of seed, of implements such as improved ploughs, harrows, drills, etc., of machinery such as sugar-cane mills and plants, the usefulness of which is experimented and established beyond any doubt by the Department of Agriculture.

But other forms of co-operations were attempted to directly help the ryot in his agricultural operations. The purpose served by and the number of such societies are noted below :—

No. of Societies.
1. For the supply of seeds, agricultural implements and manure 72
2. For the sale of agricultural produce 2
3. For lift-irrigation 1
4. For dairy-farming 1

The supply societies, started purely with the object of supplying to their members good seed, improved agricultural implements and manure did not do much work for want of men and money. But nearly seventy existing credit societies discharged this function by utilizing a portion of their capital for such purposes. Of the seed supplied, the principal one is a variety of ragi seed recommended by the Agricultural Department after extensive and exhaustive experiments and tests as being best suited to the Mysore soil. Nearly twenty-seven co-operative societies in the Bangalore Kolar and Tumkur Districts won prizes for the best ragi crops.

The supply of implements was very limited as they were not available in sufficient numbers in the season at which they were in demand. The work of supplying manure was still less. A few societies purchased a small quantity of mixed manure and supplied it to their members.

There were also sale societies for the joint-sale of agricultural produce, such as copra, areca-nut, etc. But these societies are still in their infancy and it remains to be seen how far they will work successfully, as success depends much on the loyalty, business-like habits and combined action of the members.

Taking the experience of the past several years into consideration, it has now been decided that no new special societies need be organized purely for agricultural purposes, as they can do very little work for want of men and money to start with. On the other hand, the existing credit societies will be fully availed of for taking up this agricultural work.

As DR. COLEMAN has stated in his book on Cultivation of Ragi in Mysore, ragi covers one-third of the total cultivated area and is the staple food for four-fifths of the people. The average annual value of the ragi crop in this State before the War can be taken at about four and a half crores of

MAY, 1923.]313

rupees. This represents roughly one-fourth the total value of all crops grown in the State. Similarly, it is said that there is hardly a type of agricultural implements in Mysore which does not find use in the cultivation, harvesting or threshing of ragi.

In consultation with the Director of Agriculture in Mysore it has been decided to confine our attention this year entirely to increasing the area of H-22 ragi in the ragi growing districts and arrange for the sale of improved implements, seeds and manure through the existing credit societies by utilizing a portion of their reserve fund or working capital. The chief implements recommended by the Agricultural Department, such as, Kolar Mission ploughs, cultivators, disc-harrows, Punjab Nahan sugar-cane mills and special varieties of sugar-cane seeds and special paddy mixture, will be popularized. With a view to successfully working out the scheme, the following decisions were arrived at after consulting the Director of Agriculture in Mysore.

(1) The Agricultural Department will supply information re places suitable for trying the experiment of co-operative supply of implements, seeds and manure through credit societies. The Department will also furnish a statement of annual sales of implements, seeds and manures in these places during the past five years.

(2) The Registrar will select suitable existing credit societies to transact this kind of business.

(3) Agricultural Inspectors are to keep in touch with the societies and assist them in their work of distributing agricultural supplies.

(4) Where stock remains in the hands of the societies unsold for a year, the Department of Agriculture is to arrange for their transfer to other places.

(5) Every society selected by the Registrar will set apart some money either out of its reserve fund or working capital for utilizing it to this agricultural business.

As regards the formation of special societies, such as supply societies, co-operative dairies, sale societies for the joint-sale of agricultural produce, societies for the disposal of live stock, societies for cattle breeding, insuring cattle, societies against fire and against accidents in agriculture, steps will be taken whenever the people are anxious to start such societies.

Similarly, the application of co-operative principles to industries in which small artisans are engaged, will confer a great blessing on the people engaged in them. The artisans are by nature illiterate and ignorant and they possess no business habits and methods. They work at their convenience and pleasure and are very unmindful of the future. The business carried on by the following class of people offers a good field for expansion :

Weavers (of cotton, silk, and wool), carpet manufacturers, basket-makers, carpenters, cabinet makers, metal workers, sandal-wood carvers.

314[MAY, 1923.

Societies started for these people should not only be able to finance them, but also, supply them with the raw materials required and find a sale for the manufactured articles. Weaving industry is carried on to a large extent in the Mysore State and the articles manufactured here are being sent to many places in Southern India. The majority of the weavers are addicted to bad habits and the difficulty of bringing them to work under proper discipline for a common purpose is in the way of the expansion of weavers' societies. We have a number of societies for these weavers, but only a few perform all the functions enumerated above. At the best these societies provide the members with the capital they require and to some extent raw materials also, but they do not undertake the sale of the articles manufactured by them to the best advantage, owing to fluctuations in trade and the uncertainty of the market. With the improvement of these conditions, these societies are likely to develop on a large scale.

There is one other branch of industry for which the Mysore State is famous and which is making rapid progress during the past few years and that is sericulture. Co-operative societies can help the people engaged in sericulture to a large extent. They can help them with the supply of capital required by them, supply them with good disease-free eggs and arrange to sell the silk manufactured by them in a profitable market. These societies do not require much capital to begin with, but they require constant supervision. The Superintendent of Sericulture has consented to select suitable places where such societies could be started with fair chance of success and to give them all technical advice. Special attempts will have to be made in the future for the formation and development of sericultural societies.

For the growth of the several types of societies enumerated above, a real desire to combine for the sake of mutual benefit must exist on the part of the people. The people for whose benefit a society is to be organized should at least be able to appreciate the advantages it will bring to them and the conditions which make it a success. These conditions are :—proper men to manage the working, punctuality of repayment of loans, an understanding faithfully carried out to declare existing debts and to borrow in future from no outside source and the employment of loans solely for the purposes for which they are taken. If people are desirous of starting any such societies they may at once apply to the Registrar of Co-operative Societies and he will render them all possible advice and assistance.

Before concluding this short note, it may be mentioned that the Co-operative Department is ready to help the small industrial and the depressed and the poor classes' societies in their initial stages by giving some allowance for establishment charges and by having a special Inspector to guide such societies.—JOURN. OF THE MYSORE AGRIC. & EXPT. UNION. VOL. V., No. 1.

May, 1923.]315

GENERAL.

CAMPHOR IN TONKIN.

Ch. Crevost and F. de FENIS.

This paper gives information regarding experiments recently made by the various French Colonies for the improvement of their agricultural, industrial and commercial resources, the writers having been originally instructed in 1904 by the Tonkin Government to ascertain the importance of the growth of camphor yielding plants in the Province of Bac-Giang. After a short historical account of the more recent works published on the subject of camphor from 1903 to 1920, the writers made a botanical study of camphor trees. These are classified under 3 principal species growing wild in Indo-China.

1. Cinnamomum Camphora Nees and Eberm.—Laurus Camphora L.—Camphora officinarum; grows in Yeu-the (Province of Bac-Giang) and in the Provinces of N. Annam. It is called "Rahuong" in Annamite, "May Kao chuong," "May Khao Khinh," "May Khao hom" in Thai, "Long nao" in Chinese.

2. Cinnamomum Balausae H. Lec., the wood of which has the smell of fennel. This tree has been of no importance as a producer of camphor but it may be of interest on account of its essential oil.

3. Cinnamomum Simondii H. Lec. which is very probably the camphor tree worked in Kouang-si. The species C. parthenoxylon Meissn., or false camphor (in Annamite "Vu huong") and C. ilicioides a chevalier (in Annamite "Gu huong") should doubtless be considered as synonyms of C. Simondii H. Lec. and C. balausae H. Lec. To these species should be added C. cecidodaphne var. caniflora.

Besides these camphor yielding trees other plants which furnish similar products may be mentioned, namely:—Blumea balsamifera D. C. (in Annamite "Dai bi" and "Co bang phien") which produces a levorotary borneol which can by oxidation give a levorotary camphor, identical with the camphor of Japan, except as regards rotary power. Another of the Compositæ, resembling an Inula, was found by the writers in the Yeu-the forest and some Chinese merchants have stated that a special essence called "Luc-nhi-Linh" in Chinese, is extracted from it.

The writers deal in a separate chapter with the chemical composition of camphor, its derivatives and the subject of synthetic camphor which is very important in its relation to natural camphor. Regarding synthetic camphor, it is important to note that PROF. SOMMELET of the Paris faculty of chemistry has stated that the product cannot be considered as a medicinal drug because most of the artificial camphors have no action on polarised light, while natural camphor is strongly dextrorotary, but that it can be used for the manufacture of celluloid provided that it is freed from chlorine which remains as an impurity consequent on the use of hydrochlorate of pinene as raw material.

316[MAY, 1923.

The distillation of camphor is very important and the yield is largely proportional to the kind of apparatus used. Thus with the method used in Japan and Formosa and described by DAVIDSON a yield of 2.16 % by weight is obtained. On the other hand with the apparatus of PROF. MORIYA of the College of Agriculture at the University of Tokio an average yield of 4.22 % in addition to a yield of oil of 1 to 1.50 % of the wood used, was obtained. According to this authority a smaller yield of camphor and a larger yield of oil is obtained in summer and the contrary in winter.

Weight distilled kg. Crude Camphor kg. Camphor oil kg.
In Summer 120 2.35 1.60
In Winter 120 3 0.63

During the last few years distillation of the leaves of the camphor tree, which previously was entirely neglected, has become very important and the writers, after having examined and compared the results obtained by men who have studied and inquired into the question, made experiments on samples from Tonkin. On a basis of the smell of bruised leaves, which varies with different trees, they fixed three classes of leaves each of which gave a different yield of camphor. Leaves of the first class, which smelt fairly strongly of camphor when bruised, produced from 0.48 to 0.56 %; those of the second class, which gave out a faint smell of camphor when bruised, yielded from 0.25 to 0.30 %; those of the third class, which smelt like pippins when bruised, gave no trace of camphor. The most favourable area for the growth of the camphor tree stretches from the 20th to the 25th degree of north latitude. In Formosa trees in the mountains give a higher yield than those in the plains; those growing in open places and much exposed to the sun give a higher yield than those which grow under shade in damp valleys.

Heavy, well drained, deeply tilled clay soils suit camphor trees best. The camphor tree requires plenty of potash and lime; in Ceylon 196 lb. of lime and 87 lb. of potash (in the form of the ashes of refuse from the distillation of the leaves) are used per acre.

The germination of the seeds is hastened by immersion in a vessel of tepid water at 25°: this enables the good seeds, which are heavy and sink to the bottom, to be distinguished. The fruit is pulped by means of special iron sieves. This operation facilitates the germination of the seed which takes place 3 months later. When the young plants reach a height of 30-45 cm. they are finally transplanted.

The camphor tree is also propagated by cuttings, by layering and by grafting. In Tonkin the best season for transplanting is from February to March.

The spacing between the young plants varies; it may be:—

  1. 1. 2.40 m. in squares giving about 700 plants per hectare;
  2. 2. 3 m. in squares; about 450 plants per ha.;
  3. 3. plants 1.8° m. apart in rows 4.50 m. apart; about 500 plants per ha.
MAY, 1923.]317

In Tonkin, on good soil, when 3 years old the plants are 2 m. to 2.50 m. high and when 5 or 6 years old they reach a height of 4.50 m.

The leaves are gathered by means of special apparatus.

According to the spacing in the plantations the yield obtained is —

  1. 1. 70 kg. of camphor per ha. in the first type of plantation ;
  2. 2. 45 kg. per ha. in the second ; and
  3. 3. 50 kg. per ha. in the third.

In the course of journeys made in 1920, the writers investigated the camphor resources of various districts in Tonkin (Lang-son, Bacgiang, Thaignuyen and Quang-si) and discovered some trees several centuries old which they describe in their paper.

According to E. GILDEMEISTER and FR. HOFFMANN, the industrial uses of camphor and its derivatives are the following :—

Spirit of Camphor, free of solid camphor, is used as a fuel oil by the poorer classes in Japan. It is also used as a solvent of resin in the manufacture of lacquer. The lamp-black resulting from its combustion is used in the manufacture of Indian-ink.

In Europe, safrol is extracted from essence of camphor and the residual spirit of this preparation has many uses as light or heavy oil of camphor.

Camphor forms part of the composition of celluloid. It is also largely used in pharmacy.

The writers conclude their paper with a reference to the fact that, by the local Government Decree of December 20, 1920, they procured the prohibition of the felling of camphor trees of all ages in Tonkin and they hope that the competent authorities will create a camphor Service whose duties would include :—

  1. 1. The listing and registration, village by village, of the best seed producing camphor trees ;
  2. 2. The collection from these selected trees of seed in sufficient quantity to allow the cultivation of these trees to be spread over as large an area as possible.
  3. 3. The making generally known by means of active propaganda, the various processes of extracting camphor from the leaves.
  4. 4. The management of a certain number of experimental plantations in different districts in order to ascertain the most suitable place for planting on a large scale.

5. The observation and following up of the work that is being done in Formosa in the matter of improving camphor planting and the processes of manufacturing camphor.—INTERNATIONAL SCI. & PRAC. OF AGRIC., Year XIII—No. II.

318[MAY, 1923.]

CHOLAM—SORGHUM.

AN IMPORTANT FODDER CROP.

[Department of Agriculture, Ceylon. Leaflet No. 25.]

Cholam or iringu cholam (Tamil) and iringu (Sinhalese) are the vernacular names of the great millet or sorghum Sorghum vulgare. In recent years this valuable millet has attracted a great deal of attention and has been introduced into Ceylon as a fodder crop. The special excellence of this new fodder lies in its being able to withstand extreme drought. The straw is nutritious and the yield heavy. For the drier parts of Ceylon where there is a scarcity of food for cattle this crop should be of great value.

In India the straw of cholam is used as fodder and its grain as food by a large section of the people. The grain can be made into porridge and other forms of food. The high nourishing value of the grain will be evident from the following figures :—

Varieties.—There are several varieties of sorghum most of which with a few exceptions can be grown both for fodder and grain. Peria manjel cholam, Iringu cholam, Chitrai vellai cholam, Chitrai manjel cholam are some of the notable South Indian varieties. Orange sorgho, Dwarf milo, Dawn kafir, Pink kafir, Feterita, are the chief American varieties, which have been recently introduced into Ceylon.

Of these, Peria manjel cholam is the most popular in India. It grows to an average height of 8 feet and in special cases it has been found to grow to more than 12 feet. The duration of this crop is 4-4½ months. The

MAY, 1923.]319

peculiarity of this variety is that it flowers only during the north-east monsoon. Chittrai cholam grows best as an irrigated crop, attains an average height of 7 feet, and yields heavy crops of sweet and palatable fodder. The American varieties mature quicker, and grow to an average height of 6 feet, yielding straw of good quality.

The following are the results of trials with these varieties carried on in the Experiment Station, Jaffna :—

Soil.—Cholam is grown both in poor and rich soil. Deeply cultivated fertile loams are considered the best for this crop, and can stand any amount of drought. If it is grown on rich land, the yield of grain is as little as the yield of straw is great. Low lands where there is a possibility of water-logging are unsuitable for this crop.

Cultivation.—The land should be ploughed two or three times between March and June. Cattle manure is applied at the rate of 10 cart-loads per acre, and well mixed up with the soil by ploughing. About the latter part of September after the initial rains of the north-east monsoon the land should be again ploughed, and cross-ploughed. The seeds are then sown. If it is exclusively sown for fodder 40-48 lb. is required for an acre, and the seed should be sown broadcast and thickly so that the straw may be thin and fine. If a good out-turn of grain and straw is desired then 20-30 lb. of seed has to be sown. Too much moisture at the time of sowing is prejudicial to the crop and, if there is a continuous rain during the first stages, the crop will be seriously affected and will not be able to withstand drought later on. It may also be grown as an irrigated crop.

Harvesting.—Harvesting is done in India by cutting the entire plant about 4 in. from the ground with serrated sickles. The ears are then cut from the straw, carried in big baskets to the threshing floor and heaped up. The threshing is done by treading by bullocks or by flailing. The grain is winnowed and dried in the sun before it is stored. Stored cholam should be dried occasionally, say once in every month to prevent the attack of weevils. The dry stalks should be stacked and thatched on a raised platform.

320[MAY, 1923.

Diseases and Pests.—Cholam is subject to fungoid diseases, such as "rust" and "smut" specially if the flowering occurs in rainy days. Smut can be prevented by soaking the seeds before sowing in copper sulphate solution. The crop sometimes suffers considerably through the attack of squirrels, parrots, and other birds.

Poisonous Cholam.—Stunted cholam grown under scarcity of rainfall is poisonous to cattle. If it is not possible to irrigate this crop, it should be sown at the commencement of the monsoon so that the scarcity of water at the initial stages of the crop may be avoided. Death among cattle from eating stunted and parched sorghum is common in South India. If the crop fails the best thing a cultivator can do under the circumstances is to burn the crop or use it as fuel.

Extension of Cultivation.—In Ceylon, specially in the drier parts where there is a great scarcity of fodder, a crop such as cholam is an absolute necessity and is bound to be a success. The results of the trials carried on at the Experiment Station, Jaffna, have amply shown that the crop can very well be grown in Jaffna and other parts of the Island, where conditions are similar. An acre of this crop, if cut green, will yield about 20,000 lb. at the first cutting, and another 10,000 lb. at the second and third cuttings. When dried the stalks lose about two-thirds of their weight.

Yields.—If it is grown for grain the average yield of grain is about 700 lb. and dried straw about 6,000—10,000 lb. The yield of grain is about the same as tinai (Salaria italica) and kurakkan, but the yield of straw is six times as great as tinai or kurakkan. Cholam straw is considerably better than paddy straw, and should be given at the rate of 30 lb. per bullock, well chopped up. Thus an acre of this crop is more than enough to feed a pair of bullocks for about 8 months—each bullock being allowed 35 lb. per day, and the grain will be enough to feed a man throughout an year if he is allowed 60 lb. per month.

N. SENATHI RAJA,

Farm Manager, Experiment Station, Jaffna.

BIGGER DAIRY PROFITS BY FEEDING
THE RIGHT COWS.

The records of many thousands of tested cows have been gone over in the last few years by the United States Department of Agriculture. It was found that from the lowest-producing group of cows to the highest-producing group, every jump of 50 lb. in annual butter-fat production was accompanied by an increase of about 16 dollars in income over cost of feed. The average production of the 21,234 cows whose twelve-month records were studied was 6,077 lb. of milk and 240 lb. of butter-fat, or about 50 per cent. more than the average of all the dairy cows in the country. The records show that selection of animals and better methods of feeding raised the average production rapidly during the first year or two that the cow-testing association is in operation, though the figures for subsequent years show smaller gains.—AGRIC. GAZ., N. S. W., VOL. XXXIV, Pt. 4.

During the first ten days of the month the pressure was very uniform throughout the Island and local evening thunderstorms were consequently common. Hail was reported from various inland stations on the 2nd and 6th and damage by lightning was continued on several days notably the 7th. From the 10th to the 17th thunderstorms a mild gradient from the South West which gave vigorous rain along the South West coast but whose very mildness was emphasised both by the way in which the rain failed to spread inland and by the variation in rainfall between different points only a few miles apart along the coast. Waterspouts were noticed on the 16th & 19th, giving morning rain on the 25th a faint South West gradient appeared intermittently

lightning were reported from places as far apart as Puttalam (30th), and Hambagamuwa (22nd).

A number of low country stations in the South West of the Island and reported over 6 inches, on the 24th to 25th and from this day to the end of the month there was a consistent gradient from the South West with low barometer and without much rain, a type of conditions that have frequently occurred during the presence of a storm in the Bay of Bengal and whose cause it would be out of place to discuss here (details are given in the Observatory Bulletin No. 4 pages 6 and 7).

As regards total rainfall for the month the highest occurred in the west of the Southern Province and south of the Western Province, and along a strip of the Kelani Valley running from Avissawella to Pelmadulla and extending eastward from there through the low country south of the main hills. The areas with rainfall above average include those mentioned in the last paragraph with the addition of Mannar, Negombo, Pattipola Welimada, Puttalam, and a line of stations from Maradankadawala to Nalanda. Deficits of more than two inches occurred over at least half the Island while deficits of over 5 inches were common and occurred in most cases immediately to the north or east of the areas that were above their average.

Thus Rayigam (Padukka) Ratnapura, Heli-ela and Ella Wella may be mentioned as stations in deficit immediately north or east of the largest area that was referred to above as being above average: while North-east of the strip of plentiful rain that stretched roughly from Avissawella to Pelmadulla and eastward, there were deficits.
