WEED SEEDS IN MANURES.*

T. PETCH, B.A., B.Sc.,
Botanist and Mycologist.

The following investigations were undertaken to determine whether artificial manure and manure mixtures contained weed seeds capable of germination.

2. The soil used in the experiments was sterilized by boiling in small quantities at a time. It was then left to dry in the laboratory for about three weeks, pulverised at the same time as the soil by heating. The mixed soil and sand was then filled into seed pans, watered, and left for a few days.

3. Samples of the following manures were received from Colombo firms.

Firm A.—Rape cake.

Groundnut cake.

Castor cake from India.

Castor cake from Europe "treated with sulphur."

Firm B.—Castor cake.

Groundnut cake

Rape cake.

Firm C.—Groundnut cake.

Rape cake.

Special selected cast or cake.

Ordinary cast or cake.

4. Samples of these, each weighing 100 grams, were mixed with sterilised sand and then mixed with the top layers of the soil in the seed pans to a depth of about half an inch. The pans were watered, covered with glass plates which were periodically removed for ventilation, and placed near the windows in an empty room in the laboratory. The experiment was continued for three months, without the appearance of any weeds. The control plots (2) which had been treated in the same way, but without the addition of manure were also blank.

5. As it had been suggested that seeds were introduced with the cake manures, but remained dormant until the subsequent application of Basic slag and sulphate of Potash, these, after sterilising by heating, were added to the seed pans under experiment. This treatment did not result in the production of any weeds.

6. Samples of manures were then obtained from several estates. These were as follows:—

Estate A.—Mixture consisting of Groundnut cake, crushed fish, Blood meal, Steamed bones, Nitrate of Potash.

Estate B.—Mixture consisting of Groundnut cake, Blood meal, Steamed Bone dust, Muriate of Potash, Sulphate of Ammonia, Nitrate of Potash, Conc. Superphosphate.

Estate C.—Mixture consisting of Groundnut cake, Blood Meal, Steamed Bone dust, Muriate of Potash, Sulphate of Ammonia, Nitrate of Potash, Conc. Superphosphate.

Estate D.—No. 1. Mixture containing fish, Castor cake, ordinary superphosphate, steamed bones, Bone Meal, Sulphate of Ammonia, Sulphate of Potash.

No. 2. Mixture containing Groundnut cake, Rape cake, Ammonium sulphate, Blood Meal, Steamed Bone Meal, Sulphate of Potash.

These five samples were treated in the same way as the first eleven, with equally negative results.

GEORGE BROWN.—Ed.

356[JUNE, 1923.

7. As it has frequently been stated that weeds can be grown from samples of manure, merely by moistening them and leaving them on the verandah, this rough and ready method of testing was tried. The tests, however, were made in the laboratory to prevent the possibility of wind-borne seeds obtaining access. No weeds grew in any case.

8. After the negative results of the pot trials, the remaining portion of each sample of manure, up to 4 lb. in some cases, was graded by sifting through standard sieves into portions each consisting of particles of approximately equal size, and these portions were examined with a lens for weed seeds. In all cases but one, no weed seeds were found. The exception was Mixture No. 2, Estate D. From two pounds of that mixture, seventy-five weed seeds, apparently sound, were separated. These were subjected to a germination test on damp blotting paper, but all of them proved to be dead.

9. It may be noted that Rape-cake frequently contains fragments of seeds, e.g., halves of leguminous seeds, pieces of grains of barley, which are quite evident on casual inspection. The sifting tests here adopted show that it contains weed seeds also, but so far, these have all turned out to be dead. This latter result agrees with the manufacturers' statement that the oil is extracted from rape seed by a solvent process.

10. The results of all these tests go to prove that the manures in common use do not contain viable weed seeds (i.e., seeds capable of germination). But one must bear in mind the proverbial, impossibility of proving a negative.

11. Several planters have kindly forwarded specimens of the weeds found on manured and unmanured fields respectively, or on fields manured with different mixtures. More specimens are required before any deductions can be made, and information is particularly desired as to which seeds predominate.

12. From the specimens available at present, it may be stated that the weeds complained of are all well-known Ceylon weeds. No new species have been found among the examples sent in. Many of them bear seeds which are distributed by the wind, e.g., Gynura lycopersicifolia, Crepis japonica, Emilia sonchifolia, Ageratum conyzoides, Vernonia Hookeriana, Sonchus oleraceus, etc., but the majority of the species do not. In that particular, however, it is not possible to arrive at any conclusion without information concerning the relative abundance of the various species sent in. Seeds which are distributed by adhering to animals are represented by the common Bidens pilosa and Cynoglossum micranthum.

13. It is particularly noticeable that the weeds especially complained of in up and mid-country districts are known to have been naturalised in the Nuwara Eliya district for many years. There seems to be no doubt that these weeds are now spreading on. This fact,—that the "new" weeds have been derived from higher elevations—goes far to disprove the idea that they have been introduced with manures. The sow thistle and chickweed are examples of weeds which are extending their range downwards.

14. A few particular cases may be noted in the present report. A more detailed study of the common weeds will be made as time permits.

15. The weed which is said to follow an application of Basic slag in the low-country is Peperomia Frasei. This is a very common weed, with a succulent stem and leaves, which dies down in the dry season. It is a native of Tropical America and could not be introduced with Basic slag. It may grow better on soil manured with Basic slag than elsewhere, but that point can only be decided by experiment.

16. Scoparia dulcis, usually known as coriander weed, is common in low-country districts. This is a South American plant which was first noticed about Galle in 1871. TRIMEN recorded in 1895 that it was a common

JUNE, 1923.]357

weed by roadsides in the south of the Island. It appears to be extending its range upwards and is now fairly common at Peradeniya.

17. Cardamine subumbellata—"Mustard and Cress"—which appears to be one of the chief "new" weeds is a native of Ceylon. THWAITES stated that it grew above 4000 ft. TRIMEN gave its description as "Montane Zone, in open places, rather common." It seems to have spread widely during recent years. One Superintendent writes that he has been resident in Dimbula for over 30 years but never saw this weed before 1907.

18. Cardamine subumbellata and Gnaphalium indicum (wild mignnette) are said to always follow an application of standard mixture on one estate. TRIMEN noted that the latter had recently become a common weed on estates in the hill district, having apparently been introduced about 1880.

19. The sow thistle (Sonchus spp) was stated by THWAITES to be a common weed in the Central Provinces before 1860. It appears to be extending its range in both directions.

20. Though it does not come within the scope of this Report, it may be noted for general information that the bulbs of Oxalis may be destroyed by spraying them with liquid fuel. One of the difficulties in dealing with Oxalis is the disposal of the bulbs after they are dug out. If they are deposited in a pit, and sprayed with liquid fuel they die. This method cannot be used for killing growing Oxalis among tea, as the oil kills or injures all plants. In an experiment at Hakgala in which a patch Oxalis was sprayed with liquid fuel, all the plants then above ground were killed. The young bulbs in the soil were, however, not touched and are now producing new plants, so that a second application will be necessary. A strong castor plant on the same plot was killed but it remains to be seen whether a young tree growing in the same place is affected.

THE BASIC SLAG PROBLEM.

A recent issue of the JOURNAL OF THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE OF SOUTH AFRICA contains an article on this subject from the pen of CHAS. F. JURITZ M.A., D.Sc., F.I.C., which we reproduce below:—

DR. JURITZ says:—"Three types of basic slag are obtainable under present conditions. They are:—

1. High-grade Basic Slag.—This contains a total of from 15 to 19 per cent. of total phosphoric oxide of from 80 to 95 per cent. solubility. That is to say, the slag may contain from 12 to 18 per cent. of citric-soluble phosphoric oxide.

2. Open-hearth Basic Slag, which contains between 7 and 15 per cent. of total phosphoric oxide of similar proportionate solubility to that of the first type; hence this variety of slag contains from 6 to 14 per cent. of citric-soluble phosphoric oxide.

3. Open-hearth Fluorspar Slag, containing the same proportion of total phosphoric oxide as type 2, namely, from 7 to 15 per cent, but of lower solubility, moreover, has a very wide range, extending from 6 to 50 per cent. of the total, so that apparently this fluorspar slag may contain as little as 0.4 per cent. of citric-soluble phosphoric oxide, or as much as 7.5 per cent.

Of these three types of slag, the first is the rapidly disappearing remainder of the basic slag of former days, and as DR. ROBERTSON remarks, agriculturists must face the probability of its complete disappearance. The second type is, however, considered to be of equal value with the first per unit of phosphoric oxide, but its content of phosphoric oxide is very much lower. The third type, although resembling the other two in appearance, is far inferior

358[JUNE, 1923.

to these, and may, in some cases, be practically worthless, so that purchasers of basic slag will have to watch their guarantees most rigidly in the future. It is not known how much of this third type of slag is on the market to-day, but there is little doubt that we shall have more to do with it later on.

In the United Kingdom the demand for basic slag on the part of farmers has increased tremendously during recent years, but the production of the article has by no means kept pace with this demand. The annual demand, a couple of years before the War, was just over a quarter of a million tons; it is now about half a million tons, and is likely to increase. The production was 400,000 tons per annum before the War, and rose to 700,000 tons some four years ago, but has since dropped to substantially less than the amount demanded. Under those circumstances it would be idle for South Africa to expect any basic slag from Great Britain; export of the article from that country has, in fact, been prohibited except under license.

As regards the possibility of South Africa importing basic slag from the continent of Europe, the following paragraph from the second ad interim report of the British departmental committee is significant:

“In view of the likelihood that the quality of basic slag manufactured on the continent may decrease as it has in the United Kingdom, following upon a similar change in process of manufacture, and further that the demands of farmers abroad may increase, it would be unwise for farmers in this country to rely to any serious extent on importation.”

It may be mentioned that possibilities of altering the composition of the slag produced, by introducing minor modifications into the blast furnace procedure, have been under consideration by the departmental committee, but as experiments in this direction fall outside the potentialities of the South African people, there is no need to dwell on them here. We can, nevertheless, carry on field trials in this country, and such investigation is actually in progress here, but even in the United Kingdom there are difficulties to be overcome before the various points presented can be regarded as settled.

The field experiments undertaken in the United Kingdom showed that the open-hearth fluorspar slag was less effective than the more highly soluble types. At the same time the fluorspar slag was of considerable value, and it was thought that, on sour soil, with a high rainfall, it might closely approximate to the other two types. On the other hand, its inferiority was clearly marked where the soil was not decidedly sour and the rainfall low.

When basic slag fails us we naturally look to ground mineral phosphates for aid. These rocks are also of a basic character and their phosphatic-content is usually high, but their citric-solubility is proportionately much lower than that of basic slag. The following types of rock

JUNE, 1923.]359

phosphate have been specially mentioned :—

phoric Oxide. Phosphoric Oxide.

The result of the experiments carried on under the auspices of the British departmental committee all agreed in showing rock phosphates to possess a much higher fertilising value than has hitherto been admitted. On sour soils and where the rainfall is high, there is a certain amount of evidence which suggests that they may even prove "superior to the best grades of basic slag." In every experiment they were found to be more effective than the open-hearth fluor spar slags.

For direct application the opinion, based on the experimental results, seemed to be that, of all the rock phosphates, Gafsa was the most suitable, and there was evidence that on sweet soil, or where the rainfall is low, the more soluble types of North African phosphates, namely Gafsa, Egyptian, Algerian, and Tunisian, are superior to the richer, less soluble and harder types such as Florida Pebble.

INDIAN SCIENTIFIC AGRICULTURIST, Vol. 4, No. 4.

SOIL NITROGEN AND LIVE-STOCK FARMING.

Interesting comparative experiments in live-stock farming and the direct utilisation of various crops have been carried out at the Agricultural Experiment Station, Wooster, Ohio. The rotation followed is maize, soybeans, wheat, and clover. Each area receives 2 tons of ground limestone and 700 lb. of 16 per cent. acid phosphate per acre, per rotation. In the first system all the crops except wheat are fed to live-stock or passed into the manure as bedding, and the manure is applied to the maize crop; in the second, the maize, soybeans, and wheat are removed and sold, the hay and straw being left upon or returned to the land; the clover is not harvested, but allowed to stand until ploughed under the following spring. The experiments show the superiority of live-stock farming, which increases the crop production and the nitrogen content of the soil.—

AGRIC. GAZ. of N.S.W., VOL. XXXIV, Pt. 4.

PESTS AND DISEASES.

PRELIMINARY REPORT ON BROWN BAST EXPERIMENTS IN MALAYA.

A. SHARPLES. A.R.C.S.. D.I.C. Mycologist

and

L. LAMBOURNE. F.R.H.S. Superintendent of Govt. Plantations.

A previous review* by the senior author treats of the early work carried out in Malaya to find a casual agent for Brown Bast. Some attention is devoted to the published works of various authors, more especially to that of RANDS† whose work in Java was contemporary with and paralleled that carried out in Malaya. The recent work of SANDERSON and SUTCLIFFE‡, BRYCE§, BATESON|| and FARMER and HORNE¶ was briefly considered; the latest work to appear is a detailed treatise by KEUCHENIUS** working in Sumatra

Experimental work on Brown Bast was taken up by the writers in 1919. At this time the physiological nature of the disease was recognised by most authorities working on the subject and the evidence in favour was overwhelming. More light upon the problem could be obtained only by working upon the individual factors influencing the incidence and development of the disease. This was obviously a matter for field experiments.

The way was opened up by RANDS' (loc. cit) heavy tapping experiments which showed that a high percentage of trees developed Brown Bast when tapped six times a day on three superimposed quarter cuts. BEL CRAVE adapted the heavy tapping to Malayan needs by substituting a full spiral cut, once daily, as sufficient to produce an appreciable percentage of Brown Bast in a few months' time. The experiments comparing Daily, Alternate Daily and Every Third Daily on \frac{1}{4} Spiral, \frac{1}{2} Spiral and Full Spiral cuts published in the review mentioned above were in hand when the senior writer took over.

In this first series of experiments the number of Brown Bast trees was verified by MR. F. W. SOUTH, Chief Agricultural Inspector, F.M.S. and S.S., while the yield figures were later worked out and analysed by the writers. The analysis presented many interesting features and further field experiments were planned to test as many points as could be conveniently dealt with.

* SHARPLES, A.—A consideration of recent work on the Brown Bast problem.—MALAYAN AGRICULTURAL JOURNAL, June 1922, Vol. X, No. 6.

† RANDS, R. P.—De Bruine Binnenbastziekte Van Hevea brasiliensis: Archief Von Rubber Cultuur in Ned. Indies 1919.

‡ SANDERSON, A. P. and SUTCLIFFE, H.—Brown Bast, Rubber Growers' Association 38, Eastcheap, London, E.C. 3.

§ BRYCE, G.—Bull. No. 28, Department of Agriculture, Ceylon, October 1916.

|| BATESON, E.—The Tapping of the Para Rubber Tree.—Bull, No. 23, Department of Agriculture, F.M.S.

¶ FARMER, J. B. and HORNE, A. S.—Phloem Necrosis, Brown Bast disease in Hevea brasiliensis. Ann. of Botany, Vol. XXXV, No. CXXXIX, July 1921.

** KEUCHENIUS, P. E.—Die Rindenbraune der Hevea Brasiliensis. Cent. for Bacteriologie, Parasitenkunde und Infektionskrankheiten Zweite Abteilung, Ad. 55/1921 Heft 1/4

JUNE, 1923.]361

This article will deal briefly with the more important points observed full details being reserved for a final publication. The first series of experiments indicated:—

(1) That comparative Brown Bast experiments could not be conveniently dealt with using the tapping systems commonly in vogue. A single daily cut on a quarter or half of the trees does not give an amount of Brown Bast sufficiently large to lead to any definite conclusions. Therefore drastic tapping systems have to be resorted to.

(2) Comparative results on Full Spiral tapping with different intervals, i.e., Daily, Alternate Daily and Every Third Day, showed a large percentage of Brown Bast trees in the Daily plots, a greatly reduced number in the Alternate Daily and a still further reduction in the Every Third Day plot. The Alternate Daily plots had about 400 trees each, the rest approximately 550 trees. The Brown Bast figures after seven months were:—

Daily. Alt. Daily. Every Third Day.
102 42 24
20 % 10 % 5 %

The differences are sufficiently large to warrant the statement that "On the same length of cut, Alternate Daily tapping is superior to Daily tapping from the point of view of Brown Bast, while a further improvement can be effected by extending the intervals between tapping."

(3) The yield figures are suggestive. For example total yields from the daily \frac{1}{2} Spiral plot = 1019.94 lb., from the Alternate Daily \frac{1}{2} Spiral = 523.14 lb. and Every Third Day \frac{1}{2} Spiral = 383.67 lb. A rough comparison can be made by taking the Daily \frac{1}{2} Spiral yield as standard and then multiplying the yield figures of the other two plots by two and three respectively. This gives

Daily \frac{1}{2} Spiral Alt. Daily \frac{1}{2} Spiral Every Third Day \frac{1}{2} Spiral
1019.94 523.14 \times 2 = 1046.28 383.67 \times 3 = 1151.01

These figures, taken over 7 months, fall within expectations and the yield figures of the Alternate Daily \frac{1}{4} cut and Every Third Day \frac{1}{4} cut are of a similar nature with reference to the Daily \frac{1}{4} cut. With the full Spiral system the final comparative figures show large differences as follows:—

Daily F.S. Alt. Daily F.S. Every Third Day F.S.
2802.25 2802.25 \times 2 = 5604.50 2802.25 \times 3 = 8406.75

These figures if supported by further evidence are very significant. They indicate the lack of exact knowledge regarding the response made by Hevea brasiliensis when tapping systems outside the ordinary routine are in operation. This point is of considerable importance in relation to the Brown Bast problem, for many investigators are in accord in regarding this affection as a wound response due to over-tapping. If high-yielding is a factor of importance, the results also indicate the possibility of yields being limited by the development of a high percentage of Brown Bast. In the writer's opinion it appears probable that according to type of soil and general growth conditions in any area the yield is sharply limited. Below this limit the amount of Brown Bast developed is of little importance from a practical stand-point but above the limit there is a tremendous percentage increase disproportionate with the increased yield. This point must be taken into consideration in the general question of obtaining high-yielding strains of Hevea Brasiliensis by bud-grafting and selection. The Brown Bast problem, in fact, apart from its scientific interest, is of little general importance during a period when restricted yields obtained by increasing the length of time between tapping, i.e., Daily to Alternate Daily, are the rule. The Brown Bast problem becomes of primary importance when considered as a limiting factor in the question of high yields.

362[JUNE, 1923.

The above first series of experiments indicated other points of interest. A sudden jump in number of Brown Bast cases during certain months had to be confirmed or otherwise; in view of this peculiarity it appears that to obtain a guiding line as to the behaviour of different plots with reference to Brown Bast development at least three months previous heavy tapping is necessary. These points were confirmed by many later experiments so that subsequently the experimental plots were subjected to three months' preliminary tapping on a Full Spiral, once daily.

In the second series of experiments 410 trees were taken and after the three months preliminary tapping were divided into blocks of approximately 50 trees. The small plots were then put under systems with varying lengths of cut from \frac{1}{2} Spiral to Full Spiral. These trees were 12 years old : The trees were opened up for tapping during the fourth year at 24 inches from the ground on a single V and in order to obtain time for bark renewal the second period was carried from the 36 inches to the 24 inches mark when the opposite V panel had been tapped. To get tappable bark of the same age our experimental tapping had to be carried out in virgin bark over the 36 inches mark. The more important results are mentioned below.

(1) The sudden rise followed by a long rest period indicated previously was confirmed by these and all later experiments. The 1921 experiments supported the experience gained in 1919 in that the months March to August were quiescent Brown Bast months. This suggested the possibility of wintering and low rainfall both influencing the results. However, 1922 showed May, June and July as heavy Brown Bast months and these are usual months of low rainfall which are fairly constant, year by year, in this district. As far as observations have been carried there is some difficulty in associating any external factors with the results obtained.

(2) Another notable feature in this series of experiments was the stoppage of the extension of Brown Bast at definite places marked by the different ages of tapped bark. As indicated above, the vertical sequence from above downwards was in virgin bark—this passed into renewed bark two years old at the 36 inches level and this panel passed into 4-6 years old renewed bark at the 24 inches mark. To record briefly—out of 410 trees, 133 developed Brown Bast. Of these, no extension took place after tapping was stopped in 40 trees. In another 20 trees the Brown Bast stopped at the 36 inches mark (the junction between the virgin and the youngest renewed bark); in 47 trees the Brown Bast extended to the 24 inches mark (the junction between the old and young renewed bark), and in 19 trees the affection extended to the base of the tree.

These results are of both practical and theoretical importance and have been confirmed by subsequent experiment. Details must be left to a final paper.

(3) Special importance is assigned to a plot of 44 trees, tapped on a \frac{7}{8} Spiral, the heaviest system apart from the Full Spiral. While the neighbouring seven plots were responding to experiment in a normal manner this plot was obviously abnormal. From November, 1920 to August, 1921 only two Brown Bast trees were reported. In September, 1921 a sudden increase of six Brown Bast trees was reported.

The abnormally long quiescent period might have considerable significance and tapping on this plot was continued. A control plot was obtained by continuing the tapping on one of the normal plots which had been tapped on a \frac{3}{4} Spiral.

JUNE, 1923.]363

From September, 1921 to December 1922 the abnormal plot developed Brown Bast in a normal manner. The change was correlated with a sudden increase in average tree yield. This correlation is supported by figures taken over a considerable period of time, the curves for average tree yield and percentage increase in Brown Bast cases conform closely to one another. The conclusion must be drawn that Brown Bast is closely associated with the question of high yields and it is almost certain that this affection must act as a limiting factor in the question of high-yielding trees.

The appearance of a number of Brown Bast cases is so sudden that it may be classed under the phenomena dependent on "trigger action," i.e. a sudden release followed by immediate effects. In the space of 24 hours the typical Brown Bast symptoms as known from field observations, will become obvious on numerous trees which had shown none the previous day. A most important question to be answered is "What changes take place in the physiological processes leading up to this sudden release?" It appears most probable that the Brown Bast affection is to be considered as an exhaustion process. Accepting this point of view, it has been possible to connect up many isolated observations; further, laboratory observations, previously contradictory, fall into line when this basis is utilised.

Tapping experiments have been carried out to test other points of interest, such as specific immunity, permanency of yield in good and bad yielders and their behaviour towards Brown Bast development, etc. Details of these must be left for a final article.

Another line has been taken in hand recently owing to FARMER and HORNE's researches on specimens sent from the Middle East to England for examination. These investigators describe a breaking-down of the sieve-tubes and suggest this as an incipient stage in Brown Bast. This type of abnormal behaviour is included under the term of Phloem Necrosis typified in other cases by lignification of the cellulose walls of the sieve-tubes, lignification of the sieve-tube walls is a common feature in the tapped bark of Hevea brasiliensis, moreover in trees which could not be suspected of Brown Bast. The findings of FARMER and HORNE have been given some prominence in an article in NATURE by DR. S. E. CHANDLER but the senior writer, having had this particular phase of sieve-tube changes under observation for the last three years would accept their suggestions with considerable reserve. Plots of trees, with and without lignified sieve-tubes have now been selected and similar tapping experiments to those described will be carried out to determine which develop Brown Bast most quickly. The results, up-to-date, show that trees originally non-lignified become lignified after being tapped for some time.

The line taken throughout this investigation has been with reference to the disease factor influencing future policy on Malayan plantations. Big claims have recently been made, with reference to increased yields per acre, for trees developed by bud-grafting from known high yielding trees. A forward policy is certainly desirable but the attendant risks should be fully realised,

364[JUNE, 1923.

Apart from the considerable body of evidence obtained during the present investigation which, at least, cannot be said to favour the policy urged by the supporters of bud-grafting, the general position at the present time is seldom clearly presented. If excessive yielding results in exhaustion, then high yielders will tend to show this effect sooner than average yielders. Further, this feature must be closely connected with some difference in physiological activity and the higher the yields the greater this difference becomes. Plant morphology is now recognised as an expression of physiological activity and small changes in the latter may produce far-reaching effects in plant structure. In the case of Hevea brasiliensis in Malayan plantations, an insufficient development of leaf cuticle would give many organisms a chance of effecting an entry and invading the leaf tissues. Positive evidence to this effect has already been obtained in Malaya. On one estate where bud-grafts were successfully established on three year old stocks, the leaves of the graft were badly attacked by several species of fungi usually saprophytic. This resulted owing to the leaves being too abundantly supplied with nutrient material from a root system which previously had supplied many thousand times the number of leaves. The leaves of these bud-grafted plants were pale-coloured, thin and obviously deficient in cuticle when compared with the usual type of rubber leaf.

Should the optimistic yields from bud-grafts materialise, the trees certainly will have physiological activities of a different order to those obtaining in the present day plantations. The direction will be towards accelerated vital activities, i.e. transpiration, respiration and absorption. Strong cuticular development is not usually associated with active transpiration, and it is possible that high-yielding bud-grafts may tend to develop less resistant cuticle.

At the present time there is a very dangerous organism epiphytic on rubber leaves which with little encouragement, would be able to cause much damage if it could penetrate into the leaf tissues, and it is doubtful if much could be done to check its activities. This parasitic alga has been long known as the cause of serious losses on Tea and Cloves; recently the senior writer visited Sarawak to investigate a disease of Pepper Vines which had been responsible for a reduction of exports from $2,733,301 in 1903 to $712,122 in 1920. The cause of this disease was the same parasitic alga, Cephaleuros mycoidea (Karsten). Again, rubber planting in British and Dutch Guiana has been rendered unprofitable by the attacks of a leaf fungus and it is more than possible that this organism may have a close relation in the Middle East capable of doing damage under favourable conditions.

The point to be clearly recognised is that the margin of safety is small and that exceedingly large risks are attached. It is for these reasons that we claim that the published bud-grafting results are insufficient upon which to base any definite policy, that neglect of vital factors in the published results calls for strong comment from a scientific point of view and that no great care has ever been taken to point the attendant risks. The admission that in Malaya there has been no opportunity to carry out experimental bud-grafting for ourselves does not prevent us calling attention to the shortcomings in the records presented by the published results relating to bud-grafting.—MALAYAN AGRIC. JOURN. Vol. XI, No. 2.

JUNE, 1923.]365

ROT-PROOF PAPER FOR CUT-WORMS.

The protection of young seedlings from cut-worm attack up-country has been the subject of investigation during the past few years and as attention was drawn in the PLANTERS' CHRONICLE to experiments made with rot-proof paper obtainable from the Dux Chemical Solutions Company, Limited, it was decided to have trials made in Ceylon.

This rot-proof paper has been experimented with with great success in Kenya Colony as a protecting collar for young coffee plants, which are apt to be destroyed by cut-worms. This paper which is in two grades D one ply and D two ply, is bent in the form of a ring and is pressed down round the plant. The cut-worms are unable to attack the paper shields, as they contain a certain amount of insoluble copper, which also prevents the paper from rotting.

EXPERIMENTS IN CEYLON.

Experiments were carried out with these papers by the Curator at the Hakgala Botanic Gardens, who reports:—"Pieces of the two kinds of paper each measuring 4 in. \times 2 in. were placed round seedlings of Antirrhinums, which are usually badly attacked by cut-worms. These collars were allowed to remain from January 21st to 5th April when they were removed as the plants were then large enough to withstand the attacks of cut-worms. The collars have withstood 11.79 inches of rain; and rain was heaviest in March. Throughout February when there was practically no rain, the beds containing the protected plants were watered regularly every evening. It has been observed that D. 1 ply paper has not stood the test so well as the D. 2 ply, which was practically unaffected by weather conditions. The experience of the Senior Coffee Officer, Kenya Colony, confirms the results obtained here that D. 1 ply paper is not quite satisfactory."

MR. J. J. NOCK, Curator, Hakgala, is of opinion that for seedlings of annuals any stiff paper is suitable as a protection against cut-worms, as it is only in the early stages that the seedlings are attacked. By the time such papers have rotted, rendering them useless, the seedlings are generally sufficiently matured to withstand the attacks of cut-worms; for the protection of vegetables, such as beetroot, lettuce, etc., rot-proof paper would certainly be useful, as these plants are attacked during all stages.

366[JUNE, 1923.

GENERAL.

THE LOSS OF CAFFEINE DURING
TEA-FIRING.

P. A. KEILLER,

Chemist to the Commercial Company, Colombo.

DR. HAROLD H. MANN, writing on "The Fermentation of Tea" for the Indian Tea Association in 1906, mentions that he found a white deposit on the roof and walls round the drying machines in a factory in the Duars, and that this deposit was found to contain 45.86 per cent of caffeine. He does not state what type of drier was in use.

My attention was first called to the volatilisation of caffeine in tea driers by MR. M. who pointed out a white deposit on the ceiling-boards above the Tilting-Tray Drier in a tea factory. This deposit did not appear over the Desiccator alongside. On the following day both MR. M. and myself found a similar deposit over the Tilting-Tray Drier in another factory, and again no such deposit was visible over the Desiccator. I took samples of both these deposits and found them to consist chiefly of caffeine.

Some time later I visited another factory, where only Desiccators are used, and noticed what appeared to be a faint deposit of a similar nature. There was not sufficient, however, for a sample to be taken. Some time later the Superintendent of this factory sent me a sample which he had collected but its response to tests for caffeine were faint and doubtful. A glass plate was then suspended just below the ceiling where the deposit occurred, and the plate was subsequently sent to me. It was then covered with a fairly heavy deposit which looked like ordinary tea fluff, a sample of which from a different part of the factory was sent at the same time.

I determined the percentage of caffeine in the two samples, and found as follows :—

Caffeine.
Deposit on glass ... 3.45 per cent.
Ordinary tea fluff ... 3.18 ,,

The amount of caffeine in Ceylon tea varies from 3.2 per cent. to 4.6 per cent. so that it is evident that the deposit on the glass is merely tea fluff and contains no more caffeine than would be expected in this material. Although the first two factories' samples were not analysed, there was no comparison between the response they gave to the caffeine test and that given by the third factory's samples. The two former showed abundance of caffeine, while the latter gave only a faint response.

JUNE, 1923.]367

If caffeine is driven off from tea during firing, the position and amount of the deposit, or indeed its appearance at all outside the drier, must depend on several factors unconnected with the drier itself. There must be a suitable surface at a sufficiently low temperature on which the caffeine can be deposited. If the discharge is close to the ceiling the deposit will probably form there, but if the distance between them is great there may be a very light and scarcely visible deposit. Similarly, open doors or windows may cause sufficient draught to distribute the discharge throughout the drying room so that no appreciable deposit appears in any one place. On the other hand, the construction of the drier may be such that caffeine is volatilised in one part of it and deposited in another without appearing outside at all. This deposition inside the machine probably always happens whether there is an outside deposit or not, and I have since learnt that a white coating (presumably caffeine) is very common in the ducts and flues of all types of driers, including the Desiccator.

It does not follow, therefore, that because a deposit does not appear outside a machine that no caffeine is being driven off from the tea. It is fairly certain, however, that where an outside deposit does appear, more is being lost than where complete deposition takes place inside the machine itself, and an outside deposit indicates a higher temperature in the exhaust and therefore in all parts of the machine, or a stronger draught, or a combination of these two conditions. It seems likely, too, that where these latter conditions prevail, there will be a greater loss of other volatile constituents such as essential oil than where temperature is lower or draught less as indicated by the absence of a noticeable deposit of caffeine outside the machine. To a certain extent, therefore, the appearance of a caffeine deposit outside is an indication of other and more important losses.

There is no doubt that in the three factories investigated the Desiccator does not drive caffeine outside the machine to any appreciable extent, and from the fact that the Desiccator is acknowledged to produce a better quality tea than driers of the type of Sirocco Pressure Driers, we may reasonably assume that the absence of caffeine outside is characteristic of the Desiccator and bears a relation to the quality of tea made by it.

I have not been able to find any further cases of caffeine deposits from other types of driers. As pointed out, the conditions determining their appearance are many, and in the factories which I have had an opportunity of visiting lately there were no outstanding cases of a deposit which could be sampled, but there is little doubt in my mind that in any type of drier where the temperature is high and the draught rapid for the purpose of obtaining a large output, caffeine will be carried out by the exhaust and deposited where conditions are favourable. Machines of this type admittedly produce teas of inferior quality to those fired in a Desiccator and the up-draught Sirocco, a machine without a fan. In this latter machine the

368[JUNE, 1923.

movement of air is slow and there is less liability for volatile substances to be driven off than where a fan is used, but its output is correspondingly low. The use of a fan enables the output of the Desiccator to be increased while the internal arrangement of the machine minimises loss of volatile substances including caffeine. In large driers, the Pressure Drier and Paragon types, a large output is obtained by quick drying with powerful fans, but with loss of quality by the volatilisation of the constituents which are responsible for flavour. In these machines the hot air passes through several layers of moist tea before coming in contact with the tea which has just been put in and which, therefore, should get the driest and hottest air rather than the wettest and coolest, and it does not seem to be possible with any type of drier at present on the market to combine the retention of quality of the Desiccator with the large output of the Pressure Drier, but this defect is common to all machines except the Desiccator and up-draught Sirocco.

In connection with the loss of caffeine, it is interesting to note that caffeine is only very slightly volatile at 212^{\circ}\text{F}. It is usually stated that no loss of weight occurs on heating caffeine to this temperature, but it has been established that minute crystals are deposited as a film on a cold surface under these conditions. At 248^{\circ}\text{F} a very gradual but distinct loss in weight occurs, indicating sensible volatilisation at this temperature. These facts make it probable that where a distinct deposit of caffeine occurs outside a drying machine the temperature, on some of the trays at least, is probably nearer 250^{\circ}\text{F} than the 180^{\circ} or 200^{\circ}\text{F} at which the firing is supposed to be done.

Unlike essential oils, which volatilise much more quickly in presence of water vapour than they do when dry, caffeine is not affected in this way by the presence of water. If the temperature of the tea in the drier is raised much above, say, 220^{\circ}\text{F}, caffeine will volatilise whether the tea be wet or dry, but the loss of essential oil under these conditions will be greater the more moisture there is in the tea at the time.

Minutes of the fourteenth meeting of the Estates Products Committee of the Board of Agriculture held at the Experiment Station, Peradeniya, at 2-30 p.m. on Thursday, May 10th, 1923.

Present :—The Director of Agriculture (CHAIRMAN), the Government Entomologist, the Government Agricultural Chemist, the Assistant Botanist and Mycologist, the Acting Assistant Entomologist, the Government Agent, Central Province, Kandy, the Government Agent, Northern Province, Jaffna, Lieut.-Col. MR. A. P. WALDOCK pointed out that it had been recorded on the first page of the minutes of the previous meeting that the jât had influenced the yield to the extent of 50% per cwt., the words "per cwt" were deleted. The minutes were then taken as read and confirmed.

Agenda Item I. Progress Report Experiment, Station, Peradeniya.

The CHAIRMAN commented on a few items of interest in the report. He said that as regards Shot-hole Borer attack, the tea under Dadap shade was less affected.

The vacancies in the budded rubber plot had been supplied; the plants are shooting well and making good progress. The cacao crop was less than last year and the percentage of fungus pods high. He was of opinion that this was so on all estates.

The Entomologist had found slight traces of injury to coconut leaflets by the coconut caterpillar.

JUNE, 1923.]371

MR. COLES referring to rubber asked whether it was not too late for the district planting rubber in December.

The CHAIRMAN said that the plants were budded in October and had to be planted out at once or kept for a year. It was decided to take a chance.

With regard to Shot-hole Borer MR. GARRICK said the Albizzia plot was cut 2 years ago and there has been no shade for the whole year.

MR. WALDOCK asked if the Entomologist had noticed any caterpillars on the coconut branches.

The Entomologist said he made a careful inspection but found no living caterpillars.

Agenda Item 2. Effects of Manures on Healing of Galleries made by Shot-hole Borer.

The CHAIRMAN in introducing the next item said that a preliminary report had been prepared by Messrs. JARDINE and GADD on the results of the effect of a general mixture on a plot on Sarnia estate. The report will duly appear in the next issue of the TROPICAL AGRICULTURIST. He asked MR. JARDINE briefly to review the report.

MR. JARDINE reviewed the report and stated that although final conclusions cannot be formulated until all the examinations are complete, the following conclusions are offered tentatively :—

1. The application of a complete manurial mixture at the rate of 350 lb. or 550 lb. per acre at the end of the first year resulted in an increase in the rate of healing of the Shot-hole borer galleries and a corresponding diminution in the number of open galleries.

2. The proportion of empty galleries and the mean number of inmates of the occupied galleries was not definitely affected by the application of the manure.

3. The application at the rate of 550 lb. of general mixture per acre gave no better results than the smaller application of 350 lb. per acre.

4. The application of manures has little, if any, direct effect on the shot-hole borer insect itself. It, however, increases the vigour of the bushes which are thereby enabled to repair more rapidly the damage done by the insect. Consequently where the intensity of the shot-hole borer attack is judged by the damage done to the bushes it would appear that a reduction in the shot-hole borer attack follows the application of manures.

The CHAIRMAN : This, gentlemen, is a preliminary report. The experiments are being continued and further data are being collected, but the data which were available up to the present time, I think, are sufficiently conclusive to place before you for your consideration. MR. JARDINE has briefly reviewed how the experiments were carried out and the conclusions which have been drawn from the figures secured. The figures have been very carefully checked and very carefully worked further with a view to ascertaining a probable error of the experiments and MR. GADD has collaborated with MR. JARDINE in the interpretation of the results. The results are now open for discussion.

MR. R. G. COOMBE enquired whether the experiments were a continuation of the old series, or whether they were new experiments.

The CHAIRMAN explained that these experiments did not refer to the series of which a bulletin had been issued by MESSRS. JEPSON and GADD at the end of last year. This was a new series conducted on another plot dealing with the estate mixture.

372[JUNE, 1923.

MR. GEO. BROWN said that in the individual manures the sulphate of ammonia would have had an effect on the bush quite different from the lime. The one would tend to make the bush sappy and induce vegetative growth while the other would render the wood hard. What was the relative value of each component.

The CHAIRMAN replied that the best results had been obtained by sulphate of ammonia, then nitrate of soda, followed by lime. There was a firm belief among planters that the application of manures improved the bushes after an attack of shot-hole borer and it was, therefore, necessary, to find out whether this was so.

MR. A. P. WALDOCK asked whether the manure was a pure estate mixture, or one recommended by the Department. He thought that a mixture consisting of 250 lb. fish manure, 60 lb. sulphate of ammonia and 40 lb. muriate of potash rather unusual for a tea estate.

The CHAIRMAN : This is the estate mixture.

MR. WALDOCK : It is spoken of as a general mixture and again as a complete mixture.

MR. GADD explained that the terms "complete" and "general" were synonymous.

The CHAIRMAN : Arising out of these results, it is proposed by the Department to carry out further experiments on similar lines nearer to Peradeniya, and we have had an offer of land from New Peradeniya Estate which appears to be suitable for the continuation of the experiments. It would be easier for us to supervise them and secure additional figures for the opinion of this Committee. The matter that has to be decided to-day is what mixture we shall apply as the general mixture and with a view to starting a discussion MR. JARDINE has suggestions to offer which are based on recommendations by MR. BAMBER. I would be glad if the Committee would consider these suggestions.

MR. JARDINE said that they had made their best endeavour to obtain a "representative" manure, and the following mixture had been suggested :—

Fish guano 280 lb.
Groundnut cake 160 ,,
Steamed bone meal 30 ,,
Superphosphate 40 ,,
Sulphate of Ammonia 60 ,,
Nitrate of Potash 40 ,,
Sulphate of Potash 40 ,,
Total 650 lb.

This would give a minimum of 42.3 lb. of nitrogen; 33.4 lb. phosphoric acid; 33.2 lb. potash.

After discussion the meeting decided that this general mixture might be adopted, the time of application being left to the Department.

Agenda Item 3. Increase of Lecanium Viridi on Tea and Methods of Prevention and Cure.

MR. JOHN HORSFALL in introducing the subject said that the Haputale Planters' Association had asked him to bring up this matter but he had since heard from DR. HUTSON that an article on the subject had already appeared in the TROPICAL AGRICULTURIST. This report covered his question except for two points. No mention had been made of shade. He wished to know what effect shade had.

DR. HUTSON said that he had no definite information on the point. Possibly the prevalence of shade might encourage parasitic fungus which in

JUNE, 1923.]373

turn would destroy the scale. He had certainly noticed that scale was worse in exposed areas.

MR. HORSFALL'S next question was about bad drainage and shallow root system. He thought that light forking would naturally give rise to a shallow and therefore not very satisfactory root system.

MR. BAMBER disagreed. He thought that during the last two years as a result of considerable leaf fall, a shallow root system over a very large area had been created. On account of that fact the little roots had all grown towards the surface to feed on the humus, caused by the disintegration of the leaf. In regard to forking he would recommend nothing under 8 inches depth,

MR. CAMERON : "May I know whether MR. BAMBER recommends the manure to be applied at a depth of 8 inches."

MR. BAMBER explained that this was not his advice. The fork could be inserted to a depth of 8 inches, the soil to be raised slightly and the manure put in.

The CHAIRMAN : With reference to the first point raised by MR. HORSFALL, it might be of interest to the Committee to know that in Dominica, where there is a very large cultivation of limes the plantations suffer very extensively from scale attacks. The only practical methods of handling the scale was to plant Bengal beans which is a very vigorous climber. It climbs over the trees and it is left there for a year after which it is cut off and the trees are found to be cleaned of scale by the parasitic fungus which had developed in the shade. It is apparent from this illustration that shade may induce conditions which are favourable to the spread of parasitic fungi.

DR. BRYCE said that with regard to the effect of parasitic fungi on the scale, the general tendency at the present day was to place no reliance on the parasitic fungi in regard to its controlling effects on scale. It is not possible to increase the infestation of the fungus by any method that has been hitherto tried by Mycologists.

Agenda Item 4. The Probable incidence of Disease in Tea from the death of Albizzia trees (a) Naturally, (b) as the result of over lopping.

MR. E. C. VILLIERS, who introduced this subject said that his object in bringing up this question was to ascertain the general opinion of the meeting. His enquiry was with reference to old trees. He had been instructed some years ago by his Visiting Agent to cut out all dead and dying Albizzia. He was not at all satisfied that the Albizzia trees were killing out the tea. At any rate the treatment recommended was very drastic on account of the loss of seven or eight tea bushes which were destroyed in the uprooting of the stump of the Albizzia tree. For this reason it was a very costly form of treatment. In several instances the Albizzia died out as the result of excessive lopping by coolies and not from disease ; it tended to make him believe that the incidence of disease or the trees dying had not necessarily induced or attracted disease to the field. Therefore in the case of trees dying by overlapping any such thing as the cutting out of its roots would lead to considerable cost.

He had a further instance of Albizzia dying by "ringing the bark" at the height to which the tree was desired to grow. Only in the case where the rain water had penetrated the bark did the tree die, and then no disease of tea subsequently occurred. He therefore wished to know whether it was really necessary to incur the very heavy cost and risk of losing a lot of tea bushes by uprooting the entire Albizzia tree or dead stump. In other words was it correct to condemn the Albizzia tree as

374[JUNE, 1923.

being the cause of disease or was it not more likely that the disease was present in the ground all the time and that the tea caught it or the Albizzia caught it first.

DR. BRYCE said that he would start with a reply straight away that the disease went from the Albizzia tree to the tea. In many instances if one followed the side roots of the dead Albizzia there would be found to left or to right of such roots lines of dead tea. Wherever there was dead tea, you will find Diplodia passing from the Albizzia to the tea and killing it. There was no data as to the death of Albizzia trees for the reason that there was no estate in Ceylon where the Albizzia had reached its full growth. Death was as much due to disease as to over-opping. In the case of too heavy cutting back of the tops, there was a definite fungus disease of the stem. The presence of dead timber does not attract disease but it forms a germinating ground for Diplodia. His advice was that in future Albizzias should not be permitted to grow to a large size but that they should be uprooted and replanted from time to time.

Agenda Item 5. Notes on Analyses of Some Up-country Tea Soils
Yielding both Quantity and Quality.

The CHAIRMAN said that the item had been put on the agenda in reference to an enquiry by MR. HORSFALL at the previous meeting. MR. BAMBER had carried out a number of such analyses and would give the meeting a brief account of his investigations so far.

MR. BAMBER said: Before making any remarks on these analyses I should like to say that if there is any estate that had particularly fine tea, giving up to 1,000 lb. or more per acre, I should be glad if they will send me a sample of their soils, so that I might make a full analysis of them, both physically and chemically. I think one of the reasons that made us start this analysis was to find out whether it was necessary to neutralize the acidity of the soil, and, I found that out of the soils so far analysed all of them are exceedingly acid, so that it would appear that the neutralization of acidity is not required. The main feature about them is the large proportion of organic matter and nitrogen. The nitrogen varies from '256 to '627 per cent. in the Kandapola soils, while the organic matter approximated '27 per cent. Potash was in nearly all cases about '25 per cent., the highest being '386 in the Kandapola soil. Phosphoric acid was considerably above the average for Ceylon soils. Another feature was that in all these good soils there was a large proportion of the lower oxide of iron. There was an idea that the quality of tea depended largely on iron, and certainly these figures appeared to support the belief. The representation of citric-soluble plant food was in all cases fairly good.

After giving certain other figures relating to the composition of the soils under analysis MR. BAMBER said that he would like to get for analyses samples of soils where the tea was poor or where the quality was inferior so that it might be determined if possible what was wanting in them to produce quantity and quality. He considered that an important feature was the increase of humus in the soil, since humus had a considerable influence both on root development and on the growth of bushes.

In conclusion, MR. BAMBER said he wished to have from those who intended to send samples of soils, figures relating to rainfall and if possible the prices obtained for the tea.

MR. HORSFALL said he had sent soil from a virgin patana which had just been planted and there was very little difference between that soil and a forest soil except in humus.

The CHAIRMAN said the figures were of considerable interest. MR. BAMBER will be glad to analyse further samples of soils on which good quality tea was grown—whether from up-country or low-country.

JUNE, 1923.]375

Agenda Item 6. Lime Stones of Ceylon.

The CHAIRMAN said this had been put on the agenda as he wished to draw the attention of the Committee to an article written by MR. COATES on "Ceylon Lime Stones." MR. BAMBER was now engaged in a series of analyses of lime stones and was working out their value from an agricultural point of view. He will be able to tell you how far this work has progressed. The samples from Nalanda were particularly interesting. It was possible that good quality lime stone was to be found elsewhere.

MR. BAMBER said that for some time he had been trying to find out whether the lime stone found in some of the districts of the Island could be used for manuring tea instead of procuring coral lime from the coast. He found that dolomitic lime stone had been used for many years by well-known Ceylon planters with great success. He himself had used it for a couple of years and the tea was looking wonderfully well. He had been looking up reference on the effect of Magnesia on tea and other crops and had learnt that the application of dolomitic lime stone with 25 % of magnesium could do no harm to the tea. Results certainly indicate that local lime could be used on tea with very good effect. A further consideration in its favour was that coral lime is expensive. Local lime would only cost Rs. 22 per ton instead of Rs. 52 and Rs. 60 at present for lime purchased in Colombo. He had written to some of the Government Agents for samples from the various districts and was hoping to bring out a paper on the subject in addition to what MR. COATES had written. In conclusion he said he would be glad to receive samples for making a complete series from up-country.

MR. PATTERSON exhibited a sample of lime stone and read a letter he had received from MR. BAMBER regarding lime stones. He said that he had burnt two or three thousand tons with very good results. The lime was free from impurities.

Agenda Item 7. Whether Silt Pits in Rubber are Suitable as Receptacles for Manures.

MR. GARNIER who introduced the subject said that at the meeting of the Committee of Estate Products held two months ago the general opinion expressed was that there was no advantage in forking. If this was the case it followed that plain forking was also bad. He asked for the opinion of the Committee in regard to applying manure in the silt pits.

MR. BAMBER said as regards application, he would not recommend forking the whole surface. At the same time he was strongly in favour of the pit system and filling it with leaves. Cutting pits 8 10 ft. long by 4 ft. wide and applying the manure on the leaves. It was not advisable to apply the manure too deep.

The CHAIRMAN reported to the Committee that since the last meeting the rubber plots at Peradeniya had been manured. The system of manuring had been changed. Instead of applying in trenches cut between the rows of rubber this year trenches were dug across between every four trees. The trenches were 6 inches deep.

MR. ALLEN COOMBE : Surely cutting trenches causes far more damage than forking it in ?

DR. BRYCE said that the question of forking rubber has been rather laboured. MR. PETCH'S opinion is that it is not a serious matter if the larger roots are not wounded.

MR. GARRICK : The inadvisability of forking I understand is the chance of loss of soil. Pits are better than forking.

MR. C. E. A. DIAS suggested a system of forking with long plantation forks and explained the process.

376[JUNE, 1923.

The CHAIRMAN : At the same time you don't trench in all your leaf fall. The pit system has a slight advantage in that, you get your leaves incorporated into your soil.

LIEUT.-COL. T. Y. WRIGHT : But the fact remains, Sir, that you see a greater number of roots on the surface than you did before.

MR. CAMERON : MR. WILLIAMSON carried out this system and we had a terrific wash from removal of the leaf and paddy land owners who had never before put in a claim against us for 30 years suddenly put in claims for silt and we gave it up.

The CHAIRMAN in closing the discussion said that this was a point on which there was a good deal of difference of opinion. Nevertheless it was valuable to have had this question brought up and discussed.

Agenda Items 8 & 9. Whether (a) Mimosa Invisa has been tried in Ceylon as a Cover Crop and if so with what success, (b) Have any further experiments or investigations been made with regard to cover plants for prevention of soil wash.

LIEUT.-COL. T. Y. WRIGHT suggested that items 8 and 9 on the agenda be taken together.

MR. GARNIER agreed.

The CHAIRMAN said that "Mimosa Invisa" was introduced from Java in 1917. The seed was sown in a Show plot on the Experiment Station. It made vigorous growth and was found to be excessively thorny. It had the potentiality of becoming a serious weed under Ceylon conditions and had therefore been uprooted and destroyed.

MR. BAMBER said that the plant in Malaya was not thorny.

MR. GARNIER said he saw thousands of acres in Java. It was very satisfactory and it checks the growth of weeds and prevents wash. It grows up to 15 feet. They say it keeps out elk and even elephant. The Dutch beat it down and keep it in check. It is grown between rows of rubber and there is no disadvantage. He said however it was very thorny

The CHAIRMAN said with regard to green manures tried on the Experiment station he proposed to allude to only a few of the later importations, Dolichos Hosei (Vigna Oligosperma) which does exceedingly well in the Federated Malay States grew well and made an excellent cover but we were never able to get any seed. It eventually died. There is at present a small plot just coming up. A further importation of Indigofera endecaphylla has been received from the Mooply Valley Rubber Co., Ltd., India. Different varieties of Cowpeas have been tried, also the Florida Velvet bean which has the disadvantage of being a creeper. It also does not produce seed in certain districts. Cluster beans from India did well. With regard to soil wash Desmodium trifolium (undupiyali S.) did best in the old experiments. The CHAIRMAN said that if members thought it would serve a useful purpose he would have a report published on green manures experimented with on the station. MR. AUSTIN DICKSON said it would be very valuable if the results could be published.

Agenda Item 10. Black Beetle on Coconut Estates, how to destroy them and keep back the mulch.

MR. C. E. A. DIAS said the black beetle was a very serious pest on Coconut estates especially on estates where coconut husk is used as mulch. He enquired whether the use of vaporite or any other poisonous stuff would be harmful to the coconut tree.

DR. HUTSON said that if the husks put down were covered over with about 8 in. of sand the beetles would not penetrate.

JUNE, 1923.]377

MR. C. E. A. DIAS said that it was not practicable to bury the husks and mulch 8 inches deep.

The CHAIRMAN said that vaporite was too costly for use. There was no data that vaporite had any effect on black beetle larvæ. Experiments could be tried if necessary with regard to keeping records of cost, depth the mulch should be buried and quantity of vaporite to be used.

Agenda Item 11. Investigation of the cause of the tapering of Coconut Trees.

MR. PANDITTASEKERA in introducing the subject said the tapering of coconuts was going from bad to worse in the Chilaw District and suggested that the matter be again taken up.

The CHAIRMAN said that DR. BRYCE has made investigations.

DR. BRYCE said that he visited MR. PANDITTASEKERA'S property and he was of opinion that the tapering was due to soil deficiency and lack of proper cultivation. He took specimens of roots and examined them. There was no parasitic fungi.

MR. C. E. A. DIAS said he could not agree with DR. BRYCE that it was due to bad soil conditions.

MR. PATTERSON remarked that it may be due to a bad type of plants.

SIR SOLOMON DIAS BANDARANAIKE said tapering was to be found in all districts. Certain trees were affected. It may be due to a defect in the seed put down or due to bad soil conditions. He said that he started manuring the trees as soon as they began to taper but with no results. The manure was applied every two years.

GATE MUDALIYAR A. E. RAJAPAKSE said that he would carry out the experiments in collaboration with MR. PANDITTASEKERA and report results.

Agenda Items 12, 13 and 14 were then postponed for the next meeting with the consent of the committee. The CHAIRMAN said he would thereby have an opportunity of duplicating the reports on Manning Coconut Trial Grounds, Negombo and Jaela, and of putting them in the hands of the members before the next meeting.

Agenda Item 15—What measures should be adopted to exterminate the Flying Fox from the Island.

MR. THOMAS DE MEL said that the question had come up before the Low-country Products Association and they all felt that the flying fox did not serve any useful purpose. It was the cause of much damage to fruit growers. The L. C. P. A. had corresponded with the Department of Agriculture and it was decided to bring the matter up at that meeting of the Estates Products Committee. He thought it would be very advantageous in the interest of the fruit growers to get rid of the pest. There was an impression in his mind that somebody had told him that the flying foxes even attacked coconut trees. He was not sure if that was correct but he knew very well and they all knew that flying foxes went in frequently for toddy.

The CHAIRMAN :—Have you any suggestions to make, MR. DE MEL, as to how we are to get rid of them?

MR. DE MEL. No, Sir, but there was one suggestion that the headmen be paid a nominal sum for every head produced. I am not sure who is going to pay the money but we might ask Government to pay. Shooting I find is not an effective means of getting rid of them. Once they are shot at they come back again, if not to the same place, to another place close by.

MR. CONSTANTINE observed that he had heard of people using large nets, like fishing-nets, to catch flying foxes. A section of low caste Tamil coolies, he knew, ate them.

378JUNE, 1923.

SIR SOLOMON DIAS BANDARANAIKE : With regard to the destruction of fruit, if we are to get rid of anything we ought to get rid of the bat, not the flying fox. It was the bat that did all the mischief. I am a fruit grower myself, and I have about 500 to 600 Sapodilla trees and it is very difficult to protect the fruit. The bat does not attack the coconuts nor does it attack every kind of fruit. It does not touch any fruit of the orange species. The total extinction of the bat I think will be a tremendous undertaking.

Continuing SIR SOLOMON said that very few people knew the uses of flying foxes. It was a sovereign remedy for asthma. He had that on very good medical authority. A doctor practising in Colombo had once asked him for a few flying foxes and it was then that he came to know the medical qualities of the animal. He was not certain if the droppings of flying foxes did not have any manurial worth. He had tried the experiment himself and found that the trees responded wonderfully well.

MR. H. D. GARRICK : suggested some form of gas that might completely destroy them.

The CHAIRMAN : Our experience in Peradeniya is that flying foxes have not done much damage to fruit. They appear to prefer feeding on wild fruits, particularly the wild figs. Our greatest trouble at Peradeniya is the crow.

COL. T. Y. WRIGHT : But flying foxes damage the tops of trees, don't they, Sir ?

The CHAIRMAN : Yes, they do slightly ; but I feel that no practical measure could be taken to completely exterminate them. It is rather a matter for individual owners to tackle themselves either by shooting or laying nets or thorns or by any other means. By such means one can reduce the number or even persuade them to go to one's neighbour's property.

Agenda Item 16—Does any evidence exist which points to various grass seeds having been disseminated on estates by application of Artificial Fertilizers.

MR. GEO. BROWN who introduced this subject said that he found all the information he needed in the papers tabled.

The CHAIRMAN said that these investigations carried out by MR. PETCH in 1923 and fully reported on, proved that artificial manures and manure mixtures contained no weed seeds capable of germination.

Agenda Item 17—Ceylon Kapok.

MR. A. P. WALDOCK commented on a statement that appeared in Bulletin No. 17 of the Philippines Bureau of Agriculture. viz., that Ceylon Kapok was always adulterated with the floss of Bombax malabaricum. He said the article referred to was a libel. Bombax malabaricum to his knowledge was never mixed with true kapok. He produced three samples of true kapok and Bombax malabaricum.

MR. BAMBER said that Sinhalese do not use the floss of Bombax as it makes the eye sore.

The CHAIRMAN said that he had seen an article in a London Bulletin that the buoyancy of Java kapok is better than Ceylon kapok. The floss too is longer. He mentioned some of the tricks played by traders in damping the cotton. He said that no Sinhalese will climb a Bombax malabaricum tree owing to the thorns. What is gathered is picked up from the ground.

JUNE, 1923.]379

SIR SOLOMON DIAS BANDARANAIKE enquired whether it is inferior to the ordinary kapok.

The CHAIRMAN replied in the affirmative.

MR. WALDOCK said he had sent a sample of Bombax malabaricum to England and promised a report on same when received.

The CHAIRMAN tabled a copy of the Year Book of the Department of Agriculture 1923. He said that all members have been supplied with copies. He also passed round copies of a reprint of the suggestions in connection with the "Fertilisers Ordinance of 1901."

DISTRICT AGRICULTURAL COMMITTEE,
MATALE.

Minutes of a meeting of the District Agricultural Committee held on the 19th May, 1923, at the Matale Kachcheri at 2-30 p.m. with the Assistant Government Agent, Matale, in the Chair.

There were also present Messrs. R. Senior White, C. P. Anderson, G. G. Auchinleck, Divisional Agricultural Officer, Central, N. K. Jardine, Plant Pest Inspector, F. Van Rooyen, the 3 Ratemahatmayas of the District and Mr. G. F. Abayakoon, Hon. Secretary.

1. Minutes.—Minutes of the Food Production Committee meeting held at Dambulla on the 23rd March 1923 were read and confirmed.

2. Ratemahatmaya's Report on Dambulla Show.—As the Ratemahatmaya's report was not ready it was decided to circulate it later together with a financial statement.

3. Cotton Cultivation.—Tabled letter No. 838 of 23'4'23 from the Director of Agriculture and discussed prospects of cotton of the District.

4. Price of Kapok.—Tabled letter No. 864 of 27'4'23 from the Director of Agriculture re price of kapok and discussed prospects. The Divisional Agricultural Officer mentioned that seedlings of Java kapok are available at the Nalanda Experimental Garden.

5. Preservation of Jak Trees.—Tabled letter the No. 841 of 26'4'23 from the Divisional Agricultural Officer and read the article in the March issue of the TROPICAL AGRICULTURIST by Dedigama Ratemahatmaya. Resolved to ask for information regarding the jak plantation in the Kalutara District with a view to inserting clauses regarding planting of jak in chena leases.

6. Cacao Competitions.—Discussed draft rules made by the Divisional Agricultural Officer and resolved to circulate them and obtain the opinion of the members. CHAIRMAN to send these opinions or a summary to the Director of Agriculture.

7. Plantain Bunchy Top Disease.—Considered report of 9th April from Agricultural Instructor, Matale South, and opinions thereon regarding this disease and the snail pest.

The Gliricidia maculata in the \frac{1}{2} acre plot was also partially lopped and yielded 5,270 lb. per acre.

The Dadap in the \frac{1}{2} acre Tea clearing have been lopped after an interval of 3 months and yielded 4,930 lb. of green material per acre.

RUBBER.

The spare acre plot in the Annual Economic area which was planted with budded rubber stumps on the 9th of December, 1922 in dry weather has done well. 83 out of 108 or 76.84 have succeeded. The vacancies have been supplied in April. Gliricidia maculata has been established between the rubber.

The young rubber plot next to Camphor has been ploughed and is being sown with different green manures.

The monthly allowance for tapping in all plots under tapping experiments has been marked out as decided at the last meeting of the Committee.

All drains in the Hill top and Hill side rubber have been cleaned out.

A round of removing loranthus has been done. The Castilloa plots have been mostly affected.

CACAO.

The cacao plots have all been pruned and the lopping of shade completed.

The spring crop appears to be poor. The trees are in heavy blossom and promise a good autumn crop.

There has been a re-appearance of the locust pest which did some damage to the Dadap shade trees during 1921.

The total crop of dry cacao for the year was 162.4 cwt.—3.06 cwt. per acre.

The previous season's crop was 217.3 cwt.—4.87 cwt. per acre.

The percentage of fungus pods has been very high probably due to excessive shade and heavy rains.

The "B" cacao area has been manured.

COCONUTS.

42 nuts which had fallen, naturally, from 2 Java coconut trees were planted in nursery beds as follows:—

Horizontal, Vertical, Slanting at about 45° and in a position assumed when dropped from a height on to a level piece of ground.

At an auction sale in March Rs. 63 per 1,000 nuts were obtained for unselected nuts.

A portion of the 10 acre plot covered with Illuk has been forked.

The Entomologist found slight traces of injury to coconut leaflets by Nephantis serencpa on two young palms in the 10 acre plot. The infected portions of leaflets were removed.

Arrangements have been made to have the area carefully inspected.

COFFEE.

All plots have been lightly pruned and the shade partially lopped and mulched round the plants.

Diebacks have been removed and burnt.

The crop of Robusta, Quillou, etc., is over. Seed will not be available till October or November next. Hybrid coffee berries and self sown seedlings of all varieties are available for South-West planting.

382[JUNE, 1923.

FOOD PRODUCTS.

The following crops have been replanted :—

Tubers :—Sweet Potatoes—Sealy's, Southern Queen, Black Spanish, Jersey, and Red Jersey.

Maniocs :—Ubi Putch, Ubi Pullet, Manihot Utillissima and Kerrington.

Cereals — Brazos White Corn, Adlay and Buck Wheat.

Legumes :—Groundnuts, Green and Black gram, Cowpeas.

ECONOMIC COLLECTION.

Vacancies have been supplied in the Nutmeg, Clove, Cardamom, Cinnamon, Pepper, Castilloa rubber, Ficus Vogelli, Lime and Sapan plots.

Three plots of Hibiscus sabdarifa var. Altissima have been established in the Fibre section.

A nursery of Columbian Pita plants were planted out in the fruit plots to be transplanted later. The plants arrived in bad order and fifty per cent. of those received apparently alive have already succumbed.

FODDER PLANTS.

Elephant grass.—33 shoots received from the Superintendent, Central Farm, Coimbatore, have been planted out for comparison with other grass growing on the station as Elephant grass. The shoots are all growing well.

SHOW PLOTS.

A plot of Kudzu (Pueraria thumbergiana) a long-leaved, woody leguminous vine, native of Japan, has been planted and is making good growth.

A plot of Indigofera has been planted from seed received from the Manager, Mooply Valley Rubber Co., Ltd., Palapilly P. O., South India.

A small plot of Vigna oligosperma synonym : Dolichos Hosei, received from the Federated Malay States has been planted.

A plot of Hubam Clover Mililotus alba var. Annua has been sown.

GENERAL.

The cart road from the village round the coffee area has been metalled and gravel laid.

Camphor distillation had to be abandoned as the still has been required for other investigations by the Agricultural Chemist.

The health of the coolies has been satisfactory.
