POULTRY.

DRY MASH SYSTEM OF FEEDING.

ARTHUR LITTLE,

Rhodesian Government Poultry Expert.

A correspondent, MR. J. W. MILNER, in your issue of March, asks for particulars of Dry Mash Feeding. His chief difficulty seems to be waste, which is easily remedied by using a simple hopper which I herewith describe. We use these hoppers in Rhodesia almost universally; they have also the merit of being inexpensive, and I can assure MR. MILNER there is no waste with them.

The dry mash system of feeding is suitable for breeding stock, laying stock and growing stock, and is, in my experience, infinitely preferable to wet mash, in that it has the following advantages:—

  1. (1) Better health, vigour and stamina of the birds;
  2. (2) Less danger from disease and digestive troubles;
  3. (3) The food is eaten more slowly and naturally and there is no gorging of a large amount rapidly.
  4. (4) Less labour and time in preparing and supplying the food is required and the expense of fuel for cooking is saved;
  5. (5) Each bird of the flock is more likely to obtain a sufficient supply of food for its requirements;
  6. (6) The weaker and more timid birds can obtain their food with more ease and comfort;
  7. (7) There is no waste, as in wet mash feeding; the latter, especially in a hot country, cannot be kept after the birds have had their fill, otherwise it becomes sour, and digestive troubles result, and what remains over of the mash has to be destroyed and so we have waste.

(8) Last, but not least by any means, the vitamins in the dry mash system are not destroyed as they often are by heating or cooking the food to produce wet mash.

The majority of dry food hoppers are certainly wasteful, and the birds can hook out a great deal of it with their beaks, but a hopper made from half a whisky or similar box, as follows, absolutely prevents this waste:—

Take a whisky box, saw it in half transversely; this will give two boxes each about 4\frac{1}{2} inches deep. The lower half has a bottom, but the upper half will also require to have a bottom nailed on; now, across the top of each nail lengthwise, a strip of wood, leaving about a 2 inch space between the two. The birds can feed by placing their heads through this aperture, and cannot possibly hook out the food. It will be seen that two hoppers can be made from one whisky case, and which, certainly, have the merit of cheapness. Obviously any size hopper can be made, from one for young chicks to that required for a large flock; of course, for young chicks the depth must be only 1\frac{1}{2} to 2 inches.—S. A. POULTRY MAGAZINE AND SMALL-HOLDER, Vol. XV., No. 135.

384[JUNE, 1923]

LIBRARY

THE DISEASES OF THE TEA BUSH.*

This volume by the well-known Mycologist in Ceylon has been written so as to enable the tea planter to recognise the fungus diseases which may affect the tea bush and to take the necessary steps for their control. It is illustrated with sixty-nine text figures and with three coloured plates, and these illustrations should enable the practical planter to diagnose his diseases without difficulty.

The opening chapter on the Classification of Fungi has been included, by request, in order to furnish explanations of technical terms used in the description of diseases. Subsequent chapters deal consecutively with Leaf diseases, Leaf and Stem diseases, Stem diseases and Root diseases. Under Leaf diseases, detailed descriptions are given of a large number. It is however stated that although the list of Leaf diseases of tea is assuming large dimensions it cannot be held that any of them, except the Blister Blight of Northern India, is of a character serious enough to arouse apprehension. Tea Planters in Ceylon should therefore make a careful study of the detailed description of this Blister Blight disease in order that immediate steps may be taken should it ever make its appearance in this Colony. Attention is also called to the description of the Cercospora disease which at present appears to be somewhat on the increase in certain districts on Acacias and Tea. Red rust disease of the Leaf and Stem is another disease to which the attention of planters in Ceylon is directed. This is common only on tea which is in "poor heart" and may be controlled by improved cultivation and manuring.

Under Stem diseases, a very full description is given of Branch Canker. This disease has been known in Ceylon since 1904, but is of particular importance at the present time in view of the interest that is being taken in the attacks of termites on tea. The most commonly observed termites in Ceylon tea estates are the mound-building termites which do not attack living tissues. They attack the decayed wood in branch cankers and clean them out. Branch canker may be caused by several different fungi and full accounts are given of these and of their effects on the tea bush.

Seventeen root diseases have now been recorded as attacking tea. A carefully prepared table giving particulars of how the external appearance of diseased roots may be used as a guide to diagnosis should prove to be of great value.

A chapter is included on wound covers, sprays and sprayers whilst the last two concluding chapters deal with Mycological notes and descriptions of the various fungi found on the tea bush.

The volume is of exceptional value to all interested in the tea industry and every tea planter should have a copy in his library. The excellent illustrations prepared from drawings, paintings and photographs made in the Mycological division of the Department of Agriculture, Ceylon, add materially to the value of the work to the practical man.

*The Diseases of the Tea Bush by T. PETCH B.A., B.Sc. Published by Macmillan & Co Ltd., London, Bombay, Calcutta and Madras-Price 20 Shillings net.

N. Eliya

The summary of May rainfall is very simple—there was a consistent deficit practically all over the island. This was chiefly due to the very dry period during the first half of the month when there were strong winds from the South West but very little rain, and conditions closely resembled those that occurred during the corresponding period in 1920 (including the presence of a severe storm further north in the Bay of Bengal).

On the 17th there was some heavy rain in the low country in the South West quadrant (e.g. Sunderland 8.4 Dundin 7.6 Eheliyagoda 5.8 Kanangama and Labugama 5.5 inches) and a mild continuation of rain occurred from then to the end of the month. In this period there were occasional heavy falls and some cases of hail e.g. at Diyatalawa on the 21st but it was only on the 24th that the rain was at all extensive: on which date the South West of the island came under some heavy rain.

Deficits of over 15 inches below the month's average occurred at Ambegamuwa, Kitungala and Carney and deficits of over 10 inches in Maskeliya, Ratnapura, Pelmadulla, Heneratgoda and parts of the Kelani Valley, while practically the whole of the South West quarter of the island was at least 5 inches in deficit.

The few stations that did reach their average included Badulla and one or two neighbouring estates, Pattipola, Woodside, Topawewa and Madawacheliya, also one or two in the eastern and southern provinces where the May averages are so low that to reach them does not necessitate very much rain. The stations that recorded most rain in the month were in the Eheliyagoda and Adam's Peak districts but these stations were nevertheless well below their own averages for May.

The clear weather of the first half of the month resulted in an increased range of temperature between night and day and the minimum temperature in air at Nuwara Eliya got down to 38°2 on the 9th which meant that the ground temperature was practically at freezing point.

The wind velocity for the month was decidedly above average and Humidity was as consistently below average, while amount of clouds was below it in most cases.
